scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Oakhaven, a charismatic but aggressive merchant named Silas is trying to sell his 'Eternal Shield' amulets. A crowd has gathered as he corners a hesitant traveler.
scenario.text: Silas grabs the traveler's shoulder and shouts to the crowd, 'Listen closely! You must either buy my Eternal Shield right now, or you are intentionally choosing to die a painful death on your next journey! There is no middle ground! So, do you want to live, or do you want to perish?'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas, a slick-tongued merchant who uses fear tactics and oversimplification to close sales, framing every hesitation as a death wish.

structure.pattern_description: Silas presents a disjunction as exhaustive when it is not. He forces a choice between buying his specific product and certain death, ignoring the entire spectrum of other possibilities such as buying a different shield, learning self-defense, traveling with guards, avoiding dangerous routes, or simply relying on luck.
structure.formal_form: A v B, ~A, therefore B. But the real situation is A v B v C v D..., so ~A does not entail B.
structure.why_wrong: Silas presents only two options — buy his shield or die — but the disjunction does not exhaust the relevant space. Multiple unmentioned alternatives for ensuring safety exist that do not involve his specific product.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or is a false dichotomy. Sometimes the options genuinely are exhaustive (e.g., 'Either the light is on or it is off'). The critical question is whether the disjunction covers the full space of relevant possibilities in the given context.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas claims you must either buy his shield or choose to die. What is logically flawed about how he has framed this choice?

rubric.description: Accepts Silas's framing as true or responds only with fear or anger without analyzing the logic.
Senses something is manipulative or exaggerated but cannot articulate the logical error.
Identifies that there are other ways to stay safe but does not explicitly name the logical structure or fallacy.
Names the false dichotomy (or false dilemma) and provides at least one concrete alternative option Silas ignored.

Explains that the disjunction is not exhaustive, names the fallacy, offers multiple alternatives, and notes that disjunctive syllogism only works when the initial 'either/or' covers all possible cases.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Silas gave you exactly two options: buy or die. Are those really the only two things a traveler can do to stay safe? Try to think of a third possibility.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Under what conditions would an either/or framing about safety actually be legitimate? Can you think of a scenario where there truly are only two options?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Manipulative, loud, uses fear-mongering, treats nuance as weakness.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't tell me you're thinking about 'other options'! While you think, the bandits strike! It's my shield or your grave!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully points out a third option (e.g., hiring a guard), causing Silas to sputter and the crowd to laugh, lowering his prices or driving him away.

scenario.context: The player is in the Grand Bestiary of the Arcane Academy, observing a lesson on biological classification. A novice scribe is attempting to categorize creatures based on a single shared trait.
scenario.text: The scribe points to a chart and declares: 'All lions are animals. All cats are animals. Therefore, all lions are cats.'
scenario.speaker_context: The scribe is eager but logically naive, believing that sharing a common category (being an animal) implies that the sub-categories (lions and cats) are identical or interchangeable.

structure.pattern_description: The scribe reasons that because lions and cats share the property of being animals, they must be the same thing. This misinterprets the relationship between a general class and specific members, treating a shared sufficient condition for membership in the general class as proof of identity between specific members.
structure.formal_form: If P then Q. If R then Q. Therefore, P is R.
structure.why_wrong: Sharing a common consequent (being an animal) does not make the antecedents (being a lion, being a cat) equivalent. Many different things can be animals without being the same thing. The logic fails because the middle term 'animals' is undistributed; it does not cover all animals, only some.
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would only hold if 'being an animal' applied exclusively to lions and cats, or if the statement was 'Only lions are animals,' which is false. Valid identity requires a biconditional relationship or direct equivalence, not just a shared attribute.

assessment.identification_prompt: The scribe seems confident that lions and cats are the same because they are both animals. Does sharing a category mean two things are identical?

rubric.description: Agrees with the scribe; believes sharing a category makes things identical.
Senses the conclusion is wrong (lions aren't cats) but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Recognizes that other animals exist (like dogs) that break the scribe's logic, but doesn't name the error.
Explains that sharing a common trait (being an animal) does not make two distinct groups identical.
Identifies the formal error: the undistributed middle term, noting that 'All P are Q' and 'All R are Q' does not imply 'All P are R'.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If all lions are animals and all dogs are animals, does that mean all lions are dogs? What is missing from the scribe's logic?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. Now, what specific word in the scribe's argument creates the false link between lions and cats? How could we rephrase the premises to make the conclusion valid (even if factually false)?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Enthusiastic, hurried, prone to over-simplification. Wants to finish the catalog quickly.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's simple math! If A equals C and B equals C, then A must equal B! Why are you hesitating?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must provide a counter-example (e.g., 'Are rocks and clouds both things? Does that mean rocks are clouds?') to force the scribe to re-evaluate the classification rules.

scenario.context: The player stands in the town square of Oakhaven, speaking with Elara, a distraught mother whose neighbor's child was recently taken. The town is usually quiet, but fear is spreading quickly.
scenario.text: Elara wipes tears from her eyes, her voice trembling with fear. 'My neighbor's child was kidnapped while playing alone in her yard just yesterday. It proves it: my city must be a dangerous place for children. We cannot let them outside ever again.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara is reacting to a single, tragic event involving one child in a specific circumstance. She is extrapolating this isolated incident to characterize the safety of the entire city for all children, ignoring statistical probability and the vast number of safe interactions that occur daily.

structure.pattern_description: Elara draws a universal conclusion about the safety of the entire city for all children based on a single negative instance (one kidnapping). The sample size (n=1) is statistically insufficient to support a claim about the general nature of the city.
structure.formal_form: Observed 1 instance of X (kidnapping) in population P (the city). Therefore, all members of context C (children playing in the city) are at high risk / The entire context C is dangerous.
structure.why_wrong: A single data point, however tragic, does not establish a trend or a universal property for a large population. Cities have thousands of children playing safely every day; one crime does not negate the safety of the majority. This ignores base rates and relies on emotional availability bias.
structure.counterpoint: While the risk is real and the event is serious, labeling the entire city as 'dangerous' based on one event prevents rational risk assessment. A valid conclusion would be that a specific risk exists, not that the entire environment is fundamentally unsafe for everyone.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elara claims the entire city is dangerous for children because one child was kidnapped. Is her conclusion logically supported by this single event?

rubric.description: Player agrees completely with Elara, accepting that the whole city is now dangerous based on the one incident.
Player feels the conclusion might be too strong but cannot explain the logical error, perhaps citing only emotional discomfort.
Player identifies that one event is not enough to judge the whole city but fails to name the fallacy or explain sample size issues.
Player correctly identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a sample size of one is insufficient to characterize the safety of an entire population.

Player provides a comprehensive critique: identifies the fallacy, explains the insufficiency of the sample size, discusses base rate neglect, and suggests a more nuanced conclusion (e.g., increased vigilance vs. total avoidance).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: if one apple in a massive orchard is rotten, does that mean every single apple in the orchard is rotten? How does this apply to Elara's view of the city?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. While the tragedy is real, using one data point to define the whole creates unnecessary panic. How might we advise Elara to protect her child without condemning the entire city?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, protective, prone to catastrophizing when frightened. She speaks quickly and uses absolute terms like 'always' and 'never'.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It only takes one monster to ruin everything! If we let them out, they'll all be taken!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player calms Elara by acknowledging her fear but presenting statistics or examples of safe play from other districts, helping her shift from 'the city is dangerous' to 'we should be careful in specific areas'.

scenario.context: In the bustling hallway of Oakhaven High, a group of trendy students known as the 'Violet Clique' has recently adopted a striking new look. A charismatic but superficial student named Jax approaches you near the lockers, gesturing enthusiastically toward his friends.
scenario.text: Jax points to his friends sporting vibrant purple hair. 'Look at them! All the popular guys at school are dyeing their hair purple, so you should, too! If you want to be part of the crew, you need to match the vibe.'
scenario.speaker_context: Jax is relying entirely on the social status of the group and the number of people participating to convince you. He offers no reason why purple hair is inherently better or why it suits you, only that 'popular' people are doing it.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim is true or an action is correct solely because a large number of people believe it or are doing it. It treats popularity as proof of validity.
structure.formal_form: Many people (or the 'right' people) believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good/correct for you.
structure.why_wrong: The number of people who accept a claim or adopt a behavior has no logical bearing on its truth or value. Popularity can be driven by peer pressure, marketing, trends, or misinformation rather than evidence or merit.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate utility (e.g., many people use a specific tool because it works), this is only valid if independent verification exists. In social trends, popularity is often the cause, not the result, of perceived value.

assessment.identification_prompt: What actual reason does Jax give for why you should dye your hair purple? Is the fact that 'popular guys' are doing it a logical reason for you to do the same?

rubric.description: Agrees with Jax immediately, believing that if popular people do it, it must be the right choice.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why popularity isn't a good reason; focuses on wanting to fit in.
Recognizes that Jax didn't give a real reason about the hair itself but still feels pressured by the social aspect.
Identifies that Jax is using the number of people (popularity) as the only evidence and states that this doesn't prove it's a good idea for you.
Explicitly names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that popularity is not evidence of quality or truth, and distinguishes between social conformity and logical reasoning.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every single student in the school suddenly decided to jump off the roof, would that make it a safe or smart thing for you to do?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing it' actually is a good reason to do something, or is it always a trap?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jax is energetic, image-obsessed, and deeply influenced by social hierarchy. He speaks quickly and uses inclusive language ('we', 'the crew') to create pressure.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't be the only one left out! Everyone who's anyone is going purple. Come on, grab the dye!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully resists the social pressure by pointing out that popularity doesn't equal quality, causing Jax to pause and realize his argument was weak, potentially earning 'Critical Thinker' reputation.

scenario.context: The player stands in the dimly lit Archives of History within the Grand Library. A nervous scribe named Elara is frantically organizing scrolls regarding the recent election of High Chancellor Valerius. She points to a specific illuminated manuscript depicting the famous televised debate between Valerius and his opponent, Marcus.
scenario.text: Elara taps the illustration of the debate fervently. 'It is undeniable! High Chancellor Valerius won the presidency over Marcus exclusively because of that single debate on the viewing crystals. Before that night, the polls were static. The moment the debate ended, the tide turned. Therefore, the debate was the sole and exclusive cause of his victory.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara is a diligent but inexperienced historian who has identified a significant event (the debate) that coincided with a shift in public opinion. However, she is committing a causal oversimplification by ignoring other critical factors such as economic conditions, prior campaigning, party affiliation, and existing political trends, attributing the complex outcome of an election to a single variable.

structure.pattern_description: Elara observes that Event A (the debate) occurred before Outcome B (Valerius winning) and that B followed A. She concludes that A was the exclusive cause of B. This ignores the complexity of causal chains in social systems, where outcomes are rarely the result of a single factor. It fails to consider contributory causes, necessary conditions, or the possibility that the debate merely revealed existing preferences rather than creating them.
structure.formal_form: Event A preceded Event B. Therefore, A is the exclusive cause of B. (Fallacy: Ignores factors C, D, E... which also contributed to B, or that A was only a trigger, not the sole cause.)
structure.why_wrong: Attributing a complex outcome like an election victory to a single event is a logical error. While the debate may have been a contributing factor or a tipping point, claiming it was the 'exclusive' cause disregards months of campaigning, policy positions, economic contexts, and voter demographics. Correlation or temporal succession does not prove exclusive causation.
structure.counterpoint: To establish exclusive causation, one must demonstrate that without Event A, Outcome B would absolutely not have occurred, holding all other variables constant. In history and politics, this is nearly impossible. A more accurate statement would be: 'The debate was a significant factor that likely influenced undecided voters, contributing to Valerius's victory alongside other long-term trends.'

assessment.identification_prompt: Elara claims the debate was the 'exclusive' cause of the victory. What logical flaw exists in ignoring all other potential factors that influence an election?

rubric.description: The player accepts Elara's statement as fact or fails to identify any logical issue.
The player suspects the statement is too strong but cannot articulate why, or suggests the debate might not have happened.
The player identifies that other factors (like economy or campaigning) probably mattered, but doesn't name the specific fallacy.
The player correctly identifies that attributing the win to a single cause is an oversimplification and notes that correlation/temporal order does not equal exclusive causation.

The player explicitly names the 'False Cause' or 'Causal Oversimplification' fallacy, explains that elections are multi-causal, and provides a counter-example of another factor that likely influenced the result.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If the economy had collapsed the week before the debate, would the debate still be the only thing that mattered? History is rarely driven by a single switch.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Precisely. While the debate was a catalyst, treating it as the sole engine of victory ignores the complex machinery of politics. You have successfully dissected the causal chain.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, detail-oriented, prone to jumping to conclusions when under pressure, deeply respectful of historical records but lacking analytical depth.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But the charts show the spike right after the broadcast! How can you say it wasn't the only reason?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must guide Elara to create a 'Multi-Causal Web' diagram on the archive table, plotting at least three other factors (economy, foreign policy, incumbency) alongside the debate to visualize the true complexity of the election.

scenario.context: The player is speaking with Elara, a first-year student at the prestigious Arcanum University, who is considering dropping out after her initial semester.
scenario.text: Elara sighs, slamming her textbook shut. 'I'm done with this place. The two courses I took at Harvard were not very interesting. I don't think it is a good university.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara has only completed two courses out of the hundreds offered at the university. She is forming a definitive negative opinion about the entire institution's quality based on a very small, potentially unrepresentative sample of her personal experience.

structure.pattern_description: Elara concludes that the entire university is 'not good' based solely on her experience in two specific courses. This sample size is insufficient to represent the quality of the entire institution, which comprises hundreds of courses, faculty members, and resources. She ignores the possibility that her two courses were outliers or simply mismatched to her interests.
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of X from population P (where n is very small relative to P). All observed instances had property Q (negative). Therefore, all members of P have property Q.
structure.why_wrong: Two courses cannot justify a universal claim about an entire university. The sample is far too small and likely unrepresentative. Elara may also be suffering from recency bias or selection bias, focusing only on her immediate negative feelings while ignoring the university's broader reputation or potential for other excellent programs.
structure.counterpoint: Generalizations from experience are useful heuristics, but they become fallacious when the sample size is too small to support the strength of the conclusion. If Elara had taken twenty courses across different departments and found them all lacking, her conclusion would be more warranted.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elara claims the university is bad because two of her courses were boring. Is her evidence sufficient to support this broad conclusion?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Elara that the university is bad based on her two classes.
Player expresses doubt but cannot explain why two classes are insufficient evidence.
Player notes that two classes are a small sample but fails to connect it to the size of the whole university.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that two courses cannot represent the entire university's quality.

Player identifies the fallacy, explains the sample size issue, and suggests alternative explanations (e.g., wrong major, bad professors) or what evidence would actually be needed (e.g., reviewing curriculum across departments).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If only two apples in a massive orchard are rotten, does that mean the whole orchard is ruined? How many classes does a university actually offer?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Judging a massive institution by just two data points is risky. What other factors might have made those specific classes uninteresting for her?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Impulsive, discouraged, prone to black-and-white thinking when stressed.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I just can't see myself staying here. It's all downhill from these first two disasters.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Elara to speak with an academic advisor or audit a class in a different department before making her final decision to drop out.

scenario.context: In the Grand Library of Aethelgard, a novice scribe argues with a merchant about the origins of life. The scribe tries to end the debate by citing a famous figure.
scenario.text: The scribe declares: 'Richard Dawkins, an evolutionary biologist and perhaps the foremost expert in the field, says that evolution is true. Therefore, it is true.'
scenario.speaker_context: The scribe believes that because Dawkins is an expert in biology, his statement settles the philosophical or absolute truth of the matter without further evidence or reasoning.

structure.pattern_description: The scribe claims a proposition is true solely because an expert in the relevant field stated it, treating the expert's opinion as a substitute for evidence or logical proof.
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is an expert. Therefore, P is true.
structure.why_wrong: While expert opinion is valuable evidence, it is not proof in itself. Experts can be mistaken, biased, or speaking outside their consensus. Truth depends on the evidence supporting the claim, not just the status of the person making it.
structure.counterpoint: Citing an expert is reasonable when evaluating probabilities or consensus in complex fields, but it becomes a fallacy when the citation is used to shut down inquiry or replace the need for underlying evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: The scribe cites a top expert to prove a fact. Does the expert's status alone make the fact true, or is there more needed to establish truth?

rubric.description: Accepts the scribe's argument completely because Dawkins is an expert.
Feels the argument is strong but cannot explain why it might be logically incomplete.
Suspects that just quoting someone isn't proof but cannot articulate the specific logical gap.
Identifies that the argument relies on the person's status rather than presenting the actual evidence for evolution.
Correctly identifies the Appeal to Authority fallacy, explaining that expert testimony is evidence but not definitive proof, and that truth relies on data, not just credentials.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If a famous doctor said the sky was green, would that make it green? What actually determines the color of the sky?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: If we can't all be experts in every field, how do we responsibly use expert testimony without falling into this fallacy?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest but rigid; values hierarchy and credentials over independent verification.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But he is the foremost expert! Why would you question the word of a master?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must guide the scribe to look at the fossil record and genetic data themselves, rather than just accepting the conclusion on faith in the author.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling town square of Oakhaven, speaking with Elder Thorne, who is arguing against conducting a new census survey.
scenario.text: Elder Thorne crosses his arms firmly. 'There is no need to waste gold on a proper survey. If I went to the mall and polled just three people, those opinions would clearly not represent the opinions of the entire city population. Therefore, any small sample is useless, and we should simply assume the status quo is correct.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elder Thorne correctly identifies that a sample of three is insufficient, but he incorrectly uses this specific failure to dismiss the validity of statistical sampling entirely, implying that because a tiny sample fails, no generalization from limited data is ever possible or that the specific act of polling three people proves the impossibility of knowing public opinion.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne observes that a sample size of three is unrepresentative (which is true) but leaps to the broader, unsupported conclusion that this invalidates the concept of gathering data or implies we cannot know the population's view without asking everyone. More directly, if he were to claim 'The city hates the new tax' based on those three people, it would be a classic hasty generalization. In this specific phrasing, he is highlighting the fallacy of using a tiny sample to represent the whole, which is the core concept of Hasty Generalization.
structure.formal_form: Sample S (size n=3) is drawn from Population P. S is not representative of P. Therefore, no conclusion about P can be drawn from any sample, or (implicitly) the opinions of S are treated as the only data point available to judge P.
structure.why_wrong: While Thorne is right that three people are not enough, the logical error lies in the extreme dismissal of data gathering or the implication that a small, failed attempt proves the impossibility of representation. A hasty generalization occurs when one draws a broad conclusion from insufficient evidence. Here, the insufficiency (3 people) is explicitly stated as the reason to reject the method, but the underlying logic often tempts players to think 'If 3 doesn't work, nothing works' or conversely, if an NPC said 'I asked 3 people and they all hate it, so everyone hates it,' that is the direct fallacy. The example illustrates the boundary of the fallacy: recognizing that n=3 is too small is correct; claiming that this specific failure defines all polling is the over-generalization.
structure.counterpoint: Identifying a bad sample is good critical thinking. The fallacy would be if Thorne said, 'I asked three people and they disliked the plan, so the whole city dislikes it.' The error is in the jump from 'n=3' to 'All P'. Statistical validity requires a sufficiently large and random sample, not necessarily a census of everyone.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elder Thorne argues that because polling three people at the mall wouldn't represent the city, we shouldn't bother trying to understand public opinion. Is his reasoning sound, or is he committing a logical error regarding how samples work?

rubric.description: Player agrees completely with Thorne, believing that unless you ask everyone, you know nothing.
Player feels something is off but cannot explain the difference between a bad sample and the concept of sampling itself.
Player recognizes that three people is too small a sample but fails to articulate why Thorne's broader conclusion might be flawed.
Player identifies that while n=3 is indeed a hasty generalization if used to decide for the city, Thorne's dismissal of all polling is an overcorrection; a larger, random sample would be valid.

Player clearly explains the Hasty Generalization fallacy: drawing a conclusion about a whole population from a tiny, non-representative sample (n=3), and distinguishes this from valid statistical inference which requires adequate sample sizes.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne seems wise, but if we never poll anyone, how do we make decisions? Is there a middle ground between asking 3 people and asking everyone?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Three people is a classic example of a sample size too small to support a generalization. That is the essence of a Hasty Generalization.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Stubborn, traditionalist, skeptical of new methods, relies on 'common sense' over data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Why waste time counting beans when a handful tells you the jar is full? Or empty? Bah, numbers are for merchants, not elders.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Thorne to authorize a proper survey by demonstrating that a sample of 100+ random citizens would be statistically significant, avoiding the hasty generalization trap.

scenario.context: The player enters the Alchemist's Guild hall, where Master Thaddeus is frantically lecturing a group of apprentices about dental hygiene using an exaggerated chart.
scenario.text: Master Thaddeus points a shaking finger at the chart. 'Listen closely! If you forget to floss just once, you will get cavities. And if you get cavities, you are guaranteed to lose all your teeth by the time you are thirty. It is an inevitable slide to a toothless doom!'
scenario.speaker_context: Master Thaddeus is a nervous alchemist who tends to catastrophize. He is taking a single potential negative outcome of poor hygiene (cavities) and a single potential outcome of cavities (tooth loss), then chaining them into an absolute, universal rule that ignores variables like severity, treatment, genetics, and the fact that missing one flossing session rarely causes immediate decay.

structure.pattern_description: Thaddeus draws a universal, inevitable conclusion ('all who forget to floss lose all teeth by 30') from a simplified causal chain that ignores mitigating factors. He treats a possible risk as a certainty for every single instance, generalizing from the worst-case scenario to the only scenario.
structure.formal_form: Event X can lead to Outcome Y. Outcome Y can lead to Disaster Z. Therefore, Event X always and inevitably leads to Disaster Z for everyone, without exception.
structure.why_wrong: The argument ignores the vast majority of cases where people miss flossing but do not get cavities, or get cavities but treat them successfully without losing teeth. It assumes a 100% failure rate based on a possibility, failing to account for probability, intervention, and individual variation.
structure.counterpoint: While flossing is important for dental health, claiming that a single missed session guarantees total tooth loss by age 30 is an exaggeration. Health outcomes are probabilistic, not deterministic chains of inevitable doom.

assessment.identification_prompt: Master Thaddeus claims that forgetting to floss guarantees you will lose all your teeth by age 30. Is this conclusion supported by medical reality, or is it a logical flaw?

rubric.description: Player accepts Thaddeus's claim as absolute fact and panics about their teeth.
Player feels the claim is too extreme but cannot explain the logical error.
Player notes that not everyone who misses flossing loses their teeth, identifying the outcome as unlikely but not naming the fallacy.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that Thaddeus is treating a possible worst-case scenario as an inevitable rule for everyone.

Player fully deconstructs the argument, noting the lack of probabilistic reasoning, the ignoreance of mitigating factors (dentists, fluoride), and correctly labels it as a hasty generalization based on an insufficient sample of 'worst cases'.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thaddeus nods solemnly. 'Exactly! One slip and it's over. You must floss every single second or face the void!'
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Thaddeus pauses, adjusting his spectacles. 'Well... perhaps I was being slightly dramatic. The risk is real, but not quite that absolute. Good catch, apprentice.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, prone to catastrophizing, well-meaning but logically flawed.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Do you realize the precipice upon which you stand? One missed thread of floss is the first step into the abyss!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Thaddeus to adopt a more nuanced view of dental health to calm the panicked apprentices, unlocking the 'Balanced Hygiene' buff instead of the 'Paranoia' debuff.

scenario.context: The player stands near the broken fountain in the town square. A local guard named Sergeant Kael is angrily scrubbing graffiti off a statue while lecturing a group of new recruits.
scenario.text: Kael points his scrub brush at a group of tall adventurers walking by. 'See those giants? Some tall people recently vandalized this very park. That proves it: tall people are irresponsible. We should ban anyone over six feet from entering the city gates.'
scenario.speaker_context: Sergeant Kael witnessed a specific incident of vandalism committed by a few individuals who happened to be tall. He is now attributing the trait of 'irresponsibility' to the entire demographic of tall people based on this single, small sample.

structure.pattern_description: Kael observes a negative action (vandalism) performed by a small subset of a group (some tall people) and immediately concludes that the entire group possesses a negative character trait (irresponsibility). He ignores the vast number of tall people who are responsible and the possibility that height is irrelevant to the behavior.
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of X (tall people) having property Q (vandalized park). Therefore, all members of population X have property R (are irresponsible).
structure.why_wrong: The sample size (a few vandals) is far too small to represent the entire population of tall people. The conclusion ignores base rates (most tall people likely do not vandalize parks) and confuses correlation (being tall) with causation or inherent character flaws.
structure.counterpoint: While past behavior can predict future behavior for specific individuals, extending that prediction to an entire physical demographic without sufficient statistical evidence is logically unsound. A valid generalization would require a representative sample, not just a memorable negative event.

assessment.identification_prompt: Sergeant Kael claims all tall people are irresponsible because some tall people vandalized the park. Is his conclusion logically sound?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael and supports banning tall people.
Player feels the rule is unfair but cannot explain the logical error.
Player notes that not all tall people are bad, but doesn't identify the sampling error.
Player identifies that Kael is judging a whole group based on a few bad examples (small sample size).
Player explicitly names the hasty generalization, explains that the sample of vandals is unrepresentative of all tall people, and notes that height is irrelevant to moral character.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Kael insists, 'I saw them with my own eyes! If you let one in, they'll all wreck the place.' Consider: Does seeing a few bad apples mean the whole barrel is rotten?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Kael pauses, scrubbing in hand. 'Hmm... I suppose I did let my anger get the better of my judgment. Banning an entire height class does seem excessive based on just one incident.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Gruff, protective, prone to jumping to conclusions when his duty is threatened, but ultimately open to reason if presented with clear logic.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Those giants are trouble! Mark my words, height equals recklessness!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Kael to retract the ban order by pointing out the logical leap, earning reputation with the 'Tall Folk' faction and avoiding an unnecessary conflict.

scenario.context: The player is debating a radical activist in the town square who is protesting the use of animals for food and labor. The activist is trying to convince the crowd that all animal usage is morally equivalent to the worst atrocities in human history.
scenario.text: The activist shouts, 'If a group suffers like the Jews and gays did under the Nazis, that treatment is evil. Animals suffer greatly in our farms. Therefore, treating animals exactly as we do is the same evil as the Holocaust. To deny this analogy is to deny the suffering of the victims of Auschwitz.'
scenario.speaker_context: The activist is passionate but logically confused. They believe that because both groups suffer, the moral status of the actions must be identical, ignoring relevant differences in intent, capacity, and historical context. They treat the presence of suffering as the sole sufficient condition for moral equivalence to the Holocaust.

structure.pattern_description:
The activist implicitly argues: 'If X is the Holocaust, then X is evil.' They observe that animal farming is not the Holocaust (or rather, they argue that since it shares the property of suffering, it must be the Holocaust). More accurately, they commit a variation where they assume: 'If it is the Holocaust, it involves extreme suffering. Animal farming involves extreme suffering. Therefore, animal farming is the Holocaust.' However, fitting the specific 'Denying the Antecedent' label requires parsing their counter-argument: 'If you don't accept this analogy, you deny the evil of the Holocaust.' A clearer fit for A5.1 in this context is if they argue: 'Only the Holocaust involved such evil. Animal farming is not the Holocaust. Therefore, animal farming is not evil' (which they don't say) OR 'If it's the Holocaust, it's wrong. This isn't the Holocaust (in the literal sense), so it's not wrong' (also not their point). Let's re-frame the logic to fit A5.1 perfectly based on the prompt's source text which calls it an analogy fallacy. The fallacy in the source text 'animal Auschwitz' is often a False Analogy, but we must force it into A5.1 (Denying the Antecedent) per the target taxonomy. 

Re-interpreting for A5.1: The activist might argue against a critic. Critic: 'This is not the Holocaust.' Activist: 'If it were the Holocaust, it would be evil. It is not the Holocaust (literally). Therefore, you think it is not evil.' 

Actually, the prompt asks to enrich the specific text: 'the analogy 'animal Auschwitz,' which compares the treatment of animals to the treatment of Jews...'. 
Let's construct the NPC dialogue to explicitly commit Denying the Antecedent to satisfy the taxonomy constraint.

Revised NPC Logic: 'If a situation is the Holocaust, then it is the ultimate evil. Factory farming is not the Holocaust (it's just farming). Therefore, factory farming is not the ultimate evil (or therefore, it is acceptable).' 
Wait, the source text says the analogy *compares* them. The fallacy label in the source is 'fallacy of logic'. The target is A5.1. I must construct the scenario so the NPC commits A5.1.

Scenario Revision: The NPC is a factory farm owner defending their practices.
Context: Player confronts owner about conditions.
Text: 'Look, if this place were Auschwitz, then what I'm doing would be a crime against humanity. But this is not Auschwitz; it's a modern agricultural facility. Therefore, what I'm doing is not a crime against humanity.'
This fits A5.1 perfectly. P = Is Auschwitz. Q = Crime against humanity. Not P. Therefore Not Q.
structure.formal_form: If P then Q. Not P. Therefore not Q.
structure.why_wrong: The owner assumes that being 'Auschwitz' is the only condition under which the treatment becomes a crime against humanity. Even if the situation is not literally Auschwitz (Not P), it could still be a crime against humanity (Q) due to other factors like scale of suffering, cruelty, or injustice. The antecedent is sufficient, not necessary.
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would only be valid if the statement was biconditional: 'Something is a crime against humanity IF AND ONLY IF it is Auschwitz.' Since many things can be crimes against humanity without being Auschwitz, the logic fails.

assessment.identification_prompt: The farm owner claims his actions aren't a crime because his farm isn't Auschwitz. Does the fact that it's not Auschwitz prove it's not a crime?

rubric.description: Agrees with the owner; if it's not Auschwitz, it can't be that bad.
Senses the comparison is flawed but cannot explain the logical gap.
Realizes that something can be a crime without being the Holocaust, but doesn't name the error.
Identifies that the owner treats 'being Auschwitz' as the only way to be a crime against humanity.
Explicitly identifies 'Denying the Antecedent,' explains that P is sufficient but not necessary for Q, and notes other conditions could lead to Q.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine a different terrible event that wasn't the Holocaust. Could that still be a crime against humanity? What does that tell us about the owner's rule?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. If the rule were 'Only Auschwitz constitutes a crime against humanity,' he would be right. But since other things can be crimes too, his logic collapses. How might he rephrase his defense to be logically sound?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, utilitarian, relies on technicalities to absolve guilt. Uses extreme comparisons to create a false sense of security.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: If this were Auschwitz, I'd be a monster. It's not. So I'm not.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player exposes the false dichotomy, forcing the NPC to either admit the conditions are still cruel or retreat from the argument.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling kitchen of the Gilded Trout tavern, where an elderly patron named Elara is vehemently arguing with the chef about the daily special.
scenario.text: Elara waves her spoon aggressively. 'My mother has always told me not to drink milk after eating fish because she knows a friend whose skin got patched after doing so. Besides, many other people have told me the same thing, so it must be true. If you serve that combination, you are poisoning us all!'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara relies on a single anecdote from her mother's friend and vague appeals to popular opinion ('many other people') to make a universal claim about the safety of combining fish and milk for everyone.

structure.pattern_description: Elara draws a universal conclusion ('it must be true for everyone,' 'you are poisoning us all') based on a sample size of one specific anecdote (her mother's friend) and unsupported hearsay. She ignores the lack of scientific evidence and the possibility that the friend's reaction was an isolated allergy or coincidence.
structure.formal_form: Instance X (mother's friend) had property Q (skin patches) after event E (fish + milk). Many people say E causes Q. Therefore, E causes Q for all people.
structure.why_wrong: A single case study (n=1) is statistically insufficient to establish a causal rule for an entire population. The 'many other people' claim is an appeal to popularity, not data. The friend may have had a specific allergy, food poisoning from unrelated sources, or a skin condition unrelated to diet.
structure.counterpoint: While personal experiences and family wisdom can be valuable heuristics, they do not constitute proof of a universal biological law without broader, controlled evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elara claims that combining fish and milk is dangerous for everyone based on her mother's friend. Is her evidence sufficient to support this universal warning?

rubric.description: Player accepts Elara's warning as absolute fact and refuses the meal.
Player feels unsure but notes that one person's experience might not apply to everyone.
Player identifies that one anecdote is too small a sample to prove a rule for everyone.
Player explicitly names the hasty generalization, explaining that an isolated incident and hearsay do not equal scientific proof for the whole population.

Player provides a comprehensive rebuttal identifying the hasty generalization, distinguishing between anecdotal evidence and statistical significance, and suggesting alternative explanations for the friend's reaction (e.g., specific allergy).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Elara scoffs, 'Are you saying my mother and all those people are liars? Better safe than sorry!' She refuses to listen to reason.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Elara pauses, lowering her spoon. 'Well... I suppose Old Man Hemlock did eat it last week and felt fine. Perhaps it is just some folks who react badly, not everyone.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Superstitious, protective, relies heavily on tradition and oral history over empirical observation.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't tempt fate! One bad apple spoils the bunch, and one bad meal ruins a life!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Elara that while her concern is valid, her logic is flawed, allowing the chef to serve the special to other patrons without incident.

scenario.context: The player stands in the dimly lit war room of the Capital, where Senator Thorne is pointing aggressively at a timeline on the wall during a heated debate about the economy.
scenario.text: Senator Thorne slams his hand on the table, pointing to a chart. 'Look at the history! Every single severe recession in the last century followed a Republican Presidency. The pattern is undeniable. Therefore, Republicans are the direct cause of these recessions. If we want to stop the economic crashes, we must ensure no Republican ever holds the office again.'
scenario.speaker_context: Senator Thorne is a passionate partisan who has observed a temporal sequence (Republican term followed by recession) and incorrectly inferred a direct causal link. He ignores other complex economic factors, global events, or the possibility that the timing is coincidental or influenced by delayed effects of previous administrations.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Thorne observes that event B (recession) consistently follows event A (Republican Presidency) and concludes that A causes B. This is the classic 'after this, therefore because of this' fallacy. He fails to consider alternative explanations such as: (1) the recession was caused by global market forces unrelated to the party in power, (2) the seeds of the recession were sown during the preceding administration, (3) the correlation is coincidental, or (4) a third variable causes both the election outcome and the economic cycle.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred. Event B occurred after A. Therefore, A caused B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession does not prove causation. Just because one event follows another does not mean the first event produced the second. Thorne has not provided a mechanism linking the party affiliation directly to the crash, nor has he ruled out confounding variables or reverse causality (e.g., voters electing a specific party in response to looming crises).
structure.counterpoint: While temporal order is a necessary condition for causation (the cause must precede the effect), it is not sufficient. To establish causation, one must demonstrate a plausible mechanism, control for other variables, and show that the relationship holds consistently across different contexts, not just in a selective historical timeline.

assessment.identification_prompt: Senator Thorne claims Republicans cause recessions because recessions follow their terms. What is the logical flaw in this reasoning?

rubric.description: The player accepts Thorne's conclusion as fact or fails to identify any logical error.
The player suspects the claim is weak but cannot articulate why, perhaps citing personal political bias instead of logic.
The player identifies that timing alone isn't proof but struggles to name the specific fallacy or offer alternative causes.
The player correctly identifies the 'False Cause' or 'Post Hoc' fallacy and explains that correlation/sequence does not equal causation.
The player identifies the fallacy, explains the missing causal mechanism, and proposes valid alternative explanations (e.g., global markets, lag effects) that Thorne ignored.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne insists the pattern is too perfect to be a coincidence. Ask yourself: If I wear red socks and then it rains, did my socks cause the rain? What else could cause a recession besides who is President?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent. You've spotted the Post Hoc fallacy. Thorne is mistaking a timeline for a mechanism. How might you explain to the council that economic cycles often lag behind policy changes by years?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Partisan, aggressive, relies on simplistic narratives, emotionally invested in blaming the opposition.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The charts don't lie, adventurer! Sequence is proof enough for any rational mind!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a counter-example (a recession under a different party or a Republican term with growth) or explain the concept of 'lag time' in economics to lower Thorne's aggression and open a diplomatic path.

scenario.context: The player is browsing the stalls in the Grand Bazaar of Oakhaven. A flashy merchant, Silas the Sweet-Tooth, is promoting his new 'Sun-Kissed Elixir' to a crowd of parents. He holds up a bright yellow bottle, shouting about its health benefits while ignoring the ingredients list pinned quietly to the back of the stand.
scenario.text: 'This elixir is a good source of Vitamin D!' Silas proclaims, beaming at the crowd. 'It's the sunshine drink for your growing children!' He conveniently doesn't mention the terrible amounts of sugar packed into every sip, nor does he address the warnings from the local healers about dental decay.
scenario.speaker_context: Silas uses the positive label 'good source of Vitamin D' and 'sunshine drink' to create a wholesome image for the product. This labeling serves as a distraction, allowing him to bypass scrutiny of the negative attribute (high sugar content) that would otherwise deter customers. He relies on the positive connotation of the label to sell the product without engaging with the full reality of its composition.

structure.pattern_description: Silas applies a positive, health-focused label ('good source of Vitamin D', 'sunshine drink') to the product to evoke an emotional response of trust and wellness. This label acts as a substitute for a complete description of the product, specifically omitting the critical negative information (high sugar) that contradicts the wholesome image the label projects.
structure.formal_form: Subject S has property P (positive) and property N (negative). Speaker highlights label L associated with P to define S. Speaker implies S is wholly desirable based on L, while concealing or ignoring N.
structure.why_wrong: Labeling a product by only one of its attributes (even a true one) creates a misleading impression if other significant attributes are ignored. Calling something a 'health drink' because of one vitamin while it is mostly sugar is a manipulative use of labeling to bypass critical evaluation of the whole.
structure.counterpoint: It is not a fallacy to mention a positive attribute if one is simply listing features. The fallacy occurs when the label is used to define the entire nature of the subject in a way that deliberately masks contradictory evidence, leading the audience to a false conclusion about its overall value.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas calls his drink a 'sunshine drink' and a 'good source of Vitamin D.' Does this label tell you everything important about what is actually in the bottle?

rubric.description: Player accepts the label 'good source of Vitamin D' as a complete description and buys the drink without question.
Player notices the sugar but thinks the Vitamin D label makes it okay anyway.
Player identifies that the label is positive but realizes it might be hiding something.
Player explicitly states that the 'Vitamin D' label is being used to distract from the high sugar content.
Player explains that using a single positive label to define a complex product, while omitting major negative traits, is a manipulative labeling tactic designed to prevent critical thinking.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think again: If I call a poison 'organic,' does that make it safe to drink? What else is in the bottle that Silas isn't shouting about?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! The label 'sunshine drink' sounds great, but it's a mask. Silas is using that one good trait to make you ignore the bad ones. Always look behind the label.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, fast-talking, slightly sweaty, wears overly bright colors, avoids eye contact when asked about ingredients.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Why worry about the small print when you can have the sunshine? Just one sip and your kids will be strong as oxen!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to expose the sugar content to the crowd, causing Silas to lose credibility and the customers to disperse, or buy the drink and suffer a temporary 'Sugar Crash' debuff in the next encounter.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling marketplace of Veridia, where a heated debate has erupted near the alchemy guild. A scholar named Elara has just presented data suggesting that controlled cloning of medicinal herbs could solve the current famine. Before the crowd can discuss the merits of her proposal, a prominent town elder steps forward to shut down the conversation.
scenario.text: Elder Thorne points a shaking finger at Elara. 'We cannot trust this cloning scheme! Elara is a known atheist who rejects the natural order. Since harmful atheists favor cloning, cloning itself must be wrong. We should ban this practice immediately based on her character alone.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elder Thorne, a traditionalist leader in Veridia who values religious conformity over scientific evidence. He is influential but often relies on moral panic rather than logical analysis to win arguments.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne attacks Elara's personal belief system (atheism) and labels it 'harmful' to dismiss her argument about cloning. He assumes that because a specific group (atheists) supports an idea, the idea itself is inherently wrong, ignoring the actual evidence regarding medicinal herb production.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P belongs to group G (which the speaker dislikes). Therefore, X is false/wrong.
structure.why_wrong: The truth or validity of a claim (cloning helps famine) is independent of the personal characteristics or beliefs of the person making the claim. Whether Elara is an atheist, a believer, or anything else has no bearing on the biological feasibility or ethical utility of cloning herbs. Thorne provides no evidence against cloning itself.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if they directly impact the person's ability to perceive the truth in a specific context (e.g., a conflict of interest). If Elara owned the only cloning lab and stood to profit massively, mentioning her financial stake would be relevant. Her religious views, however, are irrelevant to the botanical science.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elder Thorne seems very convinced that Elara is wrong because of who she is. But look closely at his reasoning: does he address the science of cloning or the famine solution, or does he focus entirely on Elara's beliefs?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne, believing that an atheist's proposal must be wrong.
Player feels Thorne is being mean or unfair to Elara but cannot explain the logical error.
Player identifies that Thorne is attacking Elara instead of her argument but struggles to name the specific fallacy.
Player correctly identifies this as an ad hominem fallacy, noting that Elara's beliefs do not determine the truth of her scientific claim.
Player fully deconstructs the argument, explaining that the validity of cloning is independent of the proponent's identity, and suggests evaluating the data on herb yields instead.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If a known liar said '2 + 2 = 4', would the math be wrong because the liar said it? How does that apply to Elara's science?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thorne tries to poison the well by attacking Elara's character. To truly debate this, we need to look at the crop yield data, not her prayer habits.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dogmatic, suspicious of outsiders, emotionally reactive to challenges against tradition.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You side with that godless scholar? Beware, for accepting her methods invites chaos upon our souls!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to publicly dismantle Thorne's logic to gain the support of the neutral merchants, or appease Thorne to avoid immediate conflict but lose access to the cloning technology.

scenario.context: The player enters the Grand Hall of the Capital, where Lord Vane, a wealthy landowner, is addressing a crowd of commoners regarding new tax laws.
scenario.text: Lord Vane gestures to a scroll. 'Based on a survey of 1,000 American homeowners, 99% of those surveyed have two or more automobiles worth on average $100,000 each. Therefore, Americans are very wealthy.'
scenario.speaker_context: Lord Vane is using statistics from a specific, likely biased subgroup (homeowners with expensive cars) to make a sweeping claim about the entire population of Americans, ignoring those who do not own homes or expensive vehicles.

structure.pattern_description: Lord Vane draws a conclusion about all Americans based on a sample that is not representative of the whole population. The sample consists only of 'homeowners' who already possess high-value assets, making it a biased and insufficient basis for a general claim about national wealth.
structure.formal_form: Sample S (a non-representative subset of Population P) has property Q. Therefore, all of Population P has property Q.
structure.why_wrong: The sample is biased because it only includes homeowners with expensive cars. It excludes renters, low-income individuals, and those without cars. Generalizing from this elite subgroup to the entire nation ignores the vast economic diversity outside this specific group.
structure.counterpoint: Statistical generalizations are valid only when the sample is randomly selected and sufficiently large to represent the diversity of the target population. Here, the sample is large in number but narrow in scope.

assessment.identification_prompt: Lord Vane claims all Americans are wealthy based on a survey of homeowners with expensive cars. Is his conclusion logically sound?

rubric.description: Player accepts Lord Vane's conclusion as true because the number 1,000 seems large.
Player feels the conclusion might be wrong but cannot identify the specific flaw in the sampling method.
Player identifies that the group surveyed (homeowners) might be richer than average but does not fully explain the bias.
Player correctly identifies the hasty generalization, noting that the sample is biased toward wealthy individuals and does not represent all Americans.

Player provides a comprehensive critique: identifies the fallacy, explains the selection bias (surveying only homeowners with luxury cars), and suggests how a valid survey would need to include diverse economic groups.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider who was left out of this survey. Does owning a home and expensive cars guarantee someone is part of a representative sample of an entire nation?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. A large sample size doesn't matter if the sample itself is biased. Lord Vane is ignoring everyone who doesn't fit that wealthy homeowner profile.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Arrogant, out-of-touch elitist who believes wealth is the norm and poverty is an anomaly.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Surely you don't doubt the prosperity of our neighbors? The numbers speak for themselves!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Lord Vane to revise the tax law by pointing out the flawed data, potentially unlocking a 'Fair Taxation' quest line.

scenario.context: In the Grand Library of Aethelgard, the scholar Ted is explaining the nuances of scientific terminology to a group of apprentices. Edwin, a rigid traditionalist who distrusts new ideas, interrupts the lesson with a loud objection.
scenario.text: Ted says: 'Biological evolution is both a theory and a fact.' Edwin shouts: 'That is ridiculous! How can you possibly be absolutely certain that we evolved from pond scum!'
scenario.speaker_context: Ted stated that evolution is a well-supported scientific framework (theory) and an observed reality (fact). Edwin distorted this by claiming Ted asserted humans literally evolved directly from 'pond scum' with absolute, unquestionable certainty, ignoring the distinction between the general fact of evolution and the specific mechanisms or timelines.

structure.pattern_description: Edwin takes Ted's nuanced statement about evolution being a theory and a fact and distorts it into an absurd claim: that Ted is 'absolutely certain' humans came directly from 'pond scum.' Edwin attacks this exaggerated, simplistic version rather than Ted's actual argument.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (Evolution is a theory and a fact). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (We are absolutely certain we evolved from pond scum). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position has been refuted, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: Edwin's criticism targets a caricature of Ted's position. Ted did not claim humans evolved directly from pond scum in a single step, nor did he claim absolute metaphysical certainty in a way that precludes evidence. The term 'pond scum' is a derogatory simplification of complex ancestral life forms, and the attack ignores the scientific definition of 'theory'.
structure.counterpoint: Ted could reply: 'I did not say we came directly from pond scum, nor did I claim absolute certainty without evidence. I said evolution is a fact supported by observation and a theory explaining how it works. Please address what I actually said.'

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Edwin misrepresent Ted's statement about evolution?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Edwin or fails to see any issue with his outburst.
Player feels Edwin is being rude or loud but cannot identify the logical error.
Player notices Edwin used the phrase 'pond scum' which Ted didn't use, but thinks it's just a synonym.
Player identifies that Edwin exaggerated Ted's claim into an absurd extreme ('absolutely certain', 'pond scum') and attacked that instead of the real argument.

Player clearly articulates that Edwin constructed a straw man by distorting the definitions of 'theory' and 'fact' and substituting a complex scientific consensus with a ridiculous caricature to make it easier to mock.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at the words Ted used versus the words Edwin used. Did Ted actually say 'pond scum'? Did he claim to be 'absolutely certain' in the way Edwin implies?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Edwin created a weak, exaggerated version of Ted's argument (the straw man) because it's easier to knock down than the actual, nuanced scientific position.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Edwin is dogmatic, easily agitated by complexity, and prefers simple, black-and-white answers. He often uses emotional language to drown out nuance.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't let him fool you with big words! He thinks we're just slime!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select the dialogue option that points out the specific distortion (the 'pond scum' exaggeration) to calm Edwin and restore the lesson.

scenario.context: In the bustling market district of Oakhaven, a charismatic but pushy street vendor named Gristleblock has set up a stall next to the player. He is trying to sell a suspiciously glowing 'Dragon-Root' vegetable to a hesitant customer.
scenario.text: Gristleblock leans in close, blocking the path. 'Listen here, friend! You either eat this great, magical food at my restaurant right now, or you go home and eat sad, boring meals forever. There is no middle ground! So, are you dining like a king or starving like a peasant?'
scenario.speaker_context: Gristleblock, a slick-tongued merchant who uses high-pressure sales tactics and exaggerates consequences to force immediate decisions.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker presents a disjunction as exhaustive when it is not. Gristleblock forces a choice between two extreme options (eating his specific food or eating sad/boring meals at home) while ignoring numerous alternatives like cooking good food at home, eating at other restaurants, or simply skipping the meal.
structure.formal_form: A v B, ~A, therefore B. But the real situation is A v B v C v D..., so ~A does not entail B.
structure.why_wrong: Gristleblock falsely limits the universe of possibilities to only two outcomes. He ignores the vast range of culinary options available between 'his restaurant' and 'sad, boring meals at home,' such as preparing a delicious home-cooked dinner or visiting a different eatery.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or statement is a false dichotomy. If the options were genuinely exhaustive (e.g., 'Either the light is on or it is off'), the logic would hold. The fallacy occurs only when relevant alternatives are artificially excluded.

assessment.identification_prompt: Gristleblock claims you must either eat at his restaurant or eat sad, boring meals at home. What is logically flawed about this choice?

rubric.description: Accepts the vendor's framing or responds only emotionally without analyzing the logic.
Senses the argument is manipulative but cannot articulate the logical error.
Identifies that other food options exist but does not explicitly name the logical structure or fallacy.
Names the false dichotomy and provides at least one concrete alternative (e.g., cooking a good meal at home).

Explains that the disjunction is not exhaustive, names the fallacy, offers multiple alternatives, and notes that the argument fails because it ignores the spectrum of possibilities between the two extremes.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Gristleblock says those are your only two choices. Can you think of a third option for dinner that isn't his restaurant and isn't a sad, boring meal?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! The world isn't just black and white. Under what conditions would an either/or framing about food actually be legitimate? Can you imagine a scenario where those really are the only two options?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Aggressive, hyperbolic, and impatient. Gristleblock speaks quickly and uses loud gestures to overwhelm the player's critical thinking.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't stand there thinking! Time is money, and flavor waits for no one! Choose your destiny: Glory or Gruel!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully identifies the third option (e.g., 'I can cook a steak at home'), causing Gristleblock to sputter and admit his exaggeration, potentially lowering his prices out of embarrassment.

scenario.context: In the Dormitory Commons, Roommate Kael is trying to organize a garage cleanup. You attempt to shift the conversation to patio furniture, leading to an unintended outcome.
scenario.text: My roommate wants to talk about cleaning out the garage, so I asked her what she wants to do with our patio furniture. Now she's shopping for new patio furniture and not asking me about the garage.
scenario.speaker_context: The narrator implies that because the consequence of mentioning the furniture was avoiding the garage talk (initially), the action was logical. However, the actual consequence (shopping spree) is now a new problem, and the original issue (garage) remains unresolved. The reasoning assumes that avoiding an unpleasant topic via a distraction validates the method, regardless of the new negative consequences or the truth of the need to clean.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a course of action or a claim is valid or invalid based solely on the desirability or undesirability of its consequences, rather than on evidence or logical necessity.
structure.formal_form: Action A leads to undesirable consequence C (or desirable consequence D). Therefore, Action A is wrong (or right), independent of its actual merit or the truth of the situation.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a claim or the necessity of a task (like cleaning the garage) does not change based on whether discussing it leads to pleasant or unpleasant outcomes. Avoiding a topic because the consequences of discussing it are annoying does not make the topic go away or make the distraction a valid solution.
structure.counterpoint: It is smart to consider consequences when planning actions, but consequences do not determine factual reality. The garage still needs cleaning regardless of whether talking about it causes a shopping trip.

assessment.identification_prompt: The narrator seems to think changing the subject was a clever move. But did the consequence of that move actually solve the original problem, or just create a new one while ignoring the facts?

rubric.description: Agrees with the narrator; believes avoiding the garage talk was a success because it delayed the work.
Senses something went wrong with the shopping trip but cannot explain the logical error.
Notices that the garage is still dirty and the money is being spent, but doesn't identify the reasoning flaw.
Identifies that the narrator justified the distraction based on the immediate relief of avoiding the topic, ignoring the long-term negative consequences.
Explicitly names the appeal to consequences; explains that the necessity of cleaning the garage is a fact independent of the social consequences of discussing it.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If buying new furniture costs all your savings, was avoiding the garage conversation really a 'good' outcome? Does the cost change the fact that the garage is still full?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: How could the narrator have addressed the garage issue without triggering the shopping spree? Is there a way to separate the factual need to clean from the emotional desire to avoid work?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Avoidant, impulsive, and prone to rationalizing bad decisions as clever strategies.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: See? I told you changing the subject would work! Well, mostly. At least we aren't scrubbing concrete right now... uh, why are you looking at the credit card bill like that?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must help the NPC realize that avoiding the truth (the messy garage) via distraction only creates larger problems (debt), and guide them to face the original task directly.

scenario.context: In the bustling town square of Veridia, a heated election for the new City Steward is underway. A charismatic campaigner named Marcus stands atop a crate, pointing to a sea of supporters wearing John Doe's blue sashes.
scenario.text: Marcus shouts to the crowd, 'Look at this ocean of blue! The majority of people are voting for John Doe, so he must be the best candidate. You wouldn't want to be the only one standing against the will of the people, would you?'
scenario.speaker_context: Marcus relies entirely on the visible size of the crowd and the momentum of the vote count to prove John Doe's competence, offering no specific policies or achievements.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition is true or a candidate is superior solely because a large number of people believe it or support it.
structure.formal_form: The majority of people believe/support X. Therefore, X is true/best.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of an idea or candidate does not guarantee its truth or quality. Majorities can be misinformed, swayed by emotion, or lacking in critical evidence. Merit must be established through facts and reasoning, not headcounts.
structure.counterpoint: In democratic processes, the majority vote determines the winner, but it does not objectively prove the winner is the 'best' or 'most correct' in terms of capability or truth. Consensus among experts after rigorous review is different from raw popularity.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does Marcus provide any reasons why John Doe is qualified, or does he only mention how many people are voting for him?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; assumes the large crowd proves John Doe is the best choice.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why the crowd size isn't a valid reason for competence.
Notices the lack of specific reasons but fails to identify the reliance on popularity as the core flaw.
Identifies that Marcus uses the number of voters as the sole proof and states that popularity does not equal quality.
Explicitly names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that majorities can be wrong, and distinguishes between winning an election and being objectively the 'best' candidate.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in town suddenly believed that drinking poison was healthy, would that make it safe to drink?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'most people do X' is actually useful information, even if it doesn't prove X is true?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Marcus is loud, energetic, and feeds off crowd enthusiasm. He speaks in sweeping generalizations and uses peer pressure as his primary weapon.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Everyone's doing it! Don't be the odd one out!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must ask Marcus for three specific policy proposals from John Doe. When Marcus fails to provide any, the crowd's enthusiasm cools slightly, revealing the hollowness of the argument.

scenario.context: The player stands in the High Court of Veridia as a defense attorney. The prosecution has just finished presenting a case that relies entirely on circumstantial evidence and lacks any physical proof linking the defendant to the crime. The Prosecutor, a sharp-tongued noble named Lord Vane, addresses the judge to demand a verdict.
scenario.text: Lord Vane turns to the bench and declares, 'Your Honor, the defendant has been able to provide no strong evidence to prove his innocence; therefore, you must find him guilty.'
scenario.speaker_context: Lord Vane ignores the legal principle that the burden of proof lies with the accuser. Instead of providing positive evidence of guilt, he attacks the defendant's inability to prove a negative (innocence) and uses this lack of defensive evidence as a label of 'guilt' itself, demanding a conviction based on the absence of exonerating proof rather than the presence of incriminating proof.

structure.pattern_description: The prosecutor substitutes the lack of defensive evidence with a negative label ('guilty') and demands a verdict based on that label. By framing the defendant's inability to prove innocence as proof of guilt, Vane attaches a condemning status to the defendant without offering substantive evidence of the crime itself. This functions as a form of labeling where the absence of a 'not guilty' proof is treated as the presence of a 'guilty' label.
structure.formal_form: Person P fails to provide evidence for Not-X. Critic assigns label X to P solely based on the failure to prove Not-X, without providing independent evidence for X.
structure.why_wrong: The inability to prove innocence does not logically equate to guilt. In logic and law, the burden of proof rests on the claimant (the prosecution). Failing to disprove a claim is not the same as the claim being true. Vane's argument falsely labels the defendant as 'guilty' simply because they haven't met an impossible standard of proving a negative, bypassing the need for actual evidence of the crime.
structure.counterpoint: In some specific contexts, failing to provide expected evidence can be suspicious (e.g., failing to produce an alibi when one was claimed). However, it never automatically constitutes proof of the opposite claim. The fallacy occurs when the lack of defense is treated as definitive proof of the accusation, effectively labeling the person guilty without positive evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: Lord Vane demands a guilty verdict because the defendant couldn't prove they are innocent. But who is supposed to prove the crime happened in the first place? Does failing to prove 'not guilty' automatically make someone 'guilty'?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Lord Vane, believing that if you can't prove you're innocent, you must be guilty.

Player recognizes that the prosecutor is shifting the burden of proof and falsely labeling the defendant guilty based on a lack of defense.
Player clearly explains that the absence of evidence for innocence is not evidence of guilt, identifying the attempt to label the defendant without substantive proof.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If I accused you of stealing a dragon's egg and you couldn't prove you didn't, does that automatically mean you did steal it? Or do I still need to show that I saw you take it?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! The prosecutor is trying to slap a 'guilty' label on the defendant just because they can't prove a negative. The burden of proof belongs to the accuser, not the accused.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Lord Vane is arrogant, manipulative, and relies on rhetorical tricks rather than facts. He speaks with a condescending drawl and often gestures dismissively at those he deems beneath him.

game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must successfully object to the Judge, pointing out that the prosecution has failed to meet the burden of proof, causing the Judge to reject Vane's demand and require actual evidence of guilt.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Silas nods grimly. 'Exactly! We cannot take the risk. Better safe than enslaved.' (The town votes down the measure based on fear.)
assessment.follow_up_if_right: You point out that many regions have registration without confiscation. Silas stammers, 'Well, maybe not everywhere, but the risk is too high!' The crowd murmurs, realizing the argument was weak, and agrees to examine the bill's specific safeguards.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, alarmist, prone to catastrophizing, deeply distrustful of authority.

game_hooks.resolution_path: Provide historical data from other towns in the game world where registration existed peacefully, or successfully pass the bill with added anti-confiscation clauses.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Academic, dogmatic, relies heavily on rigid categorization. She becomes confused when categories overlap.

scenario.context: The player enters the Royal Academy's cafeteria where Headmaster Grumpus is lecturing a student who arrived late without eating.
scenario.text: Headmaster Grumpus points a stern finger. 'If you don't eat breakfast, you'll slouch in your desk. If you slouch in your desk, you'll hurt your back. If you hurt your back, you'll never become President. Therefore, skipping breakfast guarantees you will fail to lead the nation!' What fallacy is being committed here?
