However, Dr. Silas is offering professional medical expertise based on general medical knowledge, not claiming his personal body is proof of the treatment's efficacy.

assessment.identification_prompt: Bram seems very confident in his rejection of the doctor. But look closely at his reason: does pointing out the doctor's weight actually prove the medicine won't work?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Bram, believing the doctor's weight invalidates his medical advice.
Player feels Bram is being rude or unfair but cannot explain why the logic is flawed.
Player identifies that Bram is attacking the doctor personally but struggles to separate the person from the argument.
Player recognizes that the doctor's weight is irrelevant to the scientific validity of the medical advice provided.
Player clearly articulates that Bram committed an ad hominem fallacy by substituting an attack on the doctor's character for a rebuttal of the medical evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If a math teacher makes a mistake on their taxes, does that mean their lesson on algebra is wrong? How is Bram's logic similar?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Bram ignored the actual data and reasoning about the cough and fatigue. He tried to win the argument by insulting the messenger instead of addressing the message.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Stubborn, pragmatic, distrustful of intellectuals, values physical strength above all.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! Don't need no lecture from someone who can't even run a mile without wheezing!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must choose dialogue options that redirect Bram's focus from the doctor's appearance back to the specific symptoms and the medical evidence presented, successfully curing Bram's illness.

scenario.context: The player stands in the Grand Library of Aethelgard, speaking with Elara, a senior scholar known for her love of literature but also her stubborn adherence to tradition. She is organizing a shelf of new arrivals when the player mentions a popular new film adaptation of a classic novel.
scenario.text: Elara scoffs without looking up from her books. 'Even without watching the movie, I just know that it would not be as good as the book. They always ruin the magic when they put it on screen.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara has likely seen a few bad adaptations in the past and is using those limited experiences to make a universal claim about all movie adaptations of books, ignoring the possibility of high-quality films.

structure.pattern_description: Elara concludes that a specific movie (which she hasn't even seen) and implicitly all movies based on books are inferior to their source material. She bases this on an unstated but implied set of past negative experiences ('They always ruin...'), treating a subset of bad adaptations as representative of the entire category.
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of X (movie adaptations) having property Q (being worse than the book). Therefore, all instances of X have property Q.
structure.why_wrong: The sample size of 'bad adaptations' Elara has encountered is insufficient to support a universal claim about every single movie adaptation. Furthermore, she is making a prediction about a specific instance without evidence, relying solely on a biased generalization. She ignores counter-examples where films have successfully captured or even enhanced the source material.
structure.counterpoint: While many adaptations do fail, stating that they 'always' fail is logically unsound. A valid assessment requires evaluating the specific movie on its own merits or acknowledging that the quality of adaptations varies widely.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elara claims the movie will definitely be worse than the book without watching it, arguing that adaptations 'always' ruin the magic. Is her conclusion logically justified?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Elara, accepting that movies are always worse than books.
Player doubts Elara but cannot explain the logical flaw, perhaps just saying 'not all movies are bad'.
Player identifies that Elara is generalizing from past experiences but fails to explicitly name the insufficient sample size or the universal nature of her claim.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, noting that Elara uses a limited set of bad examples to make a universal claim ('always') about all adaptations.

Player fully deconstructs the argument: identifies the hasty generalization, explains that the sample of bad adaptations does not represent the whole population, and points out the error of judging a specific unseen case based solely on this flawed generalization.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider: Have you ever seen a movie that was just as good as, or better than, the book? If so, does that change Elara's rule?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Just because some adaptations fail doesn't mean they all do. Elara is letting a few bad experiences cloud her judgment of something she hasn't even seen yet.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Scholarly, traditionalist, slightly dismissive of modern media, passionate about literature.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The written word allows the imagination to flourish; a camera forces a single vision upon you. It is a reduction, never an enhancement.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Elara to watch the trailer or read a review of this specific film, breaking her reliance on the generalization and opening a quest to compare the book and film directly.

scenario.context: In the bustling town square of Veridia, a heated debate is underway regarding the upcoming election. A citizen named Elias expresses concern about a candidate's policy on immigration detention. Another citizen, Mara, known for her fiery rhetoric, immediately jumps in to shut down the conversation.
scenario.text: Elias says: 'I am worried about Candidate Jones's plan to separate immigrant families in detention centers; it seems inhumane.' Mara shouts back: 'Bob Jones is a monster who likes to separate immigrant families in detention centers. How could you vote for someone like that??'
scenario.speaker_context: Elias expressed concern about a specific policy (family separation). Mara ignored the nuance of the policy discussion and instead attacked a caricature of the candidate as a 'monster' who simply 'likes' separating families, implying malicious intent rather than addressing the policy mechanics or ethics directly.

structure.pattern_description: Mara takes Elias's concern about a specific policy outcome (separation of families) and distorts it into an attack on the candidate's character and motives (calling him a 'monster' who 'likes' doing it). She attacks this exaggerated, evil version of the candidate rather than engaging with the actual policy argument Elias raised.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (Policy X is harmful). Person B restates P as P* (Person supporting X is a monster who enjoys harm). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes A's position is invalid because P* is absurd/evil.
structure.why_wrong: Mara's response does not address the ethical or practical arguments regarding family separation. Instead, she constructs an extreme version of the candidate's stance (that he enjoys the suffering) and attacks that fabrication. This diverts the conversation from the policy to an emotional ad hominem based on a distortion.
structure.counterpoint: Elias could reply: 'I didn't say he is a monster or that he enjoys it. I said the policy of separating families is harmful. Can we discuss the effects of that policy instead of attacking his character?'

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Mara's response misrepresent Elias's original point about the candidate's policy?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Mara's outrage and sees no logical error, viewing Jones simply as a monster.
Player feels Mara is being too aggressive or mean but cannot identify the logical distortion.
Player notices Mara changed the subject from the policy to the candidate's character but doesn't fully articulate the exaggeration.
Player identifies that Mara exaggerated Elias's point by claiming the candidate 'likes' separating families and is a 'monster,' attacking this distorted view instead of the policy itself.

Player clearly explains that Mara constructed a 'straw man' by attributing malicious enjoyment to the candidate, which Elias never claimed, thereby avoiding the actual argument about the policy's impact.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at what Elias actually said versus what Mara accused him of supporting. Did Elias say the candidate 'likes' hurting people, or did he criticize a specific action?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Mara created a distorted, evil version of the candidate's position (the straw man) that is easier to attack than the actual policy discussion Elias tried to have.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Mara is impulsive, emotionally driven, and tends to view political opponents as purely evil rather than mistaken. She thrives on rallying the crowd through outrage.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't listen to his excuses! He's defending a monster!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must choose a dialogue option that calmly distinguishes between the candidate's actions and the alleged malicious intent, forcing Mara to either address the policy or reveal her refusal to engage logically.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Veridia, a town councilor named Elara proposes a modest adjustment to the state minimum wage to help workers keep up with rising food costs. A wealthy merchant lord, Baron Vane, who employs most of the town's laborers, immediately shouts down the proposal from his balcony.
scenario.text: Baron Vane declares: 'People who don't support the proposed state minimum wage increase hate the poor! They want to see families starve so they can hoard gold!' The crowd murmurs, turning suspicious eyes toward Elara.
scenario.speaker_context: Elara proposed a specific economic adjustment. Baron Vane recharacterized opposition to this specific policy as a moral failure and active hatred toward the poor, an extreme position Elara never claimed.

structure.pattern_description: Baron Vane takes the specific position 'opposes this wage increase' and distorts it into the extreme, emotional position 'hates the poor and wants them to starve.' He attacks this fabricated moral failing rather than addressing the economic arguments against the wage hike.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (oppose wage hike). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (hate the poor/want starvation). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position is morally bankrupt, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: Opposing a specific economic policy does not logically equate to hating the demographic that policy aims to help. One can care deeply about the poor while believing a specific wage increase will cause job losses or inflation. Vane ignores the actual argument to attack a fake, evil motive.
structure.counterpoint: Elara could reply: 'I do not hate the poor; I love them enough to ensure this policy doesn't cost them their jobs. Let us discuss the economic data, not invented motives.'

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Baron Vane misrepresent Councilor Elara's stance on the minimum wage?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane or believes opposing the wage hike truly means hating the poor.
Player feels Vane is being unfair or too harsh but cannot explain why logically.
Player notices Vane used strong emotional words like 'hate' but doesn't identify the structural distortion of the argument.
Player identifies that Vane replaced Elara's specific policy objection with a fabricated, extreme moral stance (hating the poor) to make her easier to attack.

Player fully articulates the Straw Man structure: distinguishing the actual position (policy disagreement) from the distorted position (moral hatred) and explains why the attack on the distortion fails to refute the original point.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider: Is it possible to disagree with a specific solution without hating the people the solution is meant to help? What other reasons might someone oppose a wage increase?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Vane created a 'straw man'—a weak, fake version of Elara's argument that is easy to knock down. He avoided the hard work of debating the actual economics.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Baron Vane is flamboyant, manipulative, and relies on emotional outbursts to control crowds rather than logical debate. He wears excessive gold and speaks loudly.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: How dare you stand against the hungry children of Veridia! Your greed knows no bounds!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that calmly separate the policy from the motive, forcing Vane to either address the economics or look foolish to the crowd.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling market square of Oakhaven, where a town hall meeting is underway. A local merchant named Bob has just proposed a new system for rotating stall locations to ensure fair foot traffic for all vendors. He presented a map and a schedule showing how every vendor would benefit equally over a month. Before the crowd can discuss the merits of the plan, a rival vendor steps forward to object.
scenario.text: You can't believe Bob's idea. He's a socialist.
scenario.speaker_context: Silas, a wealthy and traditionalist spice merchant who has held the prime corner spot for decades. He is known for being dismissive of new ideas and often uses political labels to discredit opponents rather than addressing their arguments.

structure.pattern_description: Silas rejects Bob's proposal for stall rotation solely based on Bob's perceived political affiliation ('socialist'). He ignores the actual content of the proposal—the map, the schedule, and the argument for fair foot traffic—and attempts to invalidate the idea by attacking the person presenting it.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P has property Q (political label/affiliation). Therefore, X is false or should be rejected.
structure.why_wrong: The truth or validity of a proposal (like a stall rotation schedule) depends on its own logic, evidence, and feasibility, not on the political views of the person suggesting it. Even if Bob were a socialist, the math of the rotation schedule could still be fair and beneficial. Silas provides no reason why the schedule itself is flawed.
structure.counterpoint: Political affiliation might be relevant if the proposal explicitly relied on socialist economic theory to function (e.g., 'We must do this because private property is theft'). However, Bob's proposal was a practical logistics plan based on fairness and data, making the label irrelevant to its execution.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas seems very quick to dismiss Bob. Look closely at what Silas actually says: does he mention the map, the schedule, or the foot traffic numbers? Or does he focus entirely on Bob?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Silas, believing Bob's idea is bad specifically because he is a socialist.
Player feels Silas is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why the argument is logically flawed.
Player identifies that Silas is attacking Bob instead of the idea but struggles to articulate why this doesn't disprove the idea.
Player correctly identifies the ad hominem fallacy and explains that Bob's political label does not change the facts of the rotation schedule.
Player fully deconstructs the argument, noting that Silas offered zero counter-evidence regarding the map or schedule, and explicitly separates the proposer's identity from the proposal's merit.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a mathematician you disliked told you that 2+2=4, would the answer suddenly become 5? Why does Bob's label change the math of the stall schedule?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Silas tried to win the argument by labeling Bob rather than debating the schedule. A good leader evaluates the plan on its own merits, regardless of who proposed it.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Silas is stubborn, status-quo biased, and relies on rhetorical tricks to maintain his privileged position in the market.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! Don't listen to his fancy maps. We all know what kind of trouble his kind brings to a honest marketplace.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player successfully identifies the fallacy, Silas is forced to either admit he hasn't reviewed the map or attempt a weak substantive argument, allowing the town to vote on the rotation plan. If the player fails, the crowd turns against Bob, and the unfair status quo remains.

scenario.context: In the bustling guild hall of Meridia, a heated debate erupts between the veteran adventurers and the novice recruits regarding the upcoming expedition into the Whispering Caves. Tensions are high as resources are scarce.
scenario.text: A stern veteran steps forward, crossing his arms and glaring at the group. 'Stop wasting time with your hesitation! You are either a leader who charges ahead, or a follower who stays behind and cowers. There is no middle ground. So, which are you?'
scenario.speaker_context: Garrick the Bold, a high-level warrior who values decisive action above all else and often oversimplifies complex social dynamics to force compliance.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker presents a situation as having only two mutually exclusive options (leader or follower) when, in reality, a spectrum of roles and behaviors exists. This ignores possibilities such as being a collaborative team member, a strategic scout, a supportive healer, or a leader who listens before acting.
structure.formal_form: A v B (You are either A or B). Implicitly: ~A -> B and ~B -> A. However, the actual state space includes C, D, E... (e.g., collaborator, specialist, cautious planner), so the disjunction is not exhaustive.
structure.why_wrong: Garrick falsely limits the identity of the adventurers to two extremes. One can be a follower who is brave, or a leader who is cautious. The terms are not exhaustive nor strictly mutually exclusive in this context.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or statement is a fallacy. If the options were 'You are either alive or dead,' the dichotomy would be logically valid because those states are genuinely exhaustive and mutually exclusive in this context. The error lies in applying this structure to complex traits where nuance exists.

assessment.identification_prompt: Garrick claims you must be either a leader or a follower. What is flawed about this framing of the adventurers' roles?

rubric.description: Accepts Garrick's ultimatum or chooses a side without questioning the premise.
Feels the statement is unfair or too harsh but cannot explain the logical error.
Identifies that other roles exist (like a team player) but does not explicitly name the logical structure.
Identifies the false dichotomy and explains that one can be a brave follower or a cautious leader, rejecting the exhaustive nature of the choice.

Clearly articulates that the disjunction is not exhaustive, names the fallacy (False Dichotomy/Black-or-White), provides multiple specific counter-examples of hybrid roles, and explains why the logical form fails here.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Garrick says there are only two types of people. Can you think of someone who follows orders but is still brave? Or a leader who waits for advice?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Since the options aren't exhaustive, how might you respond to Garrick to show that the party needs a mix of styles, not just one extreme?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Authoritarian, impatient, binary thinker, respects strength but lacks nuance.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't give me excuses about 'teamwork.' Pick a side: lead or follow!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully points out a third option (e.g., 'We can be a coordinated unit'), causing Garrick to pause and reconsider his rigid stance, potentially unlocking a 'Unified Strategy' buff for the party.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling courtyard of Oakhaven Academy during the final round of student council elections. The air is thick with tension as the results are about to be announced. A group of students is gathered around a podium where Joseph, a quiet but diligent student known for his detailed platform on improving the library and cafeteria, has just finished his closing statement. Suddenly, Marcus, a popular athlete running against him, steps forward to address the crowd before the votes are counted.
scenario.text: Marcus crosses his arms and sneers at the crowd. 'Don't waste your vote! Joseph can't be class president, he's poor! How can someone who wears hand-me-downs possibly understand what our school needs?'
scenario.speaker_context: Marcus, a charismatic but arrogant senior and star quarterback. He relies heavily on social status and popularity to win arguments, often dismissing opponents based on their background rather than their ideas.

structure.pattern_description: Marcus attacks Joseph's financial status (being poor, wearing hand-me-downs) to disqualify him from the presidency. He ignores Joseph's actual platform regarding the library and cafeteria, treating Joseph's economic circumstance as proof that he cannot represent the school.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X (or is a candidate for role R). Person P has property Q (poverty/low status), which is irrelevant to the truth of X or ability to perform R. Therefore, P's claim should be rejected or P is unfit for R.
structure.why_wrong: A person's financial status does not determine their intelligence, leadership ability, or the validity of their policy proposals. Joseph's ideas must be evaluated on their own merits—whether they are feasible and beneficial—not on how much money his family has. Being poor does not prevent someone from understanding school needs or leading effectively.
structure.counterpoint: Personal circumstances are only relevant if they create a direct conflict of interest or inability to perform a specific duty. For example, if the role required managing a large budget and the candidate had a proven history of embezzlement, that financial history would be relevant. However, simply being poor is not a conflict of interest for a student council president.

assessment.identification_prompt: Marcus is trying to turn the crowd against Joseph. Look closely at his reason: does being poor actually stop someone from having good ideas about the library or cafeteria? What part of Joseph's argument did Marcus ignore?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Marcus or believes being poor makes Joseph unfit for president.
Player feels Marcus is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why his logic is flawed.
Player identifies that Marcus is attacking Joseph's money instead of his ideas, but struggles to articulate why this is irrelevant.
Player clearly states that financial status is irrelevant to leadership ability and notes that Marcus ignored Joseph's specific proposals.

Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, explaining that the merit of a proposal is independent of the proposer's wealth, and identifies this as a circumstantial ad hominem attack designed to distract from the real issues.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: have you ever known someone with little money who was still a great leader or had brilliant ideas? Does having less money automatically mean you know less about what a school needs?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Marcus is distracting everyone from Joseph's actual plans. By focusing on Joseph's wallet instead of his words, Marcus is hoping no one will notice he has no real counter-arguments.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Marcus is loud, confident, and relies on social proof. He gets defensive when pressed on facts and tries to bully opponents into silence.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's obvious, isn't it? You can't lead if you don't have anything to your name!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to publicly defend Joseph by restating his platform points, ask Marcus a direct question about his own policies to shift the focus, or use a 'Logic Lens' item to highlight the fallacy to the crowd, boosting Joseph's support.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Logos City, a town hall debate is underway regarding the new 'Soda Surcharge' intended to fund public health initiatives. Councilor Vane, known for his sharp tongue and tendency to exaggerate, is responding to a moderate proposal from Councilor Elara.
scenario.text: Councilor Elara argues that we should abolish the soda tax to ease the burden on low-income families. Councilor Vane scoffs and declares: 'It is a shame that my opponent wants to encourage people to eat and drink unhealthily, to poison our children, and to destroy our community's wellness just to save a few coins on sugary drinks. I say we keep the tax to stop this madness.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara proposed abolishing a specific tax for economic reasons. Vane recharacterized this as an active desire to promote unhealthy eating, poison children, and destroy community wellness, attributing malicious intent and extreme consequences she never claimed.

structure.pattern_description: Vane takes Elara's specific policy position (abolish the soda tax) and distorts it into an extreme, morally repugnant stance (wanting to poison children and destroy community wellness). He then attacks this fabricated extreme stance rather than addressing the actual economic argument.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (abolish tax). Person B restates P as distorted P* (wants to encourage unhealthy eating/poison children). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes P is false, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: Abolishing a tax is not equivalent to actively encouraging unhealthy behavior or wanting to harm children. Vane ignores the economic reasoning and attacks a caricature of Elara's motives that she never expressed.
structure.counterpoint: Councilor Elara could reply: 'I did not say I want people to eat unhealthily or poison anyone. I argued that this specific tax hurts low-income families. Let us discuss the economic impact, not imaginary motives.'

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Councilor Vane misrepresent Councilor Elara's argument about the soda tax?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane or believes Elara actually wants people to eat unhealthily.
Player feels Vane is being unfair or mean but cannot explain why logically.
Player notices Vane used strong words like 'poison' but doesn't clearly identify that he changed the argument.
Player identifies that Vane exaggerated Elara's position from 'abolish tax' to 'encourage unhealthy eating' and attacked the exaggeration.
Player explicitly names the Straw Man fallacy, distinguishes the original economic argument from the fabricated moral attack, and explains why the distortion invalidates Vane's conclusion.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at what Elara actually said versus what Vane claims she wants. Did she say she wants to poison children, or did she just want to remove a tax?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Vane built a 'straw man' by making Elara's argument look evil and extreme so it would be easier to knock down, instead of debating the actual tax policy.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Councilor Vane is a populist agitator who relies on emotional outbursts and caricatures rather than data. He speaks loudly and uses dramatic gestures.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: My opponent wants to poison our children! Can you believe the greed?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select the dialogue option that corrects the record: 'Vane, she only mentioned the tax, not promoting unhealthy habits. Stop twisting her words.'

scenario.context: The player stands in the dimly lit study of Lord Hargrove, a wealthy but superstitious noble whose estate was recently burglarized. He is pacing nervously near the window, pointing an accusatory finger at a nervous servant holding an unlit lantern.
scenario.text: Lord Hargrove slams his hand on the desk. 'It is undeniable! Because I forgot to leave my porch light on last night, someone robbed my house. The darkness invited the thieves in. If that light had been burning, this tragedy would never have occurred.'
scenario.speaker_context: Lord Hargrove is distraught and seeking a simple explanation for the crime. He assumes that the absence of light (Event A) directly caused the robbery (Event B), ignoring other factors like poor locks, lack of guards, or the thieves' prior knowledge of his schedule.

structure.pattern_description: Hargrove observes that the porch light was off before the robbery occurred and infers that the missing light caused the robbery. This is a classic post hoc ergo propter hoc error. While darkness might be a contributing factor, asserting it as the sole or primary cause without evidence ignores other necessary conditions for the crime (e.g., motive, opportunity, breached security).
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, Event A caused Event B. (Flaw: Temporal precedence does not guarantee causation; other causes may exist.)
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes causation based solely on sequence. Just because the light was off before the robbery doesn't mean the light's absence was the decisive cause. Thieves could have entered regardless of the light if other security measures were weak. Correlation or sequence is not causation.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one must show a mechanism (how darkness specifically enabled this specific entry) and rule out alternative explanations (e.g., 'The lock was picked,' or 'The guard was asleep'). A dark porch is a condition, not necessarily a cause.

assessment.identification_prompt: Lord Hargrove claims the robbery happened *because* the light was off. Is this a valid causal link, or is he confusing sequence with cause?

rubric.description: Fails to identify the flaw; agrees that the missing light definitely caused the robbery.
Suspects the logic is weak but cannot articulate why; vaguely suggests 'maybe it wasn't just the light'.
Identifies that sequence does not equal cause but struggles to name the fallacy or provide an alternative cause.
Correctly identifies the False Cause fallacy and explains that other factors (locks, guards) could be the real cause.
Masterfully deconstructs the argument, naming the 'post hoc' fallacy, explaining the difference between a condition and a cause, and proposing a rigorous method to test the actual cause.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If the light had been on, would a determined thief with bolt cutters still have been able to enter? What else might have allowed the crime to happen?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Just because the light went off before the theft doesn't mean it caused the theft. You've spotted the 'Post Hoc' trap. Now, how would you advise Lord Hargrove to actually secure his home?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, affluent, prone to superstition, and desperate for a simple solution to complex problems.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But surely you see the connection? No light, then thieves. It is the only logical conclusion!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Hargrove to invest in better locks and a night watch rather than just buying brighter bulbs, unlocking the 'Security Upgrade' quest line.

scenario.context: In the Town Square of Veridia, a heated debate erupts between two factions regarding the nature of the Crimson Plague. One group demands strict quarantine, while the other insists on normalcy to save the harvest season.
scenario.text: Some people say that the coronavirus is dangerous. Others say that it is not dangerous. That must mean that some coronavirus vaccinations are fine while others are not.
scenario.speaker_context: The speaker, a distressed merchant named Elian, ignores the medical data presented by the town healer. Instead, he argues that because the situation is confusing and the stakes (life vs. economy) are high, the truth must be a compromise, implying the validity of the vaccine depends on the desirability of the outcome rather than biological efficacy.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a factual claim (or the validity of a solution) should be accepted or rejected based on whether the consequences are desirable, rather than on evidence.
structure.formal_form: Claim P has mixed or undesirable consequences. Therefore, the truth of P (or the validity of solutions derived from P) is conditional or false.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a scientific fact (like the danger of a virus) and the efficacy of a treatment (vaccine) are independent of human desires, economic outcomes, or the existence of opposing opinions. Wishing for a middle ground does not make it biologically real.
structure.counterpoint: It is reasonable to weigh the consequences when making policy decisions (e.g., how strictly to enforce quarantine), but consequences cannot determine whether the virus is actually dangerous or whether the vaccine works.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elian suggests the vaccine's validity depends on the disagreement and the stakes. Does the danger of the virus change based on what people want to happen?

rubric.description: Agrees with Elian; believes the confusion and high stakes mean the truth must be a mix of both sides.
Feels something is off about ignoring the healer's data but cannot explain why the conclusion doesn't follow.
Notices Elian is focusing on the disagreement and the stakes rather than the medical evidence.
Identifies that Elian is rejecting a clear factual reality because the consequences of accepting it are difficult or disputed.
Explicitly names the Appeal to Consequences (or Appeal to Desire), noting that biological facts are objective and not subject to compromise based on outcomes.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone agreed the plague wasn't dangerous, would that suddenly make it safe? Or does the danger exist regardless of our opinion?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: How can we address Elian's fear about the harvest without denying the medical reality of the plague?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, pragmatic, deeply concerned with community survival and economic stability, prone to wishful thinking.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: We can't afford for the healer to be right! If the plague is that bad, we lose everything. There has to be a middle ground where some vaccines work and some don't, so we don't have to shut down the whole town!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present objective data (e.g., infection rates, lab results) to separate the factual reality of the plague from the policy decision of how to handle the harvest, calming Elian by addressing his fears without validating his flawed logic.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling cafeteria of the Academy of Reason just before midterms. A nervous student named Leo is surrounded by a pile of empty candy wrappers and soda cans, trying to convince a group of freshmen to adopt his 'study strategy.'
scenario.text: Leo slams his hand on the table, pointing triumphantly at his history test which bears a large 'A'. 'Listen up! Eating five candy bars and drinking two sodas right before a test is the secret. I did exactly that this morning, and look—I got an A on my history test! It's the sugar rush that unlocks your brain. If you want good grades, you have to copy my snack routine.'
scenario.speaker_context: Leo is a well-meaning but logically flawed student who has confused temporal succession with causation. He performed an action (eating sugar) and observed a positive outcome (getting an A), assuming the former caused the latter. He ignores alternative explanations such as his prior studying, the ease of the test, or natural ability.

structure.pattern_description: Leo observes that event B (getting an A) followed event A (eating candy and soda) and concludes that A caused B. This is the classic 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' error. He fails to consider that the correlation might be coincidental or that a third factor (like hours spent studying beforehand) was the actual cause of the good grade.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred. Event B occurred after A. Therefore, A caused B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal sequence does not prove causation. Just because the sugar intake happened before the good grade does not mean it produced the grade. Leo has not ruled out coincidence, reverse causation (unlikely here), or common causes (e.g., a student who studies hard might also treat themselves to candy).
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one would need a controlled experiment where students with similar study habits are split into groups: one eats candy, one does not. If the candy group consistently outperforms the non-candy group, only then could a causal link be suggested. Anecdotal evidence of a single instance is insufficient.

assessment.identification_prompt: Leo claims his sugar rush caused his A grade. Identify the logical flaw in his reasoning and explain why his conclusion might be wrong despite the test result.

rubric.description: The player accepts Leo's logic as true or fails to identify any flaw.
The player suspects something is wrong but cannot articulate why, or suggests sugar is bad for health rather than addressing the logic.
The player identifies that one event following another doesn't prove causation but offers no alternative explanation.
The player correctly identifies the post hoc fallacy and suggests that studying or test difficulty might be the real cause.
The player fully deconstructs the fallacy, explains the difference between correlation/temporal sequence and causation, and proposes how one could actually test Leo's hypothesis.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if you wore your lucky socks and then it rained, did your socks cause the rain? What else could have led to Leo's good grade besides the candy?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because the candy came first doesn't mean it caused the success. Leo likely got the A because he studied, not because of the sugar. Don't let coincidence trick you into bad habits!

game_hooks.npc_personality: Energetic, superstitious, confident but misguided. Leo speaks quickly and uses absolute terms like 'undeniable' and 'secret.'
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's simple science! Sugar equals smarts! Why else would I have aced it?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Leo to try taking the next test without candy but with the same amount of study time to see if the result holds, thereby teaching him about controlled variables.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Oakhaven, a street performer named Jax is trying to sell a peculiar 'luck stone' to a crowd of onlookers.
scenario.text: Jax holds up a smooth grey stone and shouts, 'Don't just stand there! Everyone in this square is buying one! Look at the line! If this many people are spending their gold on it, it must work. You don't want to be the only fool without luck, do you? Join the crowd!'
scenario.speaker_context: Jax offers no proof of the stone's magical properties, relying entirely on the fact that a crowd has formed to validate his claim.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition is true or a product is effective solely because a large number of people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or action does not constitute evidence for its truth or efficacy. Crowds can be mistaken, manipulated, or acting on misinformation.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread consensus among experts after independent verification can be meaningful, mere popularity among a general crowd without evidence is not a valid argument.

assessment.identification_prompt: What actual evidence does Jax provide that the stone brings luck? Is the size of the crowd a valid reason to buy it?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument; believes the stone must work because so many people are buying it.
Feels unsure about the logic but cannot explain why the crowd's behavior isn't proof.
Recognizes that Jax hasn't proven the stone works but fails to identify the specific flaw of using popularity as evidence.
Identifies that Jax uses the number of buyers as the sole evidence and explains that popularity does not equal truth.
Names the bandwagon fallacy, explains why popularity is not evidence, notes the social pressure tactic, and distinguishes between crowd behavior and factual proof.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in the village suddenly believed the sky was green, would that actually make the sky green?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing it' might be useful information, even if it doesn't prove something is true?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, fast-talking huckster who feeds off crowd energy and uses FOMO (fear of missing out) to drive sales.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look at that line! Do you think all these folks are wrong? Get yours before they're gone!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player points out that a crowd can be wrong, causing the bystanders to hesitate and disperse, revealing Jax's scam.

scenario.context: The player encounters a nervous student named Leo pacing outside the Registrar's office in the Academy of Reason. He is muttering to himself, visibly stressed about course selection.
scenario.text: Leo wrings his hands and says, 'If I don't take this A.P. class, then I won't do well on the exam. If I don't do well on the A.P. exam, then I can't get into a good college. If I can't get into a good college, then I'll never get a good job. If I can't get a good job, then I'm going to have to live in my parents' basement forever. Guess I'll sign up for the A.P. class.'
scenario.speaker_context: Leo is constructing a slippery slope argument where each step assumes a catastrophic and inevitable outcome from a single event (not taking one class). While the original label was 'faulty generalization', in this specific chain, the error is treating a possible negative outcome as a guaranteed universal truth for his entire future based on a single variable, effectively generalizing a worst-case scenario to the only possible reality.

structure.pattern_description: Leo assumes that a single negative event (not taking the class) will inevitably lead to a chain of extreme negative consequences ending in living in a basement. He generalizes from the possibility of failure to the certainty of a lifetime disaster, ignoring all intermediate possibilities, mitigating factors, and alternative paths to success.
structure.formal_form: Event A might lead to Event B. Event B might lead to Event C... Event Y leads to Catastrophe Z. Therefore, Event A will definitely lead to Catastrophe Z.
structure.why_wrong: The argument fails because it treats a chain of probabilistic events as a deterministic certainty. It ignores the fact that one can do well on an exam without the specific A.P. class, get into a good college without that specific exam score, or find a good job through other means. The sample size of 'one missing class' is insufficient to guarantee the 'lifetime of failure' conclusion.
structure.counterpoint: Planning for the future is rational, but assuming a single decision dictates your entire life trajectory is a hasty generalization of cause and effect. Most life outcomes are determined by hundreds of variables, not just one class.

assessment.identification_prompt: Leo believes that skipping one specific class guarantees he will end up living in his parents' basement forever. Is this conclusion supported by the evidence he provided?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Leo and signs him up for the class immediately to avoid the inevitable doom.
Player feels Leo is being too dramatic but cannot explain exactly where the logic breaks down.
Player identifies that not every step in the chain is guaranteed to happen.
Player explains that Leo is generalizing a worst-case scenario as the only outcome, ignoring alternative paths to success at each step.
Player fully deconstructs the slippery slope as a hasty generalization of causality, noting that one variable (the class) cannot determine a complex life outcome (career/housing) with 100% certainty.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: have you ever known someone who didn't take an A.P. class but still succeeded in life? Does one decision really control everything?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Leo is jumping to a massive conclusion based on a fragile chain of assumptions. One class does not define an entire lifetime.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, catastrophic thinker, prone to panic spirals.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's all over if I miss this one step! The dominoes are already falling!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player helps Leo identify the flaw in his chain reaction, reducing his anxiety and allowing him to make a rational choice about the class based on interest rather than fear.

scenario.context: The player visits the infirmary in the village of Oakhaven. A weary healer named Elara is reviewing a patient's chart with a look of confusion mixed with relief.
scenario.text: You contracted a severe cold two nights ago, yet last night you stayed up incredibly late studying by candlelight. Miraculously, you are no longer sick this morning. Therefore, your recovery must be because you stayed up really late last night.
scenario.speaker_context: Elara is a kind but logically flawed healer who often attributes recovery to the last action taken before symptoms vanish, ignoring the natural timeline of illnesses.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker observes that event B (recovery) occurred after event A (staying up late) and concludes that A caused B. This ignores the natural course of the illness, which likely would have resolved around this time regardless of the player's sleep schedule. It mistakes temporal sequence for causal connection.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, Event A caused Event B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession does not imply causation. Colds typically run a course of a few days; the recovery likely coincided with the expected end of the illness rather than being caused by sleep deprivation, which usually hinders recovery.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one must rule out coincidence and alternative explanations (like the natural immune response). A valid causal claim requires evidence that the effect would not have happened without the cause, or a known mechanism linking them. Here, the mechanism (staying up late curing a cold) is biologically implausible.

assessment.identification_prompt: Identify the logical error in Elara's conclusion about the cause of your recovery.

rubric.description: Fails to identify any logical error; accepts the conclusion that staying up late cured the cold.
Identifies that the reasoning seems flawed but cannot name the specific type of error or explain why.
Notes that correlation does not equal causation but does not explicitly address the timeline or natural recovery.
Correctly identifies the post hoc fallacy and explains that the recovery was likely due to the natural course of the illness, not the lack of sleep.

Provides a comprehensive analysis identifying the post hoc fallacy, explaining the ignorence of the illness timeline, and noting that sleep deprivation typically worsens health, making the causal claim doubly suspect.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider: If you had gone to bed early, would the cold have lasted longer? Or do colds usually go away on their own after a few days?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Just because the recovery happened after staying up late doesn't mean it happened *because* of it. This is a classic 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' error.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Well-meaning but superstitious; relies on anecdotal evidence rather than medical science.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's a miracle! The sleepless cure works! We must tell the whole village to stay awake when they are ill!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Elara to record the natural duration of colds in her logbook to see the pattern, preventing her from prescribing 'sleeplessness' to future patients.

scenario.context: The player is inspecting a row of carriages at the Grand Stable when a nervous traveler named Elian rushes over, pointing at a specific blue sedan.
scenario.text: Elian gestures frantically at the vehicle. 'Do not buy that type of car! It is poorly made and a waste of gold. A friend of mine owns one, and it continually gives him trouble. Therefore, every single one of those cars is a lemon.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elian is anxious about making a bad purchase. He has heard one negative anecdote from a single friend regarding one specific car and has extrapolated this to condemn the entire manufacturing line of that car model.

structure.pattern_description: Elian concludes that an entire class of objects (all cars of a specific type) possesses a negative quality (poorly made) based on a sample size of exactly one instance (his friend's car). This ignores statistical probability, manufacturing variances, and the possibility that the friend's car is an outlier or poorly maintained.
structure.formal_form: Instance x is a member of Population P. Instance x has Property Q (defect). Therefore, all members of Population P have Property Q.
structure.why_wrong: A sample size of one is statistically insufficient to characterize a mass-produced population. One bad experience does not prove a universal rule; it only proves that at least one defective unit exists. The argument fails to account for the vast number of functioning units of that car type likely in existence.
structure.counterpoint: Generalizations are useful heuristics when based on large, random samples. If Elian had surveyed 1,000 owners and 900 reported failures, his conclusion would be inductively strong. The fallacy lies strictly in the inadequacy of the sample size relative to the scope of the conclusion.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elian claims all cars of a certain type are defective because his friend's one car has problems. Is his conclusion logically supported by his evidence?

rubric.description: Player accepts Elian's warning as absolute truth and refuses to consider the car type.
Player feels unsure but cannot explain why one friend's experience might not apply to all cars.
Player suspects Elian is exaggerating but struggles to name the logical error or define the sample size issue.
Player identifies that one example is too small to judge the whole group and labels it a hasty generalization.

Player fully articulates that a sample of one cannot represent a mass-produced population, explains the difference between an outlier and a trend, and suggests seeking broader data (e.g., consumer reports) before deciding.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Elian nods vigorously. 'Exactly! Better safe than sorry. I'll stick to walking.' (The player misses a potentially good purchase due to fear based on insufficient data).
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Elian pauses, scratching his head. 'Well... I suppose Jim does tend to be rough on his vehicles. Maybe it's just his specific car, not the whole brand. Thanks for keeping me from panicking.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, risk-averse, prone to listening to rumors over data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I heard one bad story and now I'm terrified of the whole category!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Elian to check the 'Merchant's Guild Reliability Scroll' (a game item representing statistical data) which shows the car model has a 98% satisfaction rate.

scenario.context: In the Grand Hall of the University of Aethelgard, the Board of Trustees has gathered to review the annual budget. Autumn, the head librarian, stands before them with a grim expression, holding a ledger showing rising book costs.
scenario.text: Autumn addresses the board: "We must raise tuition to cover the cost of new books. Otherwise, the library will be forced to close. There is no other way."
scenario.speaker_context: Autumn, a passionate but stressed librarian who believes she is protecting the institution by presenting an urgent crisis.

structure.pattern_description: A disjunction is presented as exhaustive when it is not. Autumn forces a choice between raising tuition or closing the library, ignoring other viable funding sources or cost-saving measures.
structure.formal_form: A v B, ~A, therefore B. But the real situation is A v B v C v D..., so ~A does not entail B.
structure.why_wrong: Autumn presents only two options — raise tuition or close the library — but the disjunction does not exhaust the relevant space. Alternatives include seeking grants, launching a fundraising campaign, reducing administrative costs, purchasing fewer but higher-quality books, or utilizing digital resources.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or is a false dichotomy. Sometimes the options genuinely are exhaustive. The critical question is whether the disjunction covers the full space of relevant possibilities.

assessment.identification_prompt: Autumn claims the library must either raise tuition or close. What is flawed about this framing?

rubric.description: Accepts the framing as true or responds only with sympathy for the library.
Senses something is off or that there might be other ways, but cannot articulate specific alternatives.
Identifies at least one other option (e.g., fundraising) but does not connect it to the logical structure of the argument.
Names the false dichotomy and provides at least one concrete alternative to show the choice is not exhaustive.

Explains that the disjunction is not exhaustive, names the fallacy, offers multiple specific alternatives, and notes that disjunctive syllogism only works when the initial 'either/or' covers all possible cases.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Autumn gave you exactly two options. Are those really the only two things the university could do? Try to think of a third possibility for funding.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Under what conditions would an either/or framing actually be legitimate? Can you think of a scenario where raising tuition or closing really are the only two options?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest and slightly dramatic; tends to catastrophize when under pressure to make her point heard.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The ledgers don't lie, adventurer! If the tuition stays flat, the doors lock forever. It's simple math!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully identifies a third option (e.g., 'What about the Alumni Endowment Fund?'), causing Autumn to realize her panic blinded her to existing resources. She thanks the player and revises her proposal to the Board.

scenario.context: In the war room of the Capital, the High Chancellor addresses the Council of Elders. The treasury is nearly empty, and a proposal to subsidize the failing Royal Carriage Guild (the 'big automakers' of this realm) is on the table. Critics argue the funds should go to food relief instead.
scenario.text: The High Chancellor slams his hand on the map: 'If we do not bail out the Royal Carriage Guild, the entire economy of the Kingdom will collapse into dust! Our merchants will starve, our roads will fall silent, and chaos will reign. Therefore, we must immediately release the gold to the Guild.'
scenario.speaker_context: The Chancellor bypasses economic data or alternative solutions, relying entirely on the terrifying image of total societal collapse to force agreement.

structure.pattern_description: Using fear of a catastrophic outcome (economic collapse) to compel acceptance of a specific action without providing evidence that the action will prevent the outcome or that no other options exist.
structure.formal_form: Claim P (we must bail out the Guild) is supported by evoking Emotion E (fear of collapse). Agent implies P is true solely because not-P leads to E.
structure.why_wrong: The statement asserts a conditional disaster ('If we don't... collapse') as fact without evidence. It substitutes the fear of the consequence for a logical proof that the bailout is the necessary or only solution. It ignores whether the Guild is actually salvageable or if the economy depends on them.
structure.counterpoint: Fear is a valid motivator for urgency, but it does not validate the causal link between 'no bailout' and 'total collapse,' nor does it prove the bailout will work.

assessment.identification_prompt: The Chancellor paints a scary picture of the future. But does he provide any evidence that the economy will actually collapse without this specific bailout, or that the bailout will stop it?

rubric.description: Agrees with the Chancellor immediately because the idea of economic collapse is too frightening to ignore.
Feels the argument is strong due to the high stakes but senses something is missing regarding the actual plan.
Notices the Chancellor didn't offer data or alternatives, only a scary prediction.
Identifies that the argument relies on fear (appeal to emotion/fear) rather than economic evidence.
Explicitly names the fallacy, explains that the conditional claim ('collapse') is unsubstantiated, and notes that fear is being used to bypass critical evaluation of the policy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine the Guild is actually inefficient and draining resources. Would giving them more gold still prevent collapse, or might it make things worse? Does the fear of collapse prove the Guild deserves saving?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. The Chancellor is using the fear of 'chaos' to shut down debate. A logical argument would require data on the Guild's impact and a projection of outcomes with and without the bailout.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Authoritarian, dramatic, prone to hyperbole, prioritizes order over nuance.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Do you wish to see the markets burn? Do you want the people starving in the streets? Then sign the decree!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player requests an audit of the Guild's finances before voting, refusing to be swayed by the hypothetical disaster scenario.

scenario.context: In the neon-lit plaza of Neo-Veridia, a holographic billboard flickers to life featuring a charismatic sales avatar standing next to the latest Samsung Galaxy model.
scenario.text: The avatar gestures to a scrolling ticker of satisfied customers: 'Look at this! Everyone who has bought the newest Samsung Galaxy loves it! Millions of users can't be wrong. Join the crowd and get yours today before you're the only one left out!'
scenario.speaker_context: The sales avatar relies entirely on the volume of existing buyers to prove the phone's quality, offering no technical specifications or independent reviews.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or a product must be good simply because a large number of people believe it or have purchased it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or product does not constitute evidence of its truth or quality. Mass adoption can be driven by marketing, social pressure, or trends rather than factual merit.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate reliability (e.g., industry standards), it is only valid if the adopters are independent experts verifying the claim, not just consumers following a trend.

assessment.identification_prompt: What specific evidence does the avatar provide about the phone's performance? Is the number of buyers a valid reason to think the phone is good?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument; assumes that because millions bought it, the phone must be excellent.
Feels uncertain but cannot articulate why popularity is not proof of quality.
Notices the lack of technical details but fails to identify the 'everyone is doing it' logic as the core flaw.
Identifies that the speaker uses the number of buyers as the sole evidence and explains that popularity does not equal quality.
Explicitly names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains the distinction between popularity and evidence, and notes the potential role of social pressure in the advertisement.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in the city suddenly believed that drinking battery acid was healthy, would that make it true?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a scenario where knowing 'many people do X' actually is a good reason for you to do X as well?

game_hooks.npc_personality: High-energy, fast-talking holographic salesbot who thrives on FOMO (fear of missing out) and crowd metrics.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't be the odd one out! The data shows 99% satisfaction! Join the movement!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select a dialogue option pointing out that 'popularity isn't proof' to disable the hologram's persuasive field and reveal the phone's actual (mediocre) stats.

scenario.context: In the industrial district of Neo-Veridia, a town hall meeting is underway to debate new emissions regulations. A factory owner argues against limiting pollutants.
scenario.text: I think that businesses should not have to limit the amount of pollutants they release into the atmosphere because Rush Limbaugh says that there is no real evidence for industrial pollutants causing the Greenhouse Effect.
scenario.speaker_context: The speaker is a factory owner with no scientific background. They are citing Rush Limbaugh, a famous radio personality and political commentator, as the sole authority on climate science, despite Limbaugh not being a climatologist or environmental scientist.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker rejects scientific consensus on industrial pollution based solely on the opinion of a media personality who lacks expertise in atmospheric science.
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is famous/influential. A is not an expert in domain D (where P belongs). Therefore P is true.
structure.why_wrong: Fame or influence in one domain (political commentary) does not confer expertise in another (climate science). The truth of a scientific claim depends on evidence and expert consensus within that specific field, not on the opinions of non-experts.
structure.counterpoint: Citing an authority is valid only when the authority is a recognized expert in the specific field relevant to the claim. If a climatologist made this statement based on data, it would be a valid appeal to expertise.

assessment.identification_prompt: The factory owner cites a famous name to support their claim. Is this person an expert in the field of environmental science?

rubric.description: Accepts the claim because the cited person is famous or well-known.
Suspects the argument might be weak but cannot identify why the source is problematic.
Identifies that the cited person is a commentator, not a scientist, but fails to connect this to the validity of the claim.
Explains that the cited person lacks specific expertise in climate science, making their opinion insufficient evidence.
Clearly identifies the Appeal to Irrelevant Authority fallacy, distinguishes between fame and expertise, and explains that scientific claims require evidence from qualified specialists.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If a famous actor said that gravity doesn't exist, would that make it true? Why is their opinion on physics different from their opinion on acting?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Imagine if the factory owner had cited a leading climatologist instead. How would that change the strength of their argument, and what other evidence would we still need to see?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive and pragmatic; prioritizes profit and relies on popular media voices rather than academic research.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look, if Rush Limbaugh says the science isn't settled, why should I spend millions filtering smoke? He's got millions of listeners; he can't be wrong.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must present a credential check or a counter-statement from an actual atmospheric scientist to expose the domain mismatch.

scenario.context: In the neon-lit interrogation room of Sector 4, the player confronts Councilor Vane regarding allegations that he diverted public funds to hire high-end companions. When presented with bank transfer records, Vane attempts to dismiss the ethical breach.
scenario.text: I don't see what's wrong with engaging the services of a professional escort. After the trauma of the riots, the sleepless nights managing the crisis, and the sheer loneliness of this office, isn't it human to seek comfort? To deny me this small solace is cruel.
scenario.speaker_context: Vane acknowledges the action but reframes the ethical violation as a tragic necessity born of suffering, attempting to make the accuser feel guilty for questioning his coping mechanisms rather than addressing the misuse of funds.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker substitutes an emotional plea (pity for their stress/loneliness) for a logical defense of the action. They imply that because they are suffering, the rules regarding fund misappropriation should not apply or that criticizing them is an act of cruelty.
structure.formal_form: Action A is under scrutiny for violating Rule R. Agent evokes Emotion E (pity/sympathy) regarding their personal state. Agent implies A is acceptable or criticism is invalid because of E.
structure.why_wrong: The speaker's emotional state (loneliness, stress) does not change the factual nature of the action (misuse of public funds) nor does it logically negate the rule against it. The appeal targets the accuser's feelings to bypass the logical evaluation of the act.
structure.counterpoint: While stress is a valid human experience and may explain why someone made a poor choice, it does not serve as a logical justification that makes the choice itself correct or exempt from consequences.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane sounds exhausted and sympathetic. But does his description of his own suffering actually explain why using public money for escorts is acceptable?

rubric.description: Feels sorry for Vane and agrees that criticizing him is cruel; drops the inquiry.
Feels conflicted; acknowledges the funds issue but thinks his stress makes it less wrong.
Notices Vane didn't address the money trail but struggles to articulate why his feelings are irrelevant to the rule.
Identifies that Vane is using his personal suffering to deflect from the specific accusation of fund misuse.
Explicitly names the appeal to emotion/pity, separates the explanatory factor (stress) from the justificatory factor (legality/ethics), and maintains focus on the evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside how tired or lonely Vane feels for a moment. Regardless of his emotions, does the bank transfer show public money being used for private services?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. His suffering might explain his behavior, but it doesn't justify the misuse of funds. The logical link between 'I am sad' and 'This transaction is legal' is missing.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, melodramatic, prone to playing the victim to manipulate social dynamics.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think I don't know the rules? I live in a nightmare! How can you stand there with your cold logic while I'm drowning?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must acknowledge Vane's stress without accepting it as a defense, then pivot back to the ledger evidence to force a confession or administrative penalty.

scenario.context: In the bustling market of Portmere, a debate erupts over the mechanics of the new steam-carriages. A crowd gathers around a famous celebrity doctor known for her cosmetic surgeries.
scenario.text: Dra. Vicky Belo addresses the concerned citizens: 'Do not worry about the engine designs. I have examined them, and I say that all kinds of cars need fuel to start. Since I am a renowned doctor, my word on how these machines work is final.'
scenario.speaker_context: Dra. Vicky Belo is a celebrated cosmetic surgeon and celebrity. While an authority in dermatology and aesthetics, she has no stated expertise in mechanical engineering or automotive physics.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker appeals to Dra. Vicky Belo's authority as a famous doctor to settle a factual question about automotive mechanics, a field outside her expertise.
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is expert in domain D. P is in domain D*. Therefore P is true. (But D ≠ D*.)
structure.why_wrong: An authority's prestige in one field (medicine/cosmetics) does not grant them automatic expertise in an unrelated field (mechanical engineering). The truth of the claim depends on mechanical facts, not the speaker's fame.
structure.counterpoint: Citing an authority is valid when the authority is an expert in the specific domain relevant to the claim. If a mechanical engineer made this statement, it would be a strong argument, not a fallacy.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dra. Vicky Belo is a famous doctor, but what exactly is she a doctor of? Does that make her an expert on how car engines start?

rubric.description: Accepts the claim solely because Dra. Vicky Belo is a famous doctor.
Feels unsure but cannot explain why her medical fame might not apply to cars.
Notices she is a cosmetic surgeon, not a mechanic, but struggles to articulate why the distinction invalidates the argument.
Identifies that her expertise is in medicine, not automotive engineering, making her opinion irrelevant to the mechanical claim.
Names the appeal to irrelevant authority, explains the domain mismatch between cosmetics and mechanics, and clarifies that expertise is not transferable across unrelated fields.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Dra. Vicky Belo told you how to perform heart surgery, would you trust her? Now she is telling you how an engine works. Is the type of knowledge the same?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Imagine the town's only mechanic is unavailable, and Dra. Vicky Belo has read a manual on cars. Does her general intelligence make her opinion equal to that of a certified engineer?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Glamorous, confident, and accustomed to being obeyed due to her celebrity status; she often conflates fame with omniscience.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Darling, I know everything about the human body, and machines are just bodies of metal! Trust me, I'm a doctor!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a credential from a mechanical engineer or a physics textbook to counter the doctor's claim and calm the worried citizens.

scenario.context: Inside the bustling 'Gear & Gadget' shop in the steampunk city of Cogsworth, the shop foreman is trying to convince the player character, a new shift manager, to approve an expensive operational change.
scenario.text: We surveyed all the customers in the store today and they all agreed that staying open 24 hours would be a great idea. We need to put together a 24-hour schedule as soon as possible.
scenario.speaker_context: The foreman relies entirely on the unanimous opinion of the current customer base as proof that the business model change is sound, ignoring costs, staffing logistics, or actual sales data.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a course of action must be correct or beneficial simply because a large number of people support it or agree with it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: Popularity is not evidence of truth or viability. Customers may want 24-hour service because it is convenient for them, but that does not mean it is profitable or operationally feasible for the store. The argument ignores critical factors like cost and logistics.
structure.counterpoint: While customer satisfaction is important, widespread desire for a service does not automatically equate to business success. Independent analysis of costs versus revenue is required, not just a headcount of opinions.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the fact that every customer asked wants the store open 24 hours prove that the store should actually do it? What evidence is missing?

rubric.description: Agrees with the foreman; assumes that if all customers want it, it must be the right business decision.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why customer opinion alone is insufficient evidence.
Notes that other factors like cost matter but fails to identify the specific logical error of equating popularity with validity.
Identifies that the foreman uses customer consensus as the sole proof and explains that popularity does not guarantee feasibility or profit.
Names the bandwagon fallacy, explains the difference between customer desire and business viability, and points out the lack of financial or logistical evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every customer asked for free items, would that prove the store should give everything away for free?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a scenario where popular opinion actually is a reliable indicator of the best course of action?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest, slightly overwhelmed foreman who trusts the crowd's voice above all else and fears missing out on potential business.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look, the people have spoken! We can't ignore the voice of the market. Let's get those night shifts scheduled!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must request a financial projection or staffing analysis instead of approving the schedule based solely on the survey results.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Oakhaven, a heated debate erupts over the safety of the new 'Spark-Berry' energy drink. A local merchant tries to shut down the argument by citing a famous figure.
scenario.text: John interrupts the crowd, pointing at a poster of a famous actor. 'Stop worrying! That famous actor agrees with me that drinking energy drinks are bad for you. If he says they're dangerous, then it must be true.'
scenario.speaker_context: John is a persuasive but logically loose merchant. The 'famous actor' he cites is renowned for dramatic roles and charity work, not for medical expertise, nutrition, or toxicology.

structure.pattern_description: John cites a famous actor's opinion to prove a medical/health claim about energy drinks, relying on the actor's fame rather than relevant expertise.
structure.formal_form: Person A (famous/authority in domain X) says P. Therefore, P is true. (But P concerns domain Y, where A has no expertise.)
structure.why_wrong: Fame or authority in one field (acting) does not grant expertise in another (nutrition/medicine). The actor's opinion is no more reliable than a layperson's without evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Citing authority is valid when the person is a genuine expert in the specific field being discussed. If a board-certified toxicologist said the drinks were bad, that would be a strong argument, not a fallacy.

assessment.identification_prompt: John claims the actor's agreement settles the debate. What makes someone an expert on whether a drink is bad for your health, and does this actor fit that description?

rubric.description: Accepts the claim immediately because the person cited is famous.
Feels unsure but cannot explain why the actor's job matters.
Notices the actor is not a doctor but doesn't explain why that invalidates the argument.
Identifies that acting expertise does not transfer to medical or nutritional science.
Clearly names the 'Appeal to Irrelevant Authority,' explains the domain mismatch between acting and health science, and notes that evidence is needed instead of celebrity endorsement.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If that same actor told you how to fix a broken engine, would you trust him just because he's famous? Why is health different?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Now, imagine if the actor actually had a PhD in Biochemistry. Would your objection still hold, or would the argument become stronger?

game_hooks.npc_personality: John is charismatic and relies on social proof and celebrity culture to win arguments, often skipping actual evidence.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But everyone knows him! He's on every poster in the capital! Are you saying he's a liar?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must guide John to realize that while the actor might be right, his fame isn't the *reason* the drink is bad. John then agrees to look for a statement from a local healer or alchemist instead.

scenario.context: In the cozy living room of the player's childhood home, Grandma has just presented a hand-knitted sweater featuring a large, garish kitty-cat design. The player hesitates to wear it for the upcoming family holiday photo, knowing it clashes with their outfit.
scenario.text: Grandma smiles hopefully, holding up the sweater: 'I know you don't like the kitty-cat sweater that I knitted for you, but I worked so hard on it, staying up late every night for a week. It will make me so happy to see you wear it in the family holiday photo.'
scenario.speaker_context: Grandma is not arguing that the sweater looks good or fits well; she is bypassing the aesthetic critique entirely by leveraging the player's guilt and desire to make her happy.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting an emotional response (guilt, pity, affection) in place of addressing the actual merit of the claim. The speaker ignores the objective quality of the sweater to focus on the effort expended and the emotional consequence of refusal.
structure.formal_form: Claim P (You should wear the sweater) is challenged by Evidence E (It looks bad/uncomfortable). Agent evokes Emotion F (Guilt over effort, desire to please). Agent implies E should be disregarded because of F.
structure.why_wrong: The amount of effort put into making the sweater or the happiness derived from wearing it does not change the fact that the sweater may be ugly or uncomfortable. The emotional factors are irrelevant to the truth of the aesthetic judgment.
structure.counterpoint: While emotions matter in relationships, they do not validate factual claims. One can appreciate the effort (emotion) while still acknowledging the sweater is unappealing (fact).

assessment.identification_prompt: Grandma clearly put a lot of love into this gift. But does her hard work actually make the kitty-cat design look better, or is she trying to make you feel too guilty to say no?

rubric.description: Feels immediate guilt and agrees to wear the sweater, believing the effort makes the sweater good.
Feels conflicted; recognizes the sweater isn't great but feels the emotional argument is a valid reason to wear it.
Notices that Grandma didn't address whether the sweater looks good, but struggles to articulate why the emotion is a logical fallacy.
Identifies that Grandma is using guilt and her own happiness to deflect from the actual issue of the sweater's appearance.
