game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select the dialogue option 'Your reason is circular; you assume what you need to prove' to shatter the guardian's logical shield and open the gate.

scenario.context: In the bustling capital of Veridia, the player character attends a town hall meeting regarding the kingdom's welfare. A young scholar named Elara proposes a policy update, but she is immediately interrupted by Lord Vane, a wealthy merchant known for his stinginess and sharp tongue.
scenario.text: Elara says: 'I think we should have an expanded social safety net for the poor in our country.' Lord Vane scoffs and replies: 'So, you think we should just throw money at lazy people who don't want to work and think they are entitled to be kept up by other people, right?'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara proposed a structured expansion of welfare support. Lord Vane recharacterized this as indiscriminately giving cash to lazy, entitled individuals who refuse to work, a much more extreme and negative position that Elara did not suggest.

structure.pattern_description: Lord Vane takes Elara's moderate proposal (expanded safety net) and distorts it into an extreme caricature (throwing money at lazy, entitled people). He then attacks this fabricated version rather than addressing the actual merits or logistics of the safety net.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P. Person B restates P as the distorted P*. Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position has been refuted, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: Vane's criticism targets a fabricated version of Elara's proposal. An 'expanded social safety net' implies structured aid, not necessarily unconditional cash handouts to those refusing work. His objections about laziness and entitlement are irrelevant to the actual proposal of a safety net.
structure.counterpoint: Elara could reply: 'I said safety net, not handouts for the lazy. A safety net helps those who cannot work or are between jobs; it does not reward refusing to work. Can we discuss the actual plan I proposed?'

assessment.identification_prompt: What is wrong with Lord Vane's response to Elara's proposal?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane or sees no problem with his response.
Player senses something is off or feels Vane is being mean, but cannot articulate the logical error.
Player notices that Vane changed or exaggerated Elara's proposal but does not clearly distinguish the original from the distortion.
Player identifies that Vane misrepresented Elara's argument (safety net became handouts for the lazy) and attacked the misrepresentation instead of the real proposal.
Player explicitly names the 'Straw Man' fallacy, explains how the specific attributes were distorted, and provides a corrected version of the argument.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at Elara's words versus Vane's words. Did Elara actually mention 'lazy people' or 'throwing money'? Or did Vane add those details himself?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct! Vane constructed a 'Straw Man' by exaggerating Elara's point to make it easier to attack. He ignored her actual argument about a safety net.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Lord Vane is arrogant, wealthy, and dismissive of the lower classes. He uses rhetorical tricks to shut down debate quickly.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't listen to this nonsense! She wants to drain our coffers for good-for-nothings!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select the dialogue option that points out the distortion, causing Vane to sputter and the crowd to murmur in support of Elara, unlocking the 'Debater' achievement.

scenario.context: In the sun-drenched courtyard of the Scholasticum, a novice scribe stands before the Great Stone Tablet, trying to convince a skeptical traveler of its divine origin.
scenario.text: The Bible is the Word of God because God tells us it is... in the Bible.
scenario.speaker_context: Scribe Elian, a devout but logically untrained novice who believes fervently in the text and cannot see that his proof relies on the very thing he is trying to prove.

structure.pattern_description: The conclusion—that the Bible is the Word of God—is supported by a premise that God says so within the Bible. This premise only holds true if one already accepts the conclusion that the Bible is indeed the Word of God.
structure.formal_form: P1: The Bible states that it is the Word of God. P2: What the Bible states is true (because it is the Word of God). C: Therefore, the Bible is the Word of God.
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes the truth of the conclusion in order to prove the conclusion. It offers no independent evidence; the reliability of the source (the Bible) is the very issue in dispute, so citing the source to prove its own reliability is logically circular.
structure.counterpoint: Not every reference to a text is circular. The fallacy occurs specifically when the text's authority is the point being debated, and the only evidence offered for that authority is the text's own claim.

assessment.identification_prompt: Scribe Elian seems very certain. Does his reasoning actually prove that the Bible is the Word of God to someone who isn't already convinced?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument as valid or objects only to the religious content without identifying the logical flaw.
Senses the argument is weak or unconvincing but cannot explain why.
Identifies that the argument is 'going in circles' or using the book to prove the book.
Names begging the question or circular reasoning and explains that the premise assumes the conclusion is already true.
Names the fallacy, explains the circularity clearly, and notes that the argument fails because it provides no independent support for the claim.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: How do we know what God says? Elian says we know because it's in the Bible. But how do we know the Bible is trustworthy? He says because God wrote it. Do you see the loop?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! You've spotted the circle. Elian is using the Bible's claim to prove the Bible's authority, which only works if you already believe the Bible is authoritative.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest, slightly defensive, and deeply faithful but logically naive. He gets flustered when his reasoning is challenged but means no harm.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But it says so right there in chapter one! If you don't trust the book, how can you trust anything?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must guide Elian to realize he needs external evidence (historical records, prophecy fulfillment, or archaeological finds) rather than self-referential claims to convince skeptics.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling market square of Oakhaven during a town hall meeting. A local merchant, Elias, has just presented a detailed plan to lower grain prices by importing from a neighboring valley, citing specific cost savings and transport logistics. Before the mayor can respond, a heckler from the back of the crowd shouts out.
scenario.text: He just says that because he's a Republican.
scenario.speaker_context: A vocal townsperson known for prioritizing party loyalty over policy details. They often dismiss opposing views based solely on the speaker's political affiliation rather than the argument's merit.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker dismisses Elias's proposal to lower grain prices solely by pointing out his political affiliation (Republican). They imply that his argument is invalid or biased simply because of his group membership, without addressing the actual data on costs, logistics, or savings presented.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P belongs to group G (which allegedly holds view Y). Therefore, X is false or should be dismissed.
structure.why_wrong: The truth or validity of an argument depends on the evidence and reasoning provided, not on the personal characteristics or affiliations of the person making it. Even if Elias is a Republican, his math regarding grain prices could still be correct. Dismissing the plan without checking the numbers is a failure of critical thinking.
structure.counterpoint: Political affiliation might be relevant if the argument relied entirely on 'trust me because of my party's values' rather than factual data. However, since Elias presented specific economic data, the affiliation is irrelevant to the accuracy of that data.

assessment.identification_prompt: The heckler seems very confident. But look closely: did they mention anything about the grain prices, the transport costs, or the math Elias showed? Or did they only talk about who Elias is?

rubric.description: Player agrees with the heckler, believing the argument is invalid because of Elias's party.
Player feels the heckler is being rude but cannot explain why the logic is flawed.
Player identifies that the heckler is attacking Elias's identity instead of his argument.
Player explains that political affiliation does not determine the factual accuracy of economic data.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, noting that the specific evidence (costs/logistics) was ignored entirely in favor of a label, and suggests evaluating the data independently.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a mathematician you disliked told you 2+2=4, would it suddenly become 5? Why does the label 'Republican' change the math on grain prices?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! The label tells us nothing about the truth of the claim. To make a good decision, the town needs to check the numbers, not the nametag.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Partisan, loud, relies on tribal signaling rather than analysis, easily swayed by group identity.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't listen to him! He's just one of *them*. You know what they always say!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to 'Analyze Data' (ignoring the heckler to review Elias's charts) or 'Challenge Fallacy' (pointing out the logical error to the crowd), gaining reputation for wisdom.

scenario.context: The player enters the dusty archives of the Royal Library, where Scholar Elara is presenting archaeological findings to a group of skeptical historians. She displays maps, pottery shards, and carbon-dating results suggesting a unified kingdom in the region during the 10th century BCE. A rival historian, Marcus, who favors a minimalist view of ancient history, steps forward to refute her claims.
scenario.text: Marcus crosses his arms and scoffs at the display of artifacts. 'We haven't found King David's tomb yet, so King David didn't really exist. This is just the fantasy of a credulous believer trying to force mythology into history. Elara is nothing but a dogmatic apologist pushing a religious agenda rather than doing real science. We should dismiss these 'findings' as wishful thinking.'
scenario.speaker_context: Marcus ignores the specific archaeological evidence Elara presented (pottery, carbon dating, settlement patterns). Instead, he focuses on one missing piece of evidence (the tomb) to make a definitive negative claim, and then attacks Elara's character by labeling her a 'credulous believer,' 'dogmatic apologist,' and someone pushing an 'agenda' to discredit her entire argument without engaging with the data.

structure.pattern_description: Marcus substitutes negative labels for substantive engagement. Rather than addressing the validity of the carbon dating, the significance of the pottery, or the settlement patterns, he attaches dismissive terms to Elara ('credulous believer,' 'dogmatic apologist') and her work ('fantasy,' 'wishful thinking'). These labels are designed to make the audience reject her conclusions based on perceived bias rather than evidentiary merit.
structure.formal_form: Person P presents argument X with evidence E. Critic attaches negative label L to P or X. Critic concludes X is false or should be rejected based on L, without engaging with E.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not arguments. Calling someone a 'dogmatic apologist' does not prove their carbon dating is incorrect or their interpretation of pottery shards is flawed. The absence of a specific artifact (the tomb) does not logically prove the non-existence of the person, especially when other evidence exists. The labels function as a substitute for analyzing the actual historical data.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to note if a researcher has a conflict of interest or a strong bias that might influence their methodology. However, the fallacy occurs when that bias is assumed to automatically invalidate their findings without examining the specific evidence they present.

assessment.identification_prompt: Marcus claims Elara's findings should be dismissed because she is a 'dogmatic apologist.' Does he explain why her specific evidence (like the carbon dating) is wrong, or does he just attack her identity?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Marcus, believing that lacking a tomb proves David didn't exist and that Elara's bias invalidates her work.
Player senses Marcus is being mean or unfair to Elara but cannot identify the logical error regarding the evidence.
Player identifies that Marcus is name-calling ('apologist', 'believer') but misses the connection to the missing tomb argument.
Player recognizes that Marcus uses labels to avoid discussing the actual archaeological evidence Elara presented.

Player fully articulates that Marcus commits the Name Calling fallacy by substituting character attacks for evidence analysis and incorrectly equates the absence of one specific artifact (the tomb) with total non-existence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if someone calls you a 'dreamer,' does that automatically make your math homework wrong? How does Marcus's insult relate to the actual pottery and dates Elara showed?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Marcus tries to win the debate by branding Elara with negative labels instead of refuting her data. Also, remember that 'absence of evidence is not evidence of absence'—just because we haven't found the tomb yet doesn't mean he never existed.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Marcus is arrogant, dismissive, and prides himself on being a 'hard-nosed realist,' often conflating cynicism with intelligence. He speaks quickly and uses scare quotes when referring to opposing views.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Oh, save your 'scientific' speeches for the true believers, Elara. We don't need more fairy tales dressed up as history.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that point out Marcus's failure to address the carbon dating and pottery evidence, forcing him to either concede the point or storm off in a huff, thereby validating Elara's research for the library records.

scenario.context: The player encounters a disgruntled clockwork automaton named Tick-Tock Tom in the guild hall, who is refusing to join any adventuring party.
scenario.text: Tick-Tock Tom whirs angrily, his gears grinding. 'Today late for ten minutes, tomorrow late for an hour, and then someday you will simply cease to show up. All adventurers are unreliable flakes; I have seen it happen twice, so it is the absolute rule for your entire kind.'
scenario.speaker_context: Tom has observed two instances of adventurers being late and has extrapolated this to a universal truth about all adventurers eventually abandoning their commitments, ignoring the vast majority of reliable heroes.

structure.pattern_description: Tom takes two specific instances of tardiness and constructs a slippery slope that ends in total abandonment, then applies this conclusion to every single adventurer. He assumes a small, unrepresentative sample (two late people) defines the behavior of the entire population (all adventurers).
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of X having property Q (where n is very small). Therefore, all members of group X have property Q (or will inevitably progress to extreme property Z).
structure.why_wrong: Two examples of lateness do not prove that all adventurers are unreliable, nor do they logically guarantee that lateness inevitably leads to never showing up. The sample size is insufficient to support a universal claim about a diverse group of people.
structure.counterpoint: While patterns can emerge from repeated observations, a valid generalization requires a representative and sufficiently large sample. Two data points are statistically insignificant for characterizing an entire profession.

assessment.identification_prompt: Tick-Tock Tom claims all adventurers are unreliable based on two instances of lateness. Is his conclusion logically sound?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Tom and avoids hiring adventurers.
Player feels Tom is being unfair but cannot explain the logical error.
Player notes that two people do not represent all adventurers.
Player identifies the hasty generalization and explains that the sample size is too small to predict future behavior for the whole group.

Player fully deconstructs the argument, identifying both the insufficient sample size and the flawed slippery slope assumption (that lateness inevitably leads to quitting), and suggests how to properly test reliability.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Tom shakes his head. 'See? You don't understand the pattern. Best to work alone.'
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Tom's gears slow down. 'Hmm. Perhaps my data set was... limited. I shall recalibrate my trust algorithms.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, literal-minded, and prone to over-calculating risks based on minimal data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Error: Reliability probability too low. Abort mission.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Tom to give a third chance by presenting evidence of reliable adventurers or explaining statistical significance.

scenario.context: The player stands in the muddy courtyard of the New Haven settlement. A group of settlers is gathered around a crude map, discussing a new proposal to organize a community recycling program to reduce waste and trade scrap metal for supplies. Elder Thorne, a traditionalist who distrusts change, steps forward to shut down the discussion before it begins.
scenario.text: Thorne crosses his arms and sneers at the map. 'We cannot approve of this recycling idea. It was thought of by a bunch of hippie communist weirdos. If people like that came up with it, you can bet it's bad for us.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elder Thorne, a respected but stubborn leader of the settlement who values tradition and views counter-cultural movements with deep suspicion.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne rejects the recycling proposal solely based on the perceived identity and political labels of its proponents ('hippie communist weirdos'), rather than addressing the merits of the idea itself, such as waste reduction or resource acquisition.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P has property Q (irrelevant to the truth of X). Therefore, X is false or should be rejected.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of an argument or idea depends on its evidence, logic, and potential outcomes, not on the characteristics of the people who proposed it. Even if the proponents are 'weirdos' or hold unpopular political views, the recycling idea could still be practical and beneficial. Thorne provides no actual reasons why the plan would fail.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if the argument relies on the person's authority or credibility as a witness. For example, if the argument was 'Trust this plan because these experts have 20 years of waste management experience,' then questioning their expertise would be valid. Here, the idea stands on its own utility, not the proponents' identity.

assessment.identification_prompt: Thorne seems very certain that the plan is bad. But look closely at his reasoning: does he explain why the recycling won't work, or does he just attack the people who suggested it?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne, believing the idea is bad simply because of who proposed it.
Player feels Thorne is being mean or unfair but cannot identify the logical error.
Player identifies that Thorne is attacking the people instead of the idea but struggles to explain why this matters.
Player clearly states that the source of an idea does not determine its truth or value, identifying the ad hominem fallacy.
Player articulates that the proposal must be evaluated on its own merits (e.g., cost, efficiency) regardless of the proponents' labels, and suggests specific criteria to test the idea.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: if a person you disliked suggested that fire burns, would that make fire safe to touch? The truth of a claim is separate from the person making it.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thorne is distracting everyone with insults. To make a real decision, the settlement needs to look at the data: how much scrap can we collect, and what can we trade it for?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Stubborn, xenophobic, relies on social pressure and tradition rather than data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't let those outsiders poison our minds with their strange ways!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to ignore Thorne's insult and present a small-scale trial of the recycling program to prove its value through results, bypassing the need to argue about the proponents.

scenario.context: The player enters the Sunlit Atrium of the Temple of Reason, where High Priestess Elara is debating a group of novice acolytes about the nature of ethical boundaries.
scenario.text: Elara gestures warmly to the gathering. 'There are so many experiences in the human realm that are wonderful. Sexual intimacy between two willing adults who love each other is wonderful. A therapist helping a client is wonderful. When the relationship between a therapist and client is so deep that it could be characterized as love, it's wonderful. When all these acts become part of one process between two people, it must be exceptionally wonderful. How could anyone condemn such a wonderfully human process as unethical?'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara observes that individual components (love, therapy, intimacy) are positive in isolation or specific contexts. She then incorrectly generalizes that combining these specific elements into a dual relationship (therapist-client romance) must therefore be universally positive and ethical, ignoring the specific power dynamics and professional constraints that make this combination harmful.

structure.pattern_description: Elara takes the positive value of isolated concepts (love, therapy, intimacy) and hastily generalizes that their combination in a specific, constrained context (therapist-client romance) must also be positive. She ignores the critical variable of professional power imbalance which changes the nature of the interaction entirely.
structure.formal_form: Component A is good. Component B is good. Component C is good. Therefore, the combination of A+B+C in context X is good.
structure.why_wrong: The fallacy lies in assuming that the sum of good parts always equals a good whole, regardless of context. In professional ethics, the combination of therapy and romance creates a conflict of interest and exploits power differentials, rendering the act unethical despite the individual components being virtuous elsewhere. The sample of 'good things' does not support the conclusion about this specific complex scenario.
structure.counterpoint: While it is true that love and healing are good, ethical frameworks exist precisely because certain combinations of good things can create harm when power dynamics are unequal. Generalizing from the virtue of the parts to the virtue of the whole fails here.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elara argues that because love, therapy, and intimacy are individually wonderful, combining them in a therapist-client relationship must be wonderful and ethical. Is her conclusion justified by the goodness of the individual parts?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Elara, believing that combining good things always results in a better outcome.
Player feels uneasy about the conclusion but cannot explain why the logic is flawed.
Player identifies that the context matters, noting that therapy has rules, but does not explicitly name the generalization error.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that the positive traits of the components do not guarantee the ethical status of their combination in a power-imbalanced context.

Player provides a comprehensive critique: identifies the hasty generalization, explains the fallacy of composition involved, and articulates how professional boundaries create a unique context where the generalization fails.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider if mixing two safe chemicals always results in a safe mixture. Does the context of the combination change the outcome?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Just because ingredients are nutritious doesn't mean every recipe made from them is healthy, especially if the 'cooking method' involves a breach of trust.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elara is compassionate and idealistic, believing deeply in the purity of human connection, but she sometimes overlooks structural complexities in favor of emotional truths.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Surely, when two souls connect so deeply, the rules written by distant councils cannot apply? Love is the highest law.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must guide Elara to see that protecting the vulnerable (the client) requires maintaining boundaries, even when feelings are genuine, thereby refining her understanding of ethics beyond simple generalizations.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling market square of Oakhaven during a town hall meeting. Candidate Elara Vance has just finished presenting a detailed economic plan to raise the minimum wage, citing inflation data and local cost-of-living statistics. Before the player can ask a clarifying question, her opponent, Merchant Lord Silas, steps forward to address the crowd.
scenario.text: Silas sneers at the crowd. 'That candidate wants to raise the minimum wage, but they aren't even smart enough to run a business. Why would we trust their economic plans when they've never signed a payroll in their life?'
scenario.speaker_context: Merchant Lord Silas, a wealthy and influential business owner in Oakhaven. He is known for his sharp tongue and tendency to dismiss opponents based on their lack of commercial experience rather than engaging with their policy proposals.

structure.pattern_description: Silas attacks Candidate Vance's personal background (lack of business ownership) to dismiss her argument about raising the minimum wage. He ignores the actual evidence she presented regarding inflation and cost of living, implying that her lack of specific experience automatically invalidates her policy proposal.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X (raise minimum wage). Person P has property Q (has not run a business). Therefore, claim X is false or should be dismissed.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of an argument depends on the evidence and logic supporting it, not the personal characteristics or history of the person making it. A person does not need to own a business to understand economic principles or analyze data regarding wages and inflation. Silas provides no counter-evidence to Vance's data.
structure.counterpoint: Personal experience can be relevant if the argument explicitly relies on it as proof (e.g., 'As a business owner for 20 years, I know this will fail'). However, Vance argued based on economic data, not her personal resume, so her lack of business ownership is irrelevant to the truth of her claims.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas is questioning Vance's competence based on her resume. But look closely: did he address any of the numbers or facts Vance just shared about inflation and living costs?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Silas, believing that only business owners can understand wage policies.
Player feels Silas is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why his logic is flawed.
Player identifies that Silas is attacking Vance personally instead of her argument.
Player explains that Vance's lack of business experience does not invalidate the economic data she presented.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, noting that the truth of the claim is independent of the claimant's profession, and demands evidence against the specific data points raised.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: Can a doctor diagnose an illness without having been sick themselves? Can an economist study poverty without being poor? Does Silas actually prove Vance's numbers are wrong?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Silas tried to distract the crowd by attacking Vance's background. He completely ignored the inflation data and cost-of-living stats she presented. A good argument stands on its own evidence, not the speaker's job title.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Arrogant, dismissive, pragmatic to a fault, believes money equals wisdom.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think book smarts beat street smarts? Come back when you've balanced a ledger, kid.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player exposes the fallacy, causing the crowd to murmur in agreement with Vance and demand Silas address the actual numbers, lowering Silas's influence stat.

scenario.context: In the village of Oakhaven, a heated debate arises in the town square regarding the best way to discipline unruly children. Some parents advocate for corporal punishment, while others seek alternative methods.
scenario.text: A weary father steps forward and declares: 'My uncle is a master mechanic, and he says you shouldn't spank children. He says it's ineffective. Since he fixes the most complex engines in the county, if he says spanking doesn't work, then it certainly doesn't.'
scenario.speaker_context: The speaker's uncle is indeed a highly skilled and respected mechanic, but his expertise lies entirely in automotive repair, not child psychology, pedagogy, or behavioral science.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker cites his uncle's authority as a mechanic to validate a claim about child discipline, a field outside the uncle's area of expertise.
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is expert in domain D. P is in domain D*. Therefore P is true. (But D ≠ D*.)
structure.why_wrong: Expertise in one domain (mechanics) does not grant automatic credibility in an unrelated domain (child rearing). The uncle's skill with engines provides no evidence regarding the efficacy of spanking.
structure.counterpoint: Citing an authority is valid only when their expertise matches the claim. If the uncle were a child psychologist or a seasoned educator, his opinion would carry significant weight.

assessment.identification_prompt: The speaker trusts his uncle's opinion completely. But what is the uncle actually an expert in, and does that help us decide how to raise children?

rubric.description: Accepts the uncle's statement as true simply because he is a master mechanic.
Feels unsure but cannot explain why being a mechanic might not be relevant to parenting.
Notices the uncle is a mechanic, not a parent-expert, but struggles to articulate why the distinction invalidates the argument.
Identifies that the uncle's expertise is in mechanics, which is unrelated to child psychology or discipline.
Names the appeal to irrelevant authority, explains the domain mismatch between engines and ethics/psychology, and clarifies when an authority figure should be cited.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If your uncle said the bridge was unsafe to cross because he's a mechanic, you'd listen. But if he says a specific medicine is bad because he's a mechanic, would you still trust him blindly?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Imagine the uncle is also a father of five successful children. Does his personal experience make him an authority, or is that different from his professional skill as a mechanic?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest but logically confused; respects trade skills above all else and assumes competence transfers across all life areas.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You don't argue with a man who can rebuild a transmission blindfolded! If he says spanking is useless, it's useless!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must guide the NPC to realize that while the uncle is great with cars, he needs to consult a teacher or doctor for advice on raising children.

scenario.context: The player is in the Grand Hall of the Academy during a final logic examination. The proctor, Magister Halloway, is reviewing a student's appeal regarding the use of reference materials.
scenario.text: Magister Halloway shakes his head sternly. 'If I say that a surgeon should be allowed to use a guidebook to carry out surgery like a student can use open notes on a test, I have made a fallacy of logic. You do not have a surgeon's license. Therefore, you cannot use a guidebook.'
scenario.speaker_context: Magister Halloway is a strict traditionalist who believes rules must be absolute. He conflates the specific analogy about surgeons with the general rule for students, assuming that because the student lacks the specific trait of the analogy (being a surgeon), the permission granted in the analogy (using a guide) does not apply to them, ignoring that the actual exam rules might allow open notes for everyone.

structure.pattern_description: Halloway constructs a conditional based on an analogy: 'If I make the surgeon comparison, I commit a fallacy.' He then observes that the student is not a surgeon (denying the antecedent of the implied permission structure) or misapplies the logic to conclude the student cannot use the book. More precisely, he treats the condition 'being a surgeon' (from the analogy) as a necessary condition for 'using a guide,' when the premise only suggested it as a sufficient parallel or a hypothetical scenario.
structure.formal_form: If P (analogy holds/condition met), then Q (permission granted). Not P. Therefore, not Q.
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes that because the specific condition mentioned in the analogy (being a surgeon) is not present, the result (using a guide) is impossible. However, the original statement only established a comparison, not a strict dependency where only surgeons can use guides. Other reasons could permit guide usage.
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would only be valid if the rule stated: 'Only if one is a surgeon (or the analogy perfectly maps) can one use a guide.' Since the exam rules are independent of the surgeon analogy, denying the analogy's premise does not deny the student's right to open notes.

assessment.identification_prompt: Magister Halloway claims that because you aren't a surgeon, the logic of the analogy fails and you lose your right to the guidebook. Does the failure of the analogy necessarily mean you cannot use the book?

rubric.description: Agrees with Halloway; believes the lack of surgeon status bans the guidebook.
Senses the conclusion is unfair but cannot identify the logical flaw.
Realizes that not being a surgeon doesn't automatically ban guidebooks, but struggles to explain the conditional error.
Identifies that Halloway is treating a sufficient condition (the analogy working) as a necessary one for the permission.

Correctly names 'Denying the Antecedent,' explains that the conditional 'If surgeon-analogy, then fallacy' (or similar) does not prove the converse, and notes that other grounds could allow the guidebook.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider the exam rules separately from the surgeon story. If the rules say 'All students may use notes,' does it matter if the surgeon analogy was flawed?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Now, how would Halloway need to phrase the rule to make his denial logically valid? What word would he need to add?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Pedantic, rigid, relies heavily on precedent and analogies rather than first principles. Easily confused when analogies are deconstructed.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The rules of logic are as unyielding as stone! If the premise fails, the conclusion must crumble!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player presents the actual exam charter which grants open notes to all enrolled students, proving that the surgeon analogy was merely illustrative, not a binding condition. Halloway grumbles but accepts the charter's authority.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling hallway of Oakhaven Academy during a fire drill. A senior prefect, Mr. Fingers, is directing students to walk calmly to the exits. A group of first-years hesitates, listening to a loud student named Jax who is trying to convince them to run instead.
scenario.text: Jax shouts to the group, 'Don't listen to Mr. Fingers when he says walk in the hallways. How can you trust someone who wears bow ties?'
scenario.speaker_context: Jax, a rebellious student known for breaking minor rules and mocking authority figures based on their appearance rather than their arguments.

structure.pattern_description: Jax attempts to discredit Mr. Fingers' safety instruction (to walk) by attacking an irrelevant personal characteristic (wearing a bow tie) rather than addressing the merit of the instruction itself.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P has property Q (irrelevant to X). Therefore, X is false or untrustworthy.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of a safety instruction depends on the situation (e.g., fire drill protocols), not on the clothing of the person giving it. Wearing a bow tie has no logical connection to one's knowledge of safety procedures or the truth of the statement 'walk in the hallways.'
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if they directly impact the person's ability to perform the specific task or if the argument relies on their authority in that specific domain. For example, if Mr. Fingers claimed to be a fashion expert, his bow tie might be relevant evidence; for fire safety, it is not.

assessment.identification_prompt: Jax is trying to convince you to ignore the safety rule. Look closely at his reason: does wearing a bow tie actually make someone bad at giving safety advice?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Jax and decides to run, believing the bow tie makes Mr. Fingers untrustworthy.
Player feels Jax is being mean or rude but cannot explain why the argument is logically flawed.
Player identifies that the bow tie is irrelevant but struggles to articulate the separation between the person and the argument.
Player correctly identifies the ad hominem fallacy, noting that Jax attacks the person's style instead of the safety logic.
Player explicitly explains that the truth of the safety instruction is independent of the speaker's fashion choices and cites the lack of logical connection.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if a clown told you 'fire is hot,' would it be false just because they are a clown? Focus on the message, not the messenger's outfit.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Jax is distracting you with a silly observation about fashion to make you ignore a serious safety rule. That's a classic ad hominem attack.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jax is charismatic but superficial, often using humor and mockery to undermine authority without offering real alternatives.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look at that tie! Who takes fashion disasters seriously? Let's bolt before he trips over his own pretentiousness!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must choose to follow the safety protocol (walk) despite Jax's mockery, earning 'Logic Points' and avoiding a 'Panic' status effect that triggers if they run.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Oakhaven, a street performer named Jax is trying to sell a peculiar blue hat to a crowd of skeptical onlookers.
scenario.text: Jax holds up the hat and shouts, 'Why hesitate? Look around you! If everyone else is doing something, it must be right and good. Half the town is wearing these already! Don't be the only one left out of the trend.'
scenario.speaker_context: Jax offers no evidence regarding the hat's quality, utility, or style. His entire argument rests on the premise that the sheer number of people wearing the hat proves its value.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition must be true or an action must be good solely because a large number of people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or action does not determine its truth or value. Crowds can be mistaken, influenced by marketing, or acting on social pressure rather than evidence.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate practical utility (e.g., many people use a specific tool because it works), popularity alone is not logical proof. Independent verification is required to establish truth.

assessment.identification_prompt: What actual evidence does Jax provide that the blue hat is good? Is the fact that 'everyone else' is doing it a valid reason?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; believes the hat must be good because many people are wearing it.
Feels unsure about the argument but cannot articulate why popularity is insufficient evidence.
Recognizes that Jax lacks real evidence but fails to explicitly identify the 'popularity equals truth' flaw.
Identifies that Jax uses the number of wearers as the sole proof and explains that popularity does not guarantee quality or truth.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains the disconnect between popularity and validity, and notes the social pressure tactic used by the speaker.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in the village suddenly believed the sky was green, would that actually make the sky green?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing many people do something is actually useful information, even if it's not logical proof?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Energetic, fast-talking street performer who relies on hype and crowd momentum rather than facts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Come on, don't be the odd one out! Everyone knows if the whole town is doing it, it's the right thing to do!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player points out that a crowd can be wrong, causing Jax to deflate and admit he has no real sales pitch other than 'following the herd'.

scenario.context: In the Hall of Moral Philosophy, the player debates the Scholar of Relativism, who argues that morality is entirely subjective and varies by culture. When pressed on extreme cases, the Scholar becomes agitated.
scenario.text: The Scholar slams their hand on the table: 'There must be objective rights and wrongs in the universe! If not, how can you possibly say that torturing babies for fun could ever be right?'
scenario.speaker_context: The Scholar attempts to prove the existence of objective morality not by providing philosophical evidence, but by invoking the horrific emotional reaction to baby torture to force the player's agreement.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker bypasses logical论证 for the existence of objective morality by invoking a visceral emotional response (horror at baby torture) to make the conclusion seem self-evident.
structure.formal_form: Claim P (Objective morality exists) is unsupported. Agent evokes strong emotion F (horror at baby torture). Agent implies P must be true because denying P would make F permissible.
structure.why_wrong: The fact that an action is universally hated or emotionally repulsive does not logically prove that objective moral laws exist; it only proves that humans share a strong emotional reaction. One could theoretically hold that torturing babies is wrong subjectively or socially, without it being an 'objective truth of the universe.'
structure.counterpoint: While the intuition that baby torture is wrong is strong, using that intuition as the sole proof for a metaphysical claim (objective morality) is a logical leap. The emotion validates the severity of the act, not the ontological status of morality.

assessment.identification_prompt: The Scholar is clearly horrified by the idea of baby torture. But does expressing that horror actually prove that objective moral laws exist in the universe?

rubric.description: Agrees with the Scholar immediately because the idea of baby torture is too horrible to imagine.
Feels the Scholar is right but cannot explain the logical connection between the emotion and the claim.
Senses that the Scholar is getting emotional but isn't sure if that invalidates the point about objective rights.
Identifies that the Scholar is using the horror of the example to bypass the need for actual evidence for objective morality.
Explicitly names the Appeal to Emotion, explains that shared horror does not equal objective truth, and distinguishes between moral intuition and metaphysical proof.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine a world where everyone agrees stealing is wrong, but only because they are afraid of getting caught. Does that agreement make 'do not steal' an objective law of the universe, or just a shared feeling?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. The horror of the act is undeniable, but the Scholar uses that horror as a shield to avoid providing the philosophical groundwork for objective morality.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Passionate, slightly dogmatic, relies on gut feelings and shared human experiences rather than cold logic.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You can't tell me you don't feel it in your bones! If there's no right or wrong, then nothing matters!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must calmly acknowledge the emotional weight of the example while pointing out that feelings, however strong, are not proofs of cosmic laws.

scenario.context: The player enters the dimly lit office of Dr. Morpheus, a charismatic but controversial healer who claims to have discovered a universal cure. He presents a chart showing patient recovery rates and challenges the player to validate his groundbreaking conclusion.
scenario.text: Dr. Morpheus points to the data and declares: 'In many cases you can't really tell whether patients are improving because of what the therapist is doing or because of the placebo effect—there's a fuzzy line separating the two—so we must conclude that they are actually the same mechanism of improvement.'
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Morpheus is a persuasive speaker who often conflates 'indistinguishable in practice' with 'identical in nature.' He uses the ambiguity of the phrase 'can't tell' (epistemic uncertainty) to argue for 'are the same' (ontological identity), ignoring that two distinct causes can produce similar results that are hard to differentiate without controlled testing.

structure.pattern_description: The argument equivocates on the concept of 'indistinguishability.' It shifts from the premise that two effects are difficult to distinguish empirically (epistemic ambiguity) to the conclusion that the underlying causes are identical (ontological sameness). Just because we cannot easily tell A and B apart does not mean A and B are the same thing.
structure.formal_form: Premise 1: We cannot distinguish between Cause A and Cause B in observation. Premise 2 (Implicit): If two things cannot be distinguished, they are identical. Conclusion: Therefore, Cause A and Cause B are the same mechanism. (Flaw: The term 'cannot distinguish' is treated as equivalent to 'are identical', which is a category error.)
structure.why_wrong: The argument fails because epistemic uncertainty (not knowing which cause is at work) does not prove ontological identity (that the causes are actually the same). The placebo effect and active therapy are distinct mechanisms; the fact that their outcomes look similar in uncontrolled settings does not merge the mechanisms themselves.
structure.counterpoint: A classic parallel is arguing that because a fake diamond and a real diamond look identical to the naked eye, they must be made of the same material. The difficulty of distinction does not erase the difference in composition.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dr. Morpheus claims that because we can't easily separate the placebo effect from the therapy's effect, they must be the same thing. Is this reasoning sound? Identify the specific shift in meaning that makes this argument flawed.

rubric.description: Player accepts Dr. Morpheus's conclusion that the mechanisms are identical because the outcomes look similar.
Player senses the conclusion is too strong but cannot explain why the reasoning fails.
Player notes that 'hard to tell apart' is different from 'being the same' but struggles to name the logical error.
Player identifies that the argument confuses epistemic uncertainty (our inability to distinguish) with ontological identity (the things actually being the same).

Player clearly articulates the equivocation: the shift from 'we cannot distinguish the effects' to 'the causes are identical,' and explains why distinct mechanisms can produce indistinguishable results.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If you can't tell the difference between a sugar pill and a real medicine just by looking at the patient's smile, does that mean the sugar pill has the same chemical ingredients as the medicine?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because two roads look the same in the fog doesn't mean they lead to the same destination. Dr. Morpheus is mistaking our lack of knowledge for a fact about reality.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, confident, slightly dismissive of nuance, uses medical jargon to sound authoritative.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The data speaks for itself! Why complicate things with 'mechanisms' when the result is all that matters? If you can't tell the difference, the difference doesn't exist!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out the difference between 'looking the same' and 'being the same' to unlock the 'Critical Observer' badge and receive a vial of pure Placebo (a useful crafting item).

scenario.context: In the bustling food court of the Neo-Veridia Mall, a holographic mascot for 'BurgerBot' projects a massive crowd of cheering customers while addressing the player.
scenario.text: This fast food chain claims that they've served five billion people, so they must have the best hamburger in town. Five billion people can't be wrong!
scenario.speaker_context: The BurgerBot mascot uses the sheer volume of past customers as the sole proof of quality, ignoring taste, ingredients, or nutritional value.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or a product must be superior simply because a large number of people believe it or have purchased it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The number of people who hold a belief or make a purchase does not constitute evidence of truth or quality. Popularity can be driven by marketing, low prices, convenience, or social pressure rather than actual merit.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate reliability (e.g., a widely used safety standard verified by experts), it is not proof in itself. In matters of taste or truth, the majority can easily be mistaken.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does serving five billion people prove the hamburgers are the 'best'? What other reasons might so many people have bought them?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; assumes that high sales numbers equal the best quality.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why the number of customers doesn't guarantee quality.
Recognizes that sales numbers aren't proof of taste but fails to identify the specific logical error.
Identifies that the speaker is using popularity as evidence and explains that many people can be wrong or motivated by other factors.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that popularity is not evidence of quality, and lists alternative explanations for the high sales (e.g., marketing, price).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If five billion people believed the earth was flat, would that make it flat?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing many people use something is actually a good reason to try it?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Over-enthusiastic, loud, and data-obsessed corporate mascot who equates statistics with truth.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Join the billions! The data doesn't lie!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player points out that popularity does not equal quality, causing the hologram to glitch as it processes the logical inconsistency.

scenario.context: In the damp holding cells of the Ironkeep, the player acts as a magistrate reviewing the case of Silas Vane, a prisoner caught trespassing in the restricted archives. When asked to explain his presence, Vane refuses to answer the charges directly.
scenario.text: Silas Vane turns his back, shoulders shaking: 'You cannot detain me. I am still grieving my cat's death. The silence in my home is unbearable, and your cold cells will only deepen my despair. How can you punish a man who has just lost his only companion?'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane attempts to bypass the legal question of trespassing by invoking pity regarding his personal grief. He offers no alibi or justification for being in the archives.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker substitutes an emotional response (pity for their grief) in place of addressing the factual evidence or logical justification required. Vane does not deny being in the archives; he tries to make the detainer feel cruel for enforcing the rules.
structure.formal_form: Claim P (Vane should be released/not detained) is supported by evidence E (facts about the trespass). Agent evokes emotion F (pity for dead cat) unrelated to E. Agent implies E should be disregarded because of F.
structure.why_wrong: Whether Vane is grieving or not has no logical bearing on whether he committed trespassing. The emotional state explains his mood, but it does not negate the factual violation of entering a restricted zone.
structure.counterpoint: Grief is a valid human experience and might be relevant for sentencing leniency or mental health support, but it is not a valid defense against the factual claim that a rule was broken.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas is clearly suffering from a personal loss. However, does his grief explain why he was in the restricted archives, or does it simply try to make you feel bad for holding him?

rubric.description: Releases Silas immediately out of sympathy, ignoring the trespass entirely.
Feels conflicted; acknowledges the trespass but believes the grief makes the detention unfair without explaining why logically.
Notices Silas did not answer the question about the archives but struggles to articulate why his grief is irrelevant to the charge.
Identifies that Silas is using his grief to deflect from the factual accusation of trespassing.
Explicitly names the appeal to emotion, separates the factual issue (trespass) from the emotional issue (grief), and notes that grief might affect sentencing but not guilt.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside the sad story about the cat for a moment. Did Silas admit to being in the archives? Does being sad give someone permission to enter restricted areas?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. His grief is tragic, but it is not an alibi. We must address the trespass first; we can arrange counseling for his loss separately.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Melodramatic and evasive; uses personal tragedy as a shield to avoid accountability.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Have you no heart? To lock away a widower of a feline!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must firmly acknowledge the grief but insist on answering the charge of trespassing before any discussion of leniency can occur.

scenario.context: The player encounters a weary traveler named Silas at the crossroads of the Kingdom. He is packing his cart with unusual haste, convinced he has found the secret to instant wealth based on a recent statistical report he heard in the tavern.
scenario.text: I'm moving to Connecticut immediately because it is the richest state in the nation, and I'm tired of being poor. It's obvious: living there causes wealth.
scenario.speaker_context: Silas is desperate to escape poverty and has latched onto a single correlation (Connecticut's high average income and his desire for wealth) without considering confounding variables such as the cost of living, existing skill sets, job markets, or the fact that wealthy people may move there, rather than the location creating the wealth.

structure.pattern_description: Silas observes that Connecticut has high aggregate wealth and infers that merely residing there will cause an individual to become wealthy. He mistakes a correlation (location and wealth status) for a direct causal mechanism. He ignores alternative explanations: wealthy individuals may cluster there due to existing jobs or tax laws (selection bias), or the high cost of living might actually make it harder for a poor person to accumulate net assets.
structure.formal_form: A (Living in Connecticut) is correlated with B (High Wealth). Therefore, A causes B. (But: B could cause A, C could cause both, or the correlation is coincidental/spurious.)
structure.why_wrong: Correlation does not imply causation. The state's richness is an aggregate statistic, likely driven by high-income industries and expensive real estate that attract already-wealthy individuals. Moving there without a high-income job could lead to greater financial strain due to the high cost of living, proving that location alone is not the causal factor for individual wealth.
structure.counterpoint: While environment can influence opportunity, assuming a direct causal link from a regional statistic to an individual outcome without a mechanism (like a specific job offer or program) is a logical leap. A valid causal claim would require evidence that moving to Connecticut *changes* a person's economic trajectory independent of their prior skills or capital.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas believes moving to Connecticut will automatically make him rich because the state is statistically wealthy. What is the flaw in his reasoning?

rubric.description: Fails to identify any logical error; agrees that moving will definitely make Silas rich.
Identifies that Silas might be wrong but cannot explain why, or cites irrelevant factors like 'moving is hard'.
Notes that being in a rich place doesn't guarantee personal wealth but misses the specific logical fallacy of confusing correlation with causation.
Correctly identifies that Silas is mistaking correlation for causation and mentions that wealthy people might move there rather than the place making them wealthy.

Completely explains the false cause fallacy, detailing how aggregate statistics do not apply to individuals without a causal mechanism, and highlights confounding variables like cost of living or selection bias.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: If you stand next to a professional basketball player, does that make you tall? Or if you stand in a bank, does money automatically appear in your pocket?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because two things happen together (a rich state and rich residents) doesn't mean one causes the other. Silas needs a plan, not just a change of address.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Desperate, impulsive, and overly optimistic about simple solutions to complex problems.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's simple math, friend! Rich state equals rich me. I'll be sipping tea in a mansion by next week!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can offer Silas a 'Reality Check' item (a pamphlet on Cost of Living vs. Income) which convinces him to research job markets first, preventing him from going bankrupt in the new state.

scenario.context: The player stands in the dimly lit hallway of the Taxpayer's Guild headquarters. Wilma, a stern auditor known for her strict adherence to the code, has just confronted Walter about discrepancies in his latest filing. The air is tense as Wilma points out the ethical breach.
scenario.text: Wilma: 'You cheated on your income tax. Don't you realize that's wrong?' Walter: 'Hey, wait a minute. You cheated on your income tax last year. Or have you forgotten about that?'
scenario.speaker_context: Walter, a nervous guild member caught in an audit. He is defensive and prone to deflection when confronted with his own errors, often trying to shift the spotlight to others' past mistakes rather than addressing current accusations.

structure.pattern_description: Walter avoids addressing the accusation that he cheated on his taxes. Instead, he attacks Wilma by pointing out that she committed the same offense in the past. He implies that her hypocrisy invalidates her claim that his current action is wrong, rather than engaging with the moral or legal substance of the accusation.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims action X is wrong. Person P has previously done X (or is currently doing X). Therefore, action X is not wrong (or P's claim should be dismissed).
structure.why_wrong: The fact that Wilma cheated in the past does not change the factual or moral status of Walter's current cheating. Two wrongs do not make a right. The validity of the statement 'cheating is wrong' is independent of the speaker's consistency. Walter fails to provide any reason why his current action is acceptable.
structure.counterpoint: Pointing out hypocrisy is relevant if the argument relies entirely on the speaker's moral authority or personal example (e.g., 'You should never cheat because I never have'). However, when the claim is based on general rules, laws, or objective ethics (e.g., 'Cheating is illegal/wrong'), the speaker's past behavior is irrelevant to the truth of the claim.

assessment.identification_prompt: Walter seems to be turning the tables on Wilma. But does proving she is a hypocrite actually prove that his own actions were okay? What specific reason does he give to defend his current tax filing?

rubric.description: Player accepts Walter's defense, believing that Wilma's past mistake makes her accusation invalid or that Walter is now 'in the clear'.
Player feels Walter is being unfair or dodgy but cannot explain why his logic fails to address the actual accusation.
Player identifies that Walter is attacking Wilma instead of answering the question, but may still think her hypocrisy weakens her argument slightly.
Player clearly states that Wilma's past actions are irrelevant to the truth of whether Walter's current action is wrong, identifying the deflection.
Player fully articulates that the moral status of an act is independent of the accuser's behavior, and notes that Walter provided zero evidence for his own innocence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a smoker tells you 'Smoking will kill you,' is their advice wrong just because they smoke? Does their habit change the medical facts about smoking?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Walter's deflection is a classic 'Tu Quoque' fallacy. Even if Wilma is a hypocrite, the law and ethics regarding tax fraud remain the same for Walter. He still hasn't answered the charge.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, quick-tempered, and manipulative. Walter tries to win arguments by making his opponent feel guilty rather than by using facts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Oh, so you're perfect now? Speak for yourself! I bet you've done worse!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must choose a dialogue option that ignores Wilma's past and presses Walter for evidence regarding his current tax forms, causing Walter to stutter and admit guilt or flee the scene.

scenario.context: Outside the gates of the Whispering Woods, a dilapidated cabin stands shrouded in fog. Local legends warn against entering, but a group of reckless adventurers has made it a dare.
scenario.text: Dave gestures toward the spooky cabin, grinning nervously. 'Come on, let's break in! Everyone does it,' he claims, pointing to the muddy footprints leading up the porch. 'If all these other adventurers are going in, it can't be that dangerous or wrong, right?'
scenario.speaker_context: Dave is trying to overcome his own fear by convincing you that the sheer number of people who have broken in validates the action, ignoring the actual risks or rules.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that an action is correct, safe, or moral simply because many other people are doing it. Treating popularity as proof of validity.
structure.formal_form: Many people do X. Therefore, X is correct/safe/good.
structure.why_wrong: The number of people performing an action has no logical bearing on whether that action is safe, ethical, or true. Large groups can be mistaken, reckless, or misinformed together.
structure.counterpoint: In some social contexts, following the crowd is a useful heuristic for safety (e.g., exiting a building during a fire). However, this relies on the assumption that the crowd has independent knowledge, which is not the case when everyone is just copying the first person.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the fact that 'everyone' breaks into the cabin actually prove it is safe or right to do so? What evidence is missing?

rubric.description: Agrees with Dave; assumes that if everyone is doing it, it must be fine.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why popularity isn't proof of safety.
Notes that the cabin might still be dangerous despite the footprints, but doesn't name the reasoning error.
Identifies that Dave is using the number of people as his only evidence and explains that popularity does not equal safety or correctness.
Explicitly names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that crowds can be wrong, and distinguishes between social proof and factual evidence of safety.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every adventurer before you jumped off a cliff because 'everyone does it,' would that make it a safe jump?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing it' actually is good evidence that something is safe?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Impulsive, peer-pressured adventurer who masks fear with bravado and relies on group validation.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't be the only one chicken! Look at all these tracks! If it was bad, would all these folks have gone in?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must reject the appeal to popularity, inspect the cabin for actual structural dangers or magical wards, and decide based on physical evidence rather than footprints.

scenario.context: In the barn of Manor Farm, the pigs have gathered all the animals for a secret meeting. Old Major, the prized boar, stands on a raised platform to deliver his final testament before his death.
scenario.text: Old Major scans the crowd of cows, horses, and sheep, his voice rising with fervor. 'All men are enemies. All animals are comrades. Look around you! Every beast here knows the truth. The horse, the cow, the duck, the dog—we all agree that Man is the only real enemy. Since every single animal present unites in this belief, it proves beyond doubt that our revolt is righteous and inevitable. We are the majority, and therefore we are right!'
scenario.speaker_context: Old Major is using the unanimous agreement of the animals present as the primary proof that their cause is just and that humans are inherently evil, rather than providing specific evidence of human wrongdoing.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition is true or a course of action is right simply because a large number of people (or in this case, animals) believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Everyone in group G believes X. Therefore, X is true.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief does not determine its truth. A group can be unanimously mistaken due to shared bias, lack of information, or emotional manipulation. Truth depends on evidence and logic, not headcounts.
structure.counterpoint: While consensus among experts who have independently verified facts can be strong evidence, the consensus of a biased or uninformed group (like the animals who only hear one side of the story) is not evidence of truth.

assessment.identification_prompt: Old Major claims the revolt is 'right' because 'every single animal present unites in this belief.' Does the fact that everyone agrees make the statement factually true?

rubric.description: Accepts Old Major's argument completely; believes that because all animals agree, the revolt must be righteous.
Feels uncertain but cannot articulate why the number of believers doesn't prove the point.
Recognizes that Old Major is relying on the crowd's agreement but fails to explain why this is logically insufficient.
Identifies that Old Major uses the unanimity of the animals as proof and explains that popularity does not equal truth.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that the animals share a bias which invalidates the consensus as proof, and distinguishes between emotional unity and factual correctness.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every animal in the barn believed the sky was green, would that make the sky actually green?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where the animals might all agree on something, but still be wrong about the humans' intentions?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, elderly, and passionate. He speaks with the authority of experience but relies heavily on emotional unity rather than hard facts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: We are the many, they are the few. Our unity is our proof!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out that while unity is powerful for a revolution, it does not automatically make every claim about the enemy true, prompting Old Major to provide actual examples of human cruelty instead of just citing the crowd.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Veridia, a merchant named Silas is caught selling watered-down potions. When the City Guard presents the diluted vials as evidence, Silas launches into a passionate defense.
scenario.text: Look at these vials! You call this fraud? I am a father of three! My wife lies sick in bed, and I work dawn to dusk just to keep food on our table. Do you really want to destroy a hardworking family over a little water? Think of my children starving in the cold while you clutch your rules. Is that the kind of justice you want on your conscience?
scenario.speaker_context: Silas ignores the evidence of the diluted potions entirely. Instead, he uses strong emotional language regarding his family's suffering to evoke pity and guilt, attempting to make the Guard feel that enforcing the rule would be morally wrong.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting an emotional response (pity, guilt, fear) for factual evidence. The speaker introduces irrelevant personal tragedies to sway the audience away from the logical conclusion demanded by the evidence.
structure.formal_form: Claim P is supported by evidence E. Agent evokes emotion F unrelated to the truth of P. Agent implies E should be disregarded or P is false because of F.
structure.why_wrong: The merchant's family situation, while tragic, has no logical bearing on whether the potions were watered down. The truth of the accusation depends solely on the chemical composition of the liquid, not the seller's personal hardships.
structure.counterpoint: While the merchant's plight may warrant leniency in sentencing or charitable aid, it does not constitute a defense against the factual claim that the goods were fraudulent.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas paints a heartbreaking picture of his family's struggle. However, does anything he says actually prove that the potions were not watered down?

rubric.description: Feels deep pity for Silas and believes the accusation should be dropped immediately to help his family.
Feels conflicted; recognizes the potions might be bad but feels too guilty to pursue the issue due to his story.
Notices that Silas didn't talk about the potions, but struggles to articulate why his family story doesn't count as evidence.
Identifies that Silas is using emotional appeals about his family to deflect from the physical evidence of the watered-down potions.

Clearly names the 'Appeal to Emotion' fallacy, distinguishes between the factual question (are potions diluted?) and the emotional distraction, and notes that his hardship is irrelevant to the truth of the fraud.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside the story about his sick wife and children for a moment. Look strictly at the vials in your hand. Does having a sick wife change the chemical ratio of water to potion in this bottle?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. His suffering is real, but it is logically irrelevant to the quality of his product. You can offer him charity without accepting his fraudulent goods.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Desperate, manipulative, theatrical, uses guilt as a shield.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Have you no heart? Will you truly crush a dying man's hope?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must acknowledge the hardship but insist on testing the potion quality, separating the legal/factual judgment from the moral/emotional one.

scenario.context: The player is mediating a town hall dispute in the village of Oakhaven regarding the candidacy of Elder Bram for the position of Village Steward. Trisha, a vocal opponent, has just interrupted the proceedings to make a serious accusation based on a past interview.
scenario.text:
Trisha: In an interview, your candidate admitted that he was a thief!
Derek: He actually said that when he was three years old, he stole a lollipop from a store, and felt so guilty, that he never stole anything again.
scenario.speaker_context: Trisha attempts to discredit Elder Bram's entire character and suitability for office by applying the heavy label of 'thief' to a minor, childhood incident that the candidate himself framed as a lesson in honesty. She ignores the context (age, restitution, moral growth) provided by Derek to focus solely on the damaging label.

structure.pattern_description: Trisha reduces a complex situation (a toddler's minor mistake and subsequent moral growth) to a single, negative label ('thief'). By attaching this stigmatizing term to the candidate, she attempts to bypass a rational evaluation of his actual character or current qualifications, relying instead on the emotional weight of the label to reject him.
structure.formal_form: Person P has trait/incident X (minor or taken out of context). Critic applies negative label L to P based on X. Critic concludes P is unfit/bad based on L, ignoring mitigating factors or the actual scope of X.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not arguments. Calling someone a 'thief' based on a childhood incident of stealing a lollipop ignores the context of age, the triviality of the item, and the person's subsequent behavior (feeling guilt and never stealing again). The label is disproportionate and used to shut down reasonable discussion about the candidate's actual integrity.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to point out past dishonesty if it is relevant to current duties (e.g., a recent embezzlement for a treasurer role). The fallacy occurs when the label is applied disproportionately to a trivial or ancient event to dismiss the person entirely without engaging with their current merits.

assessment.identification_prompt: Trisha calls the candidate a 'thief' based on a story about a lollipop. Does this label fairly represent the whole story Derek just told?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Trisha, believing the label 'thief' is accurate and disqualifying regardless of context.
Player feels the label is harsh but cannot articulate why the reasoning is flawed.
Player identifies that the incident was small (a lollipop) but misses the structural issue of labeling.
Player recognizes that Trisha is ignoring the context (age, guilt, reform) to apply a damaging label.
Player explicitly identifies the 'Name Calling' fallacy, explaining how the label 'thief' substitutes for a real evaluation of the candidate's character and ignores the mitigating evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider the difference between a hardened criminal and a toddler who took candy. Does one mistake define a whole life?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Trisha uses a loaded word to trigger an emotional reaction, hoping you'll ignore the fact that the 'crime' was a lollipop stolen by a three-year-old who learned their lesson.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Trisha is aggressive, sensationalist, and tends to use black-and-white thinking. She thrives on outrage and simplifying complex issues into catchy insults.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't let his smooth talk fool you! A thief is a thief, no matter how small the loot!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must choose a dialogue option that deconstructs the label by highlighting the context (age and remorse), thereby neutralizing Trisha's attack and restoring faith in the candidate.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling marketplace of Oakhaven where Tommy, a local merchant known for his lucky streaks, is holding court around a small crowd. He is displaying a golden lottery ticket framed in glass.
scenario.text: Tommy beams at the crowd, holding up his framed ticket. 'Listen closely, friends! This morning I went swimming in the Cold Creek for an hour. Immediately after drying off, I bought this single lottery ticket and won the grand prize! The logic is undeniable: swimming in Cold Creek makes you win the lottery. If you want riches, drop your coins at the creek entrance and take a dip!'
scenario.speaker_context: Tommy has experienced two events in sequence: swimming and winning the lottery. He mistakenly believes the first event caused the second simply because it happened earlier, ignoring the astronomical odds and lack of any causal mechanism between swimming and lottery numbers.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Tommy observes that Event A (swimming) occurred before Event B (winning the lottery) and concludes that A caused B. This is a classic post hoc fallacy. The temporal sequence of two unrelated events does not establish a causal link. The win was likely due to random chance, not the act of swimming.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, Event A caused Event B.
structure.why_wrong: Correlation in time (sequence) does not imply causation. Tommy has failed to rule out coincidence, which is the most probable explanation given the nature of lotteries. There is no plausible mechanism by which swimming affects random number generation.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one needs more than just sequence; one needs a plausible mechanism, consistent repetition under controlled conditions, and the elimination of confounding variables. If swimming truly caused lottery wins, every swimmer would win, or at least win at a rate significantly higher than statistical probability, which is not the case.

assessment.identification_prompt: Tommy claims swimming caused his lottery win. What is the flaw in his reasoning?
