structure.why_wrong: The conclusion ignores variable rates of change, potential interventions, and historical resilience. Moving from 'things are getting worse' to 'everything will be destroyed and become Venus' is a massive leap not supported by the limited evidence of current trends alone. It treats a complex, dynamic system as having a single, linear, unavoidable fate.
structure.counterpoint: Concern about environmental trends is valid and based on data. However, predicting a specific, absolute cataclysm (turning into Venus) based solely on the existence of those trends, while ignoring counter-evidence and potential solutions, constitutes a hasty generalization of the outcome.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elder Thorne claims the planet will definitely turn into Venus because of current waste and temperature issues. Does his evidence support such a definite and extreme conclusion?

rubric.description: Player accepts Thorne's prediction as absolute fact and panics.
Player feels worried but suspects Thorne might be exaggerating without knowing why.
Player identifies that Thorne is jumping to conclusions but cannot explain the logical gap between trends and total destruction.
Player recognizes the hasty generalization, noting that current negative trends do not automatically guarantee the specific extreme outcome of becoming Venus.

Player fully articulates the fallacy: Thorne ignores mitigating factors, adaptation, and non-linear system dynamics, treating a probable risk as an inevitable, singular catastrophe based on insufficient projection.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne shakes his head sadly. 'You do not see the writing on the wall? Once the slide begins, it never stops until nothing remains!' He refuses to consider any data that suggests stabilization.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Thorne pauses, looking at his frantic sketches. 'Perhaps... perhaps I have let my fear dictate the math. The slide is steep, but maybe not infinite. We must look at the variables I ignored.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, intelligent but overwhelmed, prone to catastrophizing when stressed.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The data points are real, but the trajectory is not set in stone! We can alter the curve if we stop assuming the worst is inevitable.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player helps Thorne recalibrate his models by introducing data on renewable energy adoption and reforestation, shifting his mindset from 'doom' to 'urgent action'.

scenario.context: The player enters the Grand Hall of the University of Westshire (UWI) during orientation week. A disgruntled senior student named Kaelen is leaning against a pillar, complaining to a group of nervous freshmen.
scenario.text: Kaelen crosses his arms and scoffs, 'Don't bother unpacking your bags yet. I took two courses here last semester, and neither of them was interesting. Honestly, I don't think this is a good university at all. You're all wasting your time.'
scenario.speaker_context: Kaelen is a senior who has only taken two specific courses at UWI. He is using his limited, negative experience with just two classes to condemn the entire institution, which offers hundreds of courses and has thousands of students.

structure.pattern_description: Kaelen draws a universal conclusion about the quality of the entire university ('not a good university') based on a sample size of only two courses. This sample is statistically insignificant relative to the total number of courses offered and ignores the diversity of departments, professors, and student experiences within the institution.
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of X from population P (where n is very small relative to P). All observed instances had property Q (uninteresting). Therefore, all members of P (the university) have property Q (bad).
structure.why_wrong: Two courses cannot represent the academic quality of an entire university. The sample is too small and likely biased (perhaps Kaelen only chose difficult electives outside his major, or had two specific professors who were having a bad semester). A valid assessment would require a much larger, randomized sample of courses or broader metrics like graduation rates and research output.
structure.counterpoint: Personal experience is valuable data, but it becomes a fallacy when treated as definitive proof for a whole. If Kaelen had taken 50 courses across every department and found them all lacking, his generalization might be warranted. The error lies in the leap from 'my two classes' to 'the whole school'.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kaelen claims UWI is a bad university because his two courses were uninteresting. Is his conclusion logically supported by his evidence?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kaelen and decides to leave the university immediately.
Player feels Kaelen is being too harsh but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Player notes that two classes are not enough to judge the whole school but lacks terminology.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that the sample size (2 courses) is too small to represent the entire population (the university).
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explains the sample size issue, and suggests potential confounding variables (e.g., specific major, professor bias) that make the sample unrepresentative.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Kaelen nods vigorously. 'Exactly! Why risk three years and a fortune on a place that's clearly a dump? Come on, let's go check out the trade school instead.' (The player misses out on potential quests and alliances at UWI).
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Kaelen pauses, scratching his head. 'Well... I suppose I did skip most of the science labs. Maybe the engineering department is decent. Alright, I won't scare you off completely, but keep your eyes open.' (Kaelen becomes a neutral contact who provides side quests).

game_hooks.npc_personality: Cynical, disengaged, and prone to complaining. Kaelen represents the 'burnt-out student' archetype who projects his specific failures onto the whole system.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I've seen it all, and it's all garbage. Don't let the shiny brochures fool you.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Kaelen to give the university another chance by pointing out the flaw in his logic, unlocking the 'Critical Thinker' badge and gaining access to the Senior Common Room.

scenario.context: In the Grand Hall of Reason, the player encounters a heated debate between two scholars. Scholar Elara is arguing for a nuanced view on justice, while her opponent, Magister Thorne, interrupts to shut down her argument by attributing a crude motive to her.
scenario.text: Magister Thorne declares: 'You support capital punishment just because you want an "eye for an eye," but I have several good reasons to believe that capital punishment is fundamentally wrong.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara had not mentioned 'an eye for an eye' or simple revenge; she was arguing based on deterrence and public safety. Thorne ignored her actual arguments and replaced them with a simplistic 'revenge' motive that is easier to attack.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne misrepresents Elara's position. He claims she supports capital punishment solely for revenge ('eye for an eye'), whereas her actual argument was likely based on complex factors like deterrence or justice. He then attacks this fabricated, weaker version of her argument.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P. Person B restates P as the distorted P* (often more extreme or simplistic). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position P has been refuted.
structure.why_wrong: The criticism targets a motive ('eye for an eye') that Elara did not express. Refuting the desire for revenge does not refute the actual arguments Elara made regarding deterrence or safety. The argument fails to engage with the real position.
structure.counterpoint: Elara could reply: 'I never mentioned revenge or an "eye for an eye." My argument was based on deterrence and public safety. Please address those points instead of a motive I do not hold.'

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Magister Thorne distort Scholar Elara's argument in his response?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne or fails to see any issue with his characterization of Elara's view.
Player feels Thorne is being unfair or aggressive but cannot identify the specific logical error.
Player notices Thorne mentioned 'eye for an eye' which Elara didn't say, but doesn't fully grasp that this invalidates his counter-argument.
Player identifies that Thorne created a false version of Elara's argument (revenge) to make it easier to attack, ignoring her actual points.

Player explicitly names the 'Straw Man' fallacy, explains how the 'eye for an eye' motive was fabricated, and articulates why attacking this fabrication does not refute Elara's actual stance on deterrence/safety.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at the phrase 'just because you want an eye for an eye.' Did Elara actually say that? What happens if you attack an argument nobody actually made?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct! Thorne built a 'straw man'—a weak, fake version of Elara's argument—to knock it down easily. By focusing on revenge, he avoided having to debate her actual points about safety.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Magister Thorne is an arrogant, fast-talking debater who prefers winning through rhetorical tricks rather than honest inquiry. He often interrupts and speaks over others.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't try to hide behind complex theories! We all know you just want blood for blood!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select the dialogue option that points out the misrepresentation ('You are attacking a motive I never claimed') to gain Logic Points and calm the debate.

scenario.context: In the bustling academy of Logos, the Dean is assigning a new instructor to the advanced Computer Animation department. A student committee is debating the hire.
scenario.text: The logic teacher was hired to fill the new computer animation class. He is a great admirer of Pixar's work and will do a great job.
scenario.speaker_context: The speaker is a student council representative who assumes that because the teacher is an expert in Logic and a fan of animation, he is automatically qualified to teach the technical and artistic skills required for computer animation.

structure.pattern_description: The argument claims the teacher will succeed in computer animation solely based on his existing authority in Logic and his personal admiration for Pixar, ignoring the lack of specific expertise in animation software or technique.
structure.formal_form: Person A is an authority in Domain X (Logic) and likes Domain Y (Animation). Therefore, Person A is an authority in Domain Y.
structure.why_wrong: Expertise in one field (Logic) and enthusiasm for another (Pixar films) do not confer the technical skills or pedagogical knowledge needed to teach Computer Animation. The authority cited is irrelevant to the specific claim.
structure.counterpoint: If the teacher had a degree in Computer Science with a specialization in Graphics, citing his background would be valid. Here, only his logic credentials and fandom are cited.

assessment.identification_prompt: The speaker says the teacher will do a great job. What evidence is given for his ability to teach animation, and does his current job as a logic teacher prove he has those skills?

rubric.description: Accepts the claim that he will do a great job because he is already a teacher and likes Pixar.
Senses something is missing but cannot identify that Logic and Animation are different skill sets.
Notices the teacher teaches Logic, not Animation, but doesn't fully explain why that makes the argument weak.
Identifies that being a Logic expert and a Pixar fan does not make someone an expert in teaching Computer Animation.
Clearly articulates the domain mismatch: Logic expertise and film appreciation do not transfer to technical animation instruction, identifying this as an irrelevant appeal to authority.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If a famous math professor claimed they could perform heart surgery because they are good at numbers and admire doctors, would you trust them with a scalpel?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. What specific qualifications should the committee have asked for instead of just his current title and hobbies?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest but naive student representative who respects titles and assumes intelligence transfers across all fields.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But surely, if he can teach us to think logically, he can teach us to animate! Plus, he loves Pixar!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must guide the committee to draft a job description requiring specific animation portfolio reviews rather than relying on the candidate's current academic status.

scenario.context: The player enters the High Council Chamber where Councilor Vane is vehemently arguing against a proposal to allow medical marijuana.
scenario.text: Councilor Vane slams his hand on the table. 'I think that the use of marijuana as a medical treatment shouldn't even be considered. If we make drugs legal in a few cases, then we might eventually have to completely legalize them - which is even crazier than Proposition 215. If we want to help people out by letting them do illegal things, then let's just get rid of all our laws.'
scenario.speaker_context: Councilor Vane assumes that allowing a specific, limited exception (medical use) will inevitably lead to an extreme, unrestricted outcome (total legalization of all drugs and abolition of all laws) without providing evidence for this causal chain. He treats a small, controlled step as if it guarantees the worst possible general outcome.

structure.pattern_description: Vane argues that a limited exception (medical marijuana) will inevitably lead to a universal extreme (legalizing all drugs and removing all laws). This is a hasty generalization because it assumes a small sample of permissiveness automatically expands to cover the entire domain of legality without intermediate checks or boundaries. It ignores the possibility of maintaining strict regulations for specific cases while prohibiting others.
structure.formal_form: Event A (limited exception) is permitted. Therefore, Event B (total removal of restrictions) will inevitably occur. No evidence is provided for the causal link between the specific instance and the universal outcome.
structure.why_wrong: The argument fails because it generalizes from a single policy change to a catastrophic societal collapse without demonstrating the mechanism. Just because we allow one thing in a specific context does not mean we must allow everything in all contexts. Laws frequently contain exceptions without collapsing entirely.
structure.counterpoint: Slippery slope arguments can be valid if there is strong empirical evidence that one step reliably leads to the next. The fallacy lies in assuming the slide is inevitable without proof, effectively generalizing a minor risk into a certainty.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane claims that allowing medical marijuana means we must eventually get rid of all laws. Is this conclusion supported by the evidence he provided?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane, believing that any exception leads to total chaos.
Player feels Vane is exaggerating but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Player identifies that Vane is jumping to conclusions but mislabels it as simply being 'scared'.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, noting that a limited exception does not logically force a total removal of all laws.

Player fully deconstructs the argument, explaining that Vane generalizes a specific policy change to an extreme universal outcome without evidence of a necessary causal link, and suggests that regulated exceptions are logically distinct from total deregulation.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Vane says 'if we do X, then Y happens.' But does doing X actually force Y to happen, or is he assuming a connection that isn't there?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Vane takes one small step and pretends it proves we must take a giant leap. That is a classic hasty generalization about how laws work.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Alarmist, rigid, prone to catastrophic thinking, authoritative but logically flawed.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: One crack in the dam and the whole city drowns! We cannot start down this path!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully points out that cities have speed limits for cars but don't ban all travel; similarly, medical exceptions don't require abolishing all drug laws. Vane grudgingly admits the logic holds but remains emotionally opposed.

scenario.context: In the bustling trade district of Oakhaven, a charismatic populist named Silas Vane is campaigning for City Treasurer against an incumbent known for fiscal prudence. During a heated town hall debate, Vane attempts to discredit his opponent's economic plan.
scenario.text: Silas Vane leans into the microphone, his voice trembling with manufactured urgency: "My opponent talks about interest rates and bond yields, but I talk about your future! If you elect him, the Dow Jones will tumble, the markets will crash, and you will lose every single penny of your life savings! Do you want to see your children starve? Do you want to lose your homes? Vote for me, or say goodbye to everything you own!"
scenario.speaker_context: Vane bypasses any analysis of the opponent's actual economic policies. Instead, he invokes extreme fear of financial ruin and the suffering of families to force a vote, offering no causal evidence linking the opponent to a market crash.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting a strong emotional response (in this case, fear and panic) in place of factual evidence or logical reasoning. Vane does not explain how the opponent's policies would cause a crash; he simply asserts a catastrophic outcome to provoke terror.
structure.formal_form: Claim P (Opponent is bad/should not be elected) is supported by evoking Emotion F (Fear of ruin/starvation). Agent implies P is true because F is terrifying, without providing causal link E.
structure.why_wrong: The fear of losing money does not constitute evidence that the opponent's policies will cause a market crash. The argument relies entirely on the intensity of the emotion rather than the probability or mechanics of the claimed event.
structure.counterpoint: While economic stability is a legitimate concern, valid arguments require specific policy analysis (e.g., 'His plan increases deficit spending which historically correlates with inflation'), not hypothetical worst-case scenarios designed solely to induce panic.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas Vane paints a terrifying picture of poverty and loss. But does he provide any actual reason to believe his opponent will cause the stock market to crash?

rubric.description: Is overwhelmed by the fear of losing savings and agrees Vane is right without questioning the claim.
Feels scared but vaguely senses something is missing, yet cannot identify the lack of evidence.
Notices Vane didn't explain how the crash would happen, but still feels the emotional weight of the argument is a valid point.
Identifies that Vane is using fear of poverty to distract from the lack of economic evidence.

Explicitly names the appeal to emotion (fear), explains that the catastrophic outcome is asserted without causal proof, and distinguishes between legitimate economic worry and manipulative scare tactics.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine the opponent's plan is actually very boring and safe. Does Vane's speech change the facts of the plan, or just how you feel about it? What specific mechanism did he describe that causes the Dow to tumble?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. He skipped the 'how' and went straight to the 'ouch.' Now, how would you rephrase his concern into a logical question about fiscal policy?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, loud, prone to hyperbole, manipulative, feeds on crowd anxiety.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: They say numbers don't cry, but families do! Are you going to let a spreadsheet destroy your winter?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that calmly ask for the specific economic mechanism linking the opponent to the crash, causing Vane to stutter or pivot to another emotional plea, thereby revealing his lack of substance to the crowd.

scenario.context: The player enters the Town Hall during a heated council meeting. Councilor Thaddeus, a traditionalist known for his fiery rhetoric, is addressing the crowd regarding a proposed bill to expand marriage rights.
scenario.text: There is a radical element, a homosexual agenda that wants to redefine what marriage is. They want to say that marriage is not only one man and one woman, but it is two men or two women. What logical reason is there to keep us from stopping the expansion of that definition to include three people, or an adult and a child, or any other odd combination? It does not even have to be limited to human beings; it could be anything. There is no reason why we cannot just completely erase whatever boundaries currently exist on the definition of marriage and say it is a free-for-all where anything goes.
scenario.speaker_context: Councilor Thaddeus assumes that allowing same-sex marriage inevitably leads to absurd extremes (polygamy, bestiality, etc.) without providing evidence that these outcomes are logically connected or likely. He treats a specific policy change as a guaranteed slide into chaos based on fear rather than data.

structure.pattern_description: Thaddeus takes a specific proposal (same-sex marriage) and immediately generalizes it to an extreme, unsupported conclusion (marriage with children, animals, or groups). He assumes that because one boundary is moved, all boundaries must disappear, ignoring the possibility of defined limits between these categories.
structure.formal_form: Event A (redefining marriage to include same-sex couples) is proposed. Therefore, Events B, C, and D (polygamy, bestiality, etc.) will inevitably follow, leading to total chaos.
structure.why_wrong: The argument fails because it assumes a causal link between distinct categories without evidence. Just because the definition of marriage expands to include one new group does not logically necessitate that it must expand to include every conceivable group. It ignores the ability of society to draw rational lines between consensual adult unions and other arrangements.
structure.counterpoint: Change does not automatically mean total loss of structure. Societies frequently update definitions (e.g., voting rights) without collapsing into anarchy or removing all other restrictions.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Thaddeus claims that allowing same-sex marriage means we must also allow marriage between adults and children or animals. Is this conclusion supported by the premise?

rubric.description: Player accepts Thaddeus's fear that 'anything goes' if the definition changes.
Player feels the conclusion is extreme but cannot explain the logical gap.
Player identifies that the speaker is jumping to extremes but labels it simply as 'exaggeration'.
Player identifies the hasty generalization/slippery slope, noting that one change does not prove all boundaries will vanish.

Player fully deconstructs the argument, explaining that the sample of 'one change' does not support the universal conclusion of 'no limits,' and distinguishes between relevant and irrelevant comparisons.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thaddeus insists that once you start changing rules, you can't stop. Can you think of a time when a rule changed but other important rules stayed the same?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Just because we adjust one definition doesn't mean we lose the ability to set other necessary boundaries. Thaddeus is skipping the step where we decide what makes sense.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Alarmist, rigid, prone to catastrophic thinking, speaks with high emotional intensity.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: If we let them do this, what's next? Marrying a horse? A chair? Where does it end?!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully calms the council by pointing out that laws have specific criteria and that expanding rights for one group does not remove the criteria for others.

scenario.context: In the Hall of Public Debate, the player encounters a stubborn citizen named Joe who refuses to update his views on the city's water crisis despite new scientific data. When challenged on his rigidity, Joe defends his stance not with evidence, but by framing his stubbornness as a moral virtue.
scenario.text: Joe stands firm in his principles. 'You admire me,' he declares to the crowd, 'because I do not change my ideas and opinions simply to match what is popular or advantageous. My refusal to listen to these new reports proves my integrity.'
scenario.speaker_context: Joe attempts to bypass the lack of factual support for his views by evoking admiration for his perceived steadfastness. He conflates 'not changing one's mind' with 'having good principles,' ignoring whether the original position was correct.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting an emotional response (admiration for steadfastness) in place of addressing the factual accuracy of the claim. Joe does not discuss the water crisis data; he tries to make the audience feel that questioning him is an attack on integrity.
structure.formal_form: Claim P is unsupported by evidence. Agent evokes emotion F (admiration for consistency). Agent implies P should be accepted because holding it demonstrates virtue F.
structure.why_wrong: Whether Joe is admired for his principles does not determine if his principles are factually correct regarding the water crisis. Stubbornness in the face of contrary evidence is a vice, not a proof of truth. The emotional appeal distracts from the need for evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Consistency is generally a virtue, but only when the initial premise is sound. If the premise is false, consistency is merely stubbornness. Emotions about character do not validate factual claims.

assessment.identification_prompt: Joe wants you to admire his refusal to change his mind. But does his integrity actually prove his facts about the water crisis are correct?

rubric.description: Agrees with Joe because staying true to one's principles is always good and deserves admiration.
Feels that Joe might be right because he seems honorable, but is unsure if that proves his facts.
Notices that Joe didn't mention the water data, but struggles to explain why his 'principles' argument is a fallacy.
Identifies that Joe is using the audience's admiration for his steadfastness to avoid providing evidence for his claims.
Names the appeal to emotion, explains that factual accuracy is independent of the speaker's perceived integrity, and distinguishes between virtuous consistency and stubborn ignorance.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine Joe's principle was that the sky is green. If he refuses to change his mind about that, is he still admirable? Does his refusal make the sky green?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. Admiration for a person's character is separate from the truth of their statements. We must evaluate the water data, not Joe's resolve.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Stubborn, self-righteous, values tradition over innovation, speaks with dramatic flair.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I will not bend like a reed in the wind! A true citizen stands like an oak, even when the storm of 'new facts' blows!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a specific piece of evidence that contradicts Joe's view and explicitly state that 'being steadfast is noble, but being correct requires looking at the evidence.'

scenario.context: The player stands in the muddy town square of Oakhaven during the final hours of the mayoral election. Two candidates are addressing the crowd from a wooden podium. Candidate Elara has just finished presenting her detailed plan for repairing the flood walls, citing engineering reports and budget allocations. Her opponent, Councilor Thorne, steps up to the microphone to offer his rebuttal.
scenario.text: Thorne leans into the mic, sneering at the crowd. 'Do not listen to Elara's fancy charts! Vote for me because the other candidate is a cheat and a liar! She stole bread when she was a child, and everyone knows her family has a history of deceit. How can we trust her with our taxes?'
scenario.speaker_context: Councilor Thorne, a charismatic but aggressive politician known for mudslinging campaigns. He often avoids policy details by attacking his opponents' personal histories.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne attacks Elara's personal character (alleged childhood theft and family history) rather than addressing the substance of her flood wall proposal, such as the engineering reports or budget logic. He attempts to discredit her argument solely by discrediting her person.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X (flood walls need repair via Plan A). Person P has negative trait Q (alleged past dishonesty). Therefore, X is false or should be rejected.
structure.why_wrong: The truth or validity of a policy proposal depends on its evidence, logic, and feasibility, not on the moral character of the person proposing it. Even if Elara had lied in the past, her current engineering data could still be accurate. Thorne provides no counter-evidence to her plan, only an attack on her identity.
structure.counterpoint: Personal character is relevant only if the argument relies entirely on the speaker's testimony or integrity as a premise (e.g., 'You should believe this happened because I saw it'). However, Elara's argument relies on external data (engineering reports), making her personal history irrelevant to the plan's merit.

assessment.identification_prompt: Thorne is making a strong emotional appeal against Elara. But look closely: does he mention anything about the flood wall engineering or the budget? What is the actual basis of his rejection?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne, believing Elara's past makes her plan invalid.
Player feels Thorne is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why his logic is flawed.
Player identifies that Thorne is attacking Elara personally instead of her plan.
Player explains that Elara's past actions do not automatically make her current engineering data false.
Player fully articulates that the argument's validity is independent of the speaker's character and demands evidence regarding the flood walls specifically.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a known liar tells you '2 + 2 = 4', is the math wrong because the person is a liar? Or is the math still correct?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thorne tried to distract the crowd with insults instead of debating the facts. A good leader evaluates the plan, not just the person.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Thorne is loud, interruptive, and relies on fear and anger. He avoids eye contact when asked specific policy questions.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think I'm just being harsh? Look at her record! Would you let a thief hold the keys to the treasury?
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player successfully identifies the fallacy, the crowd murmurs in agreement with the player, and Elara is able to resume her presentation with renewed support. If the player fails, the crowd turns hostile toward Elara, and Thorne gains temporary momentum.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling town square of Oakhaven during the mayoral debate. Candidate Elara Vance has just finished presenting her detailed platform on education reform and infrastructure. Before the moderator can ask the next question, her opponent, Councilor Thorne, steps up to the microphone to respond.
scenario.text: Thorne sneers at the crowd. 'Don't let Elara's fancy words fool you. I knew her back in high school, and she almost flunked out! She can't possibly be a good choice for mayor.'
scenario.speaker_context: Councilor Thorne, a long-serving local politician known for his aggressive campaigning style and reliance on personal anecdotes over policy details.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne attacks Elara's past academic performance in high school rather than addressing her current policy proposals for education and infrastructure. He implies that her past struggles automatically disqualify her from holding office now, ignoring any evidence of growth or the relevance of her current platform.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X (Elara proposes policy changes). Person P has property Q (Elara nearly failed in high school). Therefore, X is false or P is unfit.
structure.why_wrong: A person's past academic struggles do not logically invalidate their current policy ideas or their ability to govern. The merit of Elara's platform must be evaluated on its own facts, logic, and feasibility, not on her high school transcript. Thorne provides no counter-argument to the policies themselves.
structure.counterpoint: Past behavior is only relevant if it directly predicts future failure in a specific, unchangeable way. If the role required a perfect academic record by law, or if Elara claimed 'I never struggled in school,' then Thorne's point would address a factual premise. However, for general leadership capability, past grades are not a definitive predictor.

assessment.identification_prompt: Thorne is trying to make you doubt Elara. But look closely: did he mention anything about her actual plans for the city, or did he only talk about her past?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne, believing that past failure means future inability to lead.
Player feels Thorne is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why his logic is flawed.
Player identifies that Thorne is attacking Elara personally instead of her ideas.
Player explains that high school performance is irrelevant to current policy proposals and notes the lack of counter-evidence.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, distinguishing between character attacks and policy evaluation, and articulates why the argument fails logically regardless of Elara's past.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if someone struggled in math ten years ago, does that mean they can't manage a city budget today? What evidence did Thorne give against the actual plan?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thorne ignored the substance of Elara's argument. Her high school record doesn't prove her current policies are bad. You've spotted the distraction.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Thorne is blustery, dismissive, and relies on emotional manipulation rather than facts. He gets defensive when pressed on policy details.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think grades matter? In the real world, losers stay losers. I'm the only one with real experience here!
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player correctly identifies the fallacy, Thorne stammers and is forced to pivot to a weak policy point, lowering his approval rating. If the player fails, the crowd murmurs in agreement with Thorne, boosting his momentum.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling cafeteria of the Academy, where a debate on school lunch regulations is taking place. Charlie, a student health advocate, has just presented statistics on sodium and sugar content in the current menu. Before the player can respond to the data, Bob, a known prankster who often skips meals, jumps into the conversation.
scenario.text:
Charlie: Fast food is filled with salt, fat and added sugars. We need better regulation of the industry.
Bob: That may be, but you're such a hypocrite! I saw you devour a Triple-Baconator, super-sized fries and 64 ounces of soda yesterday.
scenario.speaker_context: Bob, a charismatic but logically inconsistent student who prefers deflection over engaging with difficult topics. He often uses personal attacks to win arguments when he lacks counter-evidence.

structure.pattern_description: Bob avoids addressing Charlie's argument about the need for industry regulation based on health data. Instead, he attacks Charlie's personal consistency by pointing out Charlie's own recent consumption of fast food. He implies that because Charlie acted inconsistently with their argument, the argument itself must be false.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P has acted in a way inconsistent with X. Therefore, X is false or should be dismissed.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a claim (that fast food is unhealthy and needs regulation) is independent of the speaker's personal behavior. A smoker can correctly argue that smoking causes cancer; similarly, Charlie can correctly argue for regulation even if they occasionally eat unhealthy food. Bob provides no evidence against the salt, fat, or sugar content, nor against the need for regulation.
structure.counterpoint: Personal consistency is relevant when the argument relies entirely on the speaker's moral authority or specific expertise as a premise (e.g., 'You should do exactly as I do because I am perfect'). However, when the argument is based on objective facts (like nutritional content), the speaker's hypocrisy does not invalidate those facts.

assessment.identification_prompt: Bob seems very eager to point out Charlie's lunch choices. But look closely: did Bob actually say anything about the salt, fat, or sugar levels Charlie mentioned? Or did he just talk about Charlie?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Bob, concluding that Charlie is wrong because they are a hypocrite.
Player feels Bob is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why his logic fails regarding the regulation issue.
Player identifies that Bob is attacking Charlie personally instead of the argument, but struggles to separate the person from the claim.
Player clearly states that Charlie's eating habits do not change the factual content about salt and sugar in fast food.
Player explicitly names the 'Tu Quoque' fallacy, explains that the validity of the data is independent of the speaker's actions, and reiterates the original evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a doctor who smokes tells you smoking is bad, is the doctor lying about the health risks? Does their habit change the medical facts?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Charlie's lunch yesterday doesn't magically remove the salt from today's burgers. Bob distracted everyone from the real data. Good catch!

game_hooks.npc_personality: Deflective, quick-witted, avoids accountability, uses social pressure to silence opponents.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Oh, so now you're the health police? Did you forget your own tray yesterday, or are you just trying to look good?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player successfully isolates the factual claim from the personal attack, forcing Bob to either address the data or retreat. This unlocks the 'Logic Shield' achievement.

scenario.text: Elara frowns at the patient's chart. 'We know that if someone eats fast food for dinner, they get a stomach ache in the evening. This patient has a stomach ache this evening. Therefore, they must have eaten fast food for dinner.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara is a diligent but inexperienced healer who often confuses correlation or sufficient conditions with necessary ones. She assumes the known cause is the only possible cause.

structure.formal_form: If P then Q. Not P. Therefore not Q.
structure.why_wrong: The conditional statement only establishes that eating fast food is a sufficient condition for a stomach ache, not a necessary one. Other factors (like a virus, spicy non-fast food, or stress) could also cause a stomach ache. Denying the antecedent (not eating fast food) does not guarantee the denial of the consequent (no stomach ache).
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would only be valid if the rule was biconditional: 'You get a stomach ache if and only if you eat fast food.' Since other causes exist, the conclusion does not follow.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elara is confident that avoiding fast food guarantees no pain. Look at her logic: does the absence of the specific cause (fast food) truly rule out the effect (stomach ache)?

rubric.description: Agrees with Elara; believes no fast food means no stomach ache.
Suspects Elara might be wrong but isn't sure why.
Realizes other things could cause a stomach ache, but doesn't name the logical flaw.
Identifies that Elara treats a sufficient condition as if it were necessary.
Correctly identifies 'Denying the Antecedent', explains that P is sufficient but not necessary for Q, and notes that ~P does not imply ~Q.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about the last time you had a stomach ache. Was it always because of fast food? What else could cause it?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. If the rule were 'Only fast food causes stomach aches,' she would be right. But since it's just 'If fast food, then ache,' her logic fails. How would you phrase the rule to make her logic valid?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest, rule-bound, slightly anxious about making mistakes, relies heavily on simplified heuristics.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But the book says if you eat the bad food, you get sick! So if you didn't eat the bad food, you can't be sick! Right?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player provides an alternative cause for the stomach ache (e.g., 'I ate spoiled fruit'), proving Elara's deduction false and teaching her about necessary vs sufficient conditions.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling town square of Veridia during a festival. They encounter Grum, a grumpy old baker known for his sour disposition, arguing with a group of young travelers near the fountain.
scenario.text: Grum points a flour-dusted finger at the crowd. 'Don't listen to their promises! Democrats are all gay, and Republicans are all rich. That's just how they are, every single one of them. You can't trust a word from either side because they're all exactly the same.'
scenario.speaker_context: Grum has likely encountered a few vocal individuals from each party or seen sensationalized news clips. He is taking specific traits observed in a small, non-representative sample (or stereotypes) and applying them universally to entire political populations comprising millions of diverse individuals.

structure.pattern_description: Grum asserts universal properties ('all Democrats are gay', 'all Republicans are rich') based on an insufficient and likely biased sample. He ignores the vast diversity within both political parties, where members hold a wide range of sexual orientations and economic statuses. The sample size (his limited personal experiences or media consumption) is negligible compared to the population size (millions of voters).
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of group G having property P (where n is very small relative to the total size of G). Therefore, all members of G have property P.
structure.why_wrong: Political parties are massive coalitions of individuals with diverse backgrounds. Claiming every single member shares a specific demographic trait (like sexual orientation or wealth status) is statistically impossible and factually incorrect. The conclusion leaps far beyond what the evidence (a few examples or stereotypes) can support.
structure.counterpoint: While political parties may have demographic trends or platforms that attract certain groups, stating that 'all' members share a specific personal attribute is a logical error. Valid generalizations require representative sampling and acknowledge exceptions; absolute claims about large populations are almost always false.

assessment.identification_prompt: Grum claims that every Democrat is gay and every Republican is rich based on his observations. Is this conclusion logically sound?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Grum, accepting the stereotypes as absolute facts about both parties.
Player feels the statement is unfair or mean but cannot explain the logical flaw in the reasoning.
Player identifies that not everyone fits these descriptions but fails to name the specific logical error regarding sample size.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, noting that Grum is applying traits from a few individuals to millions of people without sufficient evidence.

Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, explaining that the sample is unrepresentative and too small to support a universal claim, and highlights the diversity within political groups that invalidates the absolute statement.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Grum seems very sure of himself. But think about the number of people in these parties. Could just a few examples really define millions of people?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Grum is taking a tiny slice of reality and pretending it represents the whole pie. That's a classic hasty generalization.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Grum is cynical, set in his ways, and relies on stereotypes rather than data. He speaks with absolute certainty despite having limited knowledge.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! Don't try to tell me about nuance, kid. I know what I see!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to challenge Grum with logic to gain 'Critical Thinking' XP and potentially soften his stance, or ignore him to avoid a tedious argument.

scenario.context: In the High Court of Veridia, a debate is underway regarding the ethics of capital punishment. A citizen named Elara argues against the death penalty, emphasizing the sanctity of all human life. The Royal Prosecutor, Lord Vane, rises to rebut her.
scenario.text: Lord Vane declares: 'What I object to most about those like Elara who oppose capital punishment is that they believe the lives of convicted murderers are more important than the lives of the police and prison guards who protect us. But, obviously, since the lives of those who protect us are of the greatest value, no one should oppose capital punishment.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara argued that taking life is inherently wrong, regardless of the crime. Lord Vane recharacterized her stance as valuing murderers' lives *more* than protectors' lives, an extreme hierarchy she never claimed, and attacked that fabrication.

structure.pattern_description: Lord Vane distorts Elara's opposition to capital punishment (based on moral principle) into a claim that she values murderers' lives above protectors' lives. He then attacks this fabricated hierarchy to conclude her position is invalid.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (opposition to execution). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (believing murderers > protectors). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position has been refuted.
structure.why_wrong: Opposing capital punishment does not logically imply believing murderers are more valuable than police. One can believe all life is sacred (equal value) and still oppose execution. Vane attacks a value judgment Elara never made.
structure.counterpoint: Elara could reply: 'I never said murderers' lives are more important. I said taking any life is wrong. Valuing the sanctity of life applies to everyone, including the guards you mention. Please address my actual argument about morality, not a fake hierarchy you invented.'

assessment.identification_prompt: How has Lord Vane misrepresented Elara's argument against capital punishment?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane or fails to see any issue with his reasoning.
Player feels Vane is being unfair or aggressive but cannot identify the logical error.
Player notices Vane changed Elara's argument but describes it vaguely as 'twisting words' without specifying the false hierarchy.
Player identifies that Vane falsely claimed Elara values murderers over protectors, and that this extreme view is not what she actually argued.
Player explicitly names the Straw Man fallacy, explains that opposing execution does not equal ranking lives, and reconstructs Elara's actual premise of equal sanctity of life.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at what Elara actually said versus what Vane claims she believes. Did she ever say murderers are MORE important than guards?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. Vane built a 'straw man' by inventing a cruel comparison Elara never made, making her easy to knock down.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Lord Vane is an aggressive, rhetorical prosecutor who relies on emotional manipulation and caricature rather than precise logic. He speaks with booming confidence.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: So you side with the killers over the keepers of peace? Is that your justice?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that clarify Elara's actual stance on the equality of life, forcing Vane to either address the real argument or retreat.

scenario.context: In the Hall of Ethics, Student Ashley confronts her peer Hannah regarding a recent scandal involving infidelity. The conversation shifts from the specific act to the nature of morality itself.
scenario.text: Ashley: It is morally wrong to cheat on your spouse; why on earth would you have done that? Hannah: But what is morality exactly? Ashley: It's a code of conduct shared by cultures. Hannah: But who creates this code? If we say it's wrong just because a culture says so, then if a culture decided cheating was good, it would be good. That means morality is arbitrary and meaningless!
scenario.speaker_context: Hannah does not address Ashley's definition or provide a counter-argument to the cultural basis of morality. Instead, she rejects the definition because accepting it would lead to the undesirable conclusion that morality is arbitrary.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a definition or factual claim must be false because accepting it would lead to undesirable, absurd, or uncomfortable consequences.
structure.formal_form: If Claim P were true, then Consequence C (which is bad/absurd) would follow. Therefore, Claim P is false.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a claim (or the validity of a definition) is independent of whether we like the implications. Unpleasant consequences do not make a fact false; they only make the reality difficult to accept.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to worry about the implications of a theory for our worldview, but those worries cannot serve as logical proof that the theory is incorrect. One must address the evidence or reasoning directly.

assessment.identification_prompt: Hannah seems distressed by where Ashley's definition might lead. Is she proving the definition wrong, or just showing she dislikes the result?

rubric.description: Agrees with Hannah; believes the definition must be wrong because it leads to absurdity.
Senses something is off but thinks Hannah is just being difficult or philosophical.
Notices Hannah focuses on the outcome ('morality is meaningless') rather than Ashley's actual argument.
Identifies that Hannah rejects the definition solely because she dislikes the consequence of it being arbitrary.
Explicitly names the Appeal to Consequences and explains that the unpleasantness of a conclusion does not invalidate the premise.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine a doctor tells you a diagnosis is serious. Would saying 'That can't be true because it would mean I'm very sick' make the diagnosis false?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: If the consequence is indeed absurd, how should one properly refute the claim without falling into this fallacy?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, intellectualizing, prone to sophistry when cornered.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But if we accept that, then nothing matters! Surely that proves the definition is flawed!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out that Hannah is arguing from fear of the conclusion rather than evidence against the definition, unlocking the 'Logic Shield' achievement.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling market square of Oakhaven, where a distressed merchant named Elias is frantically scratching his head while shouting at a crowd gathered around his shoe stall.
scenario.text: I bought these new leather shoes this morning, and immediately after putting them on, my head started itching terribly! It must be the shoes; I am clearly allergic to them!
scenario.speaker_context: Elias is a superstitious merchant who often jumps to conclusions based on timing alone. He has ignored other potential causes for his itching, such as eating shellfish for lunch, walking through poison ivy, or seasonal pollen, focusing solely on the most recent event (buying shoes) because it happened right before the symptom.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Elias observes that Event A (buying/wearing shoes) occurred immediately before Event B (head itching) and concludes that A caused B. This is a classic 'post hoc' fallacy. The temporal sequence does not prove causation. The itching could be caused by an unrelated third factor (common cause) or pure coincidence, especially since shoes touching feet rarely cause immediate head itching without other systemic symptoms.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, A caused B. (Flaw: Temporal succession does not imply causal connection.)
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes causation based solely on the order of events. It fails to consider alternative explanations (e.g., allergens in food, environment, or pre-existing conditions) or the lack of a plausible biological mechanism connecting new shoes directly to immediate head itching.
structure.counterpoint: While temporal precedence is a necessary condition for causation (the cause must happen before the effect), it is not sufficient. To establish causation, one must also demonstrate a plausible mechanism, consistency across trials, and the elimination of confounding variables. For example, if Elias wore the shoes ten times without issue and only itched after eating strawberries, the strawberries would be the more likely cause despite the shoes being worn simultaneously.

assessment.identification_prompt: Analyze Elias's claim. Does the fact that his head started itching after he put on new shoes prove the shoes are the cause? Identify the logical flaw in his reasoning.

rubric.description: Fails to identify any logical error; accepts Elias's conclusion that the shoes definitely caused the itching.
Suspects the reasoning is weak but cannot articulate why; offers vague doubts like 'maybe not' without explaining the fallacy.
Identifies that timing alone isn't proof but struggles to name the specific fallacy or suggest concrete alternative causes.
Correctly identifies the 'post hoc' fallacy and explains that correlation in time does not equal causation, offering at least one alternative cause.

Comprehensively deconstructs the argument: names the fallacy, explains the lack of mechanistic link between shoes and head itching, and lists multiple plausible alternative causes (e.g., diet, environment).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If you sneeze right after a clock strikes noon, did the clock cause the sneeze? What other things happened before your head started itching?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent deduction. Just because B follows A doesn't mean A caused B. Can you think of a scenario where checking for a common cause (like what he ate for lunch) would solve the mystery faster than blaming the shoes?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, hasty, and prone to superstition. Elias speaks quickly and gestures wildly, often jumping to the most dramatic conclusion available.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's the leather, I tell you! The curse of the tanner! My head burns the moment they touch my feet! Burn the stock before we all perish!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to calm Elias down by suggesting he check his lunch menu or the pollen count. Successfully identifying the fallacy prevents Elias from destroying his own merchandise and unlocks a discount on future purchases as a thank you.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Portmere, a traveling merchant is trying to sell a dubious 'elixir of vitality' to a crowd of skeptical townsfolk.
scenario.text: An attempt to gain a customer's trust in an advertisement is referred to as relying on the speaker's status: 'This tonic is guaranteed to cure all ailments because it was endorsed by General Thorne, the greatest military commander in the kingdom! If a hero of his stature says it works, it must be true.'
scenario.speaker_context: General Thorne is a celebrated military strategist with no training in medicine, chemistry, or biology. His expertise lies in warfare, not pharmacology.

structure.pattern_description: The merchant appeals to General Thorne's authority as a military commander to validate the medical efficacy of a tonic, a field outside the General's expertise.
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is expert in domain D. P is in domain D*. Therefore P is true. (But D ≠ D*.)
structure.why_wrong: An authority's prestige in one domain (military strategy) does not transfer automatically to unrelated domains (medicine). The General's opinion is influential but not evidence of the tonic's medical properties.
structure.counterpoint: Appealing to authority is not always fallacious. Citing a renowned royal physician on the tonic's ingredients would be reasonable. The fallacy lies specifically in the mismatch between the authority's expertise and the claim being made.

assessment.identification_prompt: The merchant cites a famous General to prove the medicine works. What exactly is the General an expert in, and does that match the product being sold?

rubric.description: Accepts the General's endorsement as proof the medicine works because he is a hero.
Is unsure why the General's opinion might not be enough but suspects something is off.
Notices the General is a soldier, not a doctor, but cannot explain why that invalidates the claim.
Identifies that the General's expertise is in war, not medicine, making his endorsement irrelevant to the cure.
Names the appeal to irrelevant authority, explains the domain mismatch between military command and pharmacology, and articulates when citing authority is legitimate.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Suppose the General told you how to win a battle. Would you trust him? Now he's telling you how to cure a fever. Is his expertise the same in both cases?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: What if the General actually studied herbalism during his campaigns? Does that change the weight of his opinion, or do we still need a dedicated medical expert?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Boastful, fast-talking, and reliant on social proof rather than facts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Who are you to question the word of General Thorne? Have you seen his statues? Buy the tonic!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player points out the domain mismatch; the merchant stammers and lowers the price or admits he has no medical proof.

scenario.context: The player enters the Town Watch barracks where Officer Grum is interrogating a nervous suspect named Tim regarding a recent arson. Tim is trying to talk his way out of custody using a clever-sounding but flawed argument.
scenario.text: Officer Grum states, 'We suspect several people of setting the fire.' Tim immediately replies, 'Therefore, I can't be under suspicion because I was alone all night.'
scenario.speaker_context: Tim is a nervous citizen trying to use wordplay to escape police scrutiny. He is conflating two different meanings of the word 'suspicion': the state of being suspected by others (passive) versus the act of suspecting others (active). He argues that because he wasn't actively suspecting others (due to being alone), he cannot be passively suspected by the police.

structure.pattern_description: The argument relies on shifting the meaning of the word 'suspicion.' In the premise ('We suspect several people'), 'suspect' is used as a verb meaning 'to believe someone is guilty.' In the conclusion ('I can't be under suspicion'), 'suspicion' refers to the status of being a suspect. Tim falsely implies that being 'alone' prevents one from being the object of suspicion, perhaps confusing 'suspecting others' with 'being suspected.'
structure.formal_form: Term T is used with meaning M1 in the premise (active suspicion of others). Term T is used with meaning M2 in the conclusion (passive status of being suspected). The argument assumes M1 implies not-M2, which is a category error.
structure.why_wrong: The fact that Tim was alone (and thus could not be actively suspecting others or participating in a group suspicion) has no logical bearing on whether the police suspect him of the crime. The police's suspicion is an external judgment based on evidence, not on Tim's social activities or his own mental state of suspecting others.
structure.counterpoint: A clearer version of this fallacy would be: 'The bank has rivers and money. I sat by the river, so I am at the bank.' Here, 'bank' shifts from a financial institution to a river edge, just as 'suspicion' shifts from an active mental state to a passive legal status.

assessment.identification_prompt: Tim claims his alibi of being 'alone' proves he cannot be 'under suspicion.' Is his reasoning valid? Identify the word that changes meaning.

rubric.description: Player accepts Tim's argument as logical or believes being alone automatically clears suspicion.
Player feels the argument is weak but cannot explain why being alone is irrelevant.
Player identifies that 'suspicion' is the key word but struggles to define the two different meanings.
Player explains that Tim confuses 'suspecting others' (which requires company) with 'being suspected by the police' (which can happen regardless of being alone).
Player fully articulates the equivocation: The police's active suspicion of Tim is independent of Tim's solitary status, rendering the conclusion non-sequitur.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: If you are alone in a room, can someone outside that room still think you committed a crime? Does your isolation stop them from suspecting you?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Tim is playing with words. The police suspect him (verb), but he argues about his own state of mind or activity (noun/gerund). Being alone doesn't make you invisible to an investigation.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Tim is slippery, anxious, and tries to use big words to sound smarter than he is. He speaks quickly to confuse the listener.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's simple logic, officer! You can't suspect a lone wolf of a pack crime! I was solitary, therefore I am innocent of your collective suspicion!
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player exposes the fallacy, Officer Grum sees through Tim's trick and presses for real evidence. If the player fails, Tim is temporarily released due to 'lack of logical cause,' only to be caught later with concrete evidence.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling market square of Oakhaven, where a nervous merchant named Silas is frantically packing his cart while shouting warnings to passersby about the local wildlife.
scenario.text: Silas points a shaking finger at a stray dog chewing on a bone nearby. 'I saw that dog eat chicken just now! It proves my theory: all dogs must only eat chicken. If you feed them anything else, you are inviting disaster!'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas has observed a single instance of one dog eating chicken and has immediately concluded that this dietary restriction applies to every dog in existence.

structure.pattern_description: Silas observes one specific instance (a single dog eating chicken) and extrapolates a universal rule ('all dogs must only eat chicken') based on this insufficient sample size. He ignores the vast diversity of canine diets and the likelihood that this specific dog simply happened to be eating chicken at that moment.
structure.formal_form: Observed 1 instance of X having property Q. Therefore, all members of population X have property Q exclusively.
structure.why_wrong: A sample size of one is statistically insignificant and cannot support a universal claim about an entire species. The observation is anecdotal and fails to account for counter-examples (dogs eating beef, vegetables, or kibble) which are common knowledge.
structure.counterpoint: While patterns can emerge from single striking events, a valid generalization requires a representative sample size large enough to rule out coincidence or unique circumstances. One data point is never enough for a universal 'all' statement.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas claims that because he saw one dog eat chicken, all dogs must only eat chicken. Is his conclusion logically sound based on the evidence provided?

rubric.description: Player accepts Silas's warning as absolute truth and avoids feeding dogs anything but chicken.
Player feels unsure but suspects Silas might be exaggerating without knowing why.
Player recognizes that one dog is not enough to judge all dogs but struggles to name the specific logical error.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, noting that a sample size of one cannot support a claim about an entire species.

Player fully deconstructs the argument, explaining that the single observation is anecdotal, ignores known biological diversity in canine diets, and incorrectly uses an existential quantifier to form a universal exclusive rule.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Are you sure one dog represents every dog in the world? What about the dogs you've seen eating kibble or bones?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Silas is jumping to a conclusion based on a single data point. One example doesn't make a rule for the whole group.

scenario.context: The player enters the dimly lit observatory of Astrologer Thorne, who is frantically scribbling notes in a large leather-bound journal. He looks exhausted, with dark circles under his eyes, convinced he has discovered a cosmic secret that controls the heavens.
scenario.text: Thorne slams his quill down and points a trembling finger at the window where the sun has just dipped below the horizon. 'I have tracked the movements of the great celestial orb for years,' he declares with manic intensity. 'The pattern is undeniable and repeats every single day without fail: Every time I go to sleep, the sun goes down. Therefore, my going to sleep causes the sun to set! If I were to stay awake forever, the sun would never set, and we would have eternal day. My fatigue is the engine of the night!'
scenario.speaker_context: Astrologer Thorne has observed a perfect temporal correlation between his own action (falling asleep) and a natural event (sunset). Because his bedtime roughly coincides with dusk, he has erroneously concluded that his personal action is the cause of the planetary rotation, ignoring the vast difference in scale and the actual astronomical mechanisms.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne observes that event B (sun setting) consistently follows event A (him going to sleep) and infers that A causes B. This is a classic post hoc ergo propter hoc ('after this, therefore because of this') error. He fails to recognize that both events are caused by a third factor (the Earth's rotation relative to the sun) and that his sleep schedule is merely adapted to the light cycle, not the driver of it.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurs. Event B occurs after A. Therefore, A causes B. (Flaw: Temporal succession does not imply causation; a common cause or coincidence may be responsible.)
structure.why_wrong: Correlation in time does not equal causation. Thorne has not demonstrated a mechanism by which his consciousness closing could stop a star's apparent motion. He ignores the obvious common cause: the time of day dictates both when the sun sets and when humans typically feel tired and go to sleep.
structure.counterpoint: To prove causation, one would need to show that preventing A (staying awake) prevents B (the sun setting), or provide a plausible physical mechanism. Since the sun sets regardless of whether Thorne sleeps, stays awake, or leaves the planet, the causal link is nonexistent. This is distinct from valid causal inference where controlled experiments isolate variables.

assessment.identification_prompt: Astrologer Thorne believes his sleep causes the sunset. Identify the logical flaw in his reasoning and explain why the correlation he observed does not prove causation.

rubric.description: The player accepts Thorne's conclusion or fails to identify any logical error.
The player states that Thorne is wrong but cannot explain why, or offers an irrelevant objection.
The player identifies that correlation does not equal causation but does not specify the actual cause or the direction of the relationship.
The player correctly identifies the post hoc fallacy and explains that the Earth's rotation (or time of day) is the common cause for both the sunset and the urge to sleep.

The player provides a comprehensive rebuttal: identifies the fallacy, explains the common cause (Earth's rotation), and notes that the causal direction is likely reversed (sunset causes sleepiness) or that the events are independent effects of a third variable.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne insists, 'But it happens every single night! How can it be a coincidence if the pattern never breaks?' Consider: Does the sun set on nights when you are already asleep? Does it set if someone else stays awake?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Precisely. Thorne has confused the sequence of events with the cause of events. Just because B follows A doesn't mean A made B happen. Often, a third factor C causes both.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Manic, sleep-deprived, overly confident in superficial patterns, prone to magical thinking.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't you see? If I drink enough coffee to stay awake, I can hold back the night forever! The fate of the realm rests on my eyelids!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must convince Thorne to test his theory by staying awake for one night (or observing that the sun sets even when he is unconscious) to break his delusion and restore his health.
