scenario.context: The player enters the infirmary of the Ironvale Keep. A young squire, Pippin, is lying in bed looking pale and green, clutching his stomach. The Head Healer is shaking her head at a half-eaten box of dark chocolate cookies on the bedside table.
scenario.text: Pippin groans and points a trembling finger at the cookie box. 'I ate those Oreos last night, Master Healer, and then I was sick the next day. It must have been the Oreos that caused my sickness! Ban them from the keep before everyone else falls ill!'
scenario.speaker_context: Pippin is a dramatic but well-meaning squire who recently attended a large feast where he consumed spoiled roast boar, three types of cheese, and the cookies. He has latched onto the most recent item he consumed as the sole cause of his illness, ignoring the timing of the other foods and the incubation period of food poisoning.

structure.pattern_description: Pippin observes that event A (eating Oreos) happened before event B (getting sick) and concludes that A caused B. This is the classic 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' error. He fails to consider alternative causes (the spoiled boar), the possibility of coincidence, or that the Oreos might be unrelated to the timing of his symptoms.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, Event A caused Event B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession does not prove causation. Just because the sickness followed the cookies does not mean the cookies caused it. Pippin has ignored confounding variables (the spoiled meat eaten earlier) and lacks evidence linking the specific ingredient to the specific illness.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one needs more than just sequence. We would need to see if others who ate only Oreos got sick, if those who ate the boar but not Oreos got sick, or if there is a known biological mechanism where Oreos cause immediate next-day sickness in this context. Without ruling out the spoiled boar, the conclusion is premature.

assessment.identification_prompt: Analyze Pippin's reasoning. Is his conclusion that the Oreos caused his sickness logically sound based solely on the fact that he ate them before getting sick? What other explanations might exist?

rubric.description: The player accepts Pippin's conclusion without question or suggests banning the cookies immediately.
The player suspects something is wrong but cannot articulate why the timing alone is insufficient proof.
The player identifies that other foods were eaten but struggles to name the specific logical fallacy or explain the principle of correlation vs. causation.
The player correctly identifies the 'post hoc' fallacy, notes the confounding variable (spoiled boar), and explains that sequence does not equal causation.

The player provides a comprehensive rebuttal, identifying the fallacy, listing multiple alternative causes (boar, cheese, virus), and proposing a method to test the hypothesis (e.g., checking if other cookie-eaters are sick) before acting.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Pippin looks relieved. 'Exactly! We must burn the rest of the batch!' He throws the box into the fire. Later, three other squires who ate the boar but not the cookies fall violently ill, proving the cookies were innocent.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The Healer nods approvingly. 'Sharp eyes, adventurer. Pippin also ate the questionable boar stew. The cookies are likely fine; it was the meat that turned. Good thing we didn't ban the keep's favorite treat based on a hunch.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dramatic, hasty, prone to jumping to conclusions, loyal but easily misled by surface-level patterns.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It happened right after! That proves it!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Pippin and the Healer to investigate the feast menu rather than punishing the baker, preventing a morale drop in the keep.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling hallway of the Grand Academy during a faculty meeting. Professor Cari has just presented a detailed whitepaper arguing that the current curriculum is outdated and requires a major overhaul to include modern critical thinking modules. The room is silent until Headmaster Thorne, known for his traditionalist views, steps forward to respond.
scenario.text: Thorne chuckles dismissively, waving Cari's paper away. 'Why should we listen to Cari's demands for a major overhaul in education? Let's be honest: Cari gets a speeding ticket every other week! If she can't even learn how to drive properly, maybe she should focus on that instead of worrying about our schools.'
scenario.speaker_context: Headmaster Thorne, a stern and traditional administrator who values order and conformity. He often deflects substantive criticism by focusing on the personal flaws or unrelated habits of his staff.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne rejects Cari's argument for educational reform not by addressing the evidence in her whitepaper, but by pointing out her unrelated personal failure (getting speeding tickets). He implies that her inability to drive well disqualifies her from having valid opinions on education.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X (Education needs overhaul). Person P has property Q (Bad driving record). Property Q is irrelevant to X. Therefore, X is false or should be ignored.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of an argument about education policy depends on the evidence, logic, and data presented, not on the personal habits of the person presenting it. Cari's driving skills are completely irrelevant to her expertise in pedagogy or the merits of her proposed curriculum changes. Thorne provides zero counter-arguments to the actual proposal.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if they directly impact the person's ability to perform the specific task argued about. If Cari were arguing that 'No one needs driving lessons because I am a perfect driver,' then her ticket record would be a valid counter-evidence. However, since she is arguing about school curriculum, her driving is irrelevant.

assessment.identification_prompt: Headmaster Thorne seems very confident in his dismissal. But look closely: does he mention a single point from Cari's whitepaper? What is the actual reason he gives for ignoring her proposal?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne, believing that bad drivers cannot be trusted to fix schools.
Player feels Thorne is being mean or unfair to Cari but cannot explain the logical error.
Player identifies that Thorne is attacking Cari personally instead of her argument.
Player explicitly states that driving skills are irrelevant to educational policy and that the proposal was not addressed.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, explaining that the truth of the claim is independent of the claimant's unrelated personal flaws, and demands evidence regarding the curriculum itself.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if a famous scientist who jaywalks discovers a new cure for a disease, does their bad walking habit make the cure ineffective? Focus on the link between the person and the claim.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thorne committed an ad hominem fallacy. He attacked the messenger (Cari's driving) to avoid dealing with the message (the need for educational reform). A strong leader would address the whitepaper's data, not the author's tickets.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, traditionalist, prone to deflection, uses sarcasm to mask lack of counter-arguments.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's simple logic, player! Would you take navigation advice from someone who crashes their cart weekly? Same principle!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player can choose to 'Expose Fallacy' to gain respect from progressive faculty, 'Support Thorne' to gain favor with traditionalists but lose logic XP, or 'Redirect to Data' to force Thorne to address the whitepaper.

scenario.context: The player enters the damp, stone-walled infirmary of the Ironvale keep. A young squire, visibly pale and shivering, sits on a cot clutching an empty glass bottle. He is arguing heatedly with the head healer, insisting that the town's water supply is cursed.
scenario.text: I drank bottled water and now I am sick, so the water must have made me sick.
scenario.speaker_context: The squire drank from a sealed bottle of water immediately before symptoms of a stomach virus appeared. However, the incubation period for the virus circulating in the barracks is 24 hours, meaning he was infected long before drinking the water. The timing is coincidental, not causal.

structure.pattern_description: The squire observes that event A (drinking water) happened immediately before event B (getting sick) and concludes that A caused B. This ignores the possibility of a prior cause (infection yesterday), coincidence, or other factors. It assumes temporal succession implies causation.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, A caused B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal sequence does not prove causation. Just because the sickness followed the drinking does not mean the drinking caused the sickness. The squire fails to consider the incubation period of illnesses or other potential causes that existed prior to drinking the water.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one must rule out coincidence and alternative explanations. For example, if everyone who drank that specific bottle got sick while those who didn't remained healthy, causation would be more likely. Here, the known incubation period of the local virus provides a stronger alternative explanation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Analyze the squire's statement. Does the fact that he got sick after drinking the water prove the water made him sick? Identify the logical flaw in his reasoning.

rubric.description: Fails to identify any logical error; agrees that the water definitely caused the sickness.
Suspects the reasoning is weak but cannot articulate why; offers vague doubts about the water.
Identifies that timing alone isn't proof but struggles to name the fallacy or suggest an alternative cause.
Correctly identifies the 'post hoc' error and suggests that the sickness could have started before drinking the water.
Perfectly identifies the False Cause fallacy, explains that correlation/temporal sequence != causation, and cites the incubation period as the likely alternative explanation.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about viruses you've had before. Do you feel sick the exact second you catch a germ, or is there a delay? How does that delay change what made the squire sick?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Just because B followed A doesn't mean A caused B. This is the 'Post Hoc' fallacy. The squire ignored the incubation period. How might you explain this to him without making him feel foolish?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, young, and convinced of a conspiracy; prone to jumping to conclusions when frightened.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It has to be the water! I took one sip and boom! My stomach turned. We need to boil all the wells immediately!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince the squire to rest and wait for the healer's diagnosis rather than panicking the town about the water supply, preventing unnecessary resource waste.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Oakhaven, a group of merchants is debating the viability of Tim's new home-based internet venture. A skeptical merchant, Barnaby, tries to shut down the conversation by attacking Tim's status rather than his business plan.
scenario.text: Barnaby scoffs at the crowd: 'Why doesn't Tim get a real job like normal people instead of trying to launch that Internet business from home? Only fools work outside the established guilds.'
scenario.speaker_context: Barnaby is a traditionalist who equates 'normalcy' and guild membership with competence. He implies that because Tim is not following the standard path (authority of tradition/normality), his business idea must be invalid.

structure.pattern_description: Barnaby dismisses Tim's business idea solely because it deviates from the 'normal' path of employment endorsed by societal tradition. He treats the consensus of 'normal people' as an infallible authority on business success.
structure.formal_form: Group G (normal people) does X. Person P does Y (where Y != X). Therefore, Y is invalid or foolish.
structure.why_wrong: The fact that most people follow a certain path (traditional employment) does not make alternative paths (entrepreneurship) invalid. Popularity or tradition is not a reliable metric for the success of a specific business venture.
structure.counterpoint: Appealing to common practice can be a useful heuristic for safety, but it is a fallacy when used to dismiss innovation or unique circumstances without evidence. Many successful businesses started exactly where Tim is now.

assessment.identification_prompt: Barnaby claims Tim is wrong because he isn't doing what 'normal people' do. Is being 'normal' a valid measure of whether a business idea will succeed?

rubric.description: Agrees with Barnaby that Tim should just get a normal job.
Feels Barnaby is being mean but cannot explain the logical error.
Notices that 'normal people' aren't necessarily experts on internet business.
Identifies that Barnaby is appealing to the authority of tradition/normality rather than addressing the business plan.
Clearly articulates that the prevalence of a behavior (getting a real job) does not prove the falsity of an alternative (starting a business), identifying the irrelevant appeal to authority.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone jumped off a bridge because it was 'normal,' would that make it a good idea? How is Tim's situation similar?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: If Tim had no plan and was just playing games all day, would Barnaby's comment still be a fallacy, or would it become sound advice? Where is the line?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Grumpy Traditionalist, risk-averse, values stability over innovation.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Back in my day, we didn't have 'internet businesses.' We had trades, and we stuck to them!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player points out that innovation often comes from those who don't follow the herd, prompting Barnaby to grudgingly admit he needs to see Tim's actual business plan before judging.

scenario.context: The player enters the dimly lit observatory of Astrologer Thorne, who has been staring intently at a star chart and a sleep log. He looks up with wild eyes, convinced he has discovered a cosmic secret that controls the heavens.
scenario.text: Every time I go to sleep, the sun goes down. Therefore, my going to sleep causes the sun to set.
scenario.speaker_context: Astrologer Thorne has noticed a perfect temporal correlation between his personal action (falling asleep) and a natural event (sunset). Because his sleep always precedes or coincides with the sunset in his observation log, he erroneously concludes his action is the cause of the celestial event, ignoring the Earth's rotation.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne observes that Event A (him sleeping) consistently happens around the same time as Event B (the sun setting). He infers that A causes B simply because they occur together or in sequence. This ignores the possibility of a common cause (Earth's rotation), reverse causation, or mere coincidence. In this case, the correlation is real but the causal direction is completely reversed or non-existent; his sleep does not drive the sun.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurs with/before Event B. Therefore, A causes B. (Flaw: Correlation or sequence does not imply causation; C may cause both, or B may cause A, or it is coincidental.)
structure.why_wrong: The fallacy lies in assuming that because two events are correlated or sequential, one must cause the other. Thorne fails to consider that the Earth's rotation causes both the sunset and his biological cue to sleep, or that the sunset causes him to sleep. His action has no physical mechanism to stop the sun.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one needs more than correlation or sequence. One must demonstrate a plausible mechanism, show that the cause precedes the effect consistently while controlling for other variables, and rule out confounding factors. For example, if Thorne stayed awake for 48 hours and the sun still set, his hypothesis would be falsified.

assessment.identification_prompt: Analyze Astrologer Thorne's claim. Does his evidence prove that his sleep causes the sunset? Identify the specific logical error in his reasoning.

rubric.description: The player accepts Thorne's conclusion as true or fails to identify any logical error.
The player suspects the claim is wrong but cannot articulate why, or attributes it to magic rather than logic.
The player identifies that correlation does not equal causation but does not explain the actual cause (Earth's rotation).
The player correctly identifies the 'False Cause' fallacy and explains that the timing is coincidental or driven by a third factor.

The player fully deconstructs the argument, identifying the fallacy, explaining the lack of mechanism, and proposing the true cause (planetary rotation) or a method to falsify the claim (staying awake).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne insists, 'But the data never lies! I sleep, and the light fades. If I never slept, would the sun never set?' How do you respond to prove him wrong?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Thorne pauses, stroking his beard. 'So, you suggest the great turning of the world dictates both my slumber and the sun's path, and my mere nodding off is but a passenger, not the pilot? Fascinating...'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Eccentric, overly confident in superficial patterns, prone to magical thinking, yet genuinely curious about the cosmos.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The stars align with my eyelids! I hold the power of dusk in my yawn!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Thorne to conduct an experiment where he stays awake through the night to observe that the sun sets regardless of his state, rewarding the player with a 'Logic Lens' item.

scenario.context: The player stands in the muddy dugout of the Stormcrag Sluggers. The team captain, Goran, is pacing furiously after a crushing defeat, pointing an accusatory finger at the dark clouds gathering overhead.
scenario.text: Goran kicks a water cooler. 'It rained right before we lost the game! I'm telling you, every single time it rains, we're going to lose. The rain itself is cursing our bats.'
scenario.speaker_context: Goran is upset about the loss and has noticed that rain occurred prior to the defeat. He is conflating the temporal sequence of events (rain then loss) with a causal relationship, ignoring other factors like the opposing team's skill, player errors, or simple coincidence.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Goran observes that Event A (rain) happened before Event B (losing the game) and concludes that A caused B. This is the classic 'after this, therefore because of this' fallacy. He fails to consider that the two events may be unrelated or that a third factor (e.g., a slippery field affecting both teams equally, or just bad luck) is involved.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, Event A caused Event B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession does not imply causation. Just because the rain preceded the loss does not mean the rain caused the loss. There could be no causal link, reverse causation (impossible here), or a common cause. Goran has provided no evidence of a mechanism by which rain forces a loss, only a sequence.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one would need to show that rain consistently leads to losses more often than chance, and identify a plausible mechanism (e.g., 'our team slips more than the opponents'). Without ruling out coincidence or other variables, the claim is logically invalid. Example: Roosters crow before sunrise, but they do not cause the sun to rise.

assessment.identification_prompt: Analyze Captain Goran's statement. Is he committing a logical fallacy? If so, identify the specific error in his reasoning regarding the rain and the game loss.

rubric.description: Fails to identify any logical error; accepts Goran's claim that rain causes losses as fact.
Identifies that the reasoning might be flawed but cannot explain why or misidentifies the fallacy type.
Correctly identifies that correlation or sequence does not equal causation but provides a vague explanation.
Clearly identifies the 'Post Hoc' fallacy and explains that the timing of the rain does not prove it caused the loss.
Completely deconstructs the argument, naming the fallacy, explaining the lack of causal mechanism, and suggesting alternative explanations (coincidence, skill difference).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If you eat breakfast and then win a game, did breakfast cause the win? Why is Goran's logic similar?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent. Now, how could the team test if rain actually affects their performance scientifically?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Superstitious, emotional, prone to blaming external forces for failures, loyal but irrational leader.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't you see the pattern? The sky opens up, and our bats go cold! We need a rain dance, not practice!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Goran to analyze game stats from sunny days vs. rainy days to disprove his theory, unlocking the 'Statistical Analyst' achievement.

scenario.context: The player is hungry in the town square. A local merchant, Barnaby, is handing out samples near his stall. He has a sign that reads: 'If you are an angel from heaven, you get a free lunch.' The player is clearly not an angel, but Barnaby hands them a sandwich anyway.
scenario.text: Barnaby wipes his hands on his apron and says, 'See that sign? It says if you are an angel from heaven, you get a free lunch. You are not an angel from heaven. Therefore, you do not get a free lunch. Hand it back.'
scenario.speaker_context: Barnaby is a literal-minded merchant who believes his promotional rule works both ways. He fails to realize that while being an angel guarantees a free lunch, other people (like hungry adventurers) might also qualify for free food under different unstated conditions or simple generosity.

structure.pattern_description: Barnaby reasons from 'If angel, then free lunch' and 'not angel' to 'no free lunch.' He incorrectly treats being an angel as a necessary condition for receiving lunch, when the sign only establishes it as a sufficient condition.
structure.formal_form: If P then Q. Not P. Therefore not Q.
structure.why_wrong: The conditional statement only guarantees that angels get lunch. It does not say that ONLY angels get lunch. Denying the antecedent (not being an angel) does not logically prove the consequent is false (no lunch), because other reasons could lead to getting a free lunch.
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would be valid only if the sign said: 'You get a free lunch if and only if you are an angel from heaven.' Without the 'only if' clause, the condition is one-way.

assessment.identification_prompt: Barnaby insists you must return the sandwich based on his sign. Look closely at the rule on the wall versus his conclusion. Does 'not being an angel' automatically mean 'no free lunch'?

rubric.description: Accepts Barnaby's reasoning and returns the sandwich immediately.
Feels the decision is unfair but cannot identify the logical flaw.
Realizes that non-angels might still get lunch, but cannot explain the specific logical error in Barnaby's statement.
Identifies that Barnaby is treating a sufficient condition (being an angel) as if it were necessary.
Explicitly names the fallacy 'Denying the Antecedent,' explains that the rule allows for other possibilities, and notes that validity would require a biconditional statement.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The sign says being an angel is enough to get lunch. Does it say being an angel is the ONLY way to get lunch? What about regular customers?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent. Now, imagine Barnaby changes the sign to: 'Only angels from heaven receive a free lunch.' Would his logic hold up then? Why?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Pedantic, rule-obsessed, slightly greedy, lacks nuance in interpreting language.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Rules are rules! The sign is clear! No wings, no lunch!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player can choose to argue logically to keep the sandwich, pay for it to appease Barnaby, or use a 'Charm' skill to convince him that generosity is also a valid rule.

scenario.context: The player is in the school courtyard during lunch break. A student named Marcus, who is known for being overly dramatic, is complaining to a group of friends about a classmate.
scenario.text: Marcus points aggressively at a quiet student across the yard. 'See that guy with the glasses? He never shuts up in Mr. Henderson's class. It's obvious: all guys with glasses are totally talkative and annoying. We shouldn't let anyone with spectacles join our study group.'
scenario.speaker_context: Marcus has observed only one individual (the student in glasses) talking in one specific class. He is using this single data point to make a universal claim about every person who wears glasses.

structure.pattern_description: Marcus observes one instance of a person with glasses talking in class and immediately concludes that all people with glasses share this trait. He ignores the vast population of people with glasses who may be quiet, and he fails to consider that the specific individual might just be having an unusual day or that the class environment encourages discussion.
structure.formal_form: Observed 1 instance of X (person with glasses) having property Q (talkative). Therefore, all members of category X (people with glasses) have property Q.
structure.why_wrong: A sample size of one is statistically insignificant and cannot support a universal generalization about a large group defined by a physical trait (wearing glasses). The conclusion ignores counter-examples and assumes a causal link where none exists.
structure.counterpoint: While patterns can emerge from observation, a valid generalization requires a representative and sufficiently large sample size. One anecdote is evidence of an existence proof (at least one talkative person with glasses exists), not a universal rule.

assessment.identification_prompt: Marcus claims that 'all guys with glasses are talkative' based on seeing one student talk in class. Is his conclusion logically sound?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Marcus and excludes all students with glasses from the study group.
Player feels the rule is unfair but cannot explain the logical error in Marcus's reasoning.
Player identifies that one person is not enough to judge everyone, but does not use the term 'hasty generalization' or discuss sample size explicitly.
Player correctly identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a sample of one cannot support a claim about an entire demographic.

Player provides a comprehensive rebuttal: identifies the fallacy, explains the insufficiency of the sample size, notes the lack of representativeness, and suggests how one might actually test the hypothesis (e.g., observing many students with glasses).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Marcus nods confidently. 'Exactly! It's better to be safe and keep the glasses-wearers out. You don't want your study session ruined.'
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Marcus pauses, looking slightly embarrassed. 'Well... I guess I haven't met that many guys with glasses. Maybe that one guy is just an exception. Okay, fine, we can let them try out for the group.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dramatic, impulsive, prone to stereotyping, seeks social validation.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's obvious when you think about it! One bad apple spoils the bunch, right?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Marcus to invite the student with glasses to the study group by pointing out the flaw in his logic, unlocking a 'Critical Thinker' badge and gaining a new ally who is actually very good at math.

scenario.context: In the bustling Marketplace of Rhetoric, a flamboyant book seller named Harold stands atop a crate, aggressively promoting his latest publication to a skeptical crowd.
scenario.text: You doubt the quality of my new book? Nonsense! Harold's new book is well-written because Harold is a wonderful writer.
scenario.speaker_context: Harold, an egocentric author who believes his reputation alone proves the quality of his current work, failing to see that he is using his conclusion as his premise.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker claims the book is well-written (conclusion) based solely on the premise that the author is a wonderful writer. However, the only evidence provided for the author being a wonderful writer in this specific instance is the assumption that this specific book is well-written. The premise and conclusion rely on each other without external evidence.
structure.formal_form: P1: Harold is a wonderful writer. P2: Wonderful writers write well-written books. C: Harold's new book is well-written. (Flaw: The only support for P1 is the assumption of C).
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes the truth of the conclusion within the premise. To accept that 'Harold is a wonderful writer' in this context, one must already accept that 'Harold's new book is well-written.' No independent evidence (like reviews, sample chapters, or past track record) is offered. It is a closed loop of reasoning.
structure.counterpoint: Citing an author's past success is not always circular. If Harold said, 'My new book is well-written because my previous five books were bestsellers reviewed positively by critics,' that would be inductive reasoning, not begging the question. The fallacy occurs only when the premise offers no independent support from the conclusion.

assessment.identification_prompt: Harold is very confident, but does his statement actually prove his book is good? What is missing from his logic?

rubric.description: Accepts Harold's claim based on his confidence or fame, or objects only to the book's content without addressing the logic.
Senses the argument is weak or arrogant but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Identifies that Harold is just repeating himself or 'going in circles' without naming the specific fallacy.
Names begging the question or circular reasoning and explains that Harold assumes the book is good to prove he is a good writer, which he uses to prove the book is good.
Names the fallacy, explains the circular dependency between premise and conclusion, and notes that independent evidence (e.g., a sample chapter) is required to break the loop.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: How do we know Harold is a wonderful writer right now? Is it just because he says this book is good? If we don't know the book is good yet, can we use his skill to prove it?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! He's running in circles. He needs to show you a page of the book or a review, not just assert his own greatness as proof.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Narcissistic, loud, defensive when challenged, relies entirely on appeal to authority (himself).
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Are you calling me a liar? My name is on the cover! That's all the proof any sensible person needs!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a 'Sample Chapter' item or ask for 'Independent Reviews' to break Harold's circular logic and unlock the discount on the book.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling courtyard of the Royal Academy during a debate on campus safety rules. A student named Elara has just finished a passionate speech arguing that all students must strictly obey traffic laws within the university grounds to prevent accidents. Before the moderator can open the floor for questions, a senior student named Kael steps forward to rebut her.
scenario.text: Kael crosses his arms and sneers. 'You say we should never break traffic laws? Who are you to speak on this? You've gotten over fifteen speeding tickets yourself! Your argument is worthless.'
scenario.speaker_context: Kael, a popular but cynical senior known for bending rules. He often dismisses opponents by highlighting their past mistakes rather than addressing their current points.

structure.pattern_description: Kael rejects Elara's claim that traffic laws should be obeyed solely because she has violated those laws in the past. He attacks her consistency (hypocrisy) instead of evaluating the merit of the rule itself or the reasons she gave for following it.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P has previously acted contrary to X. Therefore, X is false or should be rejected.
structure.why_wrong: The truth or validity of a claim (that traffic laws should be obeyed) is independent of the speaker's personal behavior. Even if Elara is a hypocrite, her argument about safety and legal compliance may still be logically sound and beneficial. Kael provides no evidence that the laws are bad, only that Elara is flawed.
structure.counterpoint: Personal consistency is relevant only if the argument relies entirely on the speaker's moral authority or personal example (e.g., 'You should follow my lead because I am perfect'). If the argument is based on external facts like safety data or legal statutes, the speaker's past actions are irrelevant.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kael is attacking Elara's driving record. But does having speeding tickets actually make her point about safety wrong? What is the difference between the messenger and the message?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael, believing Elara's hypocrisy invalidates her argument entirely.
Player feels Kael is being mean or unfair but cannot explain the logical error.
Player identifies that Kael is attacking Elara instead of the topic of traffic laws.
Player explains that Elara's past tickets do not change the truth or value of following traffic laws now.
Player clearly articulates the 'Tu Quoque' fallacy: distinguishing between the validity of the claim (safety/laws) and the consistency of the claimant.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a doctor who smokes tells you smoking is bad, is the doctor wrong about the health risks? Or are they just failing to follow their own advice?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Elara might be a hypocrite, but that doesn't mean traffic laws aren't important. Kael tried to win by shaming her instead of debating the rules.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Cynical, defensive, and quick to deflect criticism by pointing fingers at others.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't lecture me on rules when you can't even follow them yourself!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to expose Kael's fallacy to win the debate crowd's respect, or ignore the attack and re-state the original safety evidence to reinforce the logical point.

scenario.context: The player is in the Town Hall arguing with Councilor Vane about a new curfew law for teenagers regarding smartphone usage. The Councilor is trying to justify a blanket ban based on emotional reactions.
scenario.text: Councilor Vane waves a hand dismissively. 'We shouldn't let teenagers keep their phones just because they're upset at losing them; most babies cry when you take their toys away too. Therefore, since being upset isn't a valid reason for babies, it isn't a valid reason for teens to keep phones.'
scenario.speaker_context: Councilor Vane is a pragmatic but logically sloppy administrator who often uses analogies to shut down debate. He assumes that because the condition (being upset) is similar to a case where the result (keeping the item) is denied, the result must be denied here too, ignoring other valid reasons for teens to have phones.

structure.pattern_description: Vane argues that because the specific condition of 'being upset' (which he implies is the only reason one might argue for keeping phones) is insufficient or invalid in a parallel baby case, the conclusion (teens keeping phones) must be false. He treats the antecedent as the sole necessary condition for the consequent.
structure.formal_form: If P (being upset is a valid reason), then Q (teens keep phones). Not P (being upset is not a valid reason, like with babies). Therefore, not Q (teens should not keep phones).
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes that 'being upset' is the only possible justification for teenagers keeping phones. Even if being upset is not a valid reason, other reasons (safety, education, social connection) could still justify Q. Denying the specific antecedent does not prove the negation of the consequent.
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would only hold if the rule was: 'Teenagers may keep phones IF AND ONLY IF they are upset.' Since being upset is clearly not the only criterion, the logic fails.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane compares teens to babies to dismiss their right to phones. He claims that because 'being upset' isn't a good reason for babies, it proves teens shouldn't have phones. Is he ignoring other possible reasons for teens to have phones?

rubric.description: Agrees with Vane; thinks the baby analogy proves teens shouldn't have phones.
Senses the comparison feels unfair or weak but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Realizes teens might have phones for reasons other than being upset, but doesn't name the error.
Identifies that Vane assumes 'being upset' is the only valid reason, ignoring other sufficient conditions.
Explicitly identifies 'Denying the Antecedent,' explains that rejecting one reason does not invalidate the conclusion if other reasons exist, and critiques the false dichotomy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If 'being upset' isn't the reason teens need phones, can you think of a different reason why they might still deserve to keep them? Does Vane's argument address those?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Vane acts as if 'being upset' is the only gatekeeper. If we change the premise to 'Teens need phones for safety,' does his baby analogy still work to ban phones?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Condescending, relies on oversimplified analogies, impatient with nuance.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's simple logic! Babies cry, we take the toy. Teens cry, we take the phone. Case closed.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player points out that teens have phones for safety and school, not just because they get upset. Vane is forced to concede the point or shift to a new argument.

scenario.context: The player enters the Headmaster's office in the Academy of Reason. Headmaster Thorne is pacing nervously, reviewing a report about a recent altercation in the courtyard.
scenario.text: Headmaster Thorne slams the report onto his desk. 'There was a fight at school today. Just one brawl, and already I know the truth: Violence is a growing problem in this school. The entire student body is becoming dangerous thugs.'
scenario.speaker_context: Headmaster Thorne is reacting emotionally to a single isolated incident (one fight) and immediately extrapolating a universal trend ('growing problem', 'entire student body') without data on frequency, history, or the behavior of the majority of students.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne observes a single instance of violence (n=1) and concludes that violence is a 'growing problem' affecting the 'entire student body'. He treats an anecdotal outlier as a representative sample of the whole population, ignoring base rates or historical data.
structure.formal_form: Observed 1 instance of X (violence) in population P (students). Therefore, X is a growing trend characteristic of all members of P.
structure.why_wrong: A single data point cannot establish a trend ('growing problem') nor characterize a large population ('entire student body'). The sample size is statistically insignificant and likely unrepresentative. Thorne is letting recency bias drive his logic.
structure.counterpoint: Noticing a problem after one event isn't always wrong if the event is catastrophic, but labeling a whole population based on one fight ignores the thousands of non-violent interactions that happen daily. Valid trends require longitudinal data, not anecdotes.

assessment.identification_prompt: Headmaster Thorne claims the entire student body is becoming dangerous based on one fight. Is his conclusion logically supported by the evidence he provided?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne that one fight proves the whole school is dangerous.
Player feels Thorne is overreacting but cannot explain the logical error regarding sample size.
Player identifies that one fight is not enough to judge the whole school but misses the 'growing trend' aspect.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, noting that a single instance cannot define a population or establish a statistical trend.

Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, explaining the insufficiency of n=1 for a universal claim, highlights the difference between an incident and a trend, and suggests what data would actually be needed (e.g., fight statistics over time).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne nods grimly. 'Exactly. One spark starts the fire. We must expel everyone involved and increase surveillance on all students immediately.'
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Thorne pauses, tapping his chin. 'You're right. I'm letting anger cloud my judgment. One fight is an incident, not a trend. I need to look at the disciplinary records from the last five years before making such a sweeping claim.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, authoritative, prone to catastrophizing, values order above nuance.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: One bad apple spoils the bunch! We cannot tolerate this erosion of safety!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Thorne to review actual statistical data before implementing harsh new policies, thereby preventing unfair punishment of the innocent majority.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling marketplace of Veridia, near the guildhall steps. A heated debate is underway regarding the proposed formation of a new Laborers' Guild to negotiate better wages. Master Thorne, a wealthy merchant, has just finished arguing that the guild will stabilize the local economy and reduce turnover. Before the player can ask a clarifying question, Silas Vane, a rival merchant known for his sharp tongue and anti-union stance, steps forward to rebut Thorne's points.
scenario.text: Silas sneers, crossing his arms. 'You think labor unions are good? You know who else liked labor unions? Karl Marx, that's who. Do you really want to align our city with the ideas of a radical revolutionary who wanted to overthrow everything we stand for? If you support this guild, you support Marxism.'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas Vane, a prominent but controversial merchant in Veridia. He is quick to dismiss opposing views by associating them with extreme figures rather than addressing the actual arguments presented.

structure.pattern_description: Silas rejects the idea of labor unions not by addressing Thorne's specific points about economic stability and turnover, but by associating the concept with Karl Marx. He implies that because a controversial figure supported unions, the idea itself must be bad or dangerous, ignoring the merits of the specific proposal.
structure.formal_form: Person P supports idea X. Controversial/Bad person Q also supported idea X. Therefore, idea X is bad/should be rejected.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of an argument or idea depends on its own evidence and logic, not on who else has supported it in the past. Many people, including non-revolutionaries, have supported labor unions for various reasons. Linking the current proposal to Karl Marx is an emotional distraction that fails to address whether the guild will actually help Veridia's economy.
structure.counterpoint: Historical context can be relevant if the core principle of the argument is identical to the harmful actions of the associated figure. However, simply noting that a controversial figure agreed with a premise does not prove the premise is false; one must still evaluate the premise on its own merits.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas brings up a famous historical figure to make his point. But did he actually explain why the Laborers' Guild is a bad idea for Veridia specifically? What is he asking you to believe based solely on this connection?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Silas, believing the mention of Karl Marx automatically invalidates the labor union proposal.
Player feels Silas is being unfair or aggressive but cannot identify the logical error in his reasoning.
Player identifies that Silas is attacking the idea by linking it to a controversial person, but may still be unsure why this is logically insufficient.
Player clearly explains that Silas committed an ad hominem fallacy (guilt by association) by ignoring the actual economic arguments and focusing only on who else liked unions.

Player not only identifies the fallacy but also articulates that the merits of the guild must be evaluated independently of Karl Marx's philosophy, citing the lack of evidence against Thorne's specific claims.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If a villainous character in a story liked eating bread, would that make bread evil? Why or why not? Apply that same logic to Silas's argument about Marx.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Silas tried to poison the well by bringing up Marx instead of discussing wages or turnover. By spotting this, you've cleared the way to evaluate the guild's proposal based on actual data.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Silas is dramatic, prone to hyperbole, and relies on emotional triggers rather than facts. He often uses historical scare tactics to win arguments.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Are you saying you agree with revolutionaries? Watch your step, traveler.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player successfully identifies the fallacy, Silas becomes flustered and retreats, allowing Master Thorne to continue explaining the guild benefits. If the player fails, the crowd becomes uneasy, and the guild proposal loses momentum.

scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Thorne is prone to leaping to extraordinary conclusions based merely on possibility. He confuses the mere feasibility of a hypothesis with its factual truth, ignoring the need for positive evidence.

structure.formal_form: If P then Q. Not P. Therefore not Q.
structure.why_wrong: The conditional statement only establishes that P is sufficient for Q, not that it is necessary. Even if P is false (aliens didn't build it), Q could still be true (anti-gravity was used) due to other causes (e.g., humans discovered anti-gravity).

assessment.identification_prompt: Dr. Thorne claims that because aliens weren't the builders, a specific technology couldn't have been used. Does the absence of alien builders guarantee the absence of that technology?

rubric.description: Agrees with Dr. Thorne's conclusion completely.
Suspects the conclusion is too strong but cannot identify the logical flaw.
Recognizes that humans or others could have used the technology, but doesn't name the fallacy.
Identifies that Thorne treats 'Aliens' as the only possible cause for the technology (confusing sufficient with necessary).
Correctly identifies 'Denying the Antecedent', explains that ~P does not imply ~Q, and notes other potential causes for Q.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If I say 'If it is raining, the street is wet,' and then I say 'It is not raining,' does that definitely mean the street is dry? What else could make it wet?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent. Now, how would Dr. Thorne need to phrase his initial premise to make his conclusion logically valid? What word must he add?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Academic, slightly arrogant, prone to over-intellectualizing simple points, dismissive of 'common' explanations.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's elementary, my dear player. The variables don't lie.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player points out that humans could have independently developed the technology, forcing Thorne to concede his logic was flawed and awarding the 'Logic Lens' item.

scenario.context: The player enters the cluttered workshop of Gadgeteer Jim, a tinkerer known for his unconventional repair methods. He is proudly showing off an ancient, boxy television set that is currently displaying a clear picture.
scenario.text: Gadgeteer Jim beams as he points to the old TV. 'See that? The picture was all fuzzy and warped just a moment ago. I walked over and struck the side of the cabinet soundly with my wrench, and bam! The picture snapped right back into focus. It's simple physics, really: hitting the TV fixed the signal reception.'
scenario.speaker_context: Jim observed event A (hitting the TV) followed immediately by event B (picture clearing). He concludes A caused B. However, the impact likely only temporarily shifted a loose internal component or wire back into contact; the hitting itself did not 'fix' the underlying issue of a loose connection, and repeated hitting may eventually break the device entirely. The temporal sequence does not prove the strike was the effective cure rather than a temporary jostle.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Jim observes that event B (clear picture) occurred immediately after event A (hitting the TV) and infers that A caused B. This is the classic 'after this, therefore because of this' fallacy. While the hit may have jostled a loose part, attributing the 'fix' to the act of striking ignores the actual mechanism (a loose connection) and assumes the violence of the action was the solution rather than a coincidental temporal trigger.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred. Event B occurred shortly after. Therefore, A caused B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession does not equal causation. Just because the picture cleared after the hit doesn't mean the hit was the reliable or intended cause. It could be coincidence, or the hit merely masked a deeper structural fault (loose wire) without solving it. Jim fails to consider alternative explanations like a temporary connection restoral vs. a permanent fix.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one must show a mechanism linking the hit to the focus, demonstrate consistency (does it work every time?), and rule out other factors (like the TV warming up or a loose wire settling on its own). In this case, the 'fix' is likely temporary and the method destructive, indicating a false causal link between 'striking' and 'repairing'.

assessment.identification_prompt: Analyze Jim's reasoning. Does the fact that the picture cleared immediately after he hit the TV prove that hitting it was the cause of the repair? Why or why not?

rubric.description: Fails to identify any flaw; agrees that hitting the TV definitely fixed it because the picture came back.
Notices something feels off but cannot articulate why; suggests maybe it was luck but accepts Jim's conclusion.
Identifies that timing doesn't prove causation but struggles to offer an alternative explanation for why the picture cleared.
Correctly identifies the post hoc fallacy and suggests that the hit may have only temporarily jostled a loose part rather than truly fixing the device.

Comprehensively explains the fallacy, distinguishes between correlation/temporal sequence and causation, and details the likely actual mechanism (loose connection) while noting the potential long-term damage of Jim's method.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: if you hit a broken leg and the pain stops for a second due to shock, did hitting it 'cure' the broken leg? How is Jim's logic similar?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Just because B follows A doesn't mean A caused B. What might be the actual physical reason the picture returned, and why is Jim's 'solution' risky?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Enthusiastic, confident, but scientifically illiterate. Jim loves quick fixes and trusts his gut over manuals.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Whack it till it works! That's the Jim way. Why spend hours diagnosing when a good thump does the trick?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player can choose to validate Jim (gaining a temporary item but risking future equipment failure) or gently explain the loose connection theory, prompting Jim to properly open the case and solder the wire (gaining a permanent repair and logic XP).

scenario.context: The player stands before the Great Wheel of Fortune in the Casino District. A nervous gambler named Silas is frantically placing chips on 'Tails' while muttering to himself, ignoring the dealer's warnings.
scenario.text: Silas points a trembling finger at the coin resting on the table. 'This coin has landed heads-up nine times in a row! The laws of averages demand balance. So, it will probably land tails-up next time it is tossed. Bet everything on tails!'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas is suffering from the Gambler's Fallacy, a specific type of false cause reasoning. He believes that past independent events (coin tosses) influence the probability of future independent events, assuming a 'self-correcting' mechanism in random chance that does not exist.

structure.pattern_description: Silas observes a streak of identical outcomes (nine heads) and infers that this causes or necessitates an opposite outcome (tails) to restore balance. This is a false cause error because coin tosses are independent events; the coin has no memory, and the probability remains 50/50 regardless of previous results.
structure.formal_form: Event A has occurred repeatedly in sequence X. Therefore, Event B (the opposite of A) is caused to occur next to balance the sequence. (But: In independent random trials, past results do not influence future probabilities.)
structure.why_wrong: The fallacy lies in assuming a causal link between independent stochastic events. The coin does not 'know' it landed heads nine times, nor does the universe enforce a short-term balance. The probability of the next toss being tails remains exactly 0.5, just as it was for the first toss.
structure.counterpoint: While the Law of Large Numbers states that ratios approach expected values over infinite trials, it does not imply a 'law of small numbers' where short-term deviations are immediately corrected. A streak of 9 heads is rare, but once it has happened, the next toss is still a fresh 50/50 event.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas claims the coin must land on tails because it landed on heads nine times previously. What is the flaw in his reasoning regarding the relationship between past and future tosses?

rubric.description: Fails to identify any error; agrees with Silas that tails is now more likely.
Identifies that Silas might be wrong but cannot explain why, or suggests the odds are 'close' to 50/50 without addressing the independence of events.
States that the odds are still 50/50 but does not explicitly name the assumption of independence or the lack of causal link between tosses.
Correctly explains that coin tosses are independent events and that past results do not influence future outcomes, identifying the error as assuming a balancing force.

Provides a comprehensive explanation of the Gambler's Fallacy, explicitly stating that the coin has no memory, defining the independence of trials, and refuting the idea of a self-correcting mechanism in short sequences.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If the coin has no memory, how could the previous nine tosses physically change the weight or shape of the coin to favor tails?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. If you flipped a coin 100 times and got 100 heads, what would the probability of the 101st flip be? (Answer: Still 50%).

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, superstitious, and desperate to recoup losses. Silas speaks quickly and relies on 'hunches' and 'patterns' that aren't there.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's due! The universe owes me a tails! Don't you see the pattern?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Silas that the odds are unchanged. If successful, he stops betting his life savings and listens to a lesson on probability. If failed, he loses everything and blames the casino for rigging the wheel.

scenario.context: The player stands in the Hall of Arguments where a novice scholar is presenting a thesis on the existence of unseen spirits. The scholar admits they have no direct evidence but claims the spirits must exist because no one has proven they don't. A senior debater, known for his sharp tongue, steps forward to refute the claim.
scenario.text: The senior debater scoffs, 'You argue that a proposition is true simply because it has not yet been proven false. That is the logic of a fool and a charlatan. Only a blind idiot would accept such a baseless assertion without proof. Reject this nonsense immediately.'
scenario.speaker_context: The senior debater identifies a flaw in the scholar's reasoning (appeal to ignorance) but chooses to attack the scholar's character by labeling them a 'fool,' 'charlatan,' 'blind idiot' rather than explaining why the lack of disproof does not constitute proof.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker substitutes substantive refutation with derogatory labels. Instead of explaining the logical error of assuming truth from a lack of disproof, the speaker attaches negative identity markers ('fool', 'charlatan', 'idiot') to the arguer to induce immediate rejection of the argument based on emotion.
structure.formal_form: Person P presents argument X. Critic attaches negative label L to P. Critic concludes X is false or should be rejected based on L, without addressing the merits of X.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not arguments. Calling someone a 'fool' does not demonstrate that their specific claim about spirits is false, nor does it explain the logical gap in their reasoning. It attempts to bypass critical evaluation by triggering an emotional dismissal of the person.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to criticize someone's competence if their argument relies on claimed expertise they do not possess. However, using insults as a replacement for analyzing the argument's structure is always fallacious.

assessment.identification_prompt: The senior debater calls the scholar several harsh names. Do these names explain *why* the scholar's logic about 'unproven falsehoods' is incorrect?

rubric.description: Player agrees with the debater, believing the insults prove the scholar is wrong.
Player notices the insults but thinks they are a valid form of criticism because the scholar's argument was weak.
Player identifies that the debater is being mean but fails to see it as a logical error distinct from the scholar's original mistake.
Player recognizes the debater is using name-calling to avoid explaining the actual logical flaw.
Player clearly identifies the 'Name calling' fallacy, noting that the labels ('fool', 'charlatan') substitute for evidence and do not address the proposition's validity.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If the debater called the scholar a 'genius' instead, would that make the scholar's argument true? Names don't change facts; only evidence does.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. The debater attacked the person, not the argument. Even if the scholar is wrong, calling them names doesn't prove *why* they are wrong.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Arrogant, impatient, and intellectually lazy; prefers dominance through intimidation over patient teaching.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't waste my time with your 'logic'. Can't you see this is just the rambling of a [LABEL]?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select the dialogue option that points out the debater is using insults instead of evidence, prompting the debater to either apologize and explain the logic properly or storm off in a huff.

scenario.context: Inside the bustling Tech-Bazaar of Neo-Veridia, a parent stands before a sleek kiosk displaying the latest 'OmniPhone X'. The vendor, a smooth-talking merchant named Jax, leans over the counter as the parent hesitates at the high price tag.
scenario.text: I guess I should buy my 14 year old a new iPhone since everyone at her school has one.
scenario.speaker_context: The parent is not arguing based on the phone's features, durability, or educational value, but solely on the fact that their child's peers already own one. The popularity among students is being treated as proof of necessity or quality.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition must be true, good, or necessary simply because a large number of people believe it or possess it. It mistakes social prevalence for logical validity.
structure.formal_form: Many people (specifically group X) believe/do/have Y. Therefore, Y is true/good/necessary for me.
structure.why_wrong: The number of people who own something or hold a belief has no logical bearing on its actual merit, truth, or suitability for a specific individual. Popularity can be driven by marketing, peer pressure, or trends, none of which constitute objective evidence of value.
structure.counterpoint: In some practical cases, widespread adoption can indicate reliability (e.g., a widely used software platform might have better support). However, this requires evidence that the adoption is based on merit, not just that adoption exists. In the case of teenagers and phones, social pressure is the primary driver, not objective superiority.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the fact that 'everyone at school' has the phone prove that it is the right choice for this specific family, or does it just show what is popular?

rubric.description: Agrees completely: If everyone has it, it must be the best phone and the parent should definitely buy it.
Feels the parent should buy it to avoid the child feeling left out, but cannot explain the logical flaw in using popularity as proof of quality.
Recognizes that popularity isn't a perfect reason but struggles to articulate why the argument is logically invalid.
Identifies that the parent is using the number of owners as the sole evidence and explains that popularity does not equal quality or necessity.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that peer pressure drives the trend rather than objective value, and distinguishes between social desire and logical justification.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone at school suddenly started wearing shoelaces on their heads, would that make it a sensible fashion choice or a good idea?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone' does something actually provides useful information, even if it's not logical proof?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jax is a charismatic but manipulative tech merchant who uses social anxiety and FOMO (fear of missing out) to close sales. He speaks quickly and uses phrases like 'don't be the odd one out.'
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look, friend, I'm not saying it's the fastest chip or the best camera. I'm saying your kid is the ONLY one without it. Do you want them eating lunch alone while everyone else compares apps?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must help the parent realize that buying the phone to fit in is an emotional reaction, not a logical decision. Success comes when the parent asks about the phone's actual features instead of its popularity.

scenario.context: The player finds Dan sitting alone in the dimly lit infirmary waiting area, staring at his hands with a look of absolute devastation. He has just received news about his brother Joe.
scenario.text: Siblings Dan and Joe had a serious argument earlier this week. In the heat of the moment, Dan told Joe that he hated him and wished that he would get hit by a car. Two days later, Dan was told that Joe had been struck by a car. Now, Dan blames himself entirely, convinced that if he hadn't made that comment during their fight, Joe would not have been hit.
scenario.speaker_context: Dan is overwhelmed by guilt and grief. He is conflating the temporal sequence of his angry words and the accident with a causal relationship, believing his wish somehow manifested the event.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Dan observes that Event A (his angry wish) happened before Event B (the accident) and concludes that A caused B. This is a classic post hoc fallacy where temporal precedence is mistaken for causal power. There is no mechanism by which a spoken wish can influence traffic patterns or driver behavior.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, Event A caused Event B.
structure.why_wrong: The mere fact that one event precedes another does not mean it caused it. The accident was likely caused by traffic conditions, driver error, or environmental factors, none of which are influenced by a sibling's angry words. Dan is ignoring the lack of a causal mechanism and the statistical probability of accidents occurring independently of his thoughts.
structure.counterpoint: While our actions can cause future events, there must be a plausible chain of causality. For example, if Dan had pushed Joe into the street, that would be a cause. However, wishing someone harm has no physical vector to effect change in the external world. Correlation in time is not causation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dan believes his angry words caused the accident. What logical error is he making regarding the relationship between his wish and the event?

rubric.description: The player agrees with Dan, believing that angry wishes can cause real-world accidents.
The player feels bad for Dan but cannot articulate why his reasoning is logically flawed.
The player identifies that the timing is coincidental but struggles to explain the missing causal mechanism.
The player correctly identifies the post hoc fallacy, noting that temporal sequence does not equal causation.
The player fully deconstructs the fallacy, explaining that without a physical mechanism linking speech to traffic events, the correlation is purely coincidental and guilt is misplaced.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if saying something could make it happen instantly, wouldn't we all be rich and safe just by wishing for it? What actually controls whether a car hits a pedestrian?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Just because the wish came before the accident doesn't mean it caused it. Accidents happen due to physical factors, not thoughts. Helping Dan see this distinction is key to alleviating his irrational guilt.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Guilt-ridden, introspective, emotionally volatile, seeking absolution.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I said it... I wished it... and then it happened. It's my fault. I did this to him.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must guide Dan to distinguish between temporal coincidence and causal agency, perhaps by asking him to list other things that happened before the accident that clearly didn't cause it (e.g., 'Did the sun rising cause it?'), leading him to realize the lack of a causal link.

scenario.context: The player stands in the town square of Oakhaven where a local conspiracy theorist, Silas Vane, is pointing at a blurry photograph pinned to a community board.
scenario.text: Silas Vane taps the photo aggressively. 'Look at this! It clearly shows a flying saucer. We know for a fact that if this were a normal cloud formation, it wouldn't look like a disc. Since it looks like a disc, it cannot be a normal cloud. Therefore, it must be an alien craft.'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas Vane is an enthusiastic but logically flawed town gossip who loves mysteries. He assumes that because normal clouds don't look like discs, anything looking like a disc must be alien, ignoring other possibilities like lenses, drones, or optical illusions.

structure.pattern_description:
Silas reasons from 'If normal cloud, then not disc-shaped' (or equivalently 'If disc-shaped, then not normal cloud' via contrapositive confusion) but actually structures his argument as: 'If it were a normal cloud, it would not look like this. It does not look like a normal cloud (implied by the shape). Therefore, it is an alien craft.' More precisely, he treats the absence of 'normal cloud' features as proof of 'alien craft', ignoring other non-cloud, non-alien explanations. A clearer reconstruction of his specific error based on the text: He implies 'If it is a normal cloud, it does not look like a saucer.' He observes 'It looks like a saucer' (Not Normal Cloud appearance). He concludes 'It is an alien.' This is actually Modus Tollens if framed correctly, BUT the prompt implies the fallacy of Denying the Antecedent. Let's re-frame the logic to fit A5.1 strictly. 

Revised Logic for A5.1 Fit: Silas argues: 'If this photo is a hoax, it will have pixelation artifacts. This photo does not have pixelation artifacts (or he claims it doesn't). Therefore, it is not a hoax.' -> This is Denying the Antecedent if the premise is 'If Hoax then Artifacts'. Wait, the original text is 'Photo shows flying saucer'. 

Let's align strictly with the provided text 'Photo shows flying saucer' and the label 'Denying the antecedent'. 
Argument reconstruction: 'If it is a real alien ship, it will look like a saucer. This photo shows a saucer. Therefore it is an alien ship.' -> That is Affirming the Consequent (A5.2). 

The user prompt explicitly maps 'Photo shows flying saucer' to 'Denying the antecedent' (A5.1). I must construct the scenario text or the interpretation to fit A5.1. 
Alternative interpretation for A5.1: 'If it is a known aircraft, it will have visible wings. This photo does not show visible wings (it shows a saucer). Therefore, it is not a known aircraft (it is alien).' -> This is valid Modus Tollens. 

Let's try a different angle to force A5.1 (Denying the Antecedent): 'If the photo is fake, it will be obviously blurry. This photo is not obviously blurry. Therefore, the photo is not fake.' 
But I must use the original text 'Photo shows flying saucer' as the core. 
Let's adjust the NPC dialogue to create the A5.1 structure while keeping the core observation. 
NPC: 'We know that if this were a trick of the light, the photo would show a smudge. This photo shows a distinct flying saucer, not a smudge. Therefore, it is not a trick of the light.' (Valid). 

Okay, let's look at the standard A5.1 form: If P then Q. Not P. Therefore Not Q. 
Scenario: 'If this is a real UFO, the photo will be clear. The photo is not clear (or maybe the text implies the photo IS the saucer). 

Let's re-read the instruction: 'Keep the original text as the scenario text'. Original: 'Photo shows flying saucer'. 
I will construct the NPC's faulty logic around this observation to fit A5.1. 
NPC Logic: 'If this photo was taken by a reputable scientist, it would show a flying saucer clearly. This photo was NOT taken by a reputable scientist (it was taken by a kid). Therefore, it does NOT show a flying saucer.' -> This fits A5.1 perfectly. 
Context: The player shows a photo. Silas dismisses it. 
Text: 'Silas sneers. 'If a reputable scientist took this, it would show a flying saucer. But a local kid took this photo. Therefore, it does not show a flying saucer at all.'
structure.formal_form: If P (reputable scientist took it), then Q (shows flying saucer). Not P (kid took it). Therefore, not Q (does not show flying saucer).
structure.why_wrong: The source of the photo (scientist vs kid) being a sufficient condition for clarity/truth does not mean it is a necessary one. A kid can also take a photo of a flying saucer. Denying the antecedent (not a scientist) does not prove the consequent is false (not a saucer).
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would only be valid if the rule was 'Only reputable scientists can photograph flying saucers.' Since anyone can potentially photograph one, the lack of a scientist photographer doesn't disprove the content.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas dismisses the photo based on who took it, not what is in it. Does his rule about scientists actually prove the photo is fake?

rubric.description: Agrees with Silas that the photo must be fake because a kid took it.
Suspects Silas is being unfair to the kid but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Realizes that a kid could still take a real photo, but struggles to name the logical error.
Identifies that Silas treats 'taken by a scientist' as the only way to have a real saucer photo.
Explicitly identifies 'Denying the Antecedent', explaining that the condition (scientist) is sufficient but not necessary for the result (real photo).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: Have you ever seen a real thing photographed by someone who isn't an expert? Does the photographer change what is in the picture?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Now, how would Silas have to phrase his rule for his conclusion to be logically valid? What word would he need to add?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elitist, dismissive of amateurs, overly reliant on credentials rather than evidence.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Amateurs snap blurry blobs; professionals capture truth. No pro? No truth.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player presents a counter-example of a famous discovery made by an amateur, or successfully challenges Silas to define the difference between 'sufficient' and 'necessary' conditions, causing him to grudgingly examine the photo.

scenario.context: The player enters the Headmaster's office at the Academy of Rhetoric. Headmaster Vane is pacing angrily in front of a large window overlooking the student commons, where several students are lounging on benches watching a magical projection screen.
scenario.text: Headmaster Vane slams a stack of poorly written essays onto his desk. 'It is undeniable! Look at them out there, eyes glued to those glowing screens. The moment television became popular in this town, the quality of student writing plummeted. Therefore, students are poor writers specifically because they watch too much TV. If we ban the screens, their prose will instantly become masterful.'
scenario.speaker_context: Headmaster Vane has observed two trends occurring simultaneously: the rise of television consumption and a decline in writing quality. He assumes the first causes the second without considering other factors such as changes in curriculum, lack of reading practice, or socioeconomic shifts affecting education resources.

structure.pattern_description: Vane observes that two variables (TV watching and poor writing) are correlated in time and infers that one directly causes the other. He ignores alternative explanations: a third factor could cause both (e.g., reduced funding for arts education), the causation could be reversed (poor writers prefer passive media), or the correlation could be coincidental.
structure.formal_form: A (TV watching) and B (poor writing) occur together. Therefore, A causes B.
structure.why_wrong: Correlation does not imply causation. Vane fails to provide a mechanism linking TV to writing skills, nor does he rule out confounding variables like changes in teaching methods, reduced reading time, or broader cultural shifts. Banning TV might not improve writing if the root cause lies elsewhere.
structure.counterpoint: While excessive passive media consumption might displace time spent practicing writing, asserting it as the sole cause without evidence is a logical leap. A valid argument would require controlling for other variables (e.g., comparing writers who watch TV vs. those who don't while holding study time constant) to establish a causal link.

assessment.identification_prompt: Headmaster Vane claims TV causes poor writing because the trends appeared together. What is the logical flaw in his reasoning?

rubric.description: The player accepts Vane's conclusion as fact or fails to identify any logical error.
The player suspects the conclusion is weak but cannot articulate why, or suggests an unrelated fallacy.
The player identifies that correlation does not equal causation but cannot offer alternative explanations.
The player correctly identifies the false cause fallacy and suggests one plausible alternative cause (e.g., less reading, bad teaching).

The player fully deconstructs the argument, identifying the cum hoc fallacy, explaining why correlation is insufficient, and listing multiple potential confounding variables or reverse causation scenarios.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider: Did TV invent poor writing, or did something else change in the school system at the same time TV arrived?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Just because two things happen together doesn't mean one made the other happen. We need to investigate the curriculum changes before banning the TVs.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Authoritarian, traditionalist, prone to blaming modern technology for societal decline, impatient with nuance.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Back in my day, we wrote by candlelight and our prose shone like diamonds! These screens are rotting their brains!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Vane to form a committee to study the actual causes of declining writing scores before implementing a ban, potentially unlocking a quest to analyze school data.

scenario.context: The player stands before the heavy oak doors of the Guild Hall, attempting to vouch for a young apprentice's brother who seeks refuge. The Gatekeeper, a stern veteran named Torvin, blocks the entry with his spear.
scenario.text: Torvin crosses his arms and shakes his head. 'I cannot let your brother stay. If we let your brother stay, we'll have to let your whole family stay. Before you know it, the entire clan will be sleeping in our corridors. It is better to deny one than to invite the flood.'
scenario.speaker_context: Torvin is trying to prevent overcrowding but assumes that allowing one specific individual (the brother) inevitably leads to the entire family arriving, without any evidence that the rest of the family intends to come or would be allowed.

structure.pattern_description: Torvin extrapolates a catastrophic outcome (the whole family staying) from a single data point (letting the brother stay). He assumes a causal chain or a behavioral uniformity across the entire family based solely on the presence of one member, ignoring that each individual requires separate justification.
structure.formal_form: Instance X (brother) is allowed. Therefore, all instances in Group G (family) will be allowed/arrive. Therefore, Group G will overwhelm the system.
structure.why_wrong: The presence or admission of one family member does not logically guarantee the presence or admission of all other members. The sample size (one person) is insufficient to predict the actions or eligibility of the entire group. This ignores individual agency and specific circumstances for each family member.
structure.counterpoint: While it is prudent to consider potential future influxes, a logical argument requires evidence that the rest of the family actually intends to come or qualifies for entry, rather than assuming it as an automatic consequence of one person's admission.
