structure.pattern_description: The speaker claims the teacher is the 'best' based solely on the premise that he is the 'best' the speaker has known. The premise assumes the truth of the conclusion without providing independent evidence of quality.
structure.formal_form: P1: The teacher is the best I have known. C: Therefore, the teacher is the best.
structure.why_wrong: The argument offers no external criteria (such as test scores, teaching methods, or student outcomes) to support the claim. It merely restates the conclusion as the premise, creating a logical loop that proves nothing to a skeptic.
structure.counterpoint: Stating an opinion is not always fallacious; the fallacy occurs only when that opinion is presented as a logical proof for itself without independent support.

assessment.identification_prompt: Marcus sounds very sure of himself, but does his sentence actually give you a reason to believe the teacher is good?

rubric.description: Accepts Marcus's statement as a valid reason or critiques the teacher's quality without noticing the logical flaw.
Senses the statement is repetitive or unconvincing but cannot explain why logically.
Identifies that Marcus is just repeating himself or 'going in circles'.
Names the fallacy (begging the question/circular reasoning) and explains that the premise assumes the conclusion.
Names the fallacy, explains the circularity, and articulates that the argument fails because it lacks independent evidence to support the claim.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Listen closely again: Did Marcus tell you *why* the teacher is good, or did he just say the teacher is good because the teacher is good?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Marcus provided zero independent evidence. He assumed the very thing he was trying to prove.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Boastful, oblivious to logical gaps, relies on confidence over substance.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look, it's simple logic! If I say he's the best, it's because he's the best! Why don't you get it?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out the circular nature of the statement to make Marcus realize he needs actual examples to recruit new members.

scenario.context: In the Grand Hall of Grades, a haughty student blocks the Professor's podium, refusing to accept a marked exam.
scenario.text: You can't give me a C. I'm an A student!
scenario.speaker_context: Preston, a privileged academy student who believes his reputation alone dictates his performance, unable to see that he is using his claimed status as proof of the very grade he is disputing.

structure.pattern_description: The conclusion (that the student deserves an A) is assumed as the premise (that the student is an 'A student'). The speaker offers no independent evidence of performance, only a restatement of the desired outcome as a fact.
structure.formal_form: P1: I am an A student. P2: A students get As. C: Therefore, I must get an A (and this specific paper is an A paper).
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes exactly what it is trying to prove. Whether the student is truly an 'A student' is the very thing in question based on the current evidence (the C grade). Using the label 'A student' as proof ignores the need for actual performance data to support that label.
structure.counterpoint: Not every reference to past performance is circular. If the student said, 'I have received As on all ten previous assignments, so this C is an outlier,' that would be inductive reasoning based on independent evidence, not circular reasoning.

assessment.identification_prompt: Preston is very confident he deserves a better grade. What is the flaw in his reasoning when he says, 'You can't give me a C. I'm an A student!'?

rubric.description: Accepts Preston's claim or argues about the difficulty of the test without addressing the logic.
Senses Preston is being arrogant or unfair but cannot explain the logical error.
Identifies that Preston is just repeating his claim without giving real proof.
Names begging the question or circular reasoning and explains that he assumes he is an A student to prove he deserves an A.
Names the fallacy, explains the circularity, and clarifies that the label 'A student' is the conclusion needing proof, not a premise that proves the grade.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: How does Preston *know* he is an A student? Is it because of this paper, or is he assuming it to dismiss the paper's grade?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! He is using the conclusion as his own evidence. Without independent proof of his work, his reputation proves nothing.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Entitled, defensive, and relies heavily on social status rather than merit.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But everyone knows I'm top of the class! Are you saying the whole school is wrong?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a rubric or specific examples of errors in the work to break the circular loop, forcing Preston to address the actual evidence.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Veridia, a street performer named Jax is trying to sell a mysterious 'Luck Stone' to a crowd of onlookers.
scenario.text: Jax holds up a dull gray rock and shouts, 'Don't just stand there! Look at this line! Hundreds of people have bought these stones today. The mayor bought one, the blacksmith bought two, and even the skeptical scholar took one home! When this many people believe in something, there must be truth to it. You don't want to be the only one missing out on this proven luck, do you?'
scenario.speaker_context: Jax offers no demonstration of the stone's power or logical reason for its efficacy; his entire argument rests on the fact that many others have already purchased it.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or good simply because many people believe it or do it. It treats popularity as a substitute for evidence.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The number of people who believe something has no logical bearing on its truth. Popularity can be driven by social pressure, marketing, tradition, or mass hysteria, none of which constitute factual evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Widespread adoption can sometimes indicate reliability if it results from independent expert verification over time, but mere crowd behavior at a market stall is not evidence of truth.

assessment.identification_prompt: What actual evidence does Jax provide that the Luck Stone works? Is the fact that 'hundreds of people' bought one a valid reason to believe it brings luck?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; believes the stone must work because so many people bought it.
Feels hesitant about the claim but cannot articulate why popularity is not proof.
Notes that Jax provided no physical proof of luck but fails to identify the flaw in using popularity as evidence.
Identifies that Jax uses the number of buyers as his only evidence and explains that popularity does not establish truth.
Names the bandwagon fallacy, explains why popularity is irrelevant to truth, identifies the social pressure component, and distinguishes between mass belief and evidential convergence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine every person in the kingdom believed the sun revolved around the earth. Would that make it scientifically true?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'many people believe X' actually gives you a good reason to investigate X further, even if it's not proof?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, fast-talking hustler who feeds off crowd energy and uses FOMO (fear of missing out) as a primary sales tactic.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Everyone's doing it! Are you really going to stand there while the rest of us get lucky?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player points out that a crowd buying rocks doesn't make them magical, causing the crowd to disperse and Jax to pack up his stall in defeat.

scenario.context: In the coastal town of Mariner's Rest, a local scholar has just presented data suggesting high mercury levels in the region's primary catch. The town council gathers to discuss the findings, and Fisher Captain Bram stands to speak.
scenario.text: Captain Bram slams his hand on the table: 'The level of mercury in seafood may be unsafe, but what will fishers do to support their families? If we accept this, our nets rot unused and our children go hungry. We cannot believe these numbers.'
scenario.speaker_context: Bram does not challenge the scholar's testing methods, sample size, or chemical analysis. He argues that the finding must be rejected solely because accepting it would lead to severe economic hardship for the fishing community.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a factual claim should be rejected because accepting it would lead to undesirable outcomes, substituting the consequences for a critique of the evidence.
structure.formal_form: Claim P would have undesirable consequences C. Therefore P is false.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a factual claim (mercury levels) is independent of whether its consequences are pleasant or painful. While the economic impact is a valid policy concern, it does not change the chemical reality of the fish.
structure.counterpoint: Concern for the fishers' livelihoods is morally relevant when deciding how to respond to the crisis (policy), but it is logically irrelevant to determining whether the mercury levels are actually high (fact).

assessment.identification_prompt: Captain Bram highlights a tragic potential outcome. But does he provide any evidence that the scholar's mercury tests were incorrect?

rubric.description: Agrees with Bram; believes the terrible consequences prove the study is wrong.
Feels conflicted but cannot explain why the argument feels insufficient.
Notices Bram talks only about money and hunger, not about the science or data.
Identifies that Bram is rejecting the factual finding based on emotional and economic consequences rather than evidence.
Names the appeal to consequences fallacy and clearly distinguishes between the truth of the data and the policy response needed to help the fishers.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine the fishers had a guaranteed income and wouldn't go hungry. Would that make the mercury levels suddenly disappear or the study suddenly true?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: If the study is true, what should the town do to help the fishers? How is that decision different from deciding if the study is accurate?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Passionate, protective, desperate, and defensive of his community's tradition.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think I don't care about safety? I care about my crew eating tonight! Your science doesn't fill bellies!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must validate the scholar's data while proposing a separate economic aid package, showing that truth and compassion can coexist without conflating them.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Oakhaven, a young scholar named Elara presents a new method for purifying water using sand and charcoal filters. She displays data showing a 90% reduction in sickness among test families. As the crowd murmurs in approval, the town's elderly gatekeeper, Borin, steps forward to dismiss her findings.
scenario.text: Borin scoffs and waves his hand dismissively. 'We cannot accept this filtration nonsense. Elara is just a child who has never fought in the border wars and comes from a family of merchants, not healers. Why should we trust the words of someone with no battle scars and no medical training? Her idea must be false.'
scenario.speaker_context: Borin, the town gatekeeper. He is proud of his military past and deeply suspicious of anyone who hasn't 'earned their keep' through physical labor or combat. He values tradition and status over abstract data.

structure.pattern_description: Borin rejects Elara's proposal solely based on her personal attributes (age, family background, lack of military service) rather than addressing the evidence she presented regarding the filter's effectiveness. He assumes her background makes her conclusion invalid.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P has characteristic Q (irrelevant to the truth of X). Therefore, X is false.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of a claim about water filtration depends on empirical evidence and logical reasoning, not the personal history or profession of the person presenting it. Elara's data stands on its own merits; attacking her background provides no evidence that the filters fail to work.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if the argument relies on the person's specific authority or testimony. If Elara had argued, 'Trust me because I am a master healer,' then questioning her lack of medical training would be a valid critique of her premise, not an ad hominem fallacy.

assessment.identification_prompt: Borin seems very confident in his rejection. But look closely: does he mention anything about the sand, the charcoal, or the sickness rates Elara showed? Or is he talking only about Elara herself?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Borin, believing Elara's background makes her idea wrong.
Player feels Borin is being mean or unfair but cannot explain the logical error.
Player identifies that Borin is attacking Elara instead of her idea.
Player explains that Elara's background is irrelevant to the scientific data she presented.
Player fully articulates the formal structure: Borin rejects the conclusion solely based on irrelevant personal premises, ignoring the empirical evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a famous general said the sky was green, would that make it true? Conversely, if a child says 2+2=4, is she wrong because she's a child? Focus on the evidence, not the speaker.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! The merit of an idea is independent of its source. By ignoring the data and focusing on Elara's age and family, Borin commits a classic ad hominem fallacy.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Gruff, traditionalist, values martial prowess and lineage over intellect or innovation.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! What do soft-handed scholars know of real survival? I've held the gates while you were still in swaddling clothes!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to present the data again focusing strictly on the mechanics of the filter, bypassing Borin's ego, or use a 'Logic Check' to publicly expose his fallacy, swaying the crowd to support Elara.

scenario.context: In the quiet study of the Academy of Reason, the player observes a debate between two students regarding the nature of human morality. Hannah, a student known for her rigorous logic, has just presented a statistical analysis suggesting that altruism is more common than selfishness in emergency situations.
scenario.text: Hannah argues that because her friend was brainwashed as a child into thinking that people are generally good, people are not generally good.
scenario.speaker_context: Hannah, a sharp but occasionally hasty debater who tends to conflate the origin of a belief with the truth value of that belief when she feels strongly about a topic.

structure.pattern_description: Hannah rejects the claim that 'people are generally good' solely based on the origin of her friend's belief (being brainwashed as a child). She attacks the source of the belief rather than addressing the actual evidence for or against the general goodness of people.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P's belief in X originates from source S (which is flawed/biased). Therefore, X is false.
structure.why_wrong: The origin of a belief does not determine its truth. Even if the friend was 'brainwashed' to believe people are good, it is still possible that people actually are good. Hannah fails to provide evidence against the claim itself, relying entirely on the questionable history of the believer.
structure.counterpoint: Questioning the source is valid only if the source's reliability is the specific premise of the argument (e.g., 'My friend says X, and he is an expert, so X is true'). Here, the claim is about general human nature, not the friend's expertise, so the friend's upbringing is irrelevant to the truth of the matter.

assessment.identification_prompt: Hannah is focusing entirely on how her friend formed their belief. Does explaining where a belief came from prove that the belief is false?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Hannah, believing that a 'brainwashed' origin automatically makes the belief false.
Player senses Hannah is being unfair to her friend but cannot identify the logical error.
Player identifies that Hannah is attacking the friend's background rather than the argument about human nature.
Player explicitly states that the origin of a belief (genetic fallacy) does not determine its truth value.
Player explains that while the friend's belief may be poorly formed, Hannah has provided zero evidence that 'people are not generally good,' committing a genetic ad hominem.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If someone was taught that 2+2=4 by a strict teacher, does that make '2+2=4' false? How is Hannah's situation similar?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. The history of an idea is separate from its validity. To disprove that people are good, Hannah would need evidence of bad behavior, not just a critique of her friend's childhood.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Hannah is intellectually gifted but prone to rhetorical shortcuts when emotional; she respects direct logical dismantling of her errors.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But don't you see? If the root is poisoned, the fruit must be rotten! His belief is tainted, so the conclusion must be false!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player points out the distinction between the 'context of discovery' and the 'context of justification,' earning Logic Points and unlocking the 'Source Code' badge.

scenario.context: The player stands before the Great Gate of the Logic Citadel. A stone tablet above the archway reads: 'If you possess the Key of Truth, the gate shall open.' The player does not have the Key of Truth.
scenario.text: The Gatekeeper points to the tablet and states, 'The rule is clear: comparison or metaphors to relate ideas or situations that are not really that similar will not work here. The sign says if you possess the Key of Truth, the gate opens. You do not possess the Key. Therefore, the gate will not open for you. Begone.'
scenario.speaker_context: The Gatekeeper is a construct bound by literal interpretation. It mistakenly believes that possessing the Key is the only way to enter, ignoring other valid methods like solving the riddle of the Sphinx or presenting a Guild Seal.

structure.pattern_description: The Gatekeeper reasons from 'If Key, then Open' and 'No Key' to conclude 'Not Open.' It incorrectly treats the antecedent (having the Key) as a necessary condition when the rule only establishes it as sufficient.
structure.formal_form: If P then Q. Not P. Therefore not Q.
structure.why_wrong: The conditional statement only guarantees that having the Key is enough to open the gate; it does not state that it is the only way. Denying the antecedent (not having the Key) does not logically force the denial of the consequent (the gate not opening), as other conditions could also cause the gate to open.
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would be valid only if the rule were biconditional: 'You may pass if and only if you carry the Key of Truth.' The fallacy lies in interpreting a one-way conditional rule as a two-way requirement.

assessment.identification_prompt: The Gatekeeper seems certain you cannot enter without the Key. Look closely at the tablet's wording. Does 'If you have the Key, it opens' mean 'Only if you have the Key, it opens'?

rubric.description: Accepts the Gatekeeper's conclusion that entry is impossible without the Key.
Senses the Gatekeeper might be wrong but cannot articulate the logical flaw.
Realizes there might be other ways to open the gate but cannot explain the specific logical error in the Gatekeeper's deduction.
Identifies that the Gatekeeper is treating a sufficient condition (having the Key) as if it were a necessary condition.
Explicitly names the fallacy 'Denying the Antecedent,' explains the difference between sufficient and necessary conditions, and notes that validity would require a biconditional statement.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The tablet says having the Key is enough to open the gate. Does it explicitly say that lacking the Key means the gate stays shut? What else could possibly open it?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent. Now, imagine the tablet read: 'The gate opens ONLY IF you possess the Key.' Would the Gatekeeper's logic be sound in that case? What changed in the logical structure?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Rigid, literal-minded, and overly confident in its interpretation of rules. It becomes confused when presented with alternative valid conditions.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Rule 44-B: Absence of antecedent implies absence of consequent. You lack the Key. Calculation complete. Access denied.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can present a Guild Seal or solve the Sphinx's riddle to open the gate, proving the Gatekeeper's deduction false and forcing it to recalibrate its logic core.

scenario.context: In the Grand Academy's Biology Hall, Professor Aris Thorne is lecturing on the mechanisms of natural selection. A student in the front row, Kael, raises his hand to challenge the lesson, misunderstanding the scope of evolutionary ancestry.
scenario.text: Professor Thorne states: 'The theory of evolution posits that all species undergo change over time through natural selection, including humans.' Kael interrupts: 'I can't accept that! You're saying humans came directly from bugs! That's ridiculous; we don't have six legs or antennae.'
scenario.speaker_context: Professor Thorne stated that humans evolve like all species. Kael distorted this into the claim that humans evolved directly from modern bugs, a specific and absurd assertion the professor never made, and attacked that distortion.

structure.pattern_description: Kael takes the Professor's general statement about common ancestry and evolutionary change ('all species evolve') and distorts it into a specific, easily refutable claim ('humans came directly from bugs'). He then rejects the theory based on this fabricated extreme.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (humans evolve like other species). Person B restates P as distorted P* (humans came directly from bugs). Person B attacks P* (we don't have six legs). Person B concludes P is false.
structure.why_wrong: The student attacks a caricature of the theory. Evolutionary biology posits a common ancestor for insects and humans hundreds of millions of years ago, not that humans descended from modern bugs. The absence of antennae does not refute the actual theory.
structure.counterpoint: Professor Thorne could reply: 'I did not say humans came from bugs. I said we share a distant common ancestor and both undergo evolutionary change. Attacking the idea that we are insects does not disprove evolution.'

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Kael misrepresent Professor Thorne's statement about evolution?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael that the professor's statement implies humans are bugs.
Player feels Kael is being rude or loud but cannot identify the logical error.
Player notices Kael is talking about bugs while the professor talked about evolution generally, but cannot explain the distortion.
Player identifies that Kael exaggerated the professor's claim into 'humans came from bugs' to make it easier to reject.

Player explicitly names the Straw Man fallacy, explaining that Kael attacked a distorted version of the theory (direct descent from bugs) rather than the actual claim (common ancestry and evolutionary change).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely: Did the professor actually say humans are bugs, or did Kael assume that to make the argument easier to win?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct! Kael built a 'straw man' by replacing the complex truth of common ancestry with a silly claim about bugs, then knocked it down.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Kael is an impulsive student who prefers simple answers and gets frustrated by nuance, often jumping to conclusions before listening fully.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's obvious! If we evolved, we'd look like them! You can't trick me with fancy words, Professor!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that clarify the difference between 'common ancestor' and 'direct descent' to calm Kael and restore the lesson flow.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Oakhaven, a charismatic but pushy merchant named Silas is trying to sell an enchanted stereo system to a young adventurer who has just returned from a dungeon with modest loot.
scenario.text: Silas leans in close, blocking your path to the exit. 'Look, friend, the choice is simple: Either you decide that you can afford this magnificent stereo right now, or you decide not to have music for a while. There is no middle ground. So, are you buying, or are you condemning yourself to silence?'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas, a silver-tongued merchant who uses high-pressure sales tactics and frames financial decisions as lifestyle ultimatums.

structure.pattern_description: Silas presents the situation as having only two possible outcomes: buying the expensive stereo immediately or having no music at all. He ignores other viable options such as saving money for later, buying a cheaper instrument, listening to free street performers, or simply waiting for a sale.
structure.formal_form: A v B, therefore if not A then B. (Where A = Buy stereo now, B = No music). The reality is A v B v C v D...
structure.why_wrong: The disjunction is not exhaustive. One can choose not to buy the stereo now and still have music through other means or at a later time. The premise falsely limits the solution space to force a sale.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or statement is a fallacy. If the stereo were the only source of music in existence and it was about to be destroyed, the choice might be genuine. The fallacy lies in ignoring realistic alternatives that clearly exist.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas claims you must either buy the stereo now or live without music. What is logically flawed about this ultimatum?

rubric.description: Accepts Silas's framing and chooses one of the two options without question.
Feels pressured or suspicious but cannot explain why the logic is flawed.
Identifies that there are other ways to get music but does not name the logical error.
Identifies the false dichotomy and lists at least one specific alternative option (e.g., saving money, cheaper instruments).
Clearly explains that the disjunction is not exhaustive, names the false dichotomy fallacy, provides multiple alternatives, and notes how the speaker is manipulating the choice.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Silas says those are your only two choices. Can you think of a third thing you could do that involves music but doesn't require buying this specific stereo today?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Silas ignored the middle ground. Can you think of a scenario where an 'either/or' choice about purchasing something would actually be legitimate and not a fallacy?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Pushy, manipulative, speaks in absolutes, treats hesitation as failure.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't overthink it! It's black or white, friend. Rich sound or dead silence. Which will it be?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully points out a third option (e.g., 'I'll save my gold for a lute'), causing Silas to lose his composure and offer a discount or retreat, revealing his tactic failed.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Gearhaven, a young apprentice is trying to convince customers to buy a strange new health tonic. He leans heavily on his father's reputation to sell the product.
scenario.text: My dad is a master mechanic and he says that brushing your teeth twice a day is good for you. Since he is a mechanic, he knows best.
scenario.speaker_context: The speaker is the son of a renowned mechanic. While his father is an undisputed expert in engines and machinery, he has no formal training or experience in dentistry or human biology.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker argues that a health claim is true solely because a mechanic (an authority in a different field) said so.
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is expert in domain D. P is in domain D*. Therefore P is true. (But D ≠ D*.)
structure.why_wrong: Expertise is domain-specific. Being an expert in mechanics does not grant authority on dental hygiene. The father's opinion on teeth is just a personal opinion, not an expert verdict.
structure.counterpoint: If the father were a dentist, citing his opinion would be a strong argument. The fallacy occurs only because the authority's expertise does not match the subject matter.

assessment.identification_prompt: The speaker claims his father 'knows best' about teeth. What is his father's actual job, and does that job make him an expert on dental health?

rubric.description: Accepts the claim completely because the father is an expert in something.
Feels unsure but cannot explain why the father's job might be irrelevant.
Notices the father is a mechanic, not a dentist, but doesn't fully explain why that invalidates the claim.
Identifies that the father's expertise is in machines, not human biology, making his opinion on teeth unreliable.
Clearly names the appeal to irrelevant authority, explains the domain mismatch between mechanics and dentistry, and notes when citing authority would be valid.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If your father said the engine needs oil, you'd trust him. But if he said this specific berry is safe to eat, would his mechanic skills help him know that?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Imagine the town has no dentist, only this mechanic who has read many books on teeth. Does his mechanical precision make his dental advice better than a random guess, or is it still not expert testimony?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest but misguided apprentice who respects his father immensely and assumes expertise transfers to all areas of life.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But he fixes the biggest steam-engines in the city! If he can fix those, surely he knows what's good for my teeth!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must guide the apprentice to realize that while his father is smart, dental health requires a different kind of knowledge, perhaps suggesting they visit the local herbalist or dentist instead.

scenario.context: In the Grand Council Chamber, Councilor Vane is being questioned about his recent voting record on environmental regulations. Critics point out his consistent opposition to green initiatives.
scenario.text: Councilor Vane smiles reassuringly: 'While you may have concerns about my votes on the environment, I can assure you that I am an open-minded individual. What we should really discuss is my record on votes that expanded educational opportunities for all children.'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane avoids addressing the specific criticism regarding his environmental votes. Instead, he pivots to a different topic (education) where his record has positive consequences, implying that his good deeds in one area validate his stance or deflect criticism in another, unrelated area.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim or action should be accepted (or a criticism rejected) based on the positive consequences of an unrelated action, rather than addressing the evidence at hand.
structure.formal_form: Action A has undesirable implications. But Action B has desirable consequences. Therefore, Action A is acceptable (or the criticism of A is invalid).
structure.why_wrong: The validity of a specific vote or claim depends on its own merits and evidence, not on the positive outcomes of unrelated actions. Good consequences in one domain do not logically negate bad decisions or valid criticisms in another.
structure.counterpoint: It is good that Vane supported education, but that fact is irrelevant to whether his environmental votes were sound. One can be a champion for schools and still vote poorly on the environment; the two issues must be evaluated separately.

assessment.identification_prompt: Vane mentions his support for education. Does this provide any evidence that his environmental votes were correct?

rubric.description: Accepts Vane's argument; believes supporting education proves he is right about the environment.
Feels Vane is changing the subject but cannot explain why the education point doesn't fix the environment issue.
Notices Vane is talking about a different topic (education) instead of answering the question about the environment.
Identifies that Vane is using the good consequences of his education votes to distract from the criticism of his environmental votes.
Explicitly names the fallacy (Appeal to Consequences/Red Herring mix) and explains that positive outcomes in one policy area do not logically validate decisions in an unrelated policy area.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Vane had voted to cut school funding but voted correctly on the environment, would that make his environmental votes wrong?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: How can we praise Vane for his education record without letting him use it as a shield against valid criticism of his environmental record?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, deflective, uses warm fuzzy topics to avoid hard truths.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Think of the children! Surely someone who cares this much about schools can't be wrong about everything else.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must press Vane to address the specific data regarding the environmental votes, refusing to let the conversation pivot to education until the original point is resolved.

scenario.context: In the campaign war room of the Silver Spire, High Strategist Vane is reviewing the latest intelligence reports regarding the upcoming vote on the 'Charter of Unity'. The room is tense; the amendment requires a simple majority to pass, but recent surveys suggest a lack of enthusiasm rather than active hatred.
scenario.text: High Strategist Vane points to the polling data, his voice dripping with certainty. 'Because recent polling indicates that no voters in the county are strongly in favor of the proposed amendment, we can expect strong opposition to the amendment when it is voted on next month. There is no middle ground; if they aren't cheering for it, they are fighting against it.'
scenario.speaker_context: High Strategist Vane, a rigid logistician who believes nuance is a weakness and forces complex public sentiment into binary categories.

structure.pattern_description: Vane presents the spectrum of voter sentiment as exhaustive: one must either be 'strongly in favor' or 'strongly opposed.' He ignores the vast middle ground of voters who are indifferent, mildly supportive, mildly opposed, or simply undecided.
structure.formal_form: For any voter x, either StronglyFavor(x) or StronglyOppose(x). Since ~StronglyFavor(x), therefore StronglyOppose(x). This ignores the possibility of Neutral(x), MildlyFavor(x), or MildlyOppose(x).
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes that the absence of strong support necessitates strong opposition. In reality, 'not strongly in favor' includes many states such as apathy, mild agreement, or uncertainty, none of which equate to active opposition.
structure.counterpoint: Not every binary is false. If a light switch is strictly on or off, then 'not on' implies 'off.' However, human opinion is rarely binary; it exists on a continuum. The fallacy occurs when a continuum is artificially collapsed into two extremes.

assessment.identification_prompt: Strategist Vane claims that because no one strongly favors the amendment, everyone must strongly oppose it. What logical error is he making regarding the voters' options?

rubric.description: Accepts Vane's conclusion that the amendment will fail due to strong opposition without question.
Senses the conclusion is too extreme but cannot explain why the logic is flawed.
Identifies that people can be neutral or unsure, but does not name the logical structure.
Identifies the false dichotomy, noting that 'not strongly in favor' does not automatically mean 'strongly opposed'.
Fully explains the false dichotomy, lists specific alternative states (indifference, mild support), and clarifies that the disjunction presented by Vane is not exhaustive.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Vane says if they aren't cheering, they are booing. Can you think of a way a voter might feel who is neither cheering nor booing?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. If the poll showed 0% strong support, what is the most likely actual outcome if the majority are just indifferent? How does that change the strategy?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Rigid, binary-thinking bureaucrat who dislikes ambiguity and tries to force complex social situations into simple 'friend vs. foe' narratives.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You're either with the plan or you're sabotaging it! There is no 'waiting to see'!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player presents a 'Nuance Report' showing three categories of voters (Support, Oppose, Indifferent), proving Vane's binary model incorrect and preventing a wasted campaign on fighting non-existent opposition.

scenario.context: In the neon-lit corridors of the Vertex Mall, a charismatic but manipulative street vendor named 'Jax the Stylist' blocks your path. He is holding up two vastly different outfits: one is his own overpriced, flashy ensemble, and the other is a tattered, generic uniform.
scenario.text: Jax grins, flashing a gold tooth. 'Listen up, kid. You can look cool in our clothes, or you can look like a loser. There is no middle ground. So, are you buying the drip, or are you signing up for social suicide?'
scenario.speaker_context: Jax the Stylist, a smooth-talking merchant who uses social pressure and binary framing to close sales, treating any hesitation as a personal insult.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker presents a disjunction as exhaustive when it is not. Jax forces a choice between looking 'cool' in his specific clothes or looking like a 'loser,' ignoring all other possibilities such as looking cool in different clothes, looking average, or defining style independently of commercial products.
structure.formal_form: A v B, ~A, therefore B. But the real situation is A v B v C v D..., so ~A does not entail B.
structure.why_wrong: Jax falsely limits the options to only two extremes. He ignores the vast spectrum of appearance outcomes between 'cool in our clothes' and 'loser,' such as looking cool in other brands, looking neat but not 'cool,' or simply not caring about the label.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or is a false dichotomy. If the options were 'You are either alive or dead,' the disjunction might be exhaustive. The critical question is whether the presented options cover the full space of relevant possibilities.

assessment.identification_prompt: Jax claims you must either buy his clothes to look cool or be a loser. What is wrong with how he has framed your choices?

rubric.description: Accepts Jax's framing or responds only emotionally (e.g., 'I'm not a loser!').
Senses something is off or unfair but cannot articulate the logical error.
Identifies that other options exist (e.g., 'I can look cool elsewhere') but does not name the logical structure.
Names the false dichotomy and provides at least one concrete alternative scenario.

Explains that the disjunction is not exhaustive, names the fallacy, offers multiple alternatives, and notes that the argument fails because it ignores the spectrum of possibilities between the two extremes.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Jax gave you exactly two options. Are those really the only two ways to dress? Try to think of a third possibility where you don't buy his clothes but also aren't a 'loser'.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Under what conditions would an either/or framing about fashion actually be legitimate? Can you think of a scenario where there truly are only two choices?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Manipulative, hyper-confident, uses social anxiety as a weapon, speaks in absolutes.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't overthink it, hero! It's simple math: Cool Us vs. Loner You. Which side of the equation are you on?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully identifies the third option (e.g., 'I can make my own style'), causing Jax's confidence to falter and lowering his prices, or the player walks away unaffected by the pressure.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling marketplace of Oakhaven during the annual Town Hall debate. Candidate Elara Vance has just finished presenting a detailed economic plan to lower taxes for small businesses, citing growth projections and budget reallocations. Before the player can ask a clarifying question, her opponent, Councilor Thaddeus Brunt, steps up to the microphone to rebut her proposal.
scenario.text: Thaddeus sneers at the crowd. 'My opponent suggests that lowering taxes will be a good idea -- but let's be honest, this is coming from a woman who eats a pint of Ben and Jerry's each night! How can we trust her fiscal responsibility when she clearly has none for her own diet?'
scenario.speaker_context: Councilor Thaddeus Brunt, a seasoned politician known for his sharp tongue and reliance on personal attacks rather than policy details. He often uses humor and mockery to deflect from substantive arguments.

structure.pattern_description: Thaddeus attacks Elara's personal habit (eating ice cream nightly) which is completely irrelevant to her economic proposal about tax cuts. He attempts to discredit her argument about fiscal policy by mocking her personal lifestyle choices.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X (lowering taxes is good). Person P has property Q (eats ice cream nightly, irrelevant to X). Therefore, X is false or should be dismissed.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of an economic argument depends on data, logic, and evidence regarding taxes and budgets, not on the proponent's dietary habits. Elara's ice cream consumption has no logical connection to the feasibility or merit of her tax plan. Thaddeus provides zero counter-evidence to her projections.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if they directly impact the person's ability to perform the specific task argued. If Elara claimed, 'I am an expert in nutrition,' then her diet might be relevant. However, since she is arguing about economics, her diet is irrelevant.

assessment.identification_prompt: Thaddeus seems very confident in his mockery. But look closely: does eating ice cream actually prove that a tax plan is bad? What specific part of Elara's economic data did he address?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thaddeus, believing that personal habits determine fiscal competence.
Player feels Thaddeus is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why his logic is flawed.
Player identifies that Thaddeus is attacking Elara personally instead of her argument.
Player explains that dietary habits are irrelevant to economic policy and notes the lack of counter-evidence.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, identifying the disconnect between the premise (ice cream) and the conclusion (tax policy), and articulates why the argument fails logically.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a mathematician who loves pizza says 2+2=4, is the math wrong because of the pizza? Why does the same logic apply here?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thaddeus tried to distract the crowd with a joke about ice cream instead of addressing the actual numbers. That's a classic Ad Hominem attack.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Thaddeus is charismatic but shallow, often using wit to mask a lack of substantive knowledge. He thrives on crowd reaction.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think I'm being harsh? Look at her! She can't even manage her own calorie intake, let alone the town budget!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to expose the fallacy publicly to gain support from logical voters, or ignore it and let Thaddeus win the crowd with humor, affecting the town's future economic stats.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling marketplace of the capital city, where a heated debate has drawn a crowd. Bill, a local merchant, has just finished explaining his detailed concerns about the new healthcare mandate, citing specific costs and logistical hurdles. Dave, a vocal supporter of the current administration, steps forward to respond, ignoring the points entirely.
scenario.text: Bill: "I believe that the new healthcare mandate is wrong." Dave: "Of course you would say that, you're a Republican." Bill: "What about the arguments I gave to support my position?" Dave: "Those don't count. Like I said, you're a Republican, so you have to support the party line. Further, you are just a lapdog to the Republican incumbent so you can get a job, so I can't believe what you say."
scenario.speaker_context: Dave is a charismatic but aggressive town crier known for rallying crowds through emotional appeals rather than factual debate. He often dismisses opponents by labeling them rather than addressing their points.

structure.pattern_description: Dave rejects Bill's arguments solely based on Bill's political affiliation (Republican) and alleged ulterior motives (seeking a job), rather than engaging with the specific costs and logistical issues Bill raised. He assumes Bill's position is invalid because of who he is and who he supports.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P belongs to group G or has circumstance C. Therefore, claim X is false or should be dismissed.
structure.why_wrong: The truth or falsity of an argument depends on the evidence and logic provided, not on the speaker's political party or potential motives. Even if Bill is a Republican or wants a job, his arguments about costs and logistics could still be valid. Dave fails to provide any counter-evidence to Bill's specific points.
structure.counterpoint: It is reasonable to question a person's bias if they are the sole source of evidence or if their motive directly fabricates the data. However, pointing out a bias does not automatically disprove the logical structure or factual claims of an argument; the claims must still be refuted on their own merits.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dave seems very confident in dismissing Bill. But look closely: did Dave address any of the specific costs or logistical problems Bill mentioned? Or did he focus entirely on Bill's identity?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Dave, believing that being a Republican automatically makes Bill's argument wrong.
Player feels Dave is being mean or unfair but cannot explain the logical error.
Player identifies that Dave is attacking Bill instead of the argument but cannot name the specific fallacy.
Player correctly identifies that Dave is committing an Ad Hominem fallacy by ignoring the evidence and attacking Bill's affiliation.
Player explains that while Bill's bias might be relevant to his credibility, it does not logically invalidate the specific premises regarding costs and logistics without further refutation.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a person you disliked told you 'the bridge is out ahead,' would you drive off the bridge just to prove them wrong? Or would you check the bridge? Dave is telling you to ignore the 'bridge' (the argument) just because he dislikes the messenger.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Dave committed an Ad Hominem fallacy. He tried to discredit the message by attacking the messenger's party affiliation and motives, completely ignoring the actual evidence Bill presented about costs and logistics.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Combative, partisan, relies on slogans and labels rather than data. Gains influence when the crowd is emotional but loses respect among scholars.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't listen to [Player Name], they're probably working for the opposition too! What do they know about real issues?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to expose Dave's logical failure to the crowd, gaining 'Logic' reputation, or attempt to mediate by asking Dave to address the specific cost figures Bill mentioned.

scenario.context: The player enters the dimly lit tent of Madame Zora, a self-proclaimed master of 'biocognitive astral-projective hyperaffective-hypnotic-teleological-metatherapy.' She is trying to convince the player to purchase a bulk package of sessions despite having no credentials or evidence of success.
scenario.text: In the four years that I have been marketing my new and improved brand of past-life regressive biocognitive astral-projective hyperaffective-hypnotic-teleological-metatherapy (buy ten sessions and the next one is free!), not one person has proved it is worthless or that I am unethical for providing a therapy I just made up one day when I realized that no one was referring clients to me anymore. That makes clear what a worthwhile therapy this is and how exceptionally ethical I am to provide it.
scenario.speaker_context: Madame Zora attempts to validate her invented therapy by claiming that the lack of disproof equates to proof of worth. She implicitly labels any potential critic as unable to prove her wrong, and frames her own lack of evidence as a sign of her exceptional ethics, effectively labeling skepticism as a failure of the skeptic rather than a lack of merit in her product.

structure.pattern_description: While primarily an Appeal to Ignorance, this example utilizes implicit labeling to shield the argument. Zora labels her therapy as 'worthwhile' and herself as 'exceptionally ethical' solely because no one has successfully attached the negative labels of 'worthless' or 'unethical' to them yet. She treats the absence of a negative label as the presence of a positive one, bypassing the need for actual evidence.
structure.formal_form: No one has proven Claim C is false (or Person P is bad). Therefore, Claim C is true (or Person P is good/worthy). The absence of a negative label is treated as a positive label.
structure.why_wrong: The absence of disproof is not proof. Just because no one has successfully called the therapy 'worthless' does not mean it has value; it may simply mean no one has tested it, or that the burden of proof is incorrectly placed on the skeptics. Validity requires positive evidence, not just a lack of successful criticism.
structure.counterpoint: In legal systems, a defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty (a lack of a 'guilty' label implies an 'innocent' status). However, in scientific or logical claims about reality (like a therapy's effectiveness), the burden of proof lies with the person making the positive claim, not on others to disprove it.

assessment.identification_prompt: Madame Zora claims her therapy is 'worthwhile' and she is 'ethical' because no one has proved otherwise. Does the lack of a negative accusation automatically create a positive truth?

rubric.description: Player accepts Zora's logic: since no one proved her wrong, she must be right and ethical.
Player feels skeptical but cannot articulate why the lack of disproof isn't proof.
Player identifies that Zora is shifting the burden of proof but misses the labeling aspect.
Player recognizes that Zora is treating the absence of a negative label ('unproven worthless') as a definitive positive label ('worthwhile').

Player fully deconstructs the fallacy: explains that validity requires positive evidence, not just the failure of others to apply a negative label, and identifies this as a manipulation of terminology.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If I claimed I invented a magic invisible dragon that no one can see or detect, and you couldn't prove it doesn't exist, would that automatically make my dragon real and my claim trustworthy?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Zora is trying to wear the badge of 'Ethical Expert' without earning it. She thinks that because no one has torn the badge off (disproved her), she must deserve to wear it. But in logic, you have to earn the badge with evidence, not just wait for someone to fail to take it away.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, pseudo-intellectual, uses overly complex jargon to confuse listeners, and reacts to skepticism with feigned moral outrage.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You doubt me? How dare you! Can you PROVE I'm a charlatan? No? Then I am clearly a saint of science!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a simple, testable prediction for the therapy. When Zora cannot provide one without resorting to more jargon or ad hominem attacks, her 'ethical' label crumbles, revealing the lack of substance.

scenario.context: The player enters the War Room of the Citadel, where General Thorne is reviewing intelligence reports regarding the hostile nation of Drakmoor. He points aggressively at a map marked with nuclear symbols.
scenario.text: General Thorne slams his fist on the table. 'We have no choice but to launch a preemptive strike on Drakmoor immediately. The intelligence is clear: their leader, Saddam, is determined to knock us down specifically because he has developed the potential for a nuclear bomb. The existence of that potential is the sole reason for his aggression. If we remove the bomb potential, the aggression stops; if we wait, they will strike first.'
scenario.speaker_context: General Thorne assumes that the mere existence of a capability (nuclear potential) is the direct and only cause of the enemy's hostile intent. He ignores other historical, political, or ideological factors that might drive the conflict, treating the correlation between 'having bombs' and 'being aggressive' as a strict causal link where the former necessitates the latter.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne observes two factors: the enemy's aggressive stance and their nuclear potential. He infers that the nuclear potential is the specific cause of the aggression. This ignores alternative explanations: the aggression could stem from territorial disputes, ideological differences, or past grievances, regardless of nuclear status. The presence of a weapon does not automatically cause the intent to use it for aggression.
structure.formal_form: Event A (nuclear potential) is present alongside Event B (aggression). Therefore, A causes B. (Flaw: B could be caused by C, D, or E; A and B might be coincidental or both caused by a third factor like regime instability.)
structure.why_wrong: The argument commits the false cause fallacy by assuming that because two conditions exist simultaneously (nuclear capability and hostile intent), one must cause the other. It fails to consider that the leader might be aggressive due to non-nuclear reasons, or that the nuclear program is a result of the aggression/fear rather than the cause of it.
structure.counterpoint: While nuclear proliferation can increase tension, asserting it as the singular cause of a specific leader's determination to attack requires evidence of motive linking the two directly. History shows many aggressive leaders without nuclear weapons and many nuclear powers without aggressive expansionist policies. Correlation of traits does not prove causal mechanism.

assessment.identification_prompt: General Thorne claims the enemy's nuclear potential is the definite cause of their aggression. What logical error is he making regarding the relationship between these two factors?

rubric.description: Fails to identify any logical error; accepts the General's conclusion as fact.
Identifies that the General might be wrong but cannot explain the logical structure of the error.
Notes that having bombs doesn't always mean someone will attack, but misses the formal causal fallacy.
Correctly identifies that the General is confusing correlation (or co-existence) with causation, ignoring other possible motives.
Precisely articulates the False Cause fallacy, explaining that the presence of nuclear potential does not necessitate aggressive intent and listing alternative causes for the conflict.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider: Have there ever been leaders with nuclear weapons who were not aggressive? Or aggressive leaders without them? Does the weapon create the hate, or does the hate seek the weapon?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Thorne is treating a capability as a motive. By identifying this false cause, you can propose diplomatic solutions that address the actual root causes of the conflict rather than just the weaponry.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Hawkish, impulsive, relies on simplified military heuristics, distrustful of nuance.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think I'm jumping to conclusions? Look at the data! Bomb potential equals attack intent. It's simple math, cadet!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Successfully debunking the fallacy lowers the 'War Meter' and unlocks a 'Diplomatic Inquiry' quest line instead of immediate combat.

scenario.context: In the bustling town square of Veridia, the City Council is debating a modest proposal to raise the state minimum wage by $1.50 to help workers afford rising food costs. Councilor Thorne, a wealthy merchant known for his dramatic flair, stands to oppose the measure.
scenario.text: Councilor Thorne declares: 'Those who do not support this proposed minimum wage increase clearly hate the poor! They want families to starve and children to go without shoes. How can you look the needy in the eye and say no?'
scenario.speaker_context: The original proposal was a specific economic adjustment ($1.50 raise). Thorne recharacterized opposition to this specific number as a moral failure and a desire for the poor to suffer, an extreme position no one actually holds.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne takes the opponent's position (opposition to a specific $1.50 wage hike) and distorts it into an extreme, morally repugnant position (hating the poor and wanting them to starve). He then attacks this fabricated motive rather than addressing the economic arguments against the hike.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (oppose specific wage hike). Person B restates P as distorted P* (hate the poor/want them to starve). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes A is immoral, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: Opposing a specific policy proposal is not equivalent to hating the demographic that policy aims to help. Thorne ignores potential reasons for opposition (e.g., inflation concerns, small business viability) and instead attacks a fabricated malicious intent.
structure.counterpoint: Councilor, opposing this specific dollar amount is not the same as hating the poor. Many of us want to help families but believe this specific hike might cause job losses. Let's discuss the actual economic impact, not imagined hatred.

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Councilor Thorne misrepresent the arguments of those who oppose the wage increase?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne or believes opposing the wage hike truly means hating the poor.
Player feels Thorne is being unfair or too emotional but cannot explain why logically.
Player notices Thorne is exaggerating but fails to distinguish between the policy objection and the alleged motive.
Player identifies that Thorne replaced the actual argument (economic policy disagreement) with a fake one (moral hatred of the poor) to make it easier to attack.
Player explicitly names the 'Straw Man' fallacy, explains the distortion (policy vs. malice), and articulates why attacking the distortion proves nothing about the original policy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne claims anyone who says 'no' to the raise wants the poor to starve. Is it possible someone could say 'no' to the raise for a different reason, like worrying about small businesses closing?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thorne built a 'straw man'—a fake, evil version of the opposition's argument that is easy to knock down. He didn't address the actual economic concerns raised by the council.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dramatic, populist, prone to emotional manipulation, speaks in absolutes.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You dare question the wage hike? Do you want the bakers' children to go hungry? Speak true, or admit your cruelty!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must choose a dialogue option that separates the economic argument from the moral accusation, calming the crowd and forcing Thorne to address the actual numbers.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Oakhaven, a street performer named Jax is trying to sell a mysterious 'Luck Stone' to a crowd of skeptical adventurers.
scenario.text: Jax holds up a dull gray rock and shouts, 'Don't just stand there staring! Look around you—everyone in this square is buying one! The blacksmith bought two, the mayor's guard has one in each pocket, and even the shy librarian grabbed the last big one. When this many people feel this way, you know it works. You don't want to be the only adventurer without luck today, do you?'
scenario.speaker_context: Jax offers no proof of the stone's magical properties. His entire argument relies on the observation that many others are purchasing the item, implying that their collective action validates the claim.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition must be true or good simply because a large number of people believe it or are doing it. It treats popularity as a substitute for evidence.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The number of people who believe something has no logical bearing on its truth value. Popularity can be driven by social pressure, marketing, misinformation, or tradition, none of which constitute factual evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Widespread adoption can sometimes indicate utility if independent agents converge on a solution after separate investigation (e.g., many engineers choosing a specific bridge design). However, this differs from blind conformity or emotional contagion in a crowd.

assessment.identification_prompt: What actual evidence does Jax provide that the Luck Stone works? Is the fact that 'everyone is buying one' a valid reason to believe it works?

rubric.description: Finds the pitch convincing; assumes that if so many people bought it, the stone must work.
Feels hesitant about the claim but cannot explain why the popularity of the stone is not good evidence.
Notes that Jax gives no real proof of magic but fails to explicitly identify the 'popularity-as-evidence' flaw.
Identifies that Jax uses the number of buyers as his sole evidence and explains that popularity does not establish truth.
Names the bandwagon fallacy, explains why popularity is not evidence, identifies the social pressure component ('don't be the only one'), and distinguishes this from evidential convergence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Suppose every person in the kingdom believed the sky was green. Would that make the sky actually green?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where the fact that many people believe something DOES give you a good reason to take it seriously? How is that different from this scenario?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jax is a fast-talking, high-energy street hustler who thrives on crowd momentum and fear of missing out (FOMO). He speaks quickly and gestures wildly to the surrounding crowd.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Come on, don't be the odd one out! The whole town is doing it!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out that the crowd's behavior is not proof of the stone's power, causing Jax to stutter and eventually admit he has no real proof, dispersing the crowd.

scenario.context: The player approaches the heavy iron gates of the St. Aethelgard Hospital. A nervous guard named Kaelen is shouting orders at a group of travelers from the neighboring city of Abu Dhabi, refusing them entry despite their pleas for medical aid.
scenario.text: Kaelen points a shaking finger at the travelers. 'Stay back! The hospital tested three patients from Abu Dhabi this morning and found they had the plague. That is enough proof for me. I am immediately banning ALL people from Abu Dhabi from entering these gates. Every single one of you is a carrier!'
scenario.speaker_context: Kaelen is acting out of fear and urgency. He has data on exactly three individuals from a city that likely contains hundreds of thousands of people. He is extrapolating the health status of three infected patients to the entire population of Abu Dhabi without further evidence.

structure.pattern_description: Kaelen observes that three specific individuals from Abu Dhabi have a disease and concludes that every person from Abu Dhabi must also have the disease. He treats a tiny, non-representative sample (3 people) as sufficient evidence to characterize the entire population of a city.
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of X from population P (where n=3 and P is very large). All observed instances had property Q (disease). Therefore, all members of P have property Q.
structure.why_wrong: A sample size of three is statistically insignificant relative to the population of a city. The presence of disease in three individuals does not imply universal infection; it may indicate an outbreak, but barring everyone ignores the high probability that many residents are healthy. The sample is too small to support a universal claim.
structure.counterpoint: While caution is warranted when a disease is detected, a logical response involves quarantine protocols or testing more individuals, not assuming 100% infection rates based on three cases. Generalizing from such a small sample ignores basic probability.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kaelen claims that because three patients from Abu Dhabi are sick, everyone from Abu Dhabi must be sick and should be banned. Is his conclusion logically justified by the evidence he provided?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kaelen, accepting that three cases prove the whole city is infected.
Player feels the ban is harsh but cannot explain the logical flaw in the reasoning.
Player notes that three people is a small number but fails to explicitly connect it to the size of the whole city's population.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, stating that three cases are insufficient to characterize an entire city's population.

Player identifies the hasty generalization, explains the sample size error, and suggests a more logical alternative (e.g., testing more people or quarantining only the suspected) instead of a total ban.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider the population of Abu Dhabi. If it has 100,000 people, does finding 3 sick people really mean the other 99,997 are definitely sick too?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Kaelen is letting fear drive his logic. Three cases suggest a risk, but they don't prove universal infection. A better approach would be to test a larger random sample or implement targeted quarantine.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, authoritative, acting on instinct rather than reason. He prioritizes the safety of the hospital above all else, even at the cost of fairness.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I don't care about your excuses! Three is all it takes to doom us all. Turn back or face the guards!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can present a logical argument to Kaelen to lower his anxiety, convincing him to allow entry under supervised testing conditions, or expose his fallacy to a superior officer to override the ban.

scenario.context: The player visits the Grand Confectionery Guild in the capital city. Master Chocolatier Von Truffle is presenting his latest theory on health and nutrition to a crowd of eager apprentices, pointing to a map of the world.
scenario.text: Master Von Truffle taps his cane on a large map highlighting Switzerland. 'Observe the data, my young apprentices! Global chocolate consumption is highest in Switzerland, yet the people there are among the trimmest in the entire industrialized world. The evidence is right before our eyes! Therefore, it is entirely reasonable to conclude that chocolate helps keep your weight down. Eat more chocolate, and you too shall be slim!'
scenario.speaker_context: Von Truffle is a brilliant baker but a terrible logician. He has identified a genuine correlation between high chocolate consumption and low obesity rates in Switzerland but has incorrectly inferred that the chocolate causes the slimness. He ignores confounding variables such as the high cost of living, active lifestyles (hiking/skiing), portion control culture, or genetic factors that likely explain the data better than the chocolate itself.

structure.pattern_description: Von Truffle observes that two variables are correlated (high chocolate consumption and low obesity rates) and infers that one causes the other (chocolate causes weight loss). However, correlation does not establish causation. There are four possibilities: (1) chocolate causes weight loss, (2) being thin causes people to eat more chocolate, (3) a third factor (like an active lifestyle or wealthy economy) causes both, or (4) the correlation is coincidental. The fallacy lies in jumping to conclusion (1) without ruling out the others.
structure.formal_form: A and B are correlated. Therefore A causes B. (But: A could cause B, B could cause A, C could cause both, or the correlation could be coincidental.)
structure.why_wrong: Correlation between two variables does not prove that one causes the other. Von Truffle has not ruled out reverse causation, a common cause (confounding variable), or coincidence. In this case, it is highly probable that a third factor, such as a culture of physical activity or higher socioeconomic status in Switzerland, leads to both higher chocolate consumption (as a luxury good) and lower obesity rates, rather than the chocolate itself causing weight loss.
structure.counterpoint: Correlations can be evidence for causation only when combined with a plausible biological mechanism, correct temporal ordering, and the elimination of confounding variables. The classic counter-example is that ice cream sales correlate with drowning deaths, but eating ice cream does not cause drowning; rather, hot weather (a common cause) increases both swimming and ice cream consumption.

assessment.identification_prompt: Master Von Truffle claims that because Swiss people eat the most chocolate and are very thin, chocolate must cause weight loss. What is the flaw in this reasoning?

rubric.description: The player accepts Von Truffle's conclusion or fails to identify any logical error.
The player suspects the conclusion is wrong but cannot articulate why, or suggests an unrelated error.
The player identifies that correlation does not equal causation but does not offer alternative explanations.
The player explains that correlation does not imply causation and suggests that a third factor (confounder) might be responsible.

The player fully deconstructs the fallacy, explicitly stating that correlation is not causation, identifying potential confounding variables (e.g., lifestyle, economy), and explaining why the causal link is unsupported.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think again: Just because two things happen together, does that mean one makes the other happen? Could something else be causing both?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because Switzerland has high chocolate consumption and low obesity doesn't mean the chocolate makes them thin. It's likely that other factors, like an active lifestyle or diet habits, cause both. You've spotted the False Cause fallacy!

game_hooks.npc_personality: Enthusiastic, proud, slightly dogmatic about sweets, wears a flour-dusted apron and a tall chef's hat.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: More chocolate for everyone! It's the secret to a slender figure, I tell you!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player convinces Von Truffle to test his theory with a controlled experiment rather than relying on national statistics, preventing the guild from promoting a potentially unhealthy diet plan.

scenario.context: In the Grand Hall of the Academy of Reason, High Scholar Valerius stands before a panel of junior researchers. A controversial new study on a magical intervention for 'Soul Rot' has just been presented. The results are promising but limited, yet Valerius demands immediate, unconditional adoption.
scenario.text: High Scholar Valerius sweeps his robes and declares, 'Either we accept the findings of this study demonstrating that this new intervention is the best to be used for this disorder, or we must no longer call ourselves scientists, psychologists, or reasonable people.'
scenario.speaker_context: High Scholar Valerius, an arrogant academic who equates disagreement with intellectual incompetence and uses social pressure to force consensus.

structure.pattern_description: Valerius presents a disjunction as exhaustive when it is not. He forces a choice between accepting the study's specific conclusion or abandoning one's identity as a rational scientist, ignoring middle grounds like accepting the data while questioning the methodology, waiting for replication, or exploring alternative treatments.
structure.formal_form: A v B, ~A, therefore B. But the real situation is A v B v C v D..., so ~A does not entail B.
structure.why_wrong: Valerius constructs a false dilemma by suggesting that rejecting the specific claim ('this is the best intervention') necessitates rejecting the entire identity of being a scientist. One can be a reasonable person and still demand more evidence or propose different interpretations.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or is a false dichotomy. If the only two options were 'accept the proven fact' or 'deny reality,' it might be valid. However, scientific inquiry inherently involves skepticism and alternative hypotheses, making the disjunction here non-exhaustive.

assessment.identification_prompt: High Scholar Valerius claims you must either accept this study as the definitive best solution or admit you are not a reasonable scientist. What is logically flawed about this ultimatum?

rubric.description: Accepts Valerius's framing out of fear or authority, or responds only with emotional defensiveness.
Senses the threat is unfair or exaggerated but cannot identify the logical structure.
Identifies that there are other options (like asking for more data) but does not name the fallacy.
Names the false dichotomy and explains that rejecting the study's conclusion does not mean rejecting science itself.

Fully deconstructs the argument: identifies the false dichotomy, explains that the disjunction is not exhaustive (listing alternatives like peer review or replication), and notes that true scientists often question findings.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Valerius says those are your only two choices. Can you think of a way to be a 'reasonable person' who still has questions about this specific study?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Science thrives on skepticism. Under what conditions would an either/or statement about scientific acceptance actually be legitimate?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elitist, intimidating, uses ad hominem threats disguised as logical necessities, values conformity over rigorous inquiry.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Do you dare suggest there is a third option? To hesitate is to admit you do not belong in this hall!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully points out that true science requires questioning even promising results, causing Valerius to grudgingly agree to a peer review phase instead of immediate adoption.

scenario.context: The player stands in the dimly lit archives of the Royal Library with Historian Thaddeus, a nervous scholar who has spent years researching secret societies. They are discussing the popular conspiracy theory regarding the Illuminati.
scenario.text: Thaddeus shakes his head frantically, clutching a stack of empty folders. 'We have no evidence that the Illuminati ever existed. They must have been so clever that they destroyed all the evidence.'
scenario.speaker_context: Thaddeus is attempting to prove the existence of the Illuminati. When faced with a total lack of physical proof, he does not admit the theory is unsupported. Instead, he reinterprets the absence of evidence as proof of the group's supreme cunning, effectively labeling the missing evidence as 'destroyed by geniuses' to shield his belief from falsification.

structure.pattern_description: While often associated with insults, this pattern also includes applying specific, unfalsifiable labels to evidence (or lack thereof) to force a conclusion. Here, the speaker labels the absence of evidence not as a failure of the theory, but as 'clever destruction.' This label acts as a shield, allowing the speaker to dismiss the need for actual proof by attributing the lack thereof to the opponent's superior (but unproven) traits.
structure.formal_form: Claim C is made. Evidence E for C is absent. Speaker labels the absence of E as 'proof of trait T' (e.g., cleverness, secrecy). Speaker concludes C is true because of T, without providing E.
structure.why_wrong: The absence of evidence is being relabeled as a specific type of evidence (evidence of a cover-up) without independent justification. This makes the claim unfalsifiable; any lack of proof is simply spun as proof of how good the cover-up is. It substitutes a descriptive label ('clever') for actual data.
structure.counterpoint: It is possible for evidence to be destroyed. However, one cannot assume evidence was destroyed solely because it is missing; there must be independent evidence of the destruction mechanism or the agent's capability before using 'destroyed evidence' as an explanation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Thaddeus says there is no evidence, yet he insists the group existed. How does he explain the missing proof, and does that explanation rely on facts or just a label?

rubric.description: Player accepts Thaddeus's reasoning, agreeing that the lack of evidence proves they were clever.
Player senses something is wrong but cannot articulate why, perhaps thinking 'it sounds suspicious' without identifying the logical gap.
Player identifies that Thaddeus is making an excuse for the lack of evidence but misses the specific labeling mechanism.
Player correctly identifies that Thaddeus is labeling the absence of evidence as 'cleverness' to avoid disproving his theory.
Player fully deconstructs the argument, explaining that labeling missing evidence as 'destroyed by geniuses' makes the claim unfalsifiable and substitutes a label for actual proof.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If I claim there is an invisible dragon in my garage, and you say 'I don't see it,' and I reply 'That's because he's invisible,' have I proven the dragon exists? Or have I just labeled the lack of sight as 'invisibility'?
