scenario.text: Jax holds up the bottle high. 'Don't just stand there staring! Look around you—half the guild is already drinking this! The captain bought two, the scouts are chugging it down, and even the old wizard picked one up. When this many people believe in something, there must be something to it. You don't want to be the only soul without one, do you?'
scenario.speaker_context: Jax's entire pitch rests on the number of people who have already purchased. He offers no evidence that the potion grants strength or speed—just popularity.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that something must be true or good because many people believe it or do it. Treating popularity as evidence.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The number of people who believe something has no bearing on whether it is true. Popularity can be driven by social pressure, marketing, fear of missing out, or tradition—none of which constitute factual evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Widespread adoption is not always irrelevant—independent expert convergence after separate investigation can be meaningful. But that is very different from a crowd impulsively buying a potion because others are doing so.

assessment.identification_prompt: What evidence does Jax give that the potion works? Is 'everyone is buying one' a valid reason to trust it?

rubric.description: Finds the pitch convincing—if so many adventurers bought it, it must work.
Is hesitant but cannot explain why popularity is not good evidence.
Notes Jax gives no real evidence but does not explicitly address the popularity-as-evidence move.
Identifies that Jax uses the number of buyers as sole evidence and explains that popularity does not establish truth.
Names the bandwagon fallacy, explains why popularity is not evidence, identifies the social pressure component, and distinguishes popularity from evidential convergence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Suppose every person in the kingdom believed the river flowed uphill. Would that make it true?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Is there any situation where the fact that many people believe something does give reason to take it seriously?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jovial, fast-talking street performer who thrives on crowd energy and fear of missing out.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Come on, don't be the odd one out! The whole guild is doing it!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully points out that the crowd's behavior proves nothing about the potion's quality, causing Jax to stammer and admit he has no actual proof, only hype.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling market square of Oakhaven, where a grumpy town guard named Sergeant Miller is lecturing a young apprentice about a local coffee shop called 'The Roasted Bean'.
scenario.text: Sergeant Miller crosses his arms and sneers. 'That girl Annie must love The Roasted Bean. It's obvious. All girls with fair hair and pale skin love that overpriced swill. I've seen three of them in there this morning alone. If you have white hair, you drink their bean water. It's a rule.'
scenario.speaker_context: Sergeant Miller has observed only three individuals with a specific physical trait visiting a shop and has immediately concluded that this trait dictates the preference of every single person who shares it, ignoring individual taste and the vast number of counter-examples he hasn't seen.

structure.pattern_description: Miller observes a tiny, non-representative sample (three fair-haired girls) and leaps to a universal conclusion about an entire demographic ('All girls with fair hair...'). He treats a coincidental observation as a deterministic rule without sufficient evidence.
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of group G having property P (where n is very small). Therefore, all members of group G have property P.
structure.why_wrong: Three observations are statistically insignificant compared to the total population of fair-haired girls. Preferences for coffee shops are subjective and vary widely regardless of physical appearance. The sample is too small and likely biased (e.g., maybe that shop is just near a school those three attend).
structure.counterpoint: While patterns can emerge from observation, a valid generalization requires a large, random, and representative sample. Assuming a universal rule based on a handful of anecdotes ignores variability and leads to stereotypes.

assessment.identification_prompt: Sergeant Miller claims that because he saw three fair-haired girls at the coffee shop, all fair-haired girls must love it. Is his conclusion logically sound?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Miller, accepting that physical appearance dictates coffee preference.
Player feels unsure but suspects Miller might be exaggerating without knowing why.
Player identifies that three people are not enough to make a rule for everyone.
Player explicitly names the hasty generalization, noting the sample size is too small to support a claim about an entire demographic.
Player explains the flaw in sample size and representativeness, and suggests how one might actually test the hypothesis (e.g., surveying a diverse group) to avoid stereotyping.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Miller nods confidently. 'See? Logic is simple. Appearances tell the whole story.' He turns away, missing the nuance of individual choice.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Miller pauses, stroking his chin. 'Hmm. I suppose I haven't actually asked every fair-haired girl in the kingdom. Perhaps I was too quick to judge the bean water based on just a few faces.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Grumpy, authoritative, relies on stereotypes and 'common sense' rather than data, resistant to nuance but capable of learning if presented with clear logic.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't need a survey to know what folks like. My eyes tell me the truth!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Miller to try the coffee himself or speak to a fair-haired girl who hates coffee, breaking his generalized assumption.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling mess hall of the Iron Garrison. A veteran soldier named Kaelen is arguing with a young recruit about ration distributions and health standards.
scenario.text: Kaelen gestures wildly at his own lean frame. 'Look at me! My uncle eats pizza and cake every single day, and he is still thin as a rail. It is obvious that pizza and cake are not the cause of obesity. Anyone who tells you otherwise is lying.'
scenario.speaker_context: Kaelen is using a single anecdotal example (his uncle) to make a universal claim about the relationship between specific foods and weight gain for the entire human population, ignoring genetics, metabolism, and broader statistical data.

structure.pattern_description: Kaelen observes one individual (his uncle) who consumes high-calorie foods (pizza and cake) without becoming obese. From this single data point, he concludes that these foods do not cause obesity in general. This ignores the vast majority of cases where excessive consumption of such foods contributes to weight gain, as well as confounding variables like the uncle's specific metabolism or activity level.
structure.formal_form: Instance X has property P (eats pizza/cake) and lacks property Q (obesity). Therefore, no instances with property P will have property Q.
structure.why_wrong: A sample size of one is statistically insignificant for establishing a causal rule for a whole population. The uncle is likely an outlier due to unique genetic or lifestyle factors. The conclusion contradicts established nutritional science which shows a strong correlation between high-calorie processed foods and obesity in the general population.
structure.counterpoint: While individual exceptions exist (some people can eat poorly without gaining weight due to high metabolism), these exceptions do not invalidate the general rule that excessive caloric intake from nutrient-poor foods leads to weight gain for most people.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kaelen claims that pizza and cake cannot cause obesity because his uncle eats them and remains thin. Is this conclusion logically sound based on the evidence provided?

rubric.description: Player accepts Kaelen's argument as true and agrees that diet does not affect weight.
Player doubts the conclusion but attributes it to the uncle lying or Kaelen being mistaken, without identifying the logical flaw.
Player notes that one person is not enough to prove a rule but fails to name the specific fallacy or explain the role of outliers.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a single anecdote (n=1) cannot override general statistical trends regarding diet and health.

Player provides a comprehensive rebuttal: identifies the hasty generalization, explains the concept of outliers/anecdotal evidence, and suggests that valid conclusions require large, representative sample sizes rather than isolated cases.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if one person survives a fall from a great height, does that mean falling is safe for everyone? How many people would we need to study to know if food affects weight?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Your uncle might have a unique metabolism or exercise routine that compensates for his diet. Basing a universal health rule on one exception is a classic hasty generalization.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Brash, experienced but overconfident veteran who trusts personal experience over book learning or data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! Don't bore me with charts and graphs, kid. I know what I see with my own eyes!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Kaelen to reconsider his stance on rations by presenting a logbook of health statistics from the garrison, showing the correlation between diet and fitness levels across hundreds of soldiers.

scenario.context: The player stands in the war room of the High Council. Strategist Valerius is pointing at a map of the northern provinces, arguing against sending scouts to the upcoming primary election in the province of New Hampshire.
scenario.text: Valerius taps the map emphatically. 'We must not waste resources predicting the general election based on New Hampshire. Look at the history: the last time a Democrat won the New Hampshire primary, they went on to win the general election. Therefore, whoever wins the New Hampshire primary this year will certainly win the general election. It is a guaranteed predictor.'
scenario.speaker_context: Valerius is basing a universal rule about future elections on a single data point (the last Democrat winner). He ignores all other instances where the primary winner lost the general, or where non-Democrats won, treating one coincidence as a causal law.

structure.pattern_description: Valerius draws a definite conclusion about all future elections ('the winner will certainly win') based on a single observed instance ('the last Democrat winner'). He treats a sample size of one as sufficient evidence to establish a universal pattern, ignoring the complexity of electoral politics and other historical data.
structure.formal_form: Observed 1 instance of X (Democrat primary winner) having property Y (won general). Therefore, all instances of X (any primary winner) will have property Y.
structure.why_wrong: A single data point cannot establish a reliable trend or causal relationship. Electoral outcomes depend on numerous variables; relying on one past coincidence ignores counter-examples (e.g., primary winners who lost the general) and the difference between correlation and causation.
structure.counterpoint: While past performance can inform predictions, a valid inductive argument requires a representative and sufficiently large sample size. One success story does not prove a rule, especially when the underlying conditions (candidates, issues, economy) change every cycle.

assessment.identification_prompt: Valerius claims the New Hampshire primary winner is guaranteed to win the general election because it happened once for a Democrat. Is his evidence sufficient to support this absolute conclusion?

rubric.description: Player accepts Valerius's claim as fact and allocates resources based on his prediction.
Player expresses doubt but cannot explain why one example is insufficient evidence.
Player notes that one example is a small sample but fails to identify the specific logical error of generalizing from a single case.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a single past event cannot guarantee future outcomes for all cases.

Player fully deconstructs the argument: identifies the sample size of one, explains the difference between correlation and causation, and suggests looking at a broader historical dataset before making a prediction.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Valerius nods confidently. 'History repeats itself, Commander. We bet everything on New Hampshire.' (Result: Resources wasted on a failed prediction).
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Valerius pauses, reconsidering the map. 'You are right. One swallow does not make a summer, and one win does not make a rule. We need more data before committing our spies.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Valerius is a pragmatic but overconfident strategist who prefers simple heuristics over complex statistical analysis. He respects boldness but can be swayed by irrefutable logic.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Simple patterns save lives, Commander. Why complicate what the past has already decided?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Valerius to broaden his data set, unlocking the 'Statistical Analysis' side quest which reveals the true volatility of the election.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Oakhaven, a street vendor named Silas is trying to sell a peculiar blue potion to a hesitant traveler.
scenario.text: Silas holds up the bottle, gesturing to the long line of customers behind him. 'Don't just stand there staring! Everyone else is doing it, so should you. Look at that crowd; they can't all be wrong about this miracle cure.'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas avoids describing the potion's ingredients or effects, relying entirely on the visible crowd to convince the traveler of its value.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or an action correct simply because a large number of people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good/correct.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or action does not constitute evidence of its truth or efficacy. Crowds can be mistaken, misled, or acting on social pressure rather than facts.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread consensus among experts after independent verification can be meaningful, mere popularity among a general crowd without stated reasons is not evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: What actual evidence does Silas provide about the potion's effectiveness? Is the size of the crowd a valid reason to buy it?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument; assumes the crowd proves the potion works.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why the crowd's behavior isn't proof.
Notices Silas didn't explain the potion but fails to identify the 'everyone is doing it' logic as the flaw.
Identifies that Silas uses the crowd as his only evidence and states that popularity does not equal truth.
Names the bandwagon fallacy, explains that crowds can be wrong, and distinguishes between social proof and factual evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in the village suddenly believed the sky was green, would that actually make the sky green?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing it' might actually be useful information, even if it's not logical proof?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Pushy, fast-talking merchant who thrives on FOMO (fear of missing out) and crowd momentum.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Come on, don't be the odd one out! The whole town is lining up!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player rejects the potion based on lack of factual evidence, causing the crowd to disperse as they realize the vendor has no real pitch.

scenario.context: The player finds their companion, Elara, sitting on the edge of her bed in the inn, looking torn between resting and staying awake. She holds a remote control in one hand and pulls up the blankets with the other.
scenario.text: Elara sighs, 'I am going to bed or watching TV. I am exhausted, so I will go to bed; therefore, I cannot watch TV.' She sets the remote down on the nightstand and turns off the lamp.
scenario.speaker_context: Elara is a tired adventurer who believes her options are mutually exclusive. She assumes that because she chose to sleep (due to exhaustion), the option to watch TV is logically impossible, failing to see that one could theoretically watch TV in bed or that the 'or' was not an exclusive either/or constraint preventing both actions simultaneously if energy allowed, but primarily she treats the condition of 'not going to bed' as necessary for watching TV.

structure.pattern_description: Elara reasons from a disjunction or implicit conditional where she treats choosing bed as negating the possibility of TV. More formally, if we map her logic to a conditional: 'If I am not exhausted, I will watch TV' (implied), then 'I am exhausted' (Not P), therefore 'I cannot watch TV' (Not Q). Alternatively, she treats the choice of bed as logically excluding TV solely based on the exhaustion premise, denying the antecedent of a potential 'If not tired, then TV' rule.
structure.formal_form: If P then Q. Not P. Therefore not Q.
structure.why_wrong: The fact that she is exhausted and chooses bed does not logically prove she *cannot* watch TV. She could watch TV while in bed, or the original premise 'I am going to bed or watching TV' allows for both if interpreted inclusively, or simply, her exhaustion explains the choice but doesn't logically negate the capability or possibility of the other action unless explicitly stated as mutually exclusive. She denies the condition (not being exhausted) and falsely concludes the negation of the result (watching TV).
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would only be valid if the rule was 'I will watch TV IF AND ONLY IF I am not exhausted.' Since she didn't establish that exhaustion makes watching TV impossible (only that it makes bed the chosen option), the conclusion 'I cannot watch TV' is a non-sequitur derived from denying the antecedent.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elara decides to sleep because she is tired and concludes she literally cannot watch TV. Does being tired logically make watching TV impossible, or is she making a leap in logic?

rubric.description: Agrees with Elara; being tired means you can't watch TV.
Senses Elara is too strict but can't explain the logical flaw.
Realizes one can watch TV in bed, but doesn't identify the formal logical error.
Identifies that Elara treats 'not being exhausted' as a necessary condition for watching TV.
Correctly identifies 'Denying the Antecedent,' explaining that denying the condition (exhaustion) does not validly deny the possibility of the outcome (watching TV).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If you were exhausted, could you still hold a remote? Does 'I will sleep' automatically mean 'It is impossible to watch TV'?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. She assumes 'If not exhausted -> Watch TV' implies 'If exhausted -> No TV.' How could she rephrase her thought to be logically sound?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Practical but prone to rigid binary thinking when fatigued. She seeks logical closure to justify resting.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's black and white, player. If I'm beat, I'm out. No TV. That's just how the logic works.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can point out that watching TV in bed is an option, or challenge the conditional link between exhaustion and the inability to watch, freeing Elara to relax with a show if she chooses.

scenario.context: In the smog-choked industrial district of Neo-Veridia, the player confronts Factory Foreman Kael about the toxic sludge his plant is dumping into the river. When presented with data showing irreversible ecosystem collapse within a decade if current rates continue, Kael refuses to install filtration systems.
scenario.text: Kael slams his hand on the table, eyes wide with manufactured panic: 'If you don't start recycling now and shut down these lines, our entire planet will be destroyed in ten years! Do you want to be the one responsible for the end of the world? Look at the sky! Feel the heat! How can you sit there with numbers while the Earth burns?'
scenario.speaker_context: Kael uses catastrophic imagery and guilt to bypass the specific economic and technical discussion about recycling efficiency. He substitutes a visceral fear of total destruction for a reasoned debate about waste management protocols.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker attempts to win the argument by evoking intense fear and guilt rather than addressing the specific claim or evidence. The focus shifts from the feasibility of recycling to the emotional weight of planetary destruction.
structure.formal_form: Claim P (Recycling is necessary/feasible) is supported by evidence E (Data on pollution). Agent evokes extreme emotion F (Fear of apocalypse, guilt). Agent implies P must be accepted immediately or E ignored because of F.
structure.why_wrong: The emotional reality of potential planetary destruction does not validate the specific claim that immediate recycling is the only solution, nor does it address the technical constraints. Fear is being used as a substitute for logical proof or a plan of action.
structure.counterpoint: While the stakes (planetary destruction) are emotionally significant and provide urgency, they do not constitute evidence that the proposed solution (immediate recycling) is technically viable or that the timeline is accurate without further data.

assessment.identification_prompt: Foreman Kael is clearly terrified of the future, but does his outburst actually explain how recycling prevents the disaster or address the cost concerns?

rubric.description: Agrees with Kael immediately due to the scary imagery of the world ending.
Feels pressured by the guilt trip but senses something is missing from the argument.
Recognizes Kael is talking about feelings rather than the recycling plan, but cannot articulate the disconnect.
Identifies that Kael is using fear of destruction to avoid discussing the actual mechanics of the proposal.
Explicitly names the appeal to emotion, separates the validity of the threat from the validity of the solution, and requests evidence over rhetoric.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside the image of the burning world for a moment. Even if the world is in danger, has Kael explained why recycling is the specific fix, or is he just making you feel bad for hesitating?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. The stakes are high, but high stakes don't prove a specific solution works. Ask Kael for the data connecting recycling rates to the ten-year timeline.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dramatic, defensive, and prone to hyperbole; Kael uses crisis mode to deflect accountability.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: How can you ask for charts when the sky is turning orange? Don't you care about your own children?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must calm the NPC and pivot the conversation back to technical specifications and cost-benefit analysis to unlock the recycling quest line.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling kitchen of the Golden Crust Bakery. Head Baker Elara is proudly showing off her new enchanted apron to an apprentice, pointing to a tray of perfectly baked cookies as proof of its magic.
scenario.text: Elara gestures to her shimmering new apron. 'Since I got this new apron, I haven't burned a single cookie! That new apron sure does help my cooking. It must be the enchantment on the fabric.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara has noticed a temporal sequence: she acquired the apron, and subsequently, her cookies stopped burning. She assumes the apron caused the improvement. In reality, she likely started paying more attention to the oven timer or lowered the temperature around the same time she bought the apron, or it is simply a coincidence that she has had a lucky streak.

structure.pattern_description: Elara observes that event B (no burned cookies) followed event A (getting the new apron) and infers that A caused B. This is the 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' (after this, therefore because of this) fallacy. She ignores other potential causes such as improved technique, better ingredients, changes in oven calibration, or mere chance.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred. Event B occurred after A. Therefore, A caused B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession does not imply causation. Just because the apron arrived before the streak of good cookies doesn't mean the apron caused them. Elara has failed to rule out confounding variables (like her own skill improvement) or coincidence.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one would need to control for other variables. For example, if Elara wore the old apron tomorrow and burned cookies, then wore the new one and didn't, repeatedly, there might be a case. Without controlling variables, the correlation is anecdotal.

assessment.identification_prompt: Baker Elara believes her new apron is the reason her cookies aren't burning. Is her reasoning logically sound? Identify the flaw in her argument.

rubric.description: The player accepts Elara's claim that the apron causes better cooking without question.
The player suspects the apron might not be the cause but cannot explain why or offers a vague objection.
The player identifies that timing alone doesn't prove cause, noting that other things could have changed.
The player explicitly names the 'post hoc' fallacy or explains that correlation does not equal causation, offering specific alternative explanations (e.g., oven temperature, skill).

The player provides a comprehensive critique, identifying the fallacy, explaining the logical gap between sequence and causation, and proposing a method to test the actual cause (e.g., a controlled baking experiment).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if you buy a new hat and then it rains, did the hat cause the rain? What else could have changed in the kitchen besides the apron?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because the good cookies came after the new apron doesn't mean the apron made them. You've spotted the 'post hoc' trap. Maybe she just finally fixed the oven thermostat!

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elara is superstitious, enthusiastic, and deeply proud of her new gear, often attributing mundane successes to magical items.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's the weave, I tell you! The threads absorb the heat of failure!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Elara to run a blind taste test or baking trial with both aprons to prove the result is due to her skill, not the cloth. Reward: Recipe for 'Perfectly Logical Cookies'.

scenario.context: In the Grand Council Chamber of Ironhold, the City Magistrate has just presented evidence of toxic leaks at the Alchemist's Guild storage facilities. Guildmaster Vane steps forward to defend the guild against proposed fines.
scenario.text: Guildmaster Vane shouts: 'The city should not be singling out our company's problems at our chemical storage facilities! The EPA records indicate the city's very own landfill has been cited as needing improvements. The council needs to clean up its own mess before they go after us.'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane does not address the specific evidence of leaks at his facility or the safety data presented. Instead, he argues that the accusation should be dropped because the accuser (the city) is also flawed, implying that accepting the accusation would lead to the undesirable consequence of hypocrisy or unfair targeting.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a factual claim or accusation should be rejected because accepting it would lead to undesirable outcomes (such as perceived unfairness or hypocrisy), rather than addressing the evidence itself.
structure.formal_form: Accepting claim P would lead to undesirable consequence C (e.g., appearing hypocritical/unfair). Therefore, P is false or should be ignored.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a factual claim (that the guild has leaks) is independent of the moral standing of the accuser or the unpleasantness of the consequences. Whether the city landfill is also dirty does not change the chemical composition of the guild's leaks.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to argue for consistent enforcement policies (i.e., the city should fix its landfill too). However, this is a policy argument, not a refutation of the specific evidence against the guild. The guild's leaks remain a factual problem regardless of the city's issues.

assessment.identification_prompt: Guildmaster Vane is angry about being singled out. But does pointing out the city's landfill problems prove that his own storage facilities are safe?

rubric.description: Agrees with Vane; believes the city's hypocrisy proves the guild is innocent.
Feels Vane is dodging the question but cannot explain why the landfill issue is irrelevant to the leaks.
Notices Vane is talking about the city's faults instead of his own evidence, but accepts his conclusion that the investigation should stop.
Identifies that Vane is rejecting the findings based on the undesirable consequence of 'unfairness' rather than disproving the leak data.
Explicitly names the fallacy (Appeal to Consequences/Whataboutism variant), distinguishing between the truth of the leak allegation and the separate issue of city-wide enforcement consistency.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If the city landfill was perfectly clean, would that suddenly make the toxic leaks at your facility disappear?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Vane raises a valid point about consistent enforcement. How can the council address the landfill issue without letting the guild off the hook for their specific violations?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, loud, prone to deflection, uses outrage to mask guilt.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Why pick on us when the city is rotting from within? It's an outrage!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must press Vane to address the specific leak report data, forcing him to either admit the fault or provide actual counter-evidence, separating the policy complaint from the factual accusation.

scenario.context: The player enters the dimly lit Confessional of St. Jude, where Brother Thomas is pacing anxiously. He has just received news of a tragic accident involving a parishioner he argued with earlier that day.
scenario.text: Brother Thomas collapses onto the pew, clutching his rosary. 'It is my fault, entirely my fault! Earlier today, Marie and I had a heated argument. In my rage, I told her I hated her and wished she would get hit by a bus. Just hours later, I received a call... she was struck by a bus and is now in the hospital. The logic is undeniable: if I had not spoken those words, this would never have happened. My wish caused this tragedy.'
scenario.speaker_context: Brother Thomas is consumed by guilt. He has identified a temporal sequence (his angry wish followed by the accident) and incorrectly inferred a causal relationship between his thoughts/words and the external event, ignoring the statistical probability of accidents and the lack of any mechanism by which a wish could cause a bus strike.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Thomas observes that Event A (his angry wish) occurred before Event B (Marie's accident) and concludes that A caused B. This is the classic 'after this, therefore because of this' fallacy. He fails to consider that the two events are coincidental or that there are independent causes for the accident (e.g., driver error, road conditions) unrelated to his verbal outburst.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, Event A caused Event B. (Flaw: Temporal precedence does not imply causation; correlation or coincidence is possible.)
structure.why_wrong: The mere fact that one event follows another does not mean the first caused the second. Thomas has provided no evidence of a causal mechanism linking his words to the bus accident. He is confusing temporal sequence with causal necessity, likely driven by emotional guilt rather than logical evidence.
structure.counterpoint: While our actions can have consequences, establishing causation requires more than just timing. We need a plausible mechanism (how did the words physically move the bus?), consistency (do similar wishes always result in accidents?), and the elimination of other causes. In this case, traffic accidents happen regularly regardless of anyone's wishes; the timing is a tragic coincidence, not a causal link.

assessment.identification_prompt: Brother Thomas believes his angry words caused Marie's accident. Analyze his reasoning: Is there a logical connection between his wish and the event, or is he committing a specific logical fallacy? Identify the fallacy and explain why the timing alone is insufficient proof of causation.

rubric.description: The player agrees with Thomas, stating that his words definitely caused the accident because they happened first.
The player senses something is wrong but cannot identify the specific logical error, perhaps attributing it only to 'bad luck' without addressing the causal claim.
The player identifies that timing does not equal causation but fails to name the fallacy or explain the missing causal mechanism clearly.
The player correctly identifies the 'False Cause' or 'Post Hoc' fallacy and explains that temporal sequence does not prove causation, noting the lack of a mechanism.

The player provides a comprehensive analysis: identifies the Post Hoc fallacy, explains the flaw in assuming temporal precedence implies causation, explicitly states the lack of a causal mechanism, and distinguishes between coincidence and causal necessity.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thomas continues to weep, convinced he is a murderer by thought. Consider this: if you wished for rain and it rained the next day, did you cause the rain? What evidence is missing here that would be required to prove your wish actually moved the clouds?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Thomas pauses, wiping his tears. 'You mean... just because I said it first doesn't mean I made it happen? The bus driver's distraction or the road conditions were the real causes?' He takes a deep breath, the weight of false guilt beginning to lift. 'I must still apologize for my anger, but I need not carry the burden of the accident itself.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Guilt-ridden, superstitious, emotionally volatile, deeply religious but prone to magical thinking.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The universe heard my hate and answered with tragedy! I am the architect of this pain!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Thomas that correlation is not causation to clear his conscience, allowing him to visit Marie in the hospital with a clear mind rather than being paralyzed by irrational guilt.

scenario.context: The player approaches the gates of the Ironwood Academy, where Coach Thorne, a grizzled veteran of the gridiron, is arguing with the school principal about the upcoming season's roster.
scenario.text: Coach Thorne crosses his arms and blocks the gate. 'Girls should not be allowed to try out as kickers for our school football teams. It's simple: girls are just not very athletic. I saw one girl miss a catch in gym class last week; that proves none of them have the coordination for sports.'
scenario.speaker_context: Coach Thorne has observed a single instance of a girl missing a catch in a non-football context (gym class) and is using this tiny, unrepresentative sample to make a universal claim about the athletic ability of all girls and their suitability for a specific position.

structure.pattern_description: Coach Thorne draws a universal conclusion ('girls are not very athletic' and should be barred from trying out) based on a sample size of one (a single girl missing a catch in gym class). This sample is far too small to represent the entire population of girls, nor is the context (gym class catch) necessarily representative of the specific skill required (kicking a football).
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of X from population P (where n=1). The observed instance lacked property Q (athletic success). Therefore, no members of P possess property Q.
structure.why_wrong: One data point cannot support a claim about an entire gender. The sample is statistically insignificant and likely biased. Additionally, the evidence (missing a catch) does not directly correlate with the specific skill in question (kicking), making the generalization doubly flawed.
structure.counterpoint: Generalizations are useful when based on large, random, and representative samples. If Coach Thorne had data from hundreds of tryouts showing a consistent trend, his argument might have statistical weight. The fallacy lies in the insufficiency of the evidence, not the desire to predict performance.

assessment.identification_prompt: Coach Thorne claims no girls should be kickers because he saw one girl miss a catch. Is his conclusion supported by his evidence?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Coach Thorne and accepts that girls cannot be kickers based on his story.
Player feels the coach is being unfair but cannot explain the logical error in his reasoning.
Player identifies that one example is not enough to judge everyone, but does not explicitly name the fallacy or discuss sample representation.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a single instance in gym class cannot represent the athletic ability of all girls regarding football kicking.

Player provides a comprehensive rebuttal identifying the hasty generalization, noting the sample size is too small (n=1), the context is irrelevant (catching vs. kicking), and suggests that proper tryouts are the only valid way to assess individual ability.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if you met one person who was bad at math, would you say everyone in the world is bad at math? How many people would you need to test to be sure?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Judging an entire group based on a single anecdote is a classic Hasty Generalization. Every player deserves a fair tryout to prove their own skills.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Stubborn, traditionalist, relies on 'gut feeling' over data, resistant to change.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I don't need statistics to know what I saw with my own eyes! One miss is all the proof I need.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Coach Thorne to allow open tryouts by pointing out the flaw in his logic, unlocking the 'Fair Play' achievement and allowing female NPCs to join the team.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling cafeteria of the Academy of Reason just before midterms. A nervous student named Pip is frantically unwrapping a massive stash of sweets at a corner table, surrounded by empty soda cans.
scenario.text: Pip shoves a fifth candy bar into his mouth and washes it down with the last of his second soda. 'You have to try this!' he insists, eyes wide with sugar-fueled confidence. 'Eating five candy bars and drinking two sodas before a test helps me get better grades. I did that exact thing and got an A on my last test in history. It's a guaranteed strategy!'
scenario.speaker_context: Pip is a well-meaning but logically flawed student who has confused a single instance of temporal succession (eating sugar, then getting a good grade) with a causal relationship. He ignores other variables like his actual study habits, the difficulty of the specific test, or simple luck.

structure.pattern_description: Pip observes that event A (consuming large amounts of sugar) preceded event B (receiving a high grade) in one specific instance. He incorrectly concludes that A caused B. This ignores the possibility that B was caused by prior studying, that the test was easy, or that the correlation is purely coincidental. In reality, excessive sugar might even impair cognitive function due to a subsequent crash.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, Event A caused Event B. (Flaw: Temporal sequence does not prove causation; confounding variables or coincidence are ignored.)
structure.why_wrong: The fallacy lies in assuming that because one thing happened before another, it must be the cause. One data point (one test) is insufficient to establish a rule, and there is no biological mechanism suggesting massive sugar intake improves test performance; indeed, the opposite is often true. Pip likely studied hard for the history test, and the candy was irrelevant.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one needs repeated trials, control groups, and a plausible mechanism. For example, if Pip took ten tests with sugar and ten without, keeping study time constant, and consistently scored higher with sugar, only then might a causal link be suspected. Anecdotal evidence of a single success is not proof.

assessment.identification_prompt: Pip claims his sugar binge caused his 'A' grade. What logical error is he making regarding the relationship between eating candy and test scores?

rubric.description: Fails to identify any logical error; agrees with Pip that sugar causes good grades.
Identifies that the claim seems wrong but cannot explain the logical flaw, perhaps citing personal opinion only.
Notes that one example isn't enough proof but misses the specific causal fallacy name or mechanism.
Correctly identifies the false cause fallacy, explaining that temporal order (eating then grading) does not equal causation.
Provides a comprehensive analysis: identifies the post hoc fallacy, explains the lack of a causal mechanism, suggests alternative causes (studying), and notes the insufficiency of a single anecdote.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if you wear red socks and win a game, did the socks make you win? Or did you practice? What else could have caused Pip's good grade besides the candy?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because the candy came before the grade doesn't mean it caused it. Pip probably studied hard. Relying on sugar instead of study skills is a dangerous strategy based on a logical glitch.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Hyperactive, optimistic, slightly scatterbrained, relies on superstition over study.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Wait, you don't believe in the Sugar Boost? But the data is right here! *points to crumpled test paper* One A! It's science!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Pip to swap the candy for a proper study guide or a balanced meal to avoid a sugar crash during the next exam.

scenario.context: Inside the bustling Stonehaven Animal Sanctuary, the player and their party are debating which rescue animal to sponsor. The shelter is full, and resources are tight. Yasir, a passionate but impulsive volunteer, spots a scruffy puppy in the back kennel marked for euthanasia due to space constraints.
scenario.text: Yasir blocks the exit, eyes wide with panic: 'If we don't adopt that puppy today, they might put him down. Do you want to be responsible for that?'
scenario.speaker_context: Yasir bypasses the logical discussion about the party's limited gold and long-term care capacity. Instead, he attempts to force a decision by inducing immediate guilt and fear of being a 'killer' in the player's mind.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting an emotional response (guilt, pity, fear) in place of addressing the practical constraints or factual evidence. Yasir does not address whether the party can afford the dog; he tries to make the player feel morally culpable for the dog's potential death if they do not act immediately.
structure.formal_form: Claim P (We must adopt the puppy) is supported by evidence E (The puppy might be euthanized). Agent evokes emotion F (Guilt/Responsibility for death). Agent implies E should dictate action regardless of other constraints because of F.
structure.why_wrong: Whether the player feels guilty does not change the factual reality of their budget or the shelter's policies. The emotional pressure is designed to bypass rational decision-making about resource allocation, not to solve the underlying problem of overcrowding.
structure.counterpoint: Compassion is a valid motivator for charity, but it is not a logical proof that a specific action is feasible or the best course of action given limited resources. One can care deeply about the puppy and still logically conclude they cannot adopt it today.

assessment.identification_prompt: Yasir clearly cares about the puppy, and the situation is sad. But does his question about being 'responsible' actually prove that the party has the money or space to take the dog?

rubric.description: Feels intense guilt and immediately agrees to adopt the puppy to stop feeling bad, ignoring party resources.
Feels conflicted; recognizes the party is low on gold but feels too pressured by the guilt trip to argue.
Notices that Yasir didn't mention the cost or space, only the emotional consequence, but struggles to articulate the fallacy.
Identifies that Yasir is using guilt to deflect from the practical question of whether the party can actually afford the adoption.

Names the appeal to emotion (specifically appeal to guilt), explains that the puppy's fate is independent of the party's ability to pay, and proposes a logical alternative (e.g., donating what they can without adopting).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside the feeling of guilt for a moment. If the party has zero gold left, does feeling responsible suddenly create gold? What is the actual constraint here?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. The puppy's fate is tragic, but making the player feel like a murderer doesn't solve the resource problem. How can we help without breaking the party's economy?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Passionate, impulsive, deeply empathetic but logically weak. Yasir wears his heart on his sleeve and often acts before thinking through consequences.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look at those eyes! How can you even check your coin purse when a life is on the line? Just say yes!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player successfully identifies the manipulation, calms Yasir down, and chooses to donate a smaller amount to extend the puppy's stay rather than adopting it immediately, satisfying both logic and compassion.

scenario.context: In the Family Hearth, a young adventurer is being scolded by their mother for spending too many hours in the virtual realm. The adventurer attempts to deflect the criticism.
scenario.text: Your mother says, 'You spend far too much time playing video games; it's affecting your studies.' You retort, 'Well, you spend way too much time shopping!'
scenario.speaker_context: The player does not address the mother's claim about video games affecting studies. Instead, they point out an unrelated behavior of the mother, implying her claim should be rejected because she is also flawed.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a factual claim or criticism should be rejected because accepting it would lead to undesirable social outcomes or expose the critic's hypocrisy, rather than addressing the evidence.
structure.formal_form: Claim P implies undesirable consequence C (or exposes critic's flaw). Therefore, P is false.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of the mother's observation (that gaming affects studies) is independent of her own habits. Pointing out her shopping habits does not prove the gaming habit is harmless; it merely changes the subject.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to point out hypocrisy in a moral debate about fairness, but in a factual debate about cause-and-effect (gaming vs. grades), the critic's behavior is irrelevant to the truth of the claim.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does pointing out your mother's shopping habits prove that your gaming habits are not affecting your grades?

rubric.description: Believes the retort successfully disproves the mother's claim because she is a hypocrite.
Feels the retort is a good comeback but isn't sure if it logically solves the problem.
Notices the topic changed from gaming to shopping, but doesn't see why that matters for the truth of the claim.
Identifies that the player avoided addressing the evidence about gaming by attacking the mother's behavior.

Explicitly names the fallacy (often confused with Tu Quoque, but functioning here as an appeal to the consequence of admitting fault) and explains that the mother's shopping is irrelevant to the gaming grade impact.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If your mother never shopped at all, would that automatically mean your gaming is definitely hurting your grades? Or are those two separate facts?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: When is it appropriate to bring up someone else's bad habits, and when does it just serve as a distraction from the main issue?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, quick-witted, prone to deflection
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't turn this around on me! We are talking about your grades, not my receipt pile!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must apologize and address the original concern about study time to gain the 'Focus' buff, rather than winning the argument through deflection.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Veridia, the player confronts a wealthy merchant, Lord Vane, who has been accused of funding cruel animal testing facilities. When presented with documents linking his funds to the labs, Vane attempts to sway the crowd.
scenario.text: Lord Vane spreads his arms wide, addressing the gathered crowd: 'Hundreds of thousands of animals are being tortured and killed every year, and for what? So that we can modernize our beauty products and overstock our grocery stores? Is this the progress you demand? Look into the eyes of the innocent victims and tell me your ledgers matter more than their suffering!'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane acknowledges the suffering but uses graphic emotional imagery to deflect from the specific accusation that he is the one funding it. He attacks the general concept of progress to avoid addressing his own financial records.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker evokes strong feelings of pity, guilt, or outrage regarding a tragic situation to bypass the need for factual evidence or logical connection to the specific claim at hand.
structure.formal_form: Claim P (Vane funds the labs) is supported by evidence E (financial ledgers). Agent evokes emotion F (horror at animal suffering) unrelated to the truth of P. Agent implies E should be disregarded or that P is false because F is so terrible.
structure.why_wrong: The fact that animal suffering is horrific does not prove or disprove whether Lord Vane specifically funded it. The emotional weight of the tragedy is being used as a shield to prevent the examination of the financial evidence.
structure.counterpoint: While animal suffering is a valid moral concern, it is irrelevant to the factual question of who signed the checks. One can condemn the suffering and still demand proof of Vane's involvement.

assessment.identification_prompt: Lord Vane describes a terrible tragedy. But does describing the suffering of animals actually prove he didn't sign the checks found in the ledger?

rubric.description: Is overwhelmed by the description of animal suffering and agrees Vane must be innocent because he cares so much.
Feels confused; knows the suffering is bad but isn't sure if it answers the accusation about the money.
Suspects Vane is changing the subject but struggles to articulate why the emotion doesn't fit the evidence.
Identifies that Vane is using the tragedy of animal testing to distract from the specific evidence of his own funding.
Clearly names the appeal to emotion, explains that the moral horror of the act is separate from the factual question of agency/funding, and demands the ledger be addressed.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside the horror of the animal testing for a moment. If a different merchant had signed those same papers, would the animal suffering be any less real? Then why does mentioning the suffering tell us anything about who signed the papers?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. The tragedy is real, but it is being used as a smokescreen. Now that we've cleared the emotional fog, let's look at the signature on line 4 of the ledger again.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dramatic, performative, and manipulative. Vane thrives on public opinion and uses moral grandstanding to hide unethical business practices.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: How can you stand there with your cold numbers while the innocent bleed? Have you no heart?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must choose a dialogue option that acknowledges the suffering but firmly redirects the conversation back to the financial evidence, causing Vane's confidence to break.

scenario.context: In the Alchemist's Guild hall, a novice argues against increasing the dosage of a volatile potion, citing safety protocols. The senior alchemist, Master Vane, dismisses the concern with a sweeping generalization.
scenario.text: Master Vane waves away the safety chart: 'One pill is good for the constitution, so surely two will be even better. Do you wish to deny the patients their full recovery? Think of their suffering if you withhold the cure out of cowardice.'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane ignores the toxicological evidence that double the dose causes harm, instead invoking the patients' suffering and accusing the novice of cowardice to force agreement.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting an emotional response (pity for patients, shame for cowardice) in place of addressing the factual evidence regarding dosage limits. Vane does not contest the safety chart; he tries to make the novice feel guilty for questioning him.
structure.formal_form: Claim P (double dose is safe) is challenged by evidence E (toxicity data). Agent evokes emotion F (pity/shame) unrelated to E. Agent implies E should be disregarded because of F.
structure.why_wrong: The desire for patients to recover quickly does not change the chemical reality that an overdose is toxic. The emotional appeal is designed to block the safety inquiry, not answer it.
structure.counterpoint: Compassion for patients is a valid motivation for seeking cures, but it is not evidence for the safety of a specific dosage. Emotions drive the goal, not the scientific method.

assessment.identification_prompt: Master Vane mentions the patients' suffering and calls the novice a coward. Does any of this actually prove that two pills are safer than one?

rubric.description: Agrees with Vane because the patients' suffering sounds terrible and the novice seems mean.
Feels conflicted; wants to help the patients but senses the argument about cowardice is unfair.
Notices Vane did not address the safety chart but struggles to articulate why the emotional points are irrelevant to toxicity.
Identifies Vane is using pity and shame to deflect from the lack of evidence for the double dose.
Names the appeal to emotion, distinguishes the factual question (toxicity) from the emotional one (suffering), and explains that good intentions do not alter chemical facts.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside the patients' feelings for a moment. If a substance is poisonous at high levels, does wanting them to feel better change that chemical property?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. Vane is trying to make you feel bad to bypass the science. How would you restate his claim without the emotional manipulation?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Arrogant, dismissive of protocol, believes intuition and boldness outweigh careful measurement.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You hesitate? While you count drops, the fever burns! Are you a healer or a clerk?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must present the toxicity chart again and explicitly state that emotional appeals do not negate chemical limits to proceed safely.

scenario.context: In the sun-drenched plaza of Solara, a heated debate arises between locals about the safest way to achieve a summer tan. A confident traveler tries to settle the argument by citing a famous expert.
scenario.text: World-renowned physicist Dr. Patricia Mitchell assures me that exposure to natural sunlight, even exposure resulting in mild sunburn, is still significantly less of a cancer risk than brief exposure to the artificial light in a tanning bed. So I make sure to tell all of my friends that if they're looking to get a tan this summer they should do it outdoors, and not at the tanning salon!
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Patricia Mitchell is indeed a world-renowned physicist, specializing in quantum mechanics and particle physics. She is not a dermatologist, oncologist, or medical researcher specializing in UV radiation effects on human skin.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker accepts a medical claim about skin cancer risks solely because it was made by a famous physicist, ignoring the mismatch between the expert's field (physics) and the claim's domain (dermatology/oncology).
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is an expert in domain D. P is a claim in domain D*. Therefore, P is true. (Flaw: D ≠ D*).
structure.why_wrong: Expertise is domain-specific. Being an authority in physics does not automatically grant authority in medicine or biology. The prestige of the physicist makes the statement sound impressive, but it does not provide valid evidence for medical safety claims.
structure.counterpoint: Citing an authority is valid only when the authority is an expert in the specific field relevant to the claim. If Dr. Mitchell were a leading dermatologist, this would be a strong argument, not a fallacy.

assessment.identification_prompt: The speaker relies heavily on Dr. Mitchell's reputation. What is Dr. Mitchell's actual field of expertise, and does it match the topic of skin cancer risks?

rubric.description: Accepts the claim completely because Dr. Mitchell is 'world-renowned'.
Feels unsure but cannot identify why the physicist's opinion might be insufficient for a medical claim.
Notices Dr. Mitchell is a physicist, not a doctor, but fails to explain why this distinction invalidates the argument.
Identifies that physics and dermatology are different fields and states that expertise in one does not apply to the other.
Clearly names the 'Appeal to Irrelevant Authority' fallacy, explains the domain mismatch between quantum physics and oncology, and articulates that medical claims require medical expertise.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Dr. Mitchell claimed that a new engine design was efficient, would you trust her? Why does her opinion count there but perhaps not on skin cancer?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Suppose Dr. Mitchell cited a specific study she co-authored with oncologists. Would that change your evaluation of her statement? Why?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest and well-meaning but overly impressed by titles; tends to trust anyone with 'Dr.' in front of their name regardless of the subject.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But she's a WORLD-RENOWNED physicist! You can't argue with science like that!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must guide the NPC to check the specific credentials required for medical advice, perhaps by consulting the local healer or medical library to verify if physicists study skin cancer.

scenario.context: The player visits the bustling market square of Solara during a heatwave. A local merchant, Gable, is frantically selling umbrellas and blaming his sister's grooming habits for the weather.
scenario.text: Gable wipes sweat from his brow and points an accusing finger at a young woman walking by. 'Every time my sister uses hairspray, it is an extremely hot day! It is an extremely hot day right now, and I just saw her with a can in her hand. She is causing this heatwave with her vanity! We must confiscate her hairspray to cool down the city.'
scenario.speaker_context: Gable has noticed that his sister often uses hairspray on sunny days (perhaps because she goes out more when the weather is nice) or it is purely coincidental. He has mistaken a temporal correlation (or coincidence) for a causal relationship, ignoring the actual meteorological causes of the heatwave.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Gable observes that event A (sister using hairspray) and event B (extremely hot day) occur together or in sequence. He incorrectly concludes that A causes B. This ignores other possibilities: B causes A (she goes out more when it's sunny), a third factor C causes both, or the correlation is entirely coincidental.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurs before or with Event B. Therefore, A causes B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession or correlation does not prove causation. Gable provides no mechanism by which hairspray could generate city-wide heat, nor has he ruled out reverse causation (sunny weather leads to more outings and hairspray use) or coincidence. The actual cause of the heat is atmospheric pressure systems, not cosmetic products.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one must demonstrate a plausible mechanism, consistent temporal ordering, and the elimination of confounding variables. For example, if turning on a heater consistently raises room temperature via a known physical process, causation is likely. Mere coincidence, like a rooster crowing before sunrise, does not mean the crowing causes the sun to rise.

assessment.identification_prompt: Analyze Gable's argument. What logical error is he making when he claims his sister's hairspray is causing the heatwave?

rubric.description: The player accepts Gable's claim or fails to identify any logical error.
The player states that Gable is wrong but cannot explain why, or attributes it to magic/superstition without logical reasoning.
The player identifies that the two events are just happening at the same time but does not name the fallacy or explain the missing causal link.
The player correctly identifies the false cause fallacy, noting that correlation does not equal causation, and suggests an alternative explanation (e.g., she uses it because it's sunny).

The player provides a comprehensive rebuttal identifying the 'Post Hoc' fallacy, explains the lack of a causal mechanism, rules out reverse causation, and cites the actual meteorological causes of heat.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: does spraying a small can of liquid really have the power to change the weather for an entire city? What else could explain why these two things happen together?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because two things happen together doesn't mean one caused the other. Gable is confusing correlation with causation. The heat likely makes his sister want to go out, leading her to use hairspray, not the other way around.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Gable is a superstitious, easily flustered merchant who sees patterns in everything and jumps to dramatic conclusions to sell his wares or assign blame.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's obvious! She sprays, the sun burns! Stop her before she melts the market!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player convinces Gable to look at weather charts showing heatwaves occurred before hairspray was invented, or points out that his sister uses hairspray on cold days too (if true), breaking the correlation.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Veridia, a heated debate erupts over whether swallowed chewing gum stays in the stomach for years. A local merchant tries to silence the crowd's doubts.
scenario.text: The merchant shouts above the noise: 'Stop your worrying! Studies show it takes up to seven years for the human body to digest a piece of gum. This fact was confirmed by the High Alchemist of the Royal Court himself. If the greatest mind in the kingdom says it takes seven years, then it is absolute truth.'
scenario.speaker_context: The High Alchemist is a renowned expert in potion brewing and elemental transmutation, not human physiology or digestive biology.

structure.pattern_description: The merchant cites the High Alchemist's opinion as definitive proof regarding human digestion, despite the Alchemist's expertise lying in chemistry and magic, not biology.
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is expert in domain D. P is in domain D*. Therefore P is true. (But D ≠ D*.)
structure.why_wrong: An authority's prestige in one field (alchemy) does not grant them automatic expertise in an unrelated field (human digestion). The claim relies on the person's status rather than biological evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Citing an authority is valid when the authority is an expert in the specific domain of the claim. If a royal physician made this statement, the appeal would be stronger, though still requiring evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: The merchant claims the High Alchemist's word settles the debate. What is the Alchemist an expert in, and does that match the topic of digestion?

rubric.description: Accepts the merchant's claim because the High Alchemist is famous.
Feels unsure but cannot identify why the Alchemist's opinion might be irrelevant.
Notices the Alchemist works with potions, not bodies, but doesn't explain the impact.
Identifies that the Alchemist's expertise is in alchemy, not human biology.
Names the appeal to irrelevant authority, explains the domain mismatch between alchemy and digestion, and notes that status does not equal factual accuracy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If the High Alchemist told you the best way to bake bread, would you believe him just because he is smart? How is this different?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: If the Royal Physician agreed with the Alchemist, would that make the claim true? Why or why not?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Boastful and persuasive, relies heavily on titles and reputation to win arguments rather than facts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Who are you to question the High Alchemist? His word is law in matters of science!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must point out the difference between alchemy and biology to expose the flaw, causing the merchant to hesitate and the crowd to demand actual medical evidence.

scenario.context: The player stands in the dimly lit Alchemy Lab of Tower 4. Apprentice Jinx is frantically packing bags, convinced he has discovered a dangerous magical curse that he accidentally triggered.
scenario.text: I sneezed at the exact same moment the power went off. My sneeze definitely did something to make the power go off. We have to evacuate before I sneeze again and blow up the whole tower!
scenario.speaker_context: Apprentice Jinx is prone to superstition and panic. He experienced two simultaneous events (a sneeze and a power outage) and immediately assumed his biological action caused the mechanical failure, ignoring the likelihood of coincidence or an external electrical fault.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Jinx observes that Event A (sneezing) occurred at the same time as Event B (power outage) and concludes that A caused B. This is a classic false cause fallacy where temporal proximity or correlation is mistaken for causation without any mechanistic link.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred at the same time as (or immediately before) Event B. Therefore, A caused B.
structure.why_wrong: Coincidence does not imply causation. There is no plausible physical or magical mechanism by which a sneeze could trip a power circuit. The events are likely independent, or both caused by a third factor (e.g., a dust cloud causing both the sneeze and a short circuit), but Jinx has jumped to a conclusion without evidence.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one needs more than timing; one needs a plausible mechanism and the elimination of other variables. If Jinx sneezed a hundred times and the power only went off once, or if the power goes off daily at this time regardless of sneezing, the causal link dissolves.

assessment.identification_prompt: Analyze Jinx's reasoning. Is his conclusion that the sneeze caused the power outage logically sound? Why or why not?

rubric.description: The player agrees with Jinx, believing the sneeze caused the outage due to the timing.
The player suspects Jinx is wrong but cannot explain why, or attributes it to magic without critique.
The player identifies that the timing is coincidental but fails to articulate the specific logical fallacy.
The player correctly identifies the false cause fallacy, noting that correlation does not equal causation.
The player fully deconstructs the argument, identifying the lack of mechanistic link and suggesting alternative explanations (coincidence or common cause) while naming the fallacy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: have you ever sneezed before when the lights stayed on? Does a sneeze have the physical power to break an electrical circuit?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because two things happen together doesn't mean one caused the other. That's the 'False Cause' fallacy. Let's check the fuse box instead of blaming your nose.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, superstitious, prone to catastrophic thinking, loyal but easily misled.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's happening again! My nose is tingling! Don't look at me, or the lights will go out forever!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must calm Jinx down and inspect the fuse box to find a loose wire (the real cause), earning logic points and stabilizing the lab.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Neo-Veridia, a parent stands before a sleek tech kiosk run by a smooth-talking salesbot named 'Trendy'. The parent looks worried about their child starting at a new academy.
scenario.text: I guess I should buy my 12-year-old daughter an iPhone. Everyone at her new school has one, and I want her to fit in with the other kids.
scenario.speaker_context: The parent is not arguing based on the phone's features, price, or durability. Their entire justification rests on the premise that because 'everyone' else has one, it is the correct choice to make.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition is true or an action is correct solely because a large number of people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good/correct.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or action does not constitute evidence of its truth or value. Majorities can be mistaken, influenced by marketing, or acting under social pressure. The merit of the phone should be evaluated on its own specifications and the family's needs, not peer prevalence.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate reliability (e.g., many engineers using a specific tool), this is only valid if those adopters made independent, informed evaluations. In this case, the adoption is driven by social conformity ('fit in'), not independent verification of quality.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the parent provide any reasons why the iPhone is a good device, or only reasons why other people have one?

rubric.description: Agrees with the parent; assumes that if everyone has one, it must be the best choice.
Senses something is off but cannot articulate why popularity isn't a valid reason.
Notes that the parent didn't mention phone features but fails to identify the logical error in using popularity as proof.
Identifies that the argument relies entirely on the number of users and explains that popularity does not equal quality or necessity.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that 'fitting in' is a social goal not a logical proof of value, and distinguishes between social pressure and evidential support.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone at the school suddenly started jumping off the roof, would that make it a good idea for your daughter to do so too?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone' does something actually is a good reason to do it yourself?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious but well-meaning parent, easily swayed by social norms and fearful of their child being an outcast.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But the other kids... they'll all be texting on iMessage. She'll be left out of the group chats!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player helps the parent list actual criteria for a phone (budget, durability, parental controls) and realize that 'fitting in' can be achieved through conversation, not just hardware, breaking the spell of the bandwagon.

scenario.context: The player enters the Alchemist's Guild hall where Apprentice Kael is arguing with a senior mage about the properties of water.
scenario.text: Kael gestures wildly at his notes. 'It is simple logic, Master! Hydrogen is not wet. Oxygen is not wet. Therefore, water, which is just H2O, cannot possibly be wet either. Any claim that water is wet is a falsehood because its constituent parts are dry.'
scenario.speaker_context: Kael is a bright but inexperienced apprentice who assumes that properties of individual components (hydrogen and oxygen atoms) must automatically apply to the compound they form (water), ignoring emergent properties.

structure.pattern_description: Kael observes that the individual elements (hydrogen and oxygen) lack the property of 'wetness' and incorrectly concludes that the compound formed by them (water) must also lack this property. This is a fallacy of composition, a specific type of hasty generalization where one assumes the whole shares the properties of the parts without sufficient evidence.
structure.formal_form: Parts X and Y of Whole Z do not have property P. Therefore, Whole Z does not have property P.
structure.why_wrong: Properties of individual atoms do not necessarily translate to the molecules or substances they form. Wetness is an emergent property resulting from the interaction of water molecules with other surfaces, not an inherent trait of isolated hydrogen or oxygen atoms. The sample (the parts) is not representative of the behavior of the whole system.
structure.counterpoint: While some properties are preserved from parts to whole (e.g., if all bricks are red, the wall is red), many chemical and systemic properties are emergent and only exist when the parts interact in specific ways.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kael claims water cannot be wet because hydrogen and oxygen are not wet. Is his conclusion logically sound based on his evidence?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael, accepting that dry parts must make a dry whole.
Player senses something is wrong but attributes it to Kael being rude or confused, not identifying the logical error.
Player states that water is wet in reality but cannot explain why Kael's logic fails regarding the parts vs. the whole.
Player identifies that Kael is assuming the whole must share the properties of its parts, noting that this is not always true.
Player explicitly identifies the fallacy of composition/hasty generalization, explaining that wetness is an emergent property of the molecular structure, not a trait of the isolated atoms.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about salt. Sodium is a reactive metal and Chlorine is a toxic gas, but together they make table salt which is safe to eat. Do the parts always dictate the whole?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because the ingredients don't taste like cake doesn't mean the cake won't taste sweet. Emergent properties are key in alchemy.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest, overly confident in textbook logic, lacks practical lab experience.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But the equations don't lie! If A is dry and B is dry, A+B must be dry!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must provide a counter-example of emergent properties (like salt or bronze) to convince Kael to re-test his hypothesis.

scenario.context: The player enters the Headmaster's office at the Academy. Dean Halloway is reviewing a list of students nominated for the advanced 'Pre-AP' track and looks visibly frustrated.
scenario.text: Dean Halloway sighs, tossing a file onto his desk. 'I've looked at the last three cohorts of Pre-AP kids. Every single one of them was incredibly smart and creative. It's obvious now: Pre-AP kids are smart and creative. We don't even need to review the new applications; if they are in Pre-AP, they automatically qualify for the Genius Grant.'
scenario.speaker_context: Dean Halloway has observed a small, selected group of students (three cohorts) who likely underwent a screening process to enter Pre-AP in the first place. He is using this limited, potentially biased sample to make a universal claim about the inherent nature of all current and future Pre-AP students, ignoring potential exceptions or the fact that the program selects for these traits rather than creating them.

structure.pattern_description: Dean Halloway observes a specific subset of students (past Pre-AP cohorts) who possess traits of intelligence and creativity. He then leaps to a universal conclusion that ALL Pre-AP kids possess these traits, implying it is an inherent rule rather than a trend or a result of selection bias. The sample size (three cohorts) may seem large, but it is insufficient to guarantee that every single individual in the category fits the description, especially when ignoring outliers or the possibility of students struggling in the program.
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of X (Pre-AP kids) have property Q (smart/creative). Therefore, all instances of X have property Q.
structure.why_wrong: The conclusion ignores the possibility of exceptions. Not every student in an advanced program is necessarily 'smart and creative' in the way defined; some may struggle, be there due to parental pressure, or excel in only one narrow area. Furthermore, the sample is likely biased because these students were already selected for the program based on these criteria, making the reasoning circular if used to justify future selections without individual review.
structure.counterpoint: While statistical trends often show Pre-AP students score higher on average, a universal claim ('Pre-AP kids ARE smart') eliminates nuance and individual variation. Valid inductive reasoning would state 'Most Pre-AP kids tend to be...' rather than asserting an absolute rule for the entire group.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dean Halloway claims that because the past few groups of Pre-AP students were smart and creative, ALL Pre-AP kids must be smart and creative. Is this conclusion logically sound?

rubric.description: Player agrees with the Dean and skips reviewing the new applications entirely.
Player feels unsure but suspects not every kid fits the description, yet cannot explain the logical flaw.
Player identifies that the Dean is making a broad claim based on limited past examples.
Player explicitly identifies the hasty generalization, noting that past cohorts do not guarantee the traits of every individual student in the program.
