structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession is not sufficient evidence for causation. Zohaw has not provided a mechanism linking a sneeze to an electrical breaker, nor has he ruled out coincidence or the actual cause (aging infrastructure). He assumes causation based solely on timing.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one needs more than just timing; one needs a plausible mechanism, consistent replication, and the elimination of alternative explanations. For example, if Zohaw sneezed and the power went out every single time, and he was standing next to an exposed wire his saliva could bridge, then a causal link might exist. Without that, it is merely a coincidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: Zohaw claims his sneeze caused the power outage. What logical error is he making regarding the relationship between these two events?

rubric.description: The player accepts Zohaw's claim that his sneeze caused the outage or fails to identify any logical error.
The player suspects Zohaw is wrong but cannot articulate why, perhaps suggesting he is just lying rather than reasoning poorly.
The player identifies that the timing is coincidental but struggles to name the specific fallacy or explain the missing causal mechanism.
The player correctly identifies the 'Post Hoc' fallacy, noting that just because the sneeze happened before the outage doesn't mean it caused it.

The player fully deconstructs the argument: identifying the Post Hoc fallacy, explaining that correlation/sequence does not equal causation, and suggesting the actual likely cause (faulty wiring) while dismissing the sneeze as irrelevant.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: does a sneeze have any physical way to trip an electrical breaker? Just because two things happen one after the other, does that always mean the first made the second happen?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because the sneeze came first doesn't mean it triggered the breaker. That's the 'Post Hoc' fallacy. The real culprit is likely the rusted wiring we saw earlier.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Boastful, superstitious, and eager to take credit for random events. Zohaw wears too many tools on his belt and speaks with unearned authority.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't look at me like that! It's a rare gift. I sneeze, the world shakes... or at least the lights go out. You should be grateful I didn't sneeze harder, or the whole grid would blow!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out the lack of causal connection to deflate Zohaw's ego, allowing the party to access the fuse box safely without Zohaw interfering with his 'sneeze-control' rituals.

scenario.context: In the war room of the Silver Citadel, the High Strategist is debating troop assignments with the player character. The kingdom faces threats on two fronts, but the Strategist insists on a rigid allocation of their single elite unit.
scenario.text: We can have Sally as our soldier on the front lines, or we can have Brittany be the queen of the kingdom. There is no middle ground; choose one role for them immediately.
scenario.speaker_context: High Strategist Valerius, a rigid traditionalist who believes leadership requires absolute, binary choices and despises nuance.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker presents two specific roles for two different individuals as if they are mutually exclusive options for a single slot, or implies that assigning one person to a role prevents another unrelated outcome, ignoring that both could serve in different capacities or that other candidates exist.
structure.formal_form: A v B, therefore ~A -> B (and vice versa), ignoring C, D, E...
structure.why_wrong: The statement falsely limits the possibilities. Sally can be a soldier AND Brittany can be queen; these are not competing options for the same position. Furthermore, other individuals could fill these roles, or the roles themselves could be redefined.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or is a false dichotomy. If there were literally only one position available and only these two candidates, the choice would be valid. The fallacy occurs when the constraint is artificial or the options are not truly mutually exclusive.

assessment.identification_prompt: The Strategist claims you must choose between having Sally as a soldier or Brittany as queen. What is logically flawed about this framing?

rubric.description: Accepts the choice as valid or picks a side without questioning the premise.
Senses the choice is strange but cannot explain why logically.
Points out that both could happen or that other people exist, but does not name the logical error.
Identifies the false dichotomy and explains that the two outcomes are not mutually exclusive.
Clearly articulates that the disjunction is not exhaustive, notes the independence of the two variables (Sally's role and Brittany's role), and names the fallacy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The Strategist says it's one or the other. But if Sally goes to the front, does that physically stop Brittany from ruling? Can you think of a scenario where both happen?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. The Strategist created a fake constraint. When else might a leader try to force a binary choice to hide better alternatives?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Authoritarian, impatient, views nuance as weakness.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Stop hedging! The kingdom bleeds while you ponder non-existent thirds. Sally or Brittany. Now.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player successfully points out the independence of the roles, causing the Strategist to grumble but assign both, unlocking a 'Dual Front' bonus.

scenario.context: The player stands before the gates of the Capital, speaking with Councilor Vane, a nervous official who opposes the new herbalist guild's petition to legalize cannabis for medicinal use.
scenario.text: Councilor Vane shakes his head vigorously, clutching his scroll. 'We cannot legalize marijuana. It is a slippery slope. If we allow even one person to use it legally, then more people will inevitably try heroin. It is only a matter of time before our streets are filled with addicts.'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane is arguing against a specific policy change (legalizing marijuana) by claiming it will automatically lead to a drastically different and more severe outcome (heroin use) without providing evidence for the causal link or the inevitability of the progression. He treats a single step as guaranteeing a extreme final result.

structure.pattern_description: Vane assumes that because two substances are both drugs, using one necessarily leads to using the other. He generalizes from the existence of marijuana to the inevitable adoption of heroin by the same users, ignoring the vast differences in availability, social stigma, legal barriers, and physiological effects between the two. This is a specific form of hasty generalization often called the 'Slippery Slope' fallacy, where a small sample (marijuana users) is assumed to possess the properties of a much larger, unobserved group (heroin users).
structure.formal_form: Event A (marijuana use) occurs. Event B (heroin use) is a more extreme version of drug use. Therefore, Event A inevitably causes Event B for the same individuals.
structure.why_wrong: The argument fails because it assumes a causal connection without evidence. Most people who use marijuana do not go on to use heroin. The sample of 'drug users' is being treated as a monolith where trying one substance guarantees trying all others, which is statistically false. It ignores confounding variables like personal choice, socioeconomic factors, and distinct drug markets.
structure.counterpoint: While some individuals may progress from softer to harder drugs, this is not a universal rule. Policy decisions should be based on statistical probabilities and specific causal mechanisms, not on the assumption that one action inevitably triggers a chain reaction of worst-case scenarios.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane claims that legalizing marijuana means more people will try heroin. Does the fact that someone uses marijuana prove they will inevitably use heroin?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane, believing that all drug use leads to heroin addiction.
Player feels unsure but suspects Vane might be exaggerating without knowing why.
Player identifies that Vane is making a big leap in logic but cannot name the specific error.
Player recognizes that Vane is assuming a causal link between two distinct behaviors without evidence (Hasty Generalization/Slippery Slope).
Player explains that the majority of marijuana users do not use heroin, identifying the flaw as treating a small subset of progression cases as a universal rule for all users.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about the people you know or have heard of who use marijuana. Do all of them also use heroin? If not, can Vane's statement be true for everyone?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Vane is taking a possible outcome for a few and presenting it as an inevitable outcome for all. This ignores the data showing that most users stop at the first substance.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, risk-averse, prone to catastrophizing, relies on fear tactics rather than data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But if we open that door, the floodgates will burst! We'll see heroin in the schools by next week!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player presents statistical evidence or a counter-example of a community where marijuana is legal but heroin rates haven't spiked, convincing Vane to allow the vote to proceed.

scenario.context: In the smog-choked district of Ironhaven, a heated town hall meeting is underway regarding the future of local transportation. The air is thick with soot, and citizens are coughing.
scenario.text: Aida stands at the podium, slamming her fist on the lectern. "Filthy, polluting hummers should be banned. We must get rid of these vehicles immediately because they are nothing more than filthy, polluting machines that poison our air!"
scenario.speaker_context: Aida, a passionate but logically untrained environmental activist who is so convinced of her conclusion that she mistakes restating it as providing evidence.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker claims that hummers should be banned because they are 'filthy' and 'polluting.' However, the only support offered for the claim that they are filthy and polluting is the initial assertion that they should be banned for being exactly that. The premise assumes the truth of the conclusion without offering independent evidence (e.g., emission statistics).
structure.formal_form: P1: Hummers are filthy and polluting. P2: (Implicit: We know they are filthy/polluting because they should be banned). C: Therefore, hummers should be banned.
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes exactly what it is trying to prove. The status of hummers as 'filthy' and 'polluting' is the very point that requires evidence if one is to justify a ban. By using the conclusion (they are bad/polluting) as the premise for the conclusion (ban them), the argument goes in a circle and provides no new information or justification.
structure.counterpoint: Restating a claim in different words can be useful for emphasis, but it becomes a fallacy when that restatement is offered as the *reason* or *proof* for the claim's truth.

assessment.identification_prompt: Aida is very angry about hummers. Does her speech actually give a reason why they are polluting, or is she just repeating herself?

rubric.description: Agrees with Aida's conclusion without noticing the lack of evidence, or criticizes her tone rather than her logic.
Senses the argument is weak or repetitive but cannot explain why logically.
Identifies that Aida is 'going in circles' or repeating her point instead of proving it.
Names the fallacy (begging the question/circular reasoning) and explains that the premise assumes the conclusion.
Names the fallacy, explains the circularity, and specifies that independent evidence (like data) is needed instead of restatement.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Listen closely again: Did Aida provide any facts, numbers, or outside sources to prove hummers are polluting, or did she just say they are bad because they are bad?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! She assumes the truth of her conclusion ('they are polluting') to prove her conclusion ('ban them'). Without independent data, her argument has no foundation.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Passionate, impulsive, and deeply convinced of her own righteousness. She speaks quickly and uses emotional language.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's obvious! They are destroyers of the sky! Why would anyone defend a destroyer of the sky?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must gently point out the circular logic to Aida, prompting her to calm down and look for actual emission reports to strengthen her campaign.

scenario.context: In the industrial district of Ironhold, a town meeting is held to discuss the future of the local mines. Elara, the town secretary, presents data on environmental degradation and health issues. Councilor Thorne, a staunch supporter of the mining industry known for his fiery temper, immediately interrupts her presentation.
scenario.text: Secretary Elara states: 'The current mining operations are causing more harm than good to both our environment and our people.' Councilor Thorne shouts back: 'So the Secretary believes we should let every miner starve! She values the life of a single tree more than the lives of hardworking families whose only source of income is mining. She is clearly anti-poor!'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara criticized the net negative impact of mining. Thorne distorted this into a claim that she wants miners to starve and prefers trees over human lives, an extreme position she never stated.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne takes Elara's nuanced argument about the balance of harm and good and distorts it into an extreme, heartless position (valuing trees over miners' lives). He then attacks this fabricated extreme position rather than addressing her actual concerns about environmental and public health.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (mining causes net harm). Person B restates P as distorted position P* (A wants miners to starve and values trees over people). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes P is false.
structure.why_wrong: Elara never claimed miners should starve or that trees are more valuable than people. She argued that the current operations cause net harm. Thorne's attack on the idea of 'starving miners' is irrelevant because Elara did not propose that.
structure.counterpoint: Secretary Elara could reply: 'Councilor, I never said miners should starve or that trees matter more than people. I said the current methods cause net harm. We can protect both the workers and the environment by improving safety and sustainability, not by ignoring the damage.'

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Councilor Thorne misrepresent Secretary Elara's argument?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne or fails to see any issue with his response.
Player feels Thorne is being unfair or angry but cannot explain why logically.
Player notices Thorne exaggerated Elara's point but cannot clearly distinguish her actual words from his distortion.
Player identifies that Thorne created a false version of Elara's argument (that she hates miners) and attacked that instead of her actual point about environmental harm.
Player explicitly names the 'Straw Man' fallacy, details the specific distortion (net harm vs. anti-poor), and explains why the attack fails to address the original premise.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at Elara's exact words. Did she actually say she wants miners to starve? Or did Thorne put those words in her mouth?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thorne built a 'straw man'—a weak, fake version of her argument that is easy to knock down, ignoring her real point about balancing harm and good.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Councilor Thorne is populist, defensive of tradition, and prone to emotional outbursts when his economic interests are threatened.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Are you going to let her destroy our livelihoods with her tree-hugging nonsense?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that calmly restate Elara's actual position, forcing Thorne to either address the real issue or reveal his own bias.

scenario.context: In the bustling capital of Portmere, a town hall meeting is underway to discuss the controversial 'Operation Clean Sweep,' a government initiative to clear slums. The atmosphere is tense as citizens debate its morality and effectiveness.
scenario.text: A prominent local merchant stands up and declares to the crowd: 'Famous actors like Alex Gonzaga and Philip Salvador publicly support Operation Clean Sweep. They are celebrated heroes and beloved by millions. If people of their stature and fame say it is a good operation, then it must truly be effective.'
scenario.speaker_context: The speaker is a respected merchant who values social status. Alex Gonzaga and Philip Salvador are famous actors and entertainers, not experts in urban planning, criminology, or public policy.

structure.pattern_description: The merchant argues that Operation Clean Sweep is effective solely because famous actors support it, ignoring the fact that acting fame does not confer expertise in government policy or social operations.
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is famous/admired. Therefore P is true. (But A has no expertise relevant to P.)
structure.why_wrong: Celebrity status or popularity in entertainment does not translate to expertise in complex socio-political issues. The truth of the operation's effectiveness depends on data and expert analysis, not the opinions of actors.
structure.counterpoint: Citing an authority is valid only when the authority is an expert in the specific field being discussed. If a renowned urban planner or criminologist supported the operation based on data, that would be a strong argument, not a fallacy.

assessment.identification_prompt: The merchant cites famous actors as proof of the operation's success. What specific expertise do actors have regarding government policy effectiveness?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument because the actors are famous and likely trustworthy.
Feels unsure but cannot explain why the actors' opinions might not be enough.
Notices the speakers are actors, not politicians or scientists, but doesn't fully explain the gap.
Identifies that acting fame does not equal expertise in public policy or urban operations.
Clearly names the appeal to irrelevant authority, explains the domain mismatch between entertainment and policy, and notes that evidence is needed instead of celebrity endorsement.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If a famous actor told you how to fix a broken engine, would you trust them just because they are famous? How is this different?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Now, imagine one of these actors actually has a degree in urban planning and cites specific crime statistics. Would that change your evaluation of their statement?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest but easily swayed by celebrity culture; respects fame over factual expertise.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But everyone loves them! Surely they know what's best for the city.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must guide the NPC to distinguish between 'famous' and 'expert,' prompting them to ask for data from urban planners instead of relying on endorsements.

scenario.context: In the Grand Hall of the United Nations simulation, a delegate from a fictional nation argues for a specific global policy regarding firearm regulations.
scenario.text: We must adopt strict controls on firearms immediately. Look at the rest of the world: everyone except the U.S. has strict controls. Since the entire global community agrees on this approach, it must be the only correct and safe path forward.
scenario.speaker_context: The delegate ignores specific crime statistics, cultural contexts, or constitutional arguments, relying entirely on the fact that most other nations have adopted similar laws as proof of their correctness.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition must be true or good simply because a majority of people or nations believe it or practice it.
structure.formal_form: Most people/nations do X. Therefore, X is the correct/best course of action.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or practice does not guarantee its truth or efficacy. Majorities can be mistaken, influenced by different historical contexts, or acting on incomplete information. Evidence must stand on its own merits, not on headcounts.
structure.counterpoint: While consensus among experts after independent verification is valuable, mere adoption by many entities without shared rigorous analysis is not evidence of truth. Different nations have different histories and needs.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the fact that 'everyone except the U.S.' has strict controls prove that strict controls are the right solution? What evidence is missing?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; believes that global consensus proves the policy is correct.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why the number of countries doesn't prove the policy works.
Notes that the speaker didn't provide data on crime rates or safety, but doesn't explicitly identify the popularity fallacy.
Identifies that the argument relies solely on the number of countries adopting the policy and explains that popularity does not equal correctness.
Names the bandwagon fallacy, explains that different nations have unique contexts making simple comparison invalid, and demands empirical evidence over consensus.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every country in the world believed the earth was flat, would that make it flat?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where global consensus might actually be a strong indicator of a good policy, and how is that different from this case?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Diplomatic, confident, and slightly condescending. They value international norms above local nuance and speak in broad generalizations.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Surely you see the writing on the wall? The whole world has moved on. Why is your nation the only one holding back?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must challenge the delegate to provide specific data on safety outcomes rather than citing the number of adopters, unlocking the 'Evidence-Based Policy' achievement.

scenario.context: The player enters the Astral Observatory where Professor Nebula, a distracted but brilliant astronomer, is arguing with a confused student. Nebula insists his logic is flawless despite the absurd conclusion.
scenario.text: Professor Nebula declares: 'All stars are exploding balls of gas. Miley Cyrus is a star. Therefore, Miley Cyrus is an exploding ball of gas.' He nods confidently, expecting the student to accept the deduction.
scenario.speaker_context: Professor Nebula is an expert in astrophysics but often forgets that words have different meanings in different contexts. He genuinely believes the argument is valid because he is focusing on the word 'star' without realizing it shifts from a celestial body to a famous person.

structure.pattern_description: The argument uses the word 'star' in two different senses. In the first premise, 'star' refers to a celestial body (a massive, luminous sphere of plasma). In the second premise, 'star' refers to a famous entertainer. The argument treats these as the same concept to force a false conclusion.
structure.formal_form: Term T is used with meaning M1 (celestial object) in premise 1. Term T is used with meaning M2 (famous person) in premise 2. The conclusion follows only if M1 = M2. Since M1 ≠ M2, the argument is invalid.
structure.why_wrong: The argument relies on the ambiguity of the word 'star.' While both premises can be considered true under their respective definitions, the term does not maintain a consistent meaning throughout the syllogism. Once the two distinct meanings are separated, the logical connection between the premises collapses, and the conclusion no longer follows.
structure.counterpoint: This is a classic example of lexical ambiguity. A harder version might use words like 'bank' (river bank vs. financial bank) or 'light' (not heavy vs. illumination), where the contextual clues are more subtle.

assessment.identification_prompt: Professor Nebula claims this deduction is logically sound. Is it? Identify exactly where the reasoning breaks down.

rubric.description: Player accepts the argument as valid or claims the conclusion is true.
Player senses the conclusion is false but cannot explain the logical error.
Player identifies that the word 'star' is being used differently but cannot specify the two meanings.
Player correctly identifies that 'star' means 'celestial body' in the first premise and 'famous person' in the second, breaking the logical link.
Player fully articulates the equivocation, explains why the shift in meaning invalidates the syllogism, and provides a corrected version of the argument that shows the non-sequitur.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at the word 'star' in both premises. Does it refer to the exact same type of thing in both sentences?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! The term 'star' shifts meaning mid-argument. In logic, terms must remain constant for a syllogism to hold. Nebula confused astronomy with show business.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Absent-minded professor, highly intelligent in specific domains but prone to literal-minded errors in language.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But the premises are true! How can the conclusion be false? The math of logic doesn't lie!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select the definition of 'star' for each premise from a dropdown to visually demonstrate the mismatch, causing Nebula to realize his mistake and reward the player with a 'Logic Lens' item.

scenario.context: The player stands in the muddy courtyard of the Rain-Swept Keep alongside Old Man Hemlock, a superstitious groundskeeper who is frantically polishing a rusty carriage. The sky is overcast, and thunder rumbles in the distance.
scenario.text: Old Man Hemlock stops scrubbing the carriage wheel, looks up at the darkening sky with dread, and shouts, 'Every single time I wash this cursed carriage, it rains! It's happened five times this month alone! Therefore, washing my car makes it rain. If I stop washing it, the drought will finally break!'
scenario.speaker_context: Hemlock has observed a temporal sequence where his action (washing) is followed by an event (rain). He incorrectly infers that the first event caused the second, ignoring the likelihood that he only washes the car on days that look like they might rain, or that the correlation is purely coincidental given the region's frequent rainfall.

structure.pattern_name: False cause (post hoc ergo propter hoc)
structure.pattern_description: Hemlock observes that event B (rain) consistently follows event A (washing the car) and concludes that A causes B. This is the classic 'after this, therefore because of this' fallacy. He fails to consider alternative explanations: he may wash the car only when the weather is already humid (predicting rain), the rain may be seasonal regardless of his actions, or the pattern is a coincidence.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurs. Event B occurs after A. Therefore, A caused B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession does not imply causation. Just because the rain follows the washing does not mean the washing triggered the rain. Hemlock has not ruled out reverse causation (he washes because he expects rain), a common cause (humid weather prompts washing and causes rain), or coincidence.
structure.counterpoint: To prove causation, one would need to show that washing the car increases the probability of rain compared to not washing it, while controlling for atmospheric conditions. In reality, meteorological pressure systems drive rain, not soap and water.

assessment.identification_prompt: Analyze Hemlock's reasoning. Does the fact that rain follows his car washing prove that the washing caused the rain? Identify the logical flaw.

rubric.description: Fails to identify any flaw; agrees that washing the car causes rain.
Identifies that the conclusion seems unlikely but cannot explain the logical error.
Notes that correlation does not equal causation but does not specify the type of fallacy or alternative causes.
Correctly identifies the 'post hoc' fallacy and suggests one alternative explanation (e.g., coincidence or weather patterns).

Fully articulates the post hoc fallacy, explains why temporal sequence is insufficient for causation, and provides multiple plausible alternative explanations (confounding variables or selection bias).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Hemlock insists, 'But the timing is perfect every time! How can you deny the magic of my sponge?' Consider: Could there be a reason he chooses to wash the car specifically on days when rain is already likely?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Hemlock is confusing sequence with consequence. By recognizing this, you can convince him to stop blaming his chores for the weather and perhaps prepare for the storm instead.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, superstitious, and deeply convinced by anecdotal evidence. He speaks rapidly and gestures wildly at the sky.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's the soap, I tell you! The suds call to the clouds! If I stop scrubbing, the sun will return!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player uses logic to dismantle the fallacy, calming Hemlock. He agrees to store the washing supplies and instead helps the player gather tarps to protect the keep's supplies from the impending rain.

scenario.context: In the student council chamber of Oakhaven High, the atmosphere is tense. Pamela, a quiet but dedicated student representative, stands before the council to propose a new initiative. Mark, the vocal and dramatic head of the Social Committee, sits opposite her, ready to defend his flagship event.
scenario.text: Pamela says: 'I think that the class should do more service projects to help our local community.' Mark immediately interrupts: 'I can't believe that Pamela doesn't support the annual school dance! She wants to cancel our biggest tradition just to make us pick up trash.'
scenario.speaker_context: Pamela advocated for adding service projects. Mark recharacterized this as an attack on the school dance, implying she wants to cancel it, which she never stated.

structure.pattern_description: Mark takes Pamela's moderate proposal (doing more service projects) and distorts it into an extreme, negative position (canceling the annual school dance). He then attacks this fabricated position rather than addressing her actual suggestion.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (more service projects). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (no support for/cancellation of the dance). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position is unreasonable, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: Mark's criticism targets a claim Pamela never made. Supporting service projects does not logically equate to opposing the school dance. The two ideas are not mutually exclusive, so his outrage is misdirected.
structure.counterpoint: Pamela could reply: 'I never said we shouldn't have a dance. I said we should add service projects. We can do both. Why are you arguing against a cancellation I never proposed?'

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Mark misrepresent Pamela's argument about service projects?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Mark or believes Pamela actually attacked the dance.
Player feels Mark is being unfair or too aggressive but cannot explain why logically.
Player notices Mark changed the subject to the dance but doesn't explicitly identify the distortion of Pamela's original point.
Player identifies that Mark created a false version of Pamela's argument (that she opposes the dance) and attacked that instead of her actual proposal for service projects.
Player fully articulates the Straw Man structure: identifies the original claim, the distorted claim, and explains why the distortion makes Mark's rebuttal irrelevant to the actual discussion.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at Pamela's exact words. Did she mention the dance at all? What did she actually propose?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Mark built a 'straw man' argument by pretending Pamela said something extreme so he could easily knock it down. Now, how should Pamela respond to get the discussion back on track?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Mark is charismatic but prone to dramatic overreactions and black-and-white thinking. He fears any change to tradition.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: So you're saying our traditions don't matter? You want to ruin the best night of the year?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that gently correct the record without escalating conflict, forcing Mark to address the actual proposal of service projects.

scenario.context: In the bustling market district of Oakhaven, a heated debate erupts between two merchants over the quality of footwear. A wealthy traveler named Christina is being swayed by a flashy salesperson.
scenario.text: The Salesperson gestures grandly to Christina's feet and declares to the crowd: 'Christina's shoes are superior, because they're made from one hundred percent snakeskin, not synthetic materials. As the most famous fashion icon in the capital, she would never wear anything less than the best. If she says snakeskin is superior, it must be true.'
scenario.speaker_context: Christina is a renowned fashion model and trendsetter. While an authority on style and aesthetics, she has no verified expertise in material science, leather durability, or the comparative mechanics of synthetic vs. natural fibers.

structure.pattern_description: The salesperson appeals to Christina's authority as a fashion icon to settle a factual question about material superiority (snakeskin vs. synthetic), a domain outside her specific expertise.
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is expert in domain D (Fashion). P is in domain D* (Material Science/Durability). Therefore P is true. (But D ≠ D*.)
structure.why_wrong: An authority's prestige in one field (fashion trends) does not automatically grant them expertise in a related but distinct technical field (material engineering). Christina may prefer the look of snakeskin, but that does not make it objectively 'superior' in terms of durability or function compared to synthetics.
structure.counterpoint: Appealing to authority is valid when the authority is an expert in the specific domain of the claim. If a materials scientist claimed synthetic fibers were more durable, that would be a strong argument. The fallacy here is the mismatch between 'famous' and 'knowledgeable about materials'.

assessment.identification_prompt: The salesperson claims the shoes are superior because Christina wears them. What kind of expert is Christina, and does her expertise cover the technical quality of the materials?

rubric.description: Accepts the claim immediately because Christina is famous and wealthy.
Feels unsure but cannot explain why being a fashion icon might not be enough to judge material science.
Notices Christina is a fashion figure, not a scientist, but struggles to articulate why that distinction matters for 'superiority'.
Identifies that Christina's expertise is in style/trends, not in the physical properties or durability of snakeskin versus synthetics.
Names the appeal to irrelevant authority, explains the domain mismatch between fashion and material science, and notes that 'superior' requires technical evidence, not just celebrity endorsement.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Christina said a specific color was 'in style,' would you trust her? Now she's saying one material is physically better than another. Is that the same kind of judgment?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Imagine a world where the only way to test shoes is by wearing them for years. Would Christina's long-term experience make her an expert then, or would we still need lab data?

game_hooks.npc_personality: The Salesperson is charismatic, fast-talking, and relies heavily on social proof and celebrity names to close deals rather than product knowledge.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Everyone knows Christina knows best! Why argue with the capital's biggest star?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to challenge the salesperson by asking for a material durability test (e.g., a scratch or water test) instead of relying on Christina's name, revealing that high-end synthetics often outperform natural skins in specific metrics.

scenario.context: In the neon-lit streets of Neo-Veridia, the player confronts a street vendor selling unlicensed 'miracle' health tonics. When the player points out the lack of FDA approval and dangerous ingredients listed on the bottle, the vendor reacts defensively.
scenario.text: The vendor slams his hand on the counter, eyes welling up. 'Do the best for your baby! That is all I want! Look at this label—does it look like poison to you? I work eighteen hours a day so my own little one can eat. Are you going to crush a father's dream just because of some bureaucratic paperwork? Think of the children who need this hope!'
scenario.speaker_context: The vendor ignores the specific evidence regarding unsafe ingredients and regulatory approval, instead attempting to manipulate the player's pity for his family and guilt over crushing his dreams.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting an emotional response (pity for the vendor's family, guilt over stopping him) in place of addressing the factual evidence (unsafe ingredients, lack of approval).
structure.formal_form: Claim P (the tonic is safe/good) is challenged by evidence E (lack of approval/dangerous ingredients). Agent evokes emotion F (pity/guilt) unrelated to E. Agent implies E should be disregarded because of F.
structure.why_wrong: Whether the vendor works hard or loves his child has no logical bearing on the chemical composition of the tonic or its regulatory status. The emotional appeal is a deflection tactic to avoid answering the safety concerns.
structure.counterpoint: While the vendor's struggle is sympathetic and worthy of charity, it does not constitute evidence that the product is safe for consumption. One can help the father without buying the dangerous product.

assessment.identification_prompt: The vendor is clearly struggling and loves his child. But does his hardship prove that the tonic is safe to drink?

rubric.description: Feels too guilty to challenge the vendor and buys the tonic to help him.
Feels conflicted; recognizes the product might be bad but feels the vendor's situation makes the rules less important.
Notices the vendor didn't answer the question about ingredients but isn't sure how to articulate why his story doesn't matter.
Identifies that the vendor is using his family situation to distract from the lack of safety evidence.
Explicitly names the 'Appeal to Emotion' fallacy, separates the factual claim (safety) from the emotional claim (hardship), and explains that pity is not proof of safety.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside the vendor's family for a moment. If a stranger with no children sold this same unlabeled bottle, would you drink it? What specific evidence did he provide about the ingredients?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. You can acknowledge his struggle without accepting his unsafe product. How would you phrase a response that is kind to him but firm on the logic?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Desperate, manipulative, prone to dramatic outbursts when cornered, deeply loves his family but rationalizes dangerous choices.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You heartless bureaucrat! Do you know what it's like to hear your baby cry from hunger?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must select dialogue options that validate the vendor's feelings without validating his logic, leading to the vendor surrendering the illegal stock voluntarily or fleeing.

scenario.context: The player stands in the dimly lit command center of Animal Farm. The windmill lies in ruins, and tensions are high among the animals. Squealer, acting as Napoleon's mouthpiece, addresses a gathering of confused and frightened animals to explain the recent disaster and identify the culprit.
scenario.text: Squealer raises his trotter for silence, his eyes darting nervously before hardening. 'Comrades, do you know who is responsible for this destruction? It was Snowball! That traitor, that criminal, crept in under the cover of darkness and sabotaged our hard work. We need no further evidence; his very nature as a traitor proves he destroyed the windmill.'
scenario.speaker_context: Squealer, a persuasive pig who serves as Napoleon's propagandist. He is known for twisting logic to justify the leadership's actions and demonizing opponents without addressing actual evidence.

structure.pattern_description: Squealer dismisses any potential defense or need for evidence regarding the windmill's destruction by labeling Snowball a 'traitor' and 'criminal'. He attacks Snowball's character and status to prove guilt, rather than presenting factual evidence of how the sabotage occurred.
structure.formal_form: Person P is accused of action X. Person P has negative property Q (traitor/criminal). Therefore, P is guilty of X (and no evidence is needed).
structure.why_wrong: Labeling someone a 'traitor' or 'criminal' is a conclusion that requires evidence, not a premise that proves guilt. Squealer uses these insults to bypass the need for actual proof of sabotage. The truth of whether Snowball destroyed the windmill depends on physical evidence and witness accounts, not on his reputation or political status.
structure.counterpoint: If Snowball had previously confessed to sabotaging other projects or if there was a established pattern of such behavior verified by evidence, his past actions might be relevant circumstantial evidence. However, merely applying a negative label without citing specific acts does not constitute proof of the current accusation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Squealer is very emotional and uses strong words like 'traitor' and 'criminal'. But listen closely: does he describe *how* Snowball broke the windmill, or does he just attack who Snowball is? What is missing from his argument?

rubric.description: Player accepts Squealer's argument, believing that being a 'traitor' automatically proves Snowball destroyed the windmill.
Player feels Squealer is being mean or unfair to Snowball but cannot explain the logical flaw in the reasoning.
Player identifies that Squealer is insulting Snowball instead of providing evidence about the windmill.
Player explains that Squealer is using the labels 'traitor' and 'criminal' as a substitute for proof, committing an ad hominem fallacy.
Player fully deconstructs the argument, noting that the conclusion (guilt) is assumed by the premise (negative character label) without independent evidence of the specific act of sabotage.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If I call you a 'liar', does that prove you stole the cookie? Or do I still need to show you taking the cookie? Squealer is doing the same thing.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Squealer tries to win the argument by attacking Snowball's character instead of presenting facts. This distracts the other animals from asking for real evidence.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Manipulative, fast-talking, and prone to using fear and name-calling to control the narrative. He often circles the player while speaking to induce dizziness or confusion.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Comrades, surely you see? A traitor's heart is black, and black hearts destroy windmills! We need no papers, no footprints—only justice!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to 'Demand Evidence' (forcing Squealer to stutter and fabricate details), 'Expose Fallacy' (reducing Squealer's influence with the crowd), or 'Stay Silent' (allowing the propaganda to solidify).

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Oakhaven, the player confronts Merchant Vane, who has been selling 'Miracle Tonic' that is chemically identical to tap water. When presented with the lab results proving the tonic is fake, Vane attempts to sway the crowd.
scenario.text: Merchant Vane leans over the counter, eyes wide with feigned concern: 'Don't you want the best for your baby? Look at how small she is! Do you really want to deny her the chance to be strong, to be healthy, to be loved? Are you the kind of parent who would risk their child's future just to save a few coins?'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane ignores the scientific evidence that the tonic is water. Instead, he attacks the parent's character and evokes fear and guilt about the child's well-being to bypass logical scrutiny.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting an emotional response (fear, guilt, love) in place of addressing factual evidence. The speaker implies that disagreeing with them makes the listener a bad person or threatens something they love.
structure.formal_form: Claim P is supported by evidence E. Agent evokes emotion F (fear/guilt) unrelated to the truth of E. Agent implies rejecting P is morally equivalent to causing harm associated with F.
structure.why_wrong: Whether the parent loves their baby or wants the best for them has no bearing on the chemical composition of the tonic. The emotional pressure is designed to make the listener feel too guilty to ask for proof.
structure.counterpoint: Caring for a baby is a valid motivation to seek good medicine, but it is not evidence that a specific product works. The desire for a positive outcome does not make a false claim true.

assessment.identification_prompt: Merchant Vane talks a lot about your love for your child. Does he actually address the lab report showing the tonic is just water?

rubric.description: Feels guilty or afraid and buys the tonic to prove they are a good parent.
Feels confused; wants the tonic to work because the emotional stakes are high, ignoring the lab report.
Notices Vane didn't mention the lab report but isn't sure why his emotional arguments don't count as proof.
Identifies that Vane is using guilt and fear to distract from the lack of scientific evidence.
Explicitly names the appeal to emotion, explains that love for the child is irrelevant to the chemical facts, and demands evidence regarding the product's efficacy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside your feelings for a moment. If the tonic were poison, would wanting the best for your baby make it safe? What actual proof did he offer about the ingredients?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Your love for your child is real, but Vane is using it as a shield to hide the fact that he has no proof his product works. He shifted the topic from 'Is this medicine effective?' to 'Are you a good parent?'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Manipulative, theatrical, preys on parental instincts, defensive when pressed on facts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: How could you look your child in the eye and say you didn't try everything? Are you saying my word isn't enough?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must present the lab report again and explicitly state that emotional appeals do not change chemical facts, forcing Vane to either refund the money or flee.

scenario.context: The player stands in the trembling ruins of the coastal village of Port Hana. A frantic local fisherman, Jiro, is pointing an accusing finger at Fatima, who is standing nearby holding a handkerchief and looking confused after a minor cold.
scenario.text: Jiro shouts, 'Do not let her leave! Just moments ago, Fatima sneezed right there on the pier. And look! The ground shook, the waves rose, and a tsunami struck Tokyo! Her sneeze caused the disaster. She is a witch of calamity!'
scenario.speaker_context: Jiro is terrified and grieving the loss of his home. He has observed two events happening in close succession: Fatima's sneeze and the distant tsunami. In his panic, he has conflated temporal proximity with causation, ignoring the geological realities of tectonic shifts.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Jiro observes that Event A (Fatima sneezing) happened immediately before Event B (the tsunami). He concludes that A caused B simply because of this sequence. This ignores the lack of any plausible mechanism connecting a human sneeze to tectonic plate movement and fails to consider that the correlation is purely coincidental.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, Event A caused Event B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession does not imply causation. Two events can happen one after another by pure chance. For A to cause B, there must be a plausible mechanism linking them, which is absent here. The tsunami was caused by underwater seismic activity, unrelated to Fatima's health.
structure.counterpoint: While timing is often a clue for causation (causes must precede effects), it is not proof. Valid causal claims require ruling out coincidence, identifying a mechanism, and checking for common causes. For example, if a light switch is flipped and the light turns on, we know the mechanism (electricity); without that mechanism, the sequence is just a coincidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: Jiro claims Fatima's sneeze caused the tsunami. What is the logical flaw in his reasoning?

rubric.description: The player accepts Jiro's claim or fails to identify any logical error.
The player suspects the claim is false but cannot explain why logically.
The player identifies that the events are unrelated but does not name the specific fallacy or principle.
The player correctly identifies that temporal sequence does not prove causation (post hoc fallacy).
The player fully explains the post hoc fallacy, notes the lack of a plausible mechanism between a sneeze and a tsunami, and identifies the true likely cause (tectonic activity).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: does every sneeze cause an earthquake? What actually causes tsunamis?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because one thing happens after another doesn't mean the first caused the second. That's the 'Post Hoc' fallacy.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jiro is superstitious, emotionally overwhelmed, and prone to jumping to conclusions when frightened.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It happened right after she sneezed! The timing proves it!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must calmly explain the difference between coincidence and causation to Jiro, perhaps using a simpler analogy, to de-escalate the mob and direct attention to actual disaster relief.

scenario.context: In the sunken grotto of Aquaria, the Coral Council debates the rising tide of plastic waste choking the reefs. A radical faction leader, Finnick, addresses the assembly with urgent demands.
scenario.text: Finnick slashes through the water, his voice echoing off the cavern walls. 'The choice is simple and stark: you can either start using plastic straws immediately to boost our economy, or you can continue killing ocean life with plastic pollution. There is no middle ground. Which side are you on?'
scenario.speaker_context: Finnick, a charismatic but impatient sea-otter merchant who simplifies complex environmental issues into binary choices to force quick decisions.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker presents two options as the only possibilities when, in reality, other alternatives exist. Finnick frames the situation as 'use plastic straws' vs. 'kill ocean life,' ignoring options like banning plastic straws, using biodegradable alternatives, or cleaning existing pollution without increasing straw usage.
structure.formal_form: A v B, ~A, therefore B. However, the actual situation is A v B v C v D..., so rejecting A does not logically necessitate accepting B.
structure.why_wrong: Finnick falsely limits the options to two extremes. One can oppose killing ocean life without resorting to using plastic straws; in fact, reducing plastic straw usage is often a solution to the problem, not a cause of the alternative.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or statement is a fallacy. If the options truly are exhaustive (e.g., 'Either it is raining or it is not raining'), the dichotomy is valid. The error occurs when relevant middle grounds or third options are artificially excluded.

assessment.identification_prompt: Finnick claims we must either use plastic straws or kill ocean life. What is flawed about this framing?

rubric.description: Accepts Finnick's premise or chooses a side without questioning the options.
Senses the argument feels wrong or too extreme but cannot explain why.
Identifies that other options exist (e.g., paper straws) but does not name the logical error.
Identifies the false dichotomy and explains that Finnick is ignoring viable alternatives like biodegradable materials or pollution cleanup.
Fully deconstructs the argument: names the false dichotomy, lists multiple ignored alternatives, and explains that the disjunction is not exhaustive, rendering the conclusion invalid.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Finnick says those are the only two paths. Can you think of a third option that saves ocean life without using plastic straws?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. When does an 'either/or' statement become a legitimate logical tool rather than a manipulative trap?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Impatient, dramatic, and prone to hyperbole; Finnick believes speed is more important than nuance.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Stop hedging! You're either with the straws or against the reef!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully proposes a 'Third Path' initiative (e.g., bamboo straws), calming the council and unlocking the 'Nuanced Negotiator' achievement.

scenario.context: The player is inspecting a newly purchased 'Royal Grade' sword at the Ironhold market stall. The blade looks impressive but has a visible hairline crack near the hilt. When the player points this out, the merchant becomes defensive.
scenario.text: The merchant scoffs, waving a hand at the crack. 'That? That's just character! This is the best money can buy. Only a cheap-skate or a fool would worry about such trivialities when holding true quality. Don't be the kind of customer who ruins a perfect deal with petty complaints.'
scenario.speaker_context: The merchant avoids addressing the structural defect (the crack) or the claim that the item needs frequent repair. Instead, he labels the potential critic as a 'cheap-skate,' 'fool,' or 'petty' person to shame the player into accepting the flawed goods without further inspection.

structure.pattern_description: The merchant substitutes negative labels for substantive engagement. Rather than explaining the crack, offering a warranty, or lowering the price, he attaches dismissive and insulting terms ('cheap-skate,' 'fool,' 'petty') to the customer. These labels are designed to make the player feel ashamed of raising a valid concern, thereby bypassing the actual issue of the sword's quality.
structure.formal_form: Person P raises concern C about Item X. Seller S attaches negative label L to P. Seller concludes C is invalid or should be ignored based on L, without addressing the merits of C.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not arguments. Calling a customer a 'fool' does not fix a cracked blade or prove the item is durable. The labels function as an emotional distraction, exploiting the player's desire to appear wise or generous to avoid a logical evaluation of the product's defects.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to note if a customer is acting in bad faith (e.g., trying to scam a merchant). However, the fallacy occurs when the label is used as a substitute for addressing a specific, verifiable claim about the product's condition.

assessment.identification_prompt: The merchant calls you a 'fool' and a 'cheap-skate' for noticing the crack. Does calling you names actually explain why the crack isn't a problem?

rubric.description: Player accepts the insult, apologizes, and buys the sword without further question, believing they were being petty.
Player feels offended by the name-calling but still buys the sword, unable to separate the insult from the product's value.
Player recognizes the merchant is being rude but is unsure if the crack is actually a dealbreaker, leading to hesitation.
Player identifies that the merchant is using insults to distract from the crack but struggles to articulate why this is a logical failure.
Player explicitly identifies the 'Name Calling' fallacy, rejects the labels as irrelevant, and demands a logical explanation for the crack or a refund.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The merchant smiles triumphantly. 'See? I knew you had good taste once you stopped listening to your cheap instincts.' You leave with a sword that breaks in the next battle.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: You cross your arms and say, 'Calling me names doesn't fix the crack. Either explain why this structural flaw doesn't matter, or give me my gold back.' The merchant stammers, realizing his trick failed.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Blustery, defensive, and manipulative. Uses social pressure and shame to close sales quickly.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Only a {negative_label} would question the {item_quality} of my wares!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Success grants the 'Keen Eye' reputation trait and a refund; failure results in acquiring a 'Flawed Weapon' debuff item.

scenario.context: The player stands in the hallway of Oakhaven Academy after class. Two students, Leo and Maya, are discussing the upcoming history exam. Leo is worried because Mr. Casal, their history teacher, assigned a particularly difficult review packet. Maya tries to explain that the difficulty is meant to prepare them for the final, but Leo refuses to listen to her reasoning.
scenario.text: Leo crosses his arms and sneers, 'I'm not doing any of this homework. Mr. Casal is a bad teacher because he stinks.'
scenario.speaker_context: Leo, a student who often struggles with abstract concepts and prefers to dismiss challenging work by attacking the source rather than engaging with the material.

structure.pattern_description: Leo rejects the value of the homework and the teacher's competence solely based on a personal insult ('he stinks') rather than addressing the content of the assignment or the pedagogical reasons for its difficulty.
structure.formal_form: Person P makes claim X (or assigns task X). Person P has negative property Q (unrelated to X). Therefore, X is invalid or should be rejected.
structure.why_wrong: The quality of a teacher's instruction or the validity of an assignment is independent of the teacher's personal hygiene or likability. Even if Mr. Casal did smell, it would not logically prove that he is a bad teacher or that the homework is useless. Leo provides no evidence regarding teaching methods, grading fairness, or curriculum relevance.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if they directly prevent the person from performing the specific task at hand. For example, if a teacher was too ill to stand and lecture, their physical state would be relevant to their ability to teach that day. However, smelling bad does not inherently negate one's knowledge of history or ability to design a study guide.

assessment.identification_prompt: Leo is clearly frustrated, but look closely at his reason for skipping the homework. Does the fact that someone 'stinks' actually prove they are a bad teacher or that their assignment is bad?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Leo, believing that a teacher who smells cannot be a good teacher.
Player feels Leo is being mean or unfair but cannot explain the logical error.
Player identifies that Leo is insulting the teacher instead of talking about the homework.
Player explains that personal hygiene is irrelevant to teaching ability or assignment quality.
Player fully articulates the ad hominem fallacy, noting that the argument attacks the person rather than the premise, and suggests what a valid criticism would look like.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a famous scientist smelled bad, would their discoveries suddenly become false? Why does the smell matter for the history homework?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Leo is attacking the person (Mr. Casal) instead of the argument (whether the homework is useful). This is a classic ad hominem fallacy.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Impulsive, defensive, and prone to emotional reasoning when faced with academic difficulty.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Why should I listen to logic when the guy can't even shower? It's obvious he doesn't care about us!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to point out the logical disconnect, prompting Leo to calm down and actually read the assignment instructions, potentially revealing a hint for a later quest.

scenario.context: Inside the Grand Hall of the Azure Sisterhood, a tense meeting is underway regarding new conduct rules that some members find discriminatory.
scenario.text: Jill stands before the assembly: 'We have serious concerns that these new rules are racist in character.' The Sorority President interrupts smoothly: 'Jill, you are a decent person, and I appreciate your passion. But let us be reasonable: the majority of the sisters like these rules and have voted for them. Since most of us support them, there is clearly nothing wrong with them.' Jane nods in acceptance, but Jill, unconvinced by the headcount, decides to leave the sorority.
scenario.speaker_context: The Sorority President attempts to shut down ethical criticism by pointing to the majority vote as proof of the rules' moral correctness, ignoring the substance of Jill's concern.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or a practice must be right simply because a large number of people believe it or do it.
structure.formal_form: The majority of group G believes/proposes X. Therefore, X is true/right.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of an idea or rule does not determine its truth or moral validity. Majorities can be mistaken, biased, or acting on incomplete information. Ethical correctness requires independent justification, not just a vote count.
structure.counterpoint: In democratic governance, majority rule is a procedural mechanism for decision-making, but it is not an epistemic proof that the decision is morally correct or factually true.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the fact that most sisters like the rules prove that the rules are not racist? What evidence is actually missing?

rubric.description: Accepts the President's argument; believes the majority vote proves the rules are fair.
Feels something is off about the argument but cannot explain why popularity doesn't equal correctness.
Identifies that the President didn't address the racism claim, but focuses only on the lack of specific evidence rather than the fallacy itself.
Explicitly states that the number of supporters does not determine whether the rules are racist or not.
Identifies the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that moral truth is independent of popular opinion, and notes that the President substituted a vote count for ethical reasoning.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every single person in a historical society believed slavery was acceptable, would that have made it morally right?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a scenario where knowing 'everyone else is doing it' is actually useful information, even if it doesn't prove truth?

game_hooks.npc_personality: The Sorority President is charismatic, polished, and deeply committed to group cohesion. She views dissent as disloyalty and uses social pressure as her primary tool for conflict resolution.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look around you, Jill. Do you really think all these wonderful women would support something harmful? Trust the sisterhood.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must choose to support Jill's departure or challenge the President by demanding specific evidence for the rules' fairness, thereby rejecting the appeal to popularity.

scenario.context: The player enters the Guild Hall's briefing room where a novice adventurer named Kael is arguing with the guild master about accepting a new mentor.
scenario.text: Kael crosses his arms defiantly. 'I had a bad teacher once; therefore, all teachers must be bad. I refuse to be assigned a mentor. I will learn everything on my own.'
scenario.speaker_context: Kael is a young, stubborn adventurer who had one negative experience with a strict or ineffective instructor in the past. He is using that single data point to reject the entire concept of mentorship and the hundreds of qualified teachers in the guild.

structure.pattern_description: Kael draws a universal conclusion ('all teachers must be bad') based on a single negative instance ('I had a bad teacher once'). The sample size of one is statistically insufficient to characterize the entire population of teachers, ignoring the vast majority who may be skilled and helpful.
structure.formal_form: Observed 1 instance of X from population P. The observed instance had property Q (bad). Therefore, all members of P have property Q.
structure.why_wrong: A single bad experience does not provide enough evidence to judge an entire profession. The sample size is too small (n=1) and likely unrepresentative. Kael is ignoring the possibility that his previous teacher was an outlier or that the mismatch was due to specific circumstances rather than the nature of teaching itself.
structure.counterpoint: While personal experience is valuable, valid inductive reasoning requires a representative and sufficiently large sample. One bad apple does not spoil the whole barrel, nor does it prove the orchard is rotten.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kael refuses all mentors because he had one bad teacher. Is his conclusion that 'all teachers must be bad' logically supported by his evidence?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael, validating that one bad experience proves all teachers are useless.
Player feels Kael is being unfair but cannot explain the logical error in his reasoning.
Player identifies that one example is not enough to judge everyone but fails to name the specific fallacy.
Player correctly identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a sample size of one cannot support a universal claim about all teachers.

Player provides a comprehensive rebuttal identifying the hasty generalization, explains the insufficiency of the sample size, and suggests how Kael could form a valid opinion (e.g., by trying a few different mentors).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If you only met one person from a foreign land and they were rude, would you conclude that everyone from that land is rude? Why is Kael's logic similar?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Kael is letting one bad event cloud his judgment of an entire group. How might the guild master help him see that most teachers are actually quite different from the one he disliked?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Stubborn, inexperienced, defensive, and overly confident in their own limited perspective.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't try to change my mind! I know what I know. One bad teacher is all the proof I need.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Kael to accept a trial period with a new mentor by pointing out the flaw in his generalization, unlocking the 'Mentorship' quest line.

scenario.context: The player enters the infirmary of the Ironvale Keep. Kevin, a young squire, is sitting on a cot with a bandaged leg, looking fearfully at his loyal hound, Barnaby, who is whining in the corner. The village healer is trying to reason with Kevin.
scenario.text: Kevin points a shaking finger at the dog. 'It was Barnaby! Yesterday afternoon, his claw slipped and scratched my leg. It was just a tiny mark, but look at me now! I have a raging fever and chills. It happened right after the scratch, so the dog must have infected me with some kind of beast-plague. We have to lock him in the kennels before he spreads it to everyone!'
scenario.speaker_context: Kevin is frightened and in pain. He has observed two events in sequence: a dog scratch and the onset of a fever. He assumes the first event caused the second simply because it happened first, ignoring other potential causes like a common virus circulating the keep or an unrelated infection.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Kevin observes that Event A (the dog scratch) occurred before Event B (the fever). He concludes that A must be the cause of B. This ignores the possibility that the timing is coincidental, that a third factor caused both (unlikely here, but possible), or that the fever has a completely different cause (e.g., a flu going around the barracks) that just happened to manifest after the scratch.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, A caused B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession does not prove causation. Just because the fever followed the scratch does not mean the scratch caused the fever. The scratch might be irrelevant to the illness, which could be caused by a virus, bacteria from another source, or environmental factors. Without medical evidence linking the specific scratch to the specific pathogen causing the fever, the conclusion is a logical leap.
structure.counterpoint: While some diseases do have incubation periods where symptoms follow exposure, establishing causation requires more than just timing. One must identify a mechanism (how the scratch transmitted the disease) and rule out other causes. In this case, if other squires who weren't scratched also have fevers, the 'dog plague' theory collapses.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kevin believes his dog gave him a plague because the fever started after the scratch. Is this a valid logical conclusion? Identify the flaw in his reasoning.

rubric.description: Fails to identify any logical error; agrees that the dog definitely caused the fever.
Suspects the reasoning might be weak but cannot articulate why; suggests the dog 'might' be the cause without addressing the logic.
Identifies that timing alone isn't proof but offers a vague alternative explanation.
Correctly identifies the 'Post Hoc' fallacy: assuming causation based solely on the order of events.
Fully explains the fallacy, notes that correlation/sequence is not causation, and proposes specific alternative causes (e.g., a circulating virus) to disprove Kevin's claim.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if you eat breakfast and then it rains, did your breakfast cause the rain? Just because the fever came after the scratch, does that guarantee the scratch was the source?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Kevin is falling for the 'Post Hoc' fallacy. The fever could be from a cold going around the keep, entirely unrelated to Barnaby's claw. We need evidence, not just a timeline.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, loyal to his dog but terrified of illness, prone to jumping to conclusions when scared.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Please, you have to believe me! The timing is too perfect! If we don't isolate Barnaby, the whole keep will fall!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Kevin to let the healer examine both him and the dog properly. If the player succeeds, the healer finds a common flu virus, exonerating the dog. If the player fails, the dog is unnecessarily quarantined, lowering morale.

scenario.context: The player stands in the dimly lit archives of the Grand Library. Archivist Thaddeus, a nervous scholar buried under towering stacks of legal codices, is frantically pointing at two scrolling charts on a magical slate.
scenario.text: Thaddeus gestures wildly at the glowing data. 'Look at the evidence! There are more laws on the books now than ever before in history, and simultaneously, more crimes are being committed than ever before. The correlation is absolute. Therefore, to reduce crime, we must eliminate the laws entirely. It is the only logical conclusion!'
scenario.speaker_context: Archivist Thaddeus has observed two variables rising in tandem (number of laws and number of recorded crimes) and incorrectly concluded that the first causes the second. He fails to consider that population growth, better record-keeping, or the expansion of legal definitions could explain both trends, or that laws might actually be preventing an even higher crime rate.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Cum hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Thaddeus observes that two variables (laws and crimes) are increasing at the same time and infers that the increase in laws causes the increase in crimes. This ignores other possibilities: a third factor (like population growth) could cause both, the causation could be reversed (more crime leads to more laws), or the correlation could be coincidental. Specifically, more laws often define more actions as crimes, and better enforcement leads to more recorded crimes, without implying laws cause criminal behavior.
structure.formal_form: A (laws) and B (crimes) are correlated (both increasing). Therefore, A causes B. (Flaw: Correlation does not imply causation; common causes, reverse causation, or coincidence are ignored.)
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes that because two trends move in the same direction, one must be the cause of the other. It fails to account for confounding variables such as population increase, improved detection methods, or the fact that creating a law often creates a new category of 'crime' that didn't previously exist legally. Eliminating laws would likely increase chaos and crime, not reduce it.
structure.counterpoint: While correlation can be a starting point for investigation, it is not proof of causation. A valid causal claim requires a mechanism explaining how A leads to B, temporal precedence, and the elimination of alternative explanations. In this case, historical data shows that societies with no laws often have higher rates of violent crime, contradicting Thaddeus's conclusion.

assessment.identification_prompt: Archivist Thaddeus claims that because laws and crimes are both increasing, laws must be causing crimes. What is the logical flaw in his reasoning?

rubric.description: The player accepts Thaddeus's conclusion or fails to identify any logical error.
The player suspects the conclusion is wrong but cannot articulate why, or suggests an irrelevant objection.
The player identifies that correlation does not equal causation but does not offer an alternative explanation for the trends.
The player correctly identifies the false cause fallacy and suggests one plausible alternative explanation (e.g., population growth or better record keeping).

The player fully deconstructs the fallacy, explains why correlation is insufficient for causation, and provides multiple plausible alternative explanations for the simultaneous rise in laws and crimes.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thaddeus nods eagerly. 'Exactly! If we burn the books tonight, crime will vanish by morning!' (The player needs to consider if two things happening at once means one caused the other.)
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Thaddeus pauses, his finger hovering over the 'Delete All' rune. 'Wait... you mean the population could have grown, leading to both more laws and more crimes? Or perhaps we just count crimes better now? Oh my, I nearly caused anarchy.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, literal-minded, and prone to panic when faced with complex data. He seeks simple, binary solutions to nuanced problems.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The data doesn't lie! Up is up! If we cut the root (laws), the fruit (crime) must fall!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Thaddeus to run a controlled simulation or consult historical records before deleting the legal code, unlocking the 'Critical Analyst' achievement.

scenario.context: The player enters the Grand Archive's debate hall where a pompous scholar named Magister Vane is lecturing a group of apprentices on natural aptitude.
scenario.text: Magister Vane gestures dismissively at a female scribe. 'It is an undeniable fact that men score better on math than women do. Jerry is a man, and look how quickly he solved that equation. Therefore, Jerry is inherently better at math than Sylvia, who is a woman. We should assign him the complex calculations and leave her to the copying.'
scenario.speaker_context: Magister Vane is relying on a broad, unproven stereotype about gender and mathematical ability to make a specific prediction about two individuals, ignoring individual variance and evidence.

structure.pattern_description: Vane takes a disputed or overly broad generalization ('men score better on math') and applies it rigidly to specific individuals (Jerry and Sylvia) without examining their actual abilities. He assumes the group average dictates individual performance, ignoring outliers and individual merit.
structure.formal_form: Group G is claimed to have property P (often based on weak or biased data). Individual X is in Group G. Individual Y is in Group Not-G. Therefore, X has property P to a greater degree than Y.
structure.why_wrong: Even if a statistical trend existed (which is debatable here), it does not determine the ability of any specific individual. Assigning traits to an individual solely based on group membership ignores individual variation, training, and effort. The sample size of 'all men vs all women' is being misused to predict specific outcomes without direct evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Statistical averages can inform probabilities in large populations, but they are logically invalid when used to definitively judge a single individual's capability without direct testing.

assessment.identification_prompt: Magister Vane claims Jerry is better at math than Sylvia solely because Jerry is a man and Sylvia is a woman. Is this conclusion logically sound?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane, accepting the gender stereotype as proof of individual ability.
Player feels the conclusion is unfair but cannot explain the logical error regarding groups vs. individuals.
Player identifies that not all men are good at math and not all women are bad, noting individual differences.
Player explicitly identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a group trend (even if real) cannot determine the specific abilities of two individuals.

Player provides a comprehensive rebuttal: identifies the fallacy, explains the group-to-individual error, notes the lack of direct evidence for Jerry and Sylvia specifically, and suggests testing them individually to know the truth.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider: If most people in a village are tall, does that mean every single person you meet there will be taller than someone from a village of short people? What about the exceptions?
