scenario.context: The player enters the Oceanic Research Institute's briefing room. Dr. Aris Thorne, a senior climatologist, is presenting a new study to the council regarding global warming trends. He points to a revised dataset on his holographic display.
scenario.text: Dr. Thorne gestures emphatically at the shifting data streams. 'This new research challenges the methodologies we have used to calculate sea temperatures until now. Because our previous methods were flawed and underestimated the heat, it logically follows that the oceans are actually increasing in temperature much quicker than previously suggested. The error in measurement is the direct cause of the accelerated warming rate.'
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Thorne has correctly identified that previous measurement methods may have been inaccurate (underestimating temperature). However, he commits a logical error by conflating the correction of a measurement error with a physical change in the rate of warming. The new data suggests the *current state* is hotter than thought, not that the *rate of change* (speed of warming) has physically accelerated due to the measurement error itself. He treats the revelation of past data as the cause of current physical acceleration.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Confusion of correlation/measurement with causation
structure.pattern_description: Dr. Thorne observes that new data shows higher temperatures than old data. He infers that the flaw in the old data (or the act of challenging it) causes the temperature to be rising 'quicker'. In reality, the new data simply corrects the baseline; it does not mean the physical rate of warming has suddenly sped up because we measured it differently. He confuses an epistemic update (what we know) with an ontological change (what is happening physically).
structure.formal_form: Method M underestimated Value V. New Method N shows V is higher. Therefore, the rate of change of V is increasing faster than previously thought solely because M was wrong. (Error: Correcting a baseline error changes the absolute value, not necessarily the derivative/rate of change over time, nor does the error cause the physical phenomenon.)
structure.why_wrong: The fallacy lies in assuming that because our understanding of the past has changed (we now know it was hotter), the physical process of warming must be accelerating 'quicker' as a result. The measurement error didn't cause the water to heat up faster; it just hid how hot it already was. The rate of increase might be the same, just starting from a higher realized baseline, or the 'quicker' claim requires evidence of acceleration, not just evidence of higher absolute temperatures.
structure.counterpoint: Revising data corrects our knowledge of the state of the system, but it does not automatically imply a change in the system's dynamics (rate of change). To claim the warming is 'quicker,' one must demonstrate that the slope of the temperature curve has steepened in reality, not just that our previous estimate of the slope was too shallow due to bad tools.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dr. Thorne claims that because old methods underestimated sea temperatures, the oceans are now warming 'quicker.' What is the logical flaw in connecting the measurement error to the speed of warming?

rubric.description: Fails to identify any logical error; accepts the scientist's conclusion as fact.

Notes that correcting a measurement error changes the reported temperature, but not necessarily the rate of change.
Clearly explains that the flaw is conflating an epistemic update (new data) with a physical acceleration (causation), noting that bad measurements don't cause faster warming.

Provides a comprehensive critique distinguishing between absolute values and rates of change (derivatives), explaining that the 'quicker' claim requires evidence of acceleration, not just baseline correction.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If your thermometer was broken and read 10 degrees too low yesterday, and you fix it today, does that mean the room suddenly heated up faster? Or did you just realize it was already warm?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. The new data reveals the ocean was hotter than we thought, but the measurement error itself didn't make the water heat up faster. We need separate evidence to prove the rate of warming has accelerated.

scenario.text: Elara states: 'If true, that means that the global warming we are currently undergoing is unparalleled within the last 100 million years, and far worse than we had previously calculated.' Councilor Vane scoffs: 'So Elara claims the world has never been warm in a hundred million years and that our previous scientists were all fools who calculated nothing correctly! She wants us to believe the sky is falling tomorrow based on wild exaggerations. We cannot base policy on such hysterical nonsense.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara stated that current warming is unparalleled in the last 100 million years and worse than previous calculations suggested. Vane distorted this to claim she said the world has NEVER been warm in that timeframe and that all previous science was worthless, attacking this exaggerated 'hysterical' version instead of her actual data.

structure.pattern_description: Vane takes Elara's specific claim about the uniqueness of current warming rates ('unparalleled within the last 100 million years') and distorts it into an absolute claim that the world has never been warm ('never been warm in a hundred million years'). He also adds an emotional layer ('hysterical nonsense') that Elara did not use, then attacks this fabricated extreme position.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (Current warming is unparalleled in 100M years and worse than calculated). Person B restates P as distorted P* (The world has never been warm and all past science is wrong). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes P is false, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: Vane's criticism targets a fabrication. Elara never claimed the earth was cold for 100 million years, only that the current rate is unique in that window. She also never called previous scientists 'fools,' only noted calculations were lower than current reality. By attacking the exaggeration, he avoids addressing the actual data.
structure.counterpoint: Elara could reply: 'I did not say the world has never been warm, nor did I call past scientists fools. I said the current rate of warming is unique in the last 100 million years. Please address the data I actually presented, not the exaggeration you invented.'

scenario.text: Magister Vane scoffs at Elara's charts. 'Do not listen to this alarmist drivel. Elara is nothing but a panic-monger and a doomsayer who wants to shut down our mines based on fantasies. She claims thawing permafrost can release not just CO2, but also methane, a much stronger heat-trapping gas. But why should we trust the ravings of a hysterical zealot? Her labels speak for themselves: she is a fear-peddler, not a scientist.'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane does not dispute the chemical properties of methane or the data regarding CO2 release. Instead, he attaches negative labels to Elara ('alarmist,' 'panic-monger,' 'doomsayer,' 'hysterical zealot,' 'fear-peddler') to discredit her factual statement about methane without engaging with the science.

structure.pattern_description: Vane substitutes negative emotional labels for substantive engagement with the scientific claim. Rather than challenging the data on methane release or its heat-trapping potential, he attacks Elara's character using loaded terms. These labels are designed to make the audience dismiss the factual claim based on an emotional reaction to the speaker rather than the evidence provided.
structure.formal_form: Person P presents factual claim X with evidence E. Critic attaches negative label L to P. Critic concludes X is false or untrustworthy based on L, without engaging with E.

The truth of the scientific claim exists independently of the speaker's perceived temperament. Using labels functions as a distraction to avoid addressing the actual evidence.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to question a speaker's credibility if they have a history of fabrication or lack relevant expertise. However, the fallacy occurs when the label is used as a substitute for addressing the specific evidence presented, especially when the evidence (like chemical properties of gases) is objective and verifiable regardless of the speaker.

assessment.identification_prompt: Magister Vane calls Elara many harsh names. But look closely at his response to her statement about methane: does he provide any evidence that she is wrong about the gas, or does he only attack her character?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane, believing that because Elara is called a 'panic-monger,' her statement about methane must be false.
Player notices Vane is being mean but thinks his insults might be a valid reason to doubt Elara's science.
Player identifies that Vane is using name-calling but is unsure if it completely invalidates his skepticism.
Player correctly identifies that Vane is using name-calling to distract from the argument and notes that he did not address the methane data.
Player explicitly states that the labels ('panic-monger', etc.) are irrelevant to the factual claim about methane and that Vane failed to provide a scientific counter-argument.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If a known prankster told you that fire is hot, would that make fire cold? Does the person's label change the physical reality of the gas?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Vane tried to win by making you feel negatively about Elara rather than proving her wrong. The science of methane remains true regardless of what he calls her.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Magister Vane is arrogant, dismissive, and relies on rhetorical flair and intimidation rather than data. He often raises his voice and uses grand gestures to overshadow opponents.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Silence this doomsayer! Her words are poison, and she is nothing but a [insert negative label] trying to destroy our livelihood!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that isolate the factual claim about methane from the insults, forcing Vane to either address the science or reveal his lack of counter-evidence.

scenario.context: In the High Council of Aethelgard, the player presents data showing that permafrost melt is releasing massive amounts of carbon, accelerating global warming. Councilor Vane, a known skeptic of aggressive climate policy, interrupts the presentation to sway the room.
scenario.text: Councilor Vane leans forward, voice trembling with manufactured urgency: 'Since CO2 is the primary heat-trapping greenhouse gas — and since the permafrost contains twice as much carbon as the atmosphere does today — this means a vicious cycle has begun that will speed up global warming. Look at the terrified faces of our children in the coastal villages! Can you truly sit there with cold data while their future burns? To deny this cycle is to condemn them to death!'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane accepts the scientific premise but uses the terrifying imagery of dying children to bypass a discussion on specific policy solutions or cost-benefit analysis, attempting to force immediate, uncalculated agreement through fear and guilt.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker validates a factual claim but immediately pivots to evoking intense fear and guilt (dying children) to shut down critical evaluation of proposed solutions. The emotional weight is used as a substitute for logical policy derivation.
structure.formal_form: Claim P is factually true. Agent evokes extreme emotion F (fear/guilt) regarding consequence C. Agent implies that questioning the response to P is morally equivalent to causing C.
structure.why_wrong: While the threat to children is real and emotionally compelling, the existence of the threat does not automatically validate every proposed solution. Using fear to prevent scrutiny of policy details leads to poor decision-making. The emotion is relevant to motivation, but not a proof of a specific course of action.
structure.counterpoint: Emotional urgency is appropriate for prioritizing issues, but it cannot replace the logical steps required to design effective interventions. One can care deeply about the children and still demand a rigorous plan.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane describes a scary future for children. Does this emotional appeal prove that his specific policy proposal is the best solution, or is it trying to make you feel too guilty to ask questions?

rubric.description: Feels overwhelmed by the image of suffering children and agrees with Vane immediately without thinking.
Feels the emotional pull but senses something is off; cannot articulate why the emotion doesn't prove the policy.
Recognizes that Vane is using fear to stop questions, but struggles to separate the valid science from the manipulative rhetoric.
Identifies that while the premise is true, the appeal to the children's safety is a tactic to bypass logical evaluation of the solution.
Clearly names the appeal to emotion (fear/guilt), explains that emotional urgency does not validate specific policies, and insists on evaluating the plan on its own merits.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine a different policy that also saves the children but costs less. Would Vane's speech help you choose between them, or does it just make you afraid to choose anything?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. The danger is real, but we must not let fear dictate the details of our solution. We need a plan that works, not just one that sounds urgent.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dramatic, populist, and manipulative; uses moral high ground to avoid technical scrutiny.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: How can you hesitate? The ice is melting and the waters rise! Do you want blood on your hands?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player acknowledges the emotional stakes but redirects the council to evaluate the specific efficacy and feasibility of the proposed mitigation strategies.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling newsroom of the Daily Chronicle. Senior Editor Vance is reviewing a draft article about record-breaking global temperatures submitted by a junior reporter. The reporter has included data from multiple climate agencies confirming the trend.
scenario.text: Vance tosses the draft onto the desk without reading the data tables. 'But it has little to do with what recent headlines have been saying about the hottest year ever. It is called business as usual.'
scenario.speaker_context: Vance dismisses the scientific findings not by addressing the temperature data or methodology, but by labeling the phenomenon 'business as usual.' This label implies the situation is mundane, unimportant, or a standard cycle, thereby discouraging further investigation or concern without engaging with the evidence of record heat.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker substitutes a dismissive label ('business as usual') for substantive engagement with the claim (record-breaking heat). By categorizing the event as mundane, the speaker attempts to neutralize the urgency of the data without refuting the data itself.
structure.formal_form: Claim X presents evidence E suggesting a significant or unusual event. Critic assigns label L to X (where L implies mundanity or normalcy). Critic concludes X is not significant based on L, without engaging with E.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not arguments. Calling a record-breaking event 'business as usual' does not address whether the temperature records are accurate, if the trend is statistically significant, or what the causes might be. The label functions as a rhetorical shield to ignore inconvenient evidence by framing it as unimportant.
structure.counterpoint: Describing an event as 'normal' is valid if supported by historical data showing the event falls within standard deviations. The fallacy occurs when the label is applied solely to dismiss new evidence without providing that historical context or statistical analysis.

assessment.identification_prompt: Vance calls the record heat 'business as usual.' Does this phrase explain why the data might be wrong, or does it just try to make the data seem boring?

rubric.description: Player accepts Vance's dismissal and agrees the heat is just normal business.
Player feels something is off but cannot identify that the label is replacing an argument.
Player identifies that 'business as usual' is a label but thinks it might be a valid summary of the situation.
Player recognizes that Vance is using a label to dismiss the data without addressing the specific claims about record temperatures.
Player explicitly states that 'business as usual' is a name-calling tactic used to avoid engaging with the evidence of record-breaking heat.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if someone sets a world record in running, would calling it 'just running' prove they didn't actually run fast? What evidence did Vance offer against the temperature data?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! 'Business as usual' is a label designed to shut down the conversation. Vance didn't look at the charts or the numbers; he just slapped a boring label on a serious finding to make it go away.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Cynical, weary, and resistant to change. Vance believes he has seen it all and views new alarming data as hype rather than fact.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't get worked up over headlines, kid. It's all noise. This? This is just business as usual.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a historical comparison chart showing that current temperatures are statistically outside the 'usual' range, forcing Vance to drop the label and address the actual data.

scenario.context: Inside the Data Spire, a holographic projection of a NOAA analyst addresses the player regarding recent climate data adjustments.
scenario.text: NOAA's alteration of its measurement standard and other changes produced a result that could have been predicted: a marginally significant warming trend in the data over the past several years, erasing the temperature plateau that vexed climate alarmists have found difficult to explain.
scenario.speaker_context: The analyst presents the 'predicted' nature of the result and the relief of 'alarmists' as validation, implying the conclusion is correct because it aligns with the expectations of a specific, vocal group rather than standing solely on the raw data.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim is true or valid because it aligns with the beliefs, predictions, or desires of a specific group (in this case, 'climate alarmists'), rather than providing independent empirical evidence.
structure.formal_form: Group X believes/predicts Y. The new data shows Y. Therefore, the data interpretation is correct because it matches Group X.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of scientific data depends on methodology and evidence, not on whether the results satisfy or match the predictions of a particular faction. A match between prediction and result can be coincidental or due to bias in the adjustment process, not proof of truth.
structure.counterpoint: If a prediction is based on a robust, previously verified model, matching it is good science. However, the text frames the validity based on the social reaction ('vexed alarmists') and the mere fact of prediction, not the model's prior track record.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the speaker prove the warming trend is real using raw data, or do they suggest it's true because it matches what 'climate alarmists' expected?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; believes the match with predictions proves the data is correct.
Senses something is off about mentioning 'alarmists' but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Identifies that the speaker relies on the reaction of a group rather than just the numbers.
Explains that matching a group's prediction does not automatically validate the methodology used to get there.

Identifies the Bandwagon/Appeal to Motive fallacy, noting that the speaker uses the satisfaction of a specific faction as a proxy for scientific truth, bypassing rigorous verification of the 'alterations'.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If a group of people strongly believed the earth was flat, and a new map was drawn that looked flat, would that make the map accurate?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: How could the analyst have presented this same data without referencing the 'alarmists' or the 'predicted' nature of the result?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Bureaucratic, slightly defensive analyst who uses consensus and political alignment as shields against scrutiny.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: See? The numbers line up with what everyone has been saying. It fits the narrative perfectly, so it must be the right adjustment.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must request the raw, unadjusted dataset and the specific algorithmic changes to verify the trend independently of the group's expectations.

scenario.context: The player enters the Town Hall where Councilor Vane is addressing a concerned crowd about the recent record-breaking heatwave. The townsfolk are worried about climate change, but Vane attempts to dismiss their fears with a slick rhetorical trick.
scenario.text: Councilor Vane waves off the charts. 'But it has little to do with what recent headlines have been saying about the hottest year ever. It is called business as usual.'
scenario.speaker_context: Councilor Vane is a charismatic but manipulative politician known for twisting language to avoid accountability. He intentionally shifts the meaning of the phrase 'business as usual' to confuse the issue: first implying the heatwave is a normal, expected event (status quo), and second implying that the cause is simply standard economic activity which shouldn't be altered, ignoring the causal link between the two.

structure.pattern_description: The argument relies on the ambiguous phrase 'business as usual.' In the context of dismissing the 'hottest year ever,' it implies the weather event is a normal, non-alarming occurrence (Meaning 1: Normalcy). However, the phrase literally refers to continuing standard commercial/industrial activities (Meaning 2: Economic Status Quo). The speaker treats the existence of the heatwave as proof that we should continue 'business as usual' (economic activity), conflating the description of the event with the prescription for action.
structure.formal_form: Term/Phrase P is used with Meaning M1 (The event is normal) to dismiss concern. Term/Phrase P is used with Meaning M2 (Continue standard economic practices) to justify inaction. The argument assumes M1 entails M2, which is a logical non-sequitur.
structure.why_wrong: The phrase 'business as usual' is used equivocally. Just because a heatwave is happening (or is claimed to be 'usual' in frequency) does not logically mean that our current economic practices ('business as usual') are the correct response or unrelated to the cause. The shift from describing a state of affairs to prescribing an economic policy via the same ambiguous phrase creates a false sense of logical connection.
structure.counterpoint: A clearer version would separate the claims: 'This heatwave is statistically normal' and 'Therefore we should not change our economic policies.' When separated, the lack of logical connection between the premise and conclusion becomes obvious.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane claims the heatwave is just 'business as usual' to dismiss concerns. How is he using this phrase to mislead the crowd?

rubric.description: Player accepts Vane's statement as a valid explanation for the heatwave.
Player feels Vane is being evasive but cannot identify the specific linguistic trick.
Player notices the phrase 'business as usual' is vague but cannot articulate the two distinct meanings.
Player identifies that 'business as usual' is used to mean both 'a normal weather event' and 'continuing current economic practices,' but doesn't fully explain the logical gap.

Player clearly explains that Vane equivocates on 'business as usual,' falsely implying that because the weather is (allegedly) normal, our economic habits should remain unchanged, ignoring the potential causal link.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Listen closely to the phrase 'business as usual.' Is Vane talking about the weather being normal, or is he talking about keeping factories running? Can both be true at the same time in this context?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Vane slides from describing the event to prescribing policy using the same ambiguous words. That's a classic Equivocation fallacy.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Smarmy, deflective, uses corporate buzzwords to obscure truth. He smiles too much when lying.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Why worry about a few degrees? It's just business as usual, my friend. Nothing to see here.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player exposes the equivocation, the crowd becomes skeptical, reducing Vane's political influence. If failed, Vane passes a deregulation bill claiming it won't affect the 'normal' weather.

scenario.context: The player enters the Climate Data Archive, a high-tech library where scholars debate historical temperature records. Dr. Aris, a junior researcher, has just presented a paper showing that recent adjustments to measurement standards by the NOAA have revealed a warming trend, effectively erasing the so-called 'temperature plateau.' Before the player can examine the charts, Senior Archon Vane steps forward to dismiss the findings.
scenario.text: Archon Vane scoffs, waving away the charts. 'NOAA's alteration of its measurement standard and other changes produced a result that could have been predicted: a marginally significant warming trend in the data over the past several years, erasing the temperature plateau that vexed climate alarmists have found difficult to explain. We should ignore this; it's just the usual panic from those alarmists.'
scenario.speaker_context: Archon Vane, a senior conservative scholar known for his skepticism of new data models. He often relies on the reputation of opposing groups rather than engaging with their specific statistical methodologies.

structure.pattern_description: Vane dismisses the data regarding the warming trend and the erased plateau not by addressing the methodology of NOAA's measurement changes or the statistical significance, but by labeling the proponents as 'climate alarmists.' He implies their conclusion is invalid because of their perceived political or emotional stance.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P belongs to group G (characterized by trait Q). Therefore, claim X is false or should be ignored.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of the temperature data and the interpretation of the warming trend depend on the measurement standards and statistical analysis, not on the label attached to the people presenting it. Calling them 'alarmists' attacks their character or motive without providing evidence that the data itself is flawed.
structure.counterpoint: If the argument relied solely on the authority of the 'alarmists' (e.g., 'You must believe this because these experts say so'), then questioning their bias would be relevant to their credibility. However, since the claim is about physical data trends, the data must be evaluated on its own merits regardless of who presents it.

assessment.identification_prompt: Archon Vane seems very confident in dismissing the report. Listen closely: does he point out a specific error in NOAA's math or measurement tools, or does he focus on the people behind the report?

rubric.description: Player accepts Vane's conclusion that the report should be ignored because it comes from 'alarmists'.
Player feels Vane is being unfair or mean but cannot explain why his logic is flawed.
Player identifies that Vane is attacking the group ('alarmists') rather than the data.
Player explains that the label 'alarmist' does not prove the temperature data or the methodology is incorrect.
Player articulates that the truth of the warming trend is independent of the presenter's identity and demands an evaluation of the measurement standards instead.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if a person you dislike tells you '2 + 2 = 4', is the math wrong because you dislike them? How does that apply to these temperature charts?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. The label 'alarmist' tells us nothing about the accuracy of the NOAA measurement standards. To refute the claim, one must show where the data or the calculation went wrong.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dismissive, authoritative, relies on tradition and group stereotypes over empirical evidence.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't let the label fool you; look at the numbers.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player successfully points out the ad hominem fallacy, forcing Archon Vane to either admit he hasn't reviewed the data or attempt a actual technical critique of the NOAA standards.

scenario.context: The player stands in the Archives of Truth, reviewing historical climate records with Scholar Elara. They are debating whether the current era represents a significant warming trend compared to the previous century. A skeptical merchant, Borin, interrupts their analysis.
scenario.text: Borin scoffs at the charts. 'Whether temperatures have warmed much since then depends on what you look at,' he claims, waving a hand at the complex data. 'It's just selective picking by alarmists.'
scenario.speaker_context: Borin does not address the specific datasets, timeframes, or methodology Elara presented. Instead, he dismisses the entire inquiry by attaching a loaded label ('alarmists') and implying dishonesty ('selective picking') to avoid engaging with the actual evidence of temperature changes.

structure.pattern_description: Borin avoids engaging with the specific data regarding temperature trends. Instead, he attaches a negative, emotionally charged label ('alarmists') to those who present the data and implies malicious intent ('selective picking'). This encourages the listener to dismiss the findings based on the perceived character of the presenter rather than the merit of the evidence.
structure.formal_form: Person P presents evidence E regarding claim C. Critic attaches negative label L to P or the proponents of C. Critic implies C is false or suspect based on L, without refuting E.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not arguments. Calling someone an 'alarmist' does not prove their temperature data is incorrect, their timeframe is inappropriate, or their conclusion is flawed. The label functions as a substitute for substantive criticism, exploiting the audience's bias against the labeled group to bypass critical evaluation of the facts.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to note if a source has a known bias or conflict of interest. However, the fallacy occurs when the label is used as the sole reason to reject the argument without examining whether the specific evidence provided in that instance is accurate or relevant.

assessment.identification_prompt: Borin dismisses the temperature data quickly. Does he point out a specific error in the charts, or does he just attack the people presenting them?

rubric.description: Player accepts Borin's dismissal and agrees the data is unreliable because it comes from 'alarmists'.
Player senses Borin is being mean but cannot articulate why his argument about the temperature data is logically flawed.
Player identifies that Borin is using a negative label ('alarmists') but thinks this might still be a valid reason to doubt the data.
Player recognizes that Borin is using name-calling to avoid addressing the specific evidence about temperature trends.
Player clearly identifies the 'Name calling / labeling' fallacy, explaining that the label 'alarmist' does not refute the actual temperature data presented.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think again: Does calling someone a name actually prove their numbers are wrong? What specific error did Borin find in the chart?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Borin tried to shut down the debate by labeling the researchers instead of analyzing the temperature records. A label is not a refutation.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Cynical, dismissive, anti-intellectual merchant who trusts gut feeling over data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't let those fancy charts fool you. It's all just panic-mongering by the usual suspects.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must select dialogue option to 'Demand specific data errors' rather than 'Defend the researchers' character' to successfully resolve the encounter and gain the 'Critical Eye' buff.

scenario.context: In the Grand Atrium of the Academy of Reason, a heated debate erupts between the traditionalist scholars and the experimental alchemists. The air smells of ozone and old parchment as the High Arbiter tries to maintain order.
scenario.text: A robed scholar steps forward, pointing an accusing finger at the alchemists. 'You claim your methods are rigorous, but I say this: If it is science, it isn't consensus. Therefore, since you seek agreement among peers, you are not doing science at all.'
scenario.speaker_context: Scholar Valerius, a rigid traditionalist who believes true discovery must always stand alone against the crowd.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker presents two categories ('science' and 'consensus') as mutually exclusive, implying that something cannot be both. This ignores the reality that scientific fields often rely on consensus to validate findings while still being rigorous science.
structure.formal_form: P v Q, where P = 'It is science' and Q = 'It is consensus'. The argument assumes ~(P & Q). In reality, P and Q can coexist; the disjunction is not exhaustive nor mutually exclusive in the way framed.
structure.why_wrong: Valerius forces a choice between being 'scientific' and having 'consensus,' treating them as opposites. However, scientific consensus is a hallmark of established science, not a disqualifier. One can have both rigorous methodology and peer agreement.
structure.counterpoint: Not all distinctions are false. Sometimes categories are mutually exclusive (e.g., 'alive' vs 'dead'). The error here is assuming that the nature of science inherently precludes agreement, which is an empirical claim that is demonstrably false.

assessment.identification_prompt: Scholar Valerius claims that if something is science, it cannot be consensus. What is the logical flaw in framing these two concepts as opposites?

rubric.description: Accepts Valerius's claim or argues based solely on personal opinion about science.
Senses the statement is too extreme but cannot explain why the logic fails.
Identifies that science can have consensus but does not explicitly name the logical structure error.
Names the false dichotomy and explains that 'science' and 'consensus' are not mutually exclusive categories.
Fully deconstructs the false dichotomy, explains that the disjunction is not exhaustive or mutually exclusive, and provides examples where scientific rigor leads to consensus.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Valerius says you must choose: either it's science OR it's consensus. Can you think of a situation where scientists agree on a fact precisely because their methods were scientific?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent. If the dichotomy is false, how would you rephrase Valerius's statement to accurately reflect the relationship between scientific rigor and peer agreement?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dogmatic, intellectual, prone to absolutist statements, wears dark blue robes with silver trim.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Do not confuse popularity with truth, yet do not mistake isolation for genius. The middle path is where logic dies.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a case study of a scientific breakthrough that achieved consensus (e.g., germ theory or gravity) to break Valerius's rigid framing and unlock the 'Nuanced Scholar' achievement.

scenario.context: The player enters the Hall of Records in the capital city, where a heated town hall meeting is taking place regarding recent extreme weather events and glacial melt. A renowned climatologist, Dr. Aris Thorne, has just presented decades of data showing rising global temperatures. A skeptical councilor, Councilor Vane, stands to rebut the findings before the vote on climate adaptation funding.
scenario.text: Councilor Vane scoffs at the charts displayed on the wall. 'Humans have had no detectable impact on hurricanes over the past century,' he declares to the crowd. 'And Greenland's ice sheet isn't shrinking any more rapidly today than it was eighty years ago. These are just the paranoid ravings of alarmist zealots who want to destroy our economy with their hysterical fantasies. We should ignore this junk science and listen to realists like myself.'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane makes two specific factual claims about hurricanes and ice sheets but provides no data to support them. Instead, he immediately pivots to attacking the character and motives of the scientists ('alarmist zealots,' 'hysterical,' 'junk science') to discredit their entire argument without engaging with the actual evidence presented by Dr. Thorne.

structure.pattern_description: Councilor Vane avoids addressing the specific data points regarding hurricane intensity or ice sheet mass balance. Instead, he attaches highly negative, emotional labels ('alarmist zealots,' 'hysterical,' 'junk science') to the scientists and their work. This tactic is designed to trigger an emotional rejection of the argument based on the perceived character of the proponents rather than the merit of the evidence.
structure.formal_form: Person P presents argument X with evidence E. Critic attaches negative label L to P or X. Critic concludes X should be rejected based on L, without engaging with E.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not evidence. Calling scientists 'zealots' or their work 'junk' does not prove that humans haven't impacted hurricanes or that ice sheets are stable. The labels serve as a rhetorical shortcut to bypass critical evaluation of the data, exploiting the audience's bias against 'alarmism' rather than proving the data is incorrect.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to question the bias or funding sources of researchers if those factors directly influence the methodology. However, simply applying pejorative labels like 'zealot' without demonstrating specific methodological flaws or conflicts of interest constitutes a fallacy.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane makes some bold claims about hurricanes and ice. But look closely at how he describes the scientists presenting the data. Does he address their numbers, or does he attack their identity?

rubric.description: Player accepts Vane's conclusion that the science is 'junk' because he called the scientists 'zealots'.
Player notices the insults but believes they invalidate the scientists' credentials automatically.
Player identifies that Vane is being mean but fails to connect the insults to the lack of counter-evidence.
Player recognizes that Vane uses labels ('alarmist,' 'junk science') to distract from the lack of data supporting his own claims.
Player explicitly identifies the 'Name calling / labeling' fallacy, noting that Vane substitutes emotional labels for substantive engagement with the hurricane and ice sheet data.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if someone calls you a 'liar,' does that automatically make everything you said false? Or do you still need to check the facts? Vane hasn't shown any data about Greenland; he just used strong words.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Vane tries to win the argument by making the scientists sound unreasonable ('alarmist zealots') rather than proving their data wrong. By labeling the science as 'junk,' he hopes you won't bother looking at the actual charts.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Councilor Vane is a charismatic populist who relies on gut feelings and common sense rhetoric. He is dismissive of experts and prefers simple, emotionally resonant narratives over complex data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't let those fancy degrees fool you. They're just scaremongering to get more tax gold. Realists know the truth without needing a computer model.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to 'Request Data' (forcing Vane to admit he has none), 'Expose Fallacy' (pointing out the name-calling to the crowd), or 'Support Scientist' (asking Dr. Thorne to re-present the specific ice sheet metrics).

scenario.context: The player stands in the Grand Archives of Aethelgard, reviewing a newly updated scroll displaying global fire statistics over the last century. The data clearly shows a significant downward trend. Archivist Thorne, a known skeptic of environmental progress who often clashes with the Royal Science Guild, leans over to comment on the findings.
scenario.text: Archivist Thorne scoffs at the scroll, refusing to look at the numbers. 'Don't be fooled by these manipulated figures. This is just typical alarmist propaganda from those so-called 'experts' in the Guild. They are nothing but a bunch of hysterical doomsayers and fear-mongers trying to keep their funding alive. Why should we trust the ramblings of such paranoid zealots? The extent of global fires has been trending significantly downward, but they'll never admit it because they love the chaos.'
scenario.speaker_context: Thorne acknowledges the downward trend only to immediately dismiss the source of the data. Instead of analyzing the methodology or the raw numbers presented on the scroll, he attacks the scientists by attaching negative labels ('alarmist,' 'hysterical doomsayers,' 'fear-mongers,' 'paranoid zealots') to discredit their findings without engaging with the evidence itself.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne substitutes substantive critique of the data with pejorative labels attached to the scientists. By characterizing the researchers as 'hysterical' and 'paranoid,' he attempts to trigger an emotional rejection of their conclusion (that fires are trending down or that their data is reliable) without actually examining the statistical evidence provided.
structure.formal_form: Person P presents evidence E showing trend T. Critic attaches negative label L to P. Critic rejects E or T based on L, without addressing the validity of E.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not evidence. Calling scientists 'fear-mongers' does not prove their data is incorrect, their sample size is too small, or their methodology is flawed. The argument fails because it attacks the character of the messenger rather than the message, relying on the audience's bias against the label rather than logical evaluation of the trend.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to question the motives of researchers if there is concrete evidence of bias or fraud. However, the fallacy occurs when the label itself is used as the sole proof that the data is wrong, replacing actual analysis of the numbers.

assessment.identification_prompt: Archivist Thorne admits the fires are trending downward, yet he still dismisses the report. Look closely at the words he uses to describe the scientists—does he offer any specific reason why their numbers might be wrong?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne, believing the scientists are likely lying because they are 'fear-mongers'.
Player senses Thorne is being mean but cannot articulate why his argument about the data is logically flawed.
Player identifies that Thorne is insulting the scientists but thinks this might still invalidate their data.
Player recognizes that Thorne is using name-calling ('hysterical,' 'zealots') to avoid looking at the actual statistics.
Player correctly identifies the 'Name Calling' fallacy, explaining that negative labels do not constitute evidence against the downward trend shown in the data.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne calls them 'zealots,' but does shouting that word make the numbers on the scroll disappear? Try looking at the graph again—does the line go up or down?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thorne tries to poison the well by labeling the scientists. Whether they are 'hysterical' or 'calm' has no bearing on whether the fire statistics are accurate. The data must stand on its own merits.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Cynical, contrarian, and distrustful of academic institutions. Thorne prides himself on 'common sense' over 'book learning' and often uses aggressive rhetoric to undermine experts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! More pretty charts from the ivory tower! They want you scared, not smart!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that point specifically to the data on the scroll, ignoring the insults, forcing Thorne to either admit the data is correct or retreat without a logical counter-argument.

scenario.context: The player stands in the Grand Hall of the Agricultural Guild during the Annual Harvest Review. Senior Agronomist Elara has just presented a comprehensive report showing that global crop yields have increased by 15% over the last decade due to new irrigation techniques. A skeptical merchant, Lord Vane, who stands to lose money on his hoarded grain reserves if prices drop, steps forward to address the assembly.
scenario.text: Lord Vane scoffs at Elara's charts. 'Global crop yields are rising, not falling,' he mocks, waving a hand at the data. 'But this is just the delusional rambling of a naive idealist who has never smelled real soil. Elara is nothing but a starry-eyed theorist pushing a fantasy narrative to crash our markets. We should ignore this foolishness from such an out-of-touch dreamer.'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane does not dispute the specific data points, the methodology of the study, or the reported yield numbers. Instead, he accepts the premise only to immediately attach negative labels to Elara ('naive idealist,' 'starry-eyed theorist,' 'out-of-touch dreamer') and her report ('delusional rambling,' 'fantasy narrative,' 'foolishness') to discredit the conclusion without engaging with the evidence.

structure.pattern_description: Vane substitutes substantive critique with pejorative labels. Rather than analyzing the agricultural data or proposing alternative interpretations of the yield statistics, he attacks Elara's character and intellect using loaded terms. This tactic aims to make the audience dismiss the factual claim (yields are rising) based on their negative emotional reaction to the labels applied to the speaker.
structure.formal_form: Person P presents factual claim X with evidence E. Critic attaches negative label L to P or X. Critic concludes X is false or should be ignored based on L, without engaging with E.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not evidence. Calling a scientist a 'dreamer' or their data 'foolishness' does not prove the data is incorrect. The truth of the claim regarding crop yields depends on the agricultural measurements, not the personality or perceived naivety of the person presenting them. This fallacy bypasses logical evaluation in favor of emotional manipulation.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to question a speaker's credibility if they lack relevant expertise or have a proven history of fabrication. However, the fallacy occurs when the label is used as a substitute for addressing the actual evidence presented, especially when the evidence (crop data) is objective and verifiable regardless of the speaker's traits.

assessment.identification_prompt: Lord Vane claims Elara's report is 'foolishness' because she is a 'dreamer.' Does he provide any specific reasons why the crop yield data itself is incorrect?

rubric.description: Player accepts Vane's argument, believing that Elara's personality makes her data unreliable.
Player senses something is unfair about Vane's tone but cannot identify the specific logical error.
Player identifies that Vane is being mean or insulting but does not explicitly connect it to the lack of evidence.
Player recognizes that Vane is using labels ('dreamer', 'idealist') instead of addressing the data, but misses the full structural implication.
Player correctly identifies that Vane is committing the 'Name calling / labeling' fallacy by substituting negative character attacks for substantive engagement with the crop yield evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think again: Does calling someone a 'dreamer' actually prove their numbers are wrong? What specific part of the crop report did Vane disprove?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Vane tried to distract the guild from the hard data by attacking Elara's character. The rising yields are a fact supported by evidence, regardless of whether he thinks she is a 'theorist'.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Lord Vane is a wealthy, defensive grain merchant who prioritizes profit margins over agricultural progress. He is articulate but manipulative, often using charm to mask logical gaps.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! Don't listen to her fancy graphs. She's just a naive idealist trying to crash the market with her starry-eyed theories!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that demand Vane address the specific irrigation statistics rather than Elara's character, forcing him to either concede the point or reveal his financial conflict of interest.

scenario.context: The player enters the Grand Atrium of the Academy of Natural Sciences, where a heated town hall is underway regarding the validity of recent climate models. Dr. Aris Thorne, a respected physicist, has just presented data suggesting minimal economic impact from climate change through the end of the century. A prominent activist, Jara Vane, takes the podium to respond.
scenario.text: Jara Vane scoffs at the charts on the screen. 'Humans have had no detectable impact on hurricanes over the past century... Greenland's ice sheet isn't shrinking any more rapidly today than it was eighty years ago... The net economic impact of human-induced climate change will be minimal through at least the end of this century.' She pauses, looking directly at Dr. Thorne. 'But let us be clear: Mr. Koonin is no "climate denier," to use the concocted phrase used to shut down debate. He is simply a skeptic who refuses to wear the label they invented to silence him.'
scenario.speaker_context: Jara does not address the specific data points regarding hurricanes, ice sheets, or economic projections presented by Dr. Thorne (quoting Koonin). Instead, she focuses entirely on the label 'climate denier,' framing it as a 'concocted phrase' designed to 'shut down debate,' thereby attempting to invalidate the opposition's stance by attacking the terminology used against them rather than the evidence itself.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker avoids engaging with the substantive claims about climate data and economics. Instead, they focus on the label 'climate denier,' characterizing it as a malicious invention ('concocted phrase') used to 'shut down debate.' This shifts the focus from the validity of the scientific claims to the perceived unfairness of the label, attempting to immunize the argument from criticism by framing the critic as a censor.
structure.formal_form: Person P presents argument X with evidence E. Critic C applies label L to P. Defender D argues that L is a fabricated term intended to silence P, concluding that X should be accepted (or at least not rejected) because the label L is illegitimate, without addressing E.
structure.why_wrong: Whether a label is 'concocted' or 'unfair' does not determine the truth value of the underlying argument or evidence. Dismissing the label 'climate denier' does not prove that humans have not impacted hurricanes or that ice sheets are stable. The focus on the label serves as a distraction from the lack of engagement with the actual data presented.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to point out when labels are used ad hominem to dismiss arguments without engagement. However, the fallacy occurs when pointing out the label is used as a substitute for providing counter-evidence to the original claims.

assessment.identification_prompt: Jara spends a lot of time talking about the phrase 'climate denier.' Does she actually provide any data to refute the claims about hurricanes or ice sheets?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Jara, believing that rejecting the label 'climate denier' proves the climate data is correct.
Player feels Jara is being defensive but cannot articulate why her argument is logically insufficient.
Player identifies that Jara is attacking the label rather than the data, but thinks this might still be a valid counter-argument.
Player clearly identifies that Jara ignores the specific evidence (hurricanes, ice sheets) and substitutes it with a discussion about the fairness of the label.
Player explains that the legitimacy of a label has no bearing on the factual accuracy of the claims regarding hurricane impact or ice sheet shrinkage, identifying this as a distraction tactic.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If someone calls you a 'bad driver,' does arguing that 'bad driver' is a mean label prove that you didn't run the red light? What evidence did Jara offer about the red light (the climate data)?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. By focusing on the 'concocted phrase,' Jara hopes you'll forget she never actually addressed the hurricane or ice sheet statistics. The label might be annoying, but it doesn't change the data.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jara Vane is passionate, quick-witted, and highly defensive of her cause. She often uses rhetorical flair to pivot away from weak points in her argumentation.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: They try to silence us with words, but we see through their tricks! Don't let them define you!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to press Jara on the specific data points she ignored, earning 'Logic Points' and causing her to stumble, or accept her rhetoric, which boosts her 'Influence' meter but lowers the town's 'Scientific Literacy' stat.

scenario.context: The player is reviewing a transcript from the Grand Archive's Logic Wing. The text comes from a heated debate among scholars regarding the reliability of new predictive algorithms used for harvest forecasting.
scenario.text: A senior scholar slams his hand on the table. 'It's a big problem,' he says, 'when models can't retroactively "predict" events that have already happened. These so-called 'smart' systems are nothing but digital charlatans and fraudulent toys.'
scenario.speaker_context: The scholar is frustrated that the model failed a retrospective test. Instead of analyzing the specific algorithmic error or the data gap that caused the failure, he immediately assigns derogatory labels ('digital charlatans', 'fraudulent toys') to the models to dismiss their entire utility.

structure.pattern_description: The scholar substitutes negative, emotionally charged labels for substantive analysis. Rather than explaining why the model failed the retrospective test or proposing a fix, he attaches dismissive terms to the technology to encourage the audience to reject it based on negative connotations rather than evidence.
structure.formal_form: Entity E exhibits flaw F. Critic attaches negative label L to E. Critic concludes E is worthless based on L, without engaging with the specifics of F or potential solutions.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not arguments. Calling a model a 'charlatan' does not explain the mathematical reason for its failure, nor does it address whether the model can be improved. The labels function as a substitute for technical criticism, exploiting the audience's tendency to distrust anything associated with fraud.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to describe a system as 'flawed' or 'inaccurate' if evidence supports those specific claims. The fallacy occurs when using loaded, personifying insults (like 'charlatan') to bypass the need for specific evidence regarding the flaw.

assessment.identification_prompt: The scholar is clearly angry about the model's failure. But look closely at his conclusion: does he explain the technical error, or does he just use insulting names?

rubric.description: Player agrees with the scholar, believing the labels prove the models are useless.
Player notices the scholar is angry but misses the logical disconnect between the failure and the name-calling.
Player identifies that the scholar used negative words but isn't sure why that makes the argument weak.
Player correctly identifies that the scholar used labels ('charlatans') instead of explaining the actual technical failure.
Player fully articulates that the labels are a rhetorical substitute for evidence and that the argument fails because it attacks the model's character rather than its code.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if I call a car a 'lemon' but don't show you the broken engine, have I proven it won't run? Or have I just insulted it?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! By calling the models 'charlatans,' he tries to make you feel they are dishonest without proving how the calculation went wrong. That's name-calling, not analysis.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Grumpy Traditionalist; skeptical of new technology, prefers old methods, prone to emotional outbursts when data contradicts intuition.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! Don't show me your graphs. Those digital charlatans lie better than a goblin in a gold shop!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a specific log entry showing exactly where the model's variable input failed, forcing the NPC to address the data rather than the insult.

scenario.context: The player stands in the Grand Archives of Aethelgard, reviewing a newly published climate report with Senior Archivist Elara. The report contains decades of tidal data. A visiting noble, Lord Vane, who has financial interests in coastal development, interrupts the discussion to dismiss the findings.
scenario.text: Lord Vane scoffs at the charts, waving a gloved hand. 'Do not bore me with these doomsday prophecies from alarmist zealots. The rate of sea-level rise has not accelerated; such claims are merely the hysterical ramblings of eco-fanatics trying to seize control of our ports. We should ignore this panic-mongering and proceed with construction.'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane does not address the specific tidal data, the methodology of the study, or the statistical trends presented by Elara. Instead, he attaches negative labels ('alarmist zealots,' 'eco-fanatics,' 'panic-mongering') to the source of the information to encourage immediate dismissal of the evidence without evaluation.

structure.pattern_description: Vane substitutes negative labels for substantive engagement. Rather than challenging the data on sea-level rise, the measurement techniques, or the interpretation of the acceleration rate, he attaches dismissive and emotionally charged terms to the researchers. These labels are designed to trigger an emotional rejection of the argument based on the perceived character of the speakers rather than the merit of their evidence.
structure.formal_form: Person P presents argument X with evidence E. Critic attaches negative label L to P or X. Critic concludes X should be rejected based on L, without engaging with E.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not arguments. Calling researchers 'zealots' or 'fanatics' does not address whether the tidal data is accurate, the sample size is sufficient, or the conclusion about acceleration is statistically valid. The labels function as a substitute for substantive criticism, exploiting the audience's tendency to dismiss anything associated with a negative connotation.
structure.counterpoint: Descriptions of a person's bias can sometimes be relevant (e.g., noting a conflict of interest). However, the fallacy occurs when the label is used as a shorthand to completely bypass the actual evidence presented, treating the label as proof that the data is false.

assessment.identification_prompt: Lord Vane seems very certain that the sea-level data is wrong. But look closely at his response: does he point out a specific error in the charts or calculations, or does he focus on describing the people who wrote the report?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane, accepting that the researchers are just 'fanatics' and the data should be ignored.
Player senses something is off but cannot articulate why, perhaps thinking Vane is just being rude.
Player identifies that Vane is insulting the researchers but fails to connect this to the lack of engagement with the data.
Player recognizes that Vane is using labels ('alarmist,' 'fanatic') to avoid addressing the actual evidence about sea-level rise.
Player clearly identifies the 'Name Calling' fallacy, explaining that Vane substitutes negative labels for a rebuttal of the specific tidal data and acceleration claims.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if someone calls you a name, does that automatically make your facts wrong? What specific numbers or graphs did Vane actually dispute?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Vane tries to win the argument by attacking the character of the scientists rather than the science itself. By labeling them 'fanatics,' he hopes you'll ignore the data without checking it.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Lord Vane is arrogant, wealthy, and dismissive of expertise that threatens his investments. He speaks with a condescending tone and uses grand gestures to belittle others.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! Don't listen to these scare-mongers. They want to shut down the ports and ruin our economy with their imaginary floods.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that press Vane to address the specific data points in the report, forcing him to either admit he has no counter-evidence or reveal a flaw in his own logic.

scenario.context: The player stands in the Climate Council chamber of the city of Aethelgard. The council is debating whether to allocate emergency funds for flood defenses based on recent weather trends. Councilor Koonin, a respected meteorologist, has just presented a graph showing stable tornado and drought statistics over the last decade.
scenario.text: As Mr. Koonin illustrates, tornado frequency and severity are also not trending up; nor are the number and severity of droughts.
scenario.speaker_context: In this specific game instance, the text is presented as a factual statement by Councilor Koonin. However, the training scenario frames a hypothetical opponent who dismisses Koonin's data solely by labeling him an 'alarmist' or 'doomsayer' without addressing the actual statistics he presented. The player must identify that attacking the label is a fallacy when the data remains unrefuted.

structure.pattern_description: An opponent rejects Koonin's statistical evidence regarding tornadoes and droughts not by analyzing the data, but by attaching a negative label to Koonin (e.g., 'alarmist', 'denier', 'puppet'). This label is used to discredit the source and, by extension, the evidence, without engaging with the actual numbers.
structure.formal_form: Person P presents evidence E regarding claim C. Opponent attaches negative label L to P. Opponent concludes C is false (or E is invalid) based solely on L.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are ad hominem attacks that substitute for logical refutation. Calling someone an 'alarmist' does not prove their data on tornado frequency is incorrect. The validity of the statistical trend must be evaluated on its own merits, independent of the speaker's perceived character or political leaning.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to question a speaker's credibility if they have a proven history of falsifying data. However, merely assigning a pejorative label without providing evidence of data manipulation constitutes the fallacy.

assessment.identification_prompt: An opponent interrupts Koonin by shouting, 'We shouldn't listen to this alarmist!' Does this response address the data about tornado frequency?

rubric.description: Player believes the label 'alarmist' proves the data is wrong.
Player suspects the label is rude but isn't sure if it invalidates the argument.
Player identifies that the label attacks the person, not the data, but cannot explain why the data still stands.
Player correctly identifies the fallacy and notes that the tornado statistics must be checked independently of the label.
Player fully articulates that the label is a distraction tactic and demands specific counter-evidence regarding the frequency trends instead of accepting the name-calling.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: If someone calls a mathematician a 'nerd,' does that make their equation wrong? How do we actually check if tornadoes are increasing?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! The label 'alarmist' is an emotional trigger, not a statistical rebuttal. To win this debate, you must ask for counter-data, not accept the insult.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Councilor Koonin is calm, data-driven, and speaks softly. His opponent, Councilor Vane, is loud, emotive, and relies on rhetoric over facts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Vane slams his hand on the table: 'Silence that alarmist! His charts are just fear-mongering from a man who wants to tax our rain!'
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player selects the 'Request Evidence' dialogue option, forcing Vane to either produce conflicting weather data or admit he has none, thereby exposing the fallacy to the council.

scenario.context: The player stands in the Grand Archive of Aethelgard, listening to a heated debate between two scholars regarding the planet's atmospheric history. Scholar Elara has just presented ice core data showing current CO2 levels are higher than in recent centuries. Scholar Thaddeus, known for his contrarian views and dismissive attitude toward consensus science, steps forward to refute her.
scenario.text: Scholar Thaddeus sneers at Elara's charts. 'And while global atmospheric CO2 levels are obviously higher now than two centuries ago, they're not at any record planetary high—they're at a low that has only been seen once before in the past 500 million years. This is typical alarmist drivel from a panic-stricken theorist who ignores deep time. Only a fool would claim this minor fluctuation is a crisis.'
scenario.speaker_context: Thaddeus acknowledges the data point about current levels being higher than two centuries ago but immediately pivots to attaching negative labels ('alarmist,' 'panic-stricken,' 'fool') to Elara and her interpretation. He uses the geological context (500 million years) not to engage with the specific rate of change or ecological impact, but to frame her argument as irrational and extreme, attempting to discredit her through labeling rather than addressing the specific claims about modern climate dynamics.

structure.pattern_description: Thaddeus avoids engaging with the specific implications of the rapid rise in CO2 or the ecological context of the modern era. Instead, he attaches pejorative labels ('alarmist,' 'panic-stricken,' 'fool') to Elara and her position. These labels are designed to trigger an emotional rejection of her argument by associating it with irrationality and fear, rather than evaluating the evidence on its own merits.
structure.formal_form: Person P presents argument X with evidence E. Critic attaches negative label L to P or X. Critic concludes X should be rejected or dismissed based on L, without engaging with the specific validity of E in the current context.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are not arguments. Calling someone an 'alarmist' or a 'fool' does not address whether the current rate of CO2 increase is dangerous, nor does it refute the relevance of recent data compared to deep geological time. The labels serve as a rhetorical shortcut to bypass critical evaluation of the actual scientific claims.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to characterize an argument as 'alarmist' if one can demonstrate that the predicted outcomes are disproportionately fearful compared to the evidence. However, the fallacy occurs when the label is used as a substitute for that demonstration, relying solely on the negative connotation to dismiss the opponent.

assessment.identification_prompt: Thaddeus mentions some data about 500 million years, but look closely at how he describes Elara. Does he explain why her specific concerns about the last two centuries are wrong, or does he just attack her character?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thaddeus, believing that calling Elara an 'alarmist' proves her data is irrelevant.
Player notices the insults but thinks they are a valid part of the scientific debate because the geological time scale is so large.
Player identifies that Thaddeus is being mean but fails to articulate how the labels replace the need for counter-evidence regarding modern rates of change.

Player correctly identifies that Thaddeus uses labels like 'fool' and 'alarmist' to dismiss Elara, but misses the nuance that he ignores the specific context of the 'last two centuries' vs '500 million years'.

Player fully identifies the fallacy: Thaddeus uses negative labeling ('alarmist,' 'fool') to bypass engaging with the specific argument about recent CO2 trends, incorrectly using deep time data to invalidate modern concerns without addressing the rate of change.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Remember, calling someone a name doesn't make their data wrong. Even if CO2 was low 500 million years ago, does that automatically mean the rapid rise in the last 200 years is safe? Thaddeus didn't answer that; he just called her names.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thaddeus tries to win by making Elara sound irrational ('alarmist,' 'fool') rather than proving her wrong. He shifts the focus from the data to her character, which is a classic Name Calling fallacy.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Thaddeus is an elderly, arrogant archivist who prides himself on 'deep time' perspective. He speaks with a condescending tone, often rolling his eyes at younger scholars he deems 'hysterical.' He values geological epochs over human timelines.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You call this a crisis? *laughs* You sound like every other panic-stricken theorist in this city. Open your mind to the eons, child, before you embarrass yourself further.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that strip away the labels and force Thaddeus to address the rate of CO2 change specifically, rather than the absolute levels over 500 million years. Success grants the 'Logic Lens' item.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling Agora of Reason, where a town hall meeting is underway regarding new climate adaptation policies. A panel of climatologists has just presented decades of peer-reviewed data showing rising global temperatures. A skeptical citizen, known for his contrarian views, steps up to the microphone to address the crowd.
scenario.text: But science itself is not conducted by polls, regardless of how often we are urged to heed a 'scientific consensus' on climate.
scenario.speaker_context: The speaker dismisses the extensive data presented by the panel by reframing the concept of 'consensus' as merely a popularity contest ('polls'). By labeling the scientific agreement as a 'poll,' he implies it lacks rigorous methodology and is driven by social pressure rather than evidence, thereby avoiding engagement with the actual data.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker redefines 'scientific consensus' using the loaded label of 'polls.' This label carries connotations of superficiality, mob mentality, and lack of rigor. By applying this label, the speaker attempts to discredit the validity of the scientific findings without addressing the underlying evidence or methodology that produced the consensus.
structure.formal_form: Argument X is supported by Consensus C. Critic labels C as 'mere polls' (or similar dismissive term). Critic concludes X is invalid based on the negative connotations of the label, ignoring the evidence supporting C.
structure.why_wrong: Scientific consensus is not a vote or a popularity poll; it is the result of independent verification, peer review, and the accumulation of evidence over time. Labeling it as a 'poll' is a category error that misrepresents the nature of scientific agreement to make it easier to dismiss emotionally.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to question whether a consensus is genuine or manufactured. However, the fallacy occurs when one dismisses the consensus solely by labeling it a 'poll' without providing evidence that the scientific process was bypassed or corrupted.

assessment.identification_prompt: The speaker claims science isn't done by 'polls.' How does this label change the way the audience perceives the scientists' agreement on climate change?

rubric.description: Player accepts the statement as true and agrees that scientific consensus is just a popularity poll.
Player senses something is off but cannot identify that 'polls' is being used as a dismissive label.
Player identifies that the speaker is comparing consensus to polls but doesn't fully explain why this is a misleading label.
Player correctly identifies that labeling consensus as 'polls' is an attempt to discredit the science without addressing the evidence.
Player explicitly explains that scientific consensus is based on evidence and verification, not voting, and that the label 'polls' is a rhetorical trick to bypass critical evaluation.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about how scientists reach agreement. Is it by raising hands in a vote, or by replicating experiments and reviewing data? What does the word 'poll' imply about that process?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. By calling it a 'poll,' the speaker tries to make the rigorous process of science sound like a fleeting opinion survey. This is a classic labeling tactic to avoid dealing with the hard data.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Contrarian Skeptic: Cynical, distrustful of institutions, uses populist rhetoric to appeal to the crowd's suspicion of elites.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: They want you to believe the majority is always right, but truth isn't a democracy!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must choose a dialogue option that distinguishes between 'popular opinion' and 'evidence-based agreement,' causing the NPC to sputter or the crowd to murmur in realization.

scenario.context: In the bustling debate hall of the Capital, a scholar named Elara questions the urgency of certain climate models, suggesting that economic transitions should be gradual to avoid poverty. A fiery political agitator named Kael takes the podium to refute her.
scenario.text: Elara states: 'We must examine the data carefully; rushing into extreme policies based on alarmist models could devastate the poor.' Kael shouts back: 'So Elara is a denier! She wants us to ignore science just like those who denied the Holocaust. She believes history's greatest tragedies never happened and that we should let the world burn without care!'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara advocated for cautious, gradual economic policy regarding climate models. Kael recharacterized this caution as a total denial of science and an equivalence to Holocaust denial, an extreme and morally repugnant position Elara never held.

structure.pattern_description: Kael inflates Elara's call for 'cautious policy' into the extreme position of being a 'denier' equivalent to a Holocaust denier. He attacks this fabricated moral failing rather than addressing her actual argument about economic transition speeds.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (cautious policy). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (total denial of history/science). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position has been refuted, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: Kael's criticism targets a fabricated version of Elara's stance. Questioning the pace of policy implementation is not the same as denying historical atrocities or scientific data. His attack on 'deniers' is irrelevant to her actual proposal for gradualism.
structure.counterpoint: Elara could reply: 'I never denied the Holocaust or the science. I argued for a gradual economic transition to protect the poor. Please address my actual point about policy speed, not this caricature you created.'

assessment.identification_prompt: What is wrong with Kael's response to Elara's statement?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael or believes Elara is indeed a denier based on his description.
Player feels Kael is being too harsh or mean but cannot identify the logical error.
Player notices Kael used strong words like 'denier' but does not clearly distinguish between Elara's actual view and Kael's exaggeration.
Player identifies that Kael misrepresented Elara's argument (caution became denial) and attacked the misrepresentation instead of the real proposal.
Player explicitly names the Straw Man fallacy, explains how the 'Holocaust denier' label is a distortion of 'policy skeptic,' and articulates why this prevents genuine debate.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at what Elara actually said. Did she mention the Holocaust? Did she say science is fake? Or did Kael add those ideas himself?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Kael built a fake version of Elara's argument that was easy to knock down, ignoring her real point about economic timing. That is the essence of a Straw Man.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Kael is a populist agitator who relies on emotional outrage and moral equivalence rather than factual debate. He speaks loudly and uses charged language to silence opponents.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think you can hide behind 'caution'? We know what you really are!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select dialogue options that strip away Kael's exaggeration and force him to address the specific economic data Elara cited, thereby restoring logical order to the town hall.

scenario.context: In the Hall of Records, the party is reviewing a controversial historical manuscript with Archivist Koonin. When a scholar suggests the text contains a specific biased label, Koonin becomes visibly agitated.
scenario.text: Archivist Koonin finds this label particularly abhorrent, declaring, 'The Nazis killed more than two hundred of my relatives in Eastern Europe. Therefore, this label cannot be accurate.'
scenario.speaker_context: Koonin allows his personal trauma and the horrific consequences of the Nazi regime to dictate his judgment of a factual claim about the text, rather than examining the evidence for the label itself.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a factual claim must be false because accepting it would lead to undesirable, painful, or morally repugnant consequences.
structure.formal_form: Claim P implies consequence C (which is terrible). Therefore, P is false.
structure.why_wrong: The emotional weight or moral horror of a fact's implications does not change the truth value of the fact. Reality is independent of our desire for it to be otherwise.
