game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Do you doubt the power of the tithe? Would you let your child freeze in Limbo for the sake of a few gold coins?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to expose the fallacy to lower the crowd's donation rate (gaining Logic XP), donate anyway to gain Favor with the Church, or walk away.

scenario.context: The player stands in the scorching courtyard of the Sunspire Observatory with Meteorologist Kael, who is frantically adjusting his instruments while looking at a data slate.
scenario.text: Kael points to the reading, his voice trembling with urgency. 'Look at this! It is significantly warmer here in Las Vegas this year compared to last year. This single data point proves it: global warming is rapidly accelerating out of control right now!' He turns to the player, expecting immediate agreement on the crisis.
scenario.speaker_context: Kael is comparing temperature data from only two specific years (last year and this year) in one specific location (Las Vegas) to draw a massive, universal conclusion about the global climate trend. He ignores long-term data sets, global averages, and natural year-to-year variability.

structure.pattern_description: Kael observes a temperature increase in one location over a two-year period and immediately concludes that global warming is 'rapidly accelerating.' He treats a sample size of two years in one city as sufficient evidence for a global, long-term climatological trend, ignoring the need for decades of global data to establish such a pattern.
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of X (where n=2 years) in location L have property Q (warmer). Therefore, the entire global system P has property R (rapidly accelerating warming).
structure.why_wrong: Climate trends are determined by long-term data (typically 30+ years) across the entire globe, not by comparing two consecutive years in a single desert city. Year-to-year weather fluctuations are normal and do not necessarily indicate a shift in the underlying climate trend. The sample is too small in both time and geographic scope to support the conclusion.
structure.counterpoint: While this specific year might indeed be part of an accelerating trend, Kael's reasoning is flawed because the evidence provided (one year's difference in one city) is insufficient to prove it. A valid argument would require citing long-term global temperature anomalies.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kael claims that because Las Vegas is warmer this year than last, global warming is rapidly accelerating. Does his evidence support this broad conclusion?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael, accepting that one hot year in one city proves global acceleration.
Player expresses doubt but cannot explain why the evidence is weak.
Player notes that one city or two years might not be enough, but lacks specific terminology.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that two data points in one location cannot define a global trend.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, noting the insufficiency of the sample size (time and space) and distinguishing between local weather variability and global climate patterns.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Kael insists, 'But the heat is undeniable! If you can't trust your own senses and the latest numbers, what can you trust?'
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Kael pauses, lowering his slate. 'You're right... I let my fear jump ahead of the data. One hot summer doesn't make a climate trend. I need to look at the thirty-year averages.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, impulsive, and prone to alarmism; Kael cares deeply about the environment but lacks patience for statistical rigor.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The numbers don't lie! Well, maybe they do if you don't look at enough of them...
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Kael to calm down and consult the long-term global archives before raising the alarm, preventing a panic in the observatory.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Logos City, a charismatic street preacher named Crowder stands atop a crate, surrounded by a mesmerized crowd nodding in unison.
scenario.text: Crowder points to the sea of faces and shouts, 'Look at them all! They know the truth. If everyone believes it, you should too! Don't be the only fool standing apart from the crowd.'
scenario.speaker_context: Crowder offers no facts, data, or logical reasons for his claim. His entire argument rests on the sheer number of people who appear to agree with him.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition is true or good solely because a large number of people believe it or do it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe X. Therefore, X is true.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief has no logical connection to its truth. History is full of widely held beliefs that were false (e.g., the earth is flat). Truth depends on evidence, not headcounts.
structure.counterpoint: While consensus among experts after rigorous investigation can be evidence, mere popular opinion without underlying verification is not a valid proof of truth.

assessment.identification_prompt: What actual evidence does Crowder provide to support his claim? Is the size of the crowd a valid reason to believe him?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument immediately because 'so many people can't be wrong'.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why the crowd size doesn't prove the point.
Recognizes that Crowder gave no facts, but fails to explicitly identify the 'popularity equals truth' error.
Identifies that the speaker uses the number of believers as the only evidence and states that popularity does not equal truth.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains the disconnect between popularity and truth, and notes the social pressure tactic used to silence dissent.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in this room suddenly believed that drinking poison was healthy, would that make it safe to drink?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing what 'everyone believes' might actually be useful information, even if it doesn't prove something is true?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, loud, and manipulative; feeds off group energy and fears isolation.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't stand there alone! Join the majority! They know!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out a historical example where the majority was wrong to break the crowd's trance.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling town square of Oakhaven, listening to a heated debate between two council members regarding a new environmental decree. Councilor Vane, a wealthy merchant who owns a fleet of heavy transport wagons (Hummers), is arguing passionately against a proposed ban on his vehicles.
scenario.text: Councilor Vane shouts over the crowd, 'If we ban Hummers just because they are bad for the environment, eventually the government will ban all cars! We cannot allow this slippery slope; therefore, we should not ban Hummers.'
scenario.speaker_context: Councilor Vane is conflating a specific regulation on a specific type of high-emission vehicle with a hypothetical, extreme future where all transportation is banned. He assumes that one small step (banning Hummers) inevitably leads to an absurd extreme (banning all cars) without providing evidence for this causal chain.

structure.pattern_description: While the original label was 'faulty generalization', the core error here is treating a single regulatory action as representative of an unlimited series of future actions. The speaker generalizes from one instance (banning Hummers) to a universal rule (the government will ban everything). Note: In strict logical taxonomy, this is often called a 'Slippery Slope', but within the context of generalization errors, it represents generalizing a specific intent to a boundless scope without sufficient evidence of such intent.
structure.formal_form: Event A (banning X) has occurred or is proposed. Therefore, Event Z (banning everything) will inevitably follow. No evidence is provided for the chain of events between A and Z.
structure.why_wrong: The argument fails because it assumes a causal chain without justification. Banning a specific harmful item does not logically imply that all items of that category will be banned. It ignores the possibility of nuanced regulations that target only specific harmful subsets.
structure.counterpoint: Regulations are often specific and targeted. Just because the government regulates one dangerous or harmful thing (like lead paint or toxic waste) does not mean they will regulate all things. Each case must be judged on its own merits.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane claims that banning Hummers means the government will eventually ban all cars. Is this conclusion supported by the evidence he provided?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane, believing that any ban leads to total prohibition.
Player feels Vane is exaggerating but cannot explain the logical gap.
Player identifies that banning one thing doesn't mean banning everything, but misses the lack of causal evidence.
Player identifies the hasty generalization/slippy slope, noting that Vane assumes an inevitable chain of events without proof.

Player fully deconstructs the argument, explaining that specific regulations do not generalize to universal bans and articulates why the sample (one ban) is insufficient to predict the extreme outcome (total ban).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: If the school bans cheating on tests, does that mean they will eventually ban students from thinking at all? Where is the line drawn?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Vane is jumping to a worst-case scenario without showing how we get there. We can ban harmful vehicles without banning all transportation.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, defensive, and prone to dramatic exaggeration to protect his financial interests.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It starts with my wagons, mark my words! Next they'll come for your carriages, then your horses, and soon we'll all be walking barefoot in the mud!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to support a targeted ban that includes exemptions for essential services, disproving Vane's fear of a total ban while still addressing the environmental concern.

scenario.context: In the bustling tech district of Neo-Veridia, a street vendor named Jax is trying to sell the latest model of the 'iSphere' smartphone to a crowd of skeptical students.
scenario.text: Jax holds up the sleek device and shouts, 'Don't waste time comparing specs or reading reviews! iPhones are the best phone because everyone has them. Look around—half the city is holding one right now. You don't want to be the only person left out of the loop, do you?'
scenario.speaker_context: Jax avoids discussing battery life, camera quality, or price. His entire argument relies on the premise that the device's quality is proven solely by its high adoption rate.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or a product must be superior simply because a large number of people believe it or possess it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of an idea or product does not constitute evidence of its truth or quality. Popularity can result from marketing, social pressure, or trends, none of which verify actual merit.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate reliability (e.g., a safety standard adopted by all experts after rigorous testing), mere popularity among the general public without independent verification is not proof of quality.

assessment.identification_prompt: What specific evidence does Jax provide about the phone's features? Is the fact that 'everyone has one' a valid reason to call it the best?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument; assumes that if everyone buys it, it must be the best phone.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why popularity isn't proof of quality.
Notices Jax didn't mention features but fails to identify the logical error in using popularity as evidence.
Identifies that Jax uses the number of owners as the sole evidence and explains that popularity does not equal quality.
Names the bandwagon fallacy, explains why popularity is irrelevant to technical merit, identifies the social pressure tactic, and distinguishes between trends and evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in the city suddenly started believing the sky was green, would that make the sky actually green?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing it' might actually be useful information, even if it doesn't prove something is true?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Fast-talking, energetic street hustler who relies on FOMO (fear of missing out) and crowd momentum to make sales.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Come on, don't be the odd one out! Everyone knows this is the one to get!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully points out that Jax provided zero technical specs, causing the crowd to hesitate and Jax to stumble over his pitch, admitting he doesn't actually know the specs himself.

scenario.context: In the Council Chamber of the Iron City, Councilor Vane argues against a proposed reform to hiring practices intended to address historical inequities.
scenario.text: We must eliminate affirmative action. We can't rely on laws to end racial prejudice.
scenario.speaker_context: Vane does not provide evidence that the specific policy fails or data showing it causes harm. Instead, he asserts the policy must be rejected because the desired outcome (ending prejudice) cannot be achieved by law, implying the negative consequence of failure is reason enough to discard the effort without testing its actual efficacy.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a course of action or factual claim should be rejected solely because the anticipated consequences are undesirable or because the desired consequence is deemed unachievable, rather than addressing the merit of the action itself.
structure.formal_form: Action A would lead to undesirable consequence C (or fail to lead to desired consequence D). Therefore, Action A is invalid/false.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of a policy or the truth of a claim depends on evidence and logic, not on whether the outcomes are pleasant or whether we wish them to be true. Assuming a method fails because the goal is hard to achieve ignores empirical testing.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to discuss whether a policy is effective. However, Vane skips the evaluation of effectiveness and jumps straight to rejection based on his belief that laws cannot change hearts, which is an assumption about consequences, not an analysis of the policy's mechanics.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane claims we must stop the policy because it won't work. Does he offer proof that it won't work, or just state a negative outcome?

rubric.description: Agrees with Vane; believes the difficulty of ending prejudice means the policy should be dropped immediately.
Senses something is missing but cannot identify that evidence is lacking.
Notices Vane focuses on the result (prejudice continuing) rather than the policy details.
Identifies that Vane rejects the policy based on a predicted failure (consequence) rather than evidence of that failure.
Explicitly names the appeal to consequences and explains that the difficulty of a goal does not invalidate the methods used to pursue it without proof.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If we decided never to try anything difficult because it might fail, would we ever solve any problems?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: How could Vane rephrase his argument to be a valid critique based on evidence rather than a prediction of failure?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Cynical, pragmatic, weary of idealistic reforms, speaks with finality.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think laws change minds? Look at history. We try, we fail, and society fractures. Why waste resources on what cannot be done?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present data from a pilot program or logical reasoning showing that legal frameworks can influence behavior, separating the 'difficulty of the goal' from the 'validity of the method'.

scenario.context: The player enters the neon-lit office of Influencer Max, a self-proclaimed 'Economic Guru' who believes social media metrics drive global markets. He is pointing excitedly at a dual-axis graph on his wall.
scenario.text: Look at this! The economy grows as the number of likes on my Instagram account continues to increase. Clearly, the two are linked. If I can just get more engagement, I can fix the recession single-handedly!
scenario.speaker_context: Max has observed two trends occurring simultaneously: a rising stock market and his own growing follower count. He mistakenly concludes that his likes are causing economic growth, ignoring that both are likely driven by broader factors like technological adoption, population growth, or general optimism, or that the correlation is purely coincidental.

structure.pattern_description: Max observes that two variables (Instagram likes and economic growth) are correlated over time and infers that one causes the other. This is a classic 'cum hoc ergo propter hoc' (with this, therefore because of this) error. He fails to consider that a third variable might cause both, that the causation could be reversed, or that the correlation is spurious.
structure.formal_form: A and B are correlated. Therefore A causes B. (Flaw: Ignores common cause C, reverse causation, or coincidence.)
structure.why_wrong: Correlation does not imply causation. Just because two trends move in the same direction does not mean one drives the other. Max has not provided a mechanism for how Instagram likes create economic value, nor has he ruled out confounding variables like general digitalization or population increases that affect both metrics.
structure.counterpoint: While correlations can hint at causal relationships, establishing causation requires a plausible mechanism, controlled experiments, or ruling out alternative explanations. For instance, ice cream sales and drowning incidents are correlated, but buying ice cream doesn't cause drowning; hot weather causes both.

assessment.identification_prompt: Max claims his Instagram likes are causing the economy to grow. What is the logical flaw in his reasoning?

rubric.description: The player agrees with Max or fails to identify any logical error.
The player suspects something is wrong but cannot articulate why, perhaps calling it 'unlikely' without logical basis.
The player identifies that correlation does not equal causation but does not offer alternative explanations.
The player correctly identifies the false cause fallacy and suggests that a third factor might be influencing both trends.

The player fully deconstructs the argument, identifying the cum hoc fallacy, explaining the lack of a causal mechanism, and proposing specific confounding variables (e.g., technology adoption) that explain the correlation.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: did your likes actually build the factories or hire the workers? Or could something else be making both numbers go up?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because two lines on a graph move together doesn't mean one is pulling the other. You've spotted the false cause fallacy.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Narcissistic, overconfident, tech-obsessed, and prone to magical thinking regarding social media metrics.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't you see the pattern? My engagement rate is the leading indicator! We need to boost my next post to save the market!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Max to look for underlying economic indicators rather than vanity metrics, unlocking the 'Critical Analyst' badge.

scenario.context: In the Family Hearth inn, you have just presented the monthly ledger to your mother, showing that the household phone bill has exceeded the budget limit due to your usage. She looks concerned about the extra cost.
scenario.text: You quickly interject: 'But Mom, you don't understand! My math class is incredibly hard this semester, and I actually got an A on my test today! If you focus on this bill, it might stress me out so much that I'll fail the next one.'
scenario.speaker_context: You do not address the factual issue of the overage or provide a plan to pay it. Instead, you argue that the bill should be ignored or forgiven because accepting responsibility for it would lead to the undesirable consequence of poor academic performance.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a factual claim or necessary action should be rejected because accepting it would lead to undesirable outcomes, substituting the consequences for a critique of the evidence or logic.
structure.formal_form: Claim P (the bill is due/usage was high) would have undesirable consequences C (stress leading to failing math). Therefore, P is false or should be ignored.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a factual claim (that the bill is over the limit) or the validity of a rule (that overages must be paid) does not depend on whether the consequences are pleasant. Bad outcomes resulting from a fact do not make the fact untrue.
structure.counterpoint: It is legitimate to ask for leniency or a payment plan based on your hard work and stress (policy/action), but that is different from implying the bill isn't actually due or that the overspending didn't happen (truth/fact).

assessment.identification_prompt: You mentioned your math grade to avoid talking about the bill. Does getting an A change the fact that the bill is over the limit?

rubric.description: Agrees that the math grade means the bill doesn't matter or isn't really an issue.
Feels the argument is manipulative but cannot explain why the math grade is irrelevant to the bill amount.
Notices the speaker is talking about school stress instead of the phone usage data.
Identifies that the speaker is rejecting the need to pay the bill based on feared consequences rather than addressing the overage itself.
Explicitly names the appeal to consequences and distinguishes between the factual reality of the debt and the policy decision of how to handle it given the student's stress.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If you had failed the math test instead, would that make the phone bill even higher or more real?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: How could you rephrase your argument to legitimately ask for help with the bill based on your hard work, without committing a logical fallacy?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious teenager, defensive, quick to deflect criticism with emotional appeals.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Wait, before you say anything about the numbers, look at this test score! Do you really want to risk my GPA over a few dollars?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must gently point out that the test score and the phone bill are two separate issues, validating the student's stress while insisting the bill must still be addressed.

scenario.context: In the high council of the Kingdom of Aethelgard, the realm is suffering from smog-choked cities and dying forests. A young eco-mage named Elara proposes a modest initiative to incentivize merchants to switch their carriages to mana-efficient models, starting with the capital city.
scenario.text: Elara says: 'We should encourage merchants to adopt mana-efficient carriages like the Prius-model to reduce our ecological footprint.' Lord Vane, a traditionalist who owns the royal stables, stands to oppose her. He declares: 'So the Senator thinks we can solve all our ecological problems simply by driving a Prius! She believes this one small change will magically fix the climate, restore the forests, and end the smog overnight, ignoring the complex industrial causes entirely.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara proposed a specific, incremental step (incentivizing efficient carriages). Lord Vane recharacterized this as a belief that this single action alone solves 'all' ecological problems, an extreme and naive position Elara never claimed.

structure.pattern_description: Lord Vane inflates Elara's modest proposal (adopting efficient carriages as one solution) into an extreme position (believing this single act solves ALL ecological problems) and then attacks the extreme version. His criticism targets the fabricated claim that she thinks it's a panacea, not her actual suggestion.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (we should do X to help). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (A thinks doing X alone solves everything). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position has been refuted, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: Vane's criticism targets a fabricated version of Elara's argument. Elara suggested a helpful step, not a total solution. Attacking the idea that 'one thing fixes everything' is irrelevant because Elara never claimed that.
structure.counterpoint: Elara could reply: 'I never claimed driving a Prius solves every problem. I suggested it as one effective step among many. Please address the actual proposal of incentivizing efficiency, not a fantasy version where I ignore other causes.'

assessment.identification_prompt: What is logically flawed about Lord Vane's response to Elara's proposal?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane or believes Elara's plan is indeed insufficient to solve everything.
Player senses Vane is being unfair or aggressive but cannot identify the logical error.
Player notices Vane exaggerated Elara's claim but fails to distinguish between her actual point and his distortion.
Player identifies that Vane misrepresented Elara's argument (changing 'one solution' to 'the only solution') and attacked the misrepresentation.

Player explicitly names the 'Straw Man' fallacy, explains how Vane constructed the extreme position, and articulates why attacking that extreme position does not refute Elara's actual modest proposal.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at the words Elara used versus the words Vane put in her mouth. Did she say this would solve 'all' problems, or just help?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct! Vane built a straw man by exaggerating her claim to make it easier to knock down. He attacked a position she never held.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Lord Vane is a gruff, defensive traditionalist who feels threatened by change and uses rhetorical bullying to protect his interests.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! Naive idealism! You think a shiny new carriage fixes the whole world?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select the dialogue option that clarifies Elara's actual stance, causing Vane to sputter and the council to vote on the pilot program.

scenario.context: In the bustling town square of Logos, a heated debate surrounds the recent election results. A fervent supporter stands atop a crate, shouting down any doubters.
scenario.text: The president of Honduras is a good leader because he is a leader of the country. This is an example of which common fallacy?
scenario.speaker_context: Citizen Marco, a loyalist who believes that holding the office of president automatically proves one's virtue and competence, unable to see that he is using the conclusion as his only evidence.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker claims the president is a 'good leader' (conclusion) solely because he is a 'leader of the country' (premise). The argument assumes that being a leader inherently makes one good, which is exactly what needs to be proven. The premise offers no independent evidence of goodness.
structure.formal_form: P1: The president is a leader of the country. P2: All leaders of the country are good leaders (unstated assumption equivalent to the conclusion). C: Therefore, the president is a good leader.
structure.why_wrong: This is a classic case of circular reasoning. The argument restates the conclusion as the premise. To accept the premise ('he is a leader, therefore he is good') requires already accepting the conclusion ('he is good'). It provides zero external evidence like policy success or moral character.
structure.counterpoint: Not all statements about leaders are circular. If the speaker said, 'He is a good leader because he reduced poverty by 20%,' that would be a valid argument with independent evidence, even if one disagrees with the data.

assessment.identification_prompt: Citizen Marco is very loud and confident. Does his reason actually prove that the president is 'good', or is he just repeating himself in a different way?

rubric.description: Agrees with Marco or criticizes the president without addressing the logic of the statement.
Feels the argument is weak or unconvincing but cannot explain why.
Identifies that Marco is going in circles or assuming what he tries to prove.
Correctly identifies the fallacy as 'begging the question' or 'circular reasoning' and explains that being a leader does not automatically mean being a good one.
Names the fallacy, explains the circular structure, and explicitly states that the premise provides no independent support for the conclusion.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if someone said 'This food is delicious because it tastes good,' are they giving you a real reason, or just saying the same thing twice?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Marco assumes that holding the position makes him good, which is the very thing he needed to prove. You've spotted the circle.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Passionate, loud, slightly dogmatic, lacks self-awareness regarding logic.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's obvious! He leads, therefore he leads well! Why do you question the obvious?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out the circular nature of the argument to calm the crowd and unlock the 'Critical Thinker' badge, allowing access to the Town Hall.

scenario.context: In the school cafeteria, two students are arguing over a missing lunchbox. A group of onlookers has gathered, and one student attempts to justify an act of retaliation based on past events.
scenario.text: Jimmy stole Tommy's lunch in the past. Therefore, it is acceptable for Tommy to steal Jimmy's lunch today.
scenario.speaker_context: The speaker argues that because a negative event occurred previously (Jimmy stealing), a reciprocal negative action (Tommy stealing) is now morally acceptable, ignoring the actual ethical principles regarding theft and focusing only on the outcome of 'evening the score'.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that an action is right or a claim is true solely because of the perceived positive or negative consequences of accepting it, rather than based on evidence or ethical principles.
structure.formal_form: Action A leads to consequence C (which feels satisfying/just). Therefore, Action A is morally acceptable.
structure.why_wrong: The moral validity of an action (like stealing) does not change based on past events or the emotional satisfaction of retaliation. Two wrongs do not make a right; the consequence of 'getting even' does not validate the act of theft itself.
structure.counterpoint: While it is understandable to feel angry about a past wrong, the consequence of feeling satisfied by retaliation does not make the retaliatory act ethically correct. Justice requires addressing the initial wrong through proper channels, not committing a new one.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the fact that Jimmy stole first actually make it okay for Tommy to steal, or is the speaker just focusing on the feeling of revenge?

rubric.description: Agrees completely; believes stealing back is fine because Jimmy started it.
Feels it might be wrong but thinks it's fair because of what happened before.
Notices the argument is about 'getting even' but isn't sure if that justifies the action.
Identifies that the speaker is using the past event to justify a new bad action without ethical proof.
Clearly states that the consequences (revenge/satisfaction) do not determine the morality of the action; theft remains wrong regardless of history.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Jimmy stole a car, would it be okay for Tommy to steal a car back? Where do we draw the line if 'past wrongs' make 'current wrongs' okay?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. The consequence of 'feeling even' doesn't change the rule that stealing is wrong. How should Tommy actually handle the situation instead?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Impulsive, vindictive, and focused on immediate fairness rather than rules.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's only fair! He took mine, so I take his. That makes it right!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must guide the NPC to see that retaliation creates a cycle of bad behavior rather than solving the original problem, perhaps suggesting reporting to a teacher or mediator instead.

scenario.context: You are attending the Grand Masquerade in the capital city, a neutral ground where nobles and commoners mingle. The conversation has drifted to household companions, and a flamboyant noble seeks to categorize your allegiance.
scenario.text: At a recent cocktail party, the conversation has turned to family pets, and your friend asks you, "Are you a cat or a dog person?"
scenario.speaker_context: Lord Valerius, a socialite who believes nuance is boring and insists everyone must pick a side in every debate.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker presents a choice between two options (cat person or dog person) as if they are the only possible options, ignoring other possibilities such as liking both, liking neither, or preferring entirely different animals.
structure.formal_form: A v B. (Implied: You must be A or B). Reality: A v B v C v D...
structure.why_wrong: The disjunction is not exhaustive. One can love both cats and dogs, love neither, or prefer birds, reptiles, or no pets at all. Framing it as an exclusive either/or forces an artificial constraint on reality.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or question is a fallacy. If the question were 'Is this coin currently showing heads or tails?' (assuming it cannot land on its edge), the dichotomy would be valid and exhaustive.

assessment.identification_prompt: Lord Valerius insists you must be either a cat person or a dog person. What is logically flawed about this framing?

rubric.description: Accepts the premise and chooses one option without question.
Feels the question is limiting but cannot explain why logically.
Identifies that other options exist (e.g., liking both) but does not name the logical error.
Identifies the false dichotomy and explains that the options provided do not cover all possibilities.
Clearly names the false dichotomy, lists multiple excluded alternatives (both, neither, other animals), and explains why the disjunctive syllogism fails here.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Valerius says those are the only two types of people. Can you think of someone who loves both? Or someone who hates both?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. By excluding the middle ground and other categories, he creates a forced choice. Can you think of a scenario where an either/or question about pets would actually be valid?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic but intellectually lazy; reduces complex issues to team sports to win arguments quickly.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Come now, don't hedge! You're either Team Fur-and-Meow or Team Bark-and-Loyalty. Which banner do you fly under?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player points out a third option (e.g., 'I'm a hamster person' or 'I love both'), causing Valerius to laugh and admit he oversimplified, granting the player 'Nuance Points'.

scenario.context: In the bustling food court of the Grand Bazaar, a tourist asks a local guide for a restaurant recommendation. The guide points to a specific chain with a line out the door.
scenario.text: You should definitely eat at the Cheesecake Factory. It is the best restaurant in the city because it is always crowded.
scenario.speaker_context: The guide assumes that high customer volume is proof of superior quality, ignoring other reasons for crowds like marketing, location, or lack of alternatives.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or a product must be good solely because many people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people do/believe X. Therefore, X is good/true.
structure.why_wrong: Popularity is not a logical guarantee of quality or truth. Crowds can be caused by factors unrelated to merit, such as effective advertising, low prices, novelty, or simply being the only option available.
structure.counterpoint: While popularity can sometimes indicate quality through collective experience (wisdom of the crowd), it only becomes evidence if the crowd is knowledgeable and independent. Mere foot traffic is not independent verification of food quality.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the fact that the restaurant is crowded prove the food is the 'best'? What other reasons might there be for a long line?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; assumes crowds equal quality.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why the crowd size might be misleading.
Recognizes that crowds don't guarantee quality but fails to identify the specific logical error.
Identifies that the speaker uses popularity as the sole evidence and notes that crowds can exist for bad reasons.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that popularity is not evidence of merit, and lists alternative causes for the crowd (e.g., marketing, location).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If a movie has a huge opening weekend but terrible reviews, is it still a 'good' movie just because many people bought tickets?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where a large crowd WOULD be a reliable sign of quality? What makes that situation different?

game_hooks.npc_personality: A well-meaning but uncritical local guide who relies on heuristics and social proof rather than deep analysis.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look at that line! Everyone knows the Cheesecake Factory is the best because it's always packed.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out that the crowd could be due to the restaurant's central location or a coupon promotion, not necessarily the food quality, convincing the NPC to check reviews instead.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling hallway of Oakhaven High during election week. A group of students is gathered around a bulletin board covered in campaign posters. Two students, Bill and Sarah, are debating the merits of Jenny's candidacy for class president.
scenario.text: Bill says Jenny would make a good class president, but Bill makes bad grades, so we shouldn't vote for Jenny.
scenario.speaker_context: Bill, a student known for struggling academically but who is vocal about school politics. He is trying to dissuade others from supporting Jenny by attacking his own credibility rather than hers, or implying his lack of status invalidates his support.

structure.pattern_description: The argument dismisses a claim (Jenny is a good candidate) based on a characteristic of the person making the supporting statement (Bill has bad grades), rather than addressing the qualities of the candidate herself. It incorrectly assumes that the speaker's academic performance determines the validity of their opinion on leadership.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X is true. Person P has property Q (bad grades). Therefore, X is false (or we should not accept X).
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a claim or the quality of a candidate is independent of the personal characteristics of the person endorsing them. Bill's grades have no logical connection to Jenny's ability to lead the student body. The argument attacks the messenger instead of evaluating the message.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if the argument relies on the person's specific expertise. If Bill claimed, 'Jenny will fix the math curriculum because I am a math genius,' then his grades would be relevant evidence. Since he is just offering an opinion on her character, his grades are irrelevant.

assessment.identification_prompt: Bill is trying to convince you not to vote for Jenny. Look closely at his reason: does he mention anything about Jenny's plans or behavior, or is he talking entirely about himself?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Bill and decides not to vote for Jenny based on his grades.
Player feels Bill's argument is weak but cannot explain why his grades matter or don't matter.
Player identifies that Bill is talking about himself, not Jenny, but accepts the conclusion anyway.
Player recognizes that Bill's grades are irrelevant to Jenny's qualifications and identifies the attack on the speaker.
Player explicitly states that the validity of an endorsement does not depend on the endorser's unrelated personal traits and demands evidence about Jenny herself.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if a student with straight A's said Jenny was a bad candidate, would that automatically make it true? Why does Bill's report card change the facts about Jenny?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Bill's academic record tells us nothing about Jenny's leadership skills. To make a fair decision, we need to look at Jenny's platform, not Bill's report card.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Bill is defensive and easily swayed by social hierarchy; he assumes academic success equals moral or leadership authority.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look, I'm not saying she's evil, but come on, I barely pass Algebra. If even I think she's okay, doesn't that mean something's wrong? Or wait, if I say she's good, does my bad grade make it a lie?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player helps the group separate the speaker from the argument, prompting them to list three actual reasons to vote for or against Jenny based on her campaign promises.

scenario.context: The player is walking along the cobblestone path toward the city gates when they encounter a flustered merchant named Elias who has just dodged a cyclist.
scenario.text: On my walk to work this morning, a woman on her bike nearly ran me off the sidewalk! I hadn't realized that cyclists were so aggressive and rude!
scenario.speaker_context: Elias is shaken after a single near-miss incident with one cyclist. He immediately concludes that the entire group of cyclists possesses negative traits (aggressive, rude) based solely on this one interaction.

structure.pattern_description: Elias observes one instance of a cyclist behaving poorly and extrapolates this behavior to the entire population of cyclists. He ignores the vast number of cyclists who may ride safely and politely, treating a sample size of one as statistically significant.
structure.formal_form: Observed 1 instance of X (cyclist) having property Q (aggressive/rude). Therefore, all members of group X have property Q.
structure.why_wrong: A single data point is insufficient to characterize a large and diverse group. The behavior of one individual does not represent the norm for the entire category. Elias is likely suffering from recency bias, where the startling nature of the event overshadows all his previous neutral or positive observations of cyclists.
structure.counterpoint: While it is rational to be cautious after a bad experience, forming a universal belief about a group's character requires a representative sample size, not just a single anecdote.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elias claims all cyclists are aggressive and rude because one nearly hit him. Is his conclusion logically sound?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Elias, stating that cyclists are indeed dangerous based on his story.
Player feels Elias is being unfair but cannot explain the logical error.
Player identifies that one person does not represent the whole group but lacks specific terminology.
Player correctly identifies the hasty generalization, noting the sample size of one is too small to judge all cyclists.

Player identifies the fallacy, explains the insufficiency of the sample size, and suggests alternative explanations (e.g., the cyclist was having a bad day, an accident, or was in a hurry) to refute the universal claim.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If you met one person from a distant land who was rude, would you say everyone from that land is rude? Why is this situation different?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Judging a whole group by one member is a classic hasty generalization. What other factors could explain that specific cyclist's behavior?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, prone to overreaction, speaks quickly when stressed.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Did you see that? She almost knocked me into the mud! It's true what they say, every last one of those pedal-pushers is a menace!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player calms Elias down by pointing out he only saw one rider, prompting him to apologize for his rash judgment and continue to work safely.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling Grand Ballroom of the Capital, where Lord Ponce, a notoriously eager matchmaker, is cornering guests near the punch bowl.
scenario.text: Lord Ponce grabs your shoulder with excitement. 'French people are great at kissing. Julie is French. Get me a date with her immediately!'
scenario.speaker_context: Lord Ponce has likely met one or two French individuals who were good kissers, or perhaps he has only heard rumors about Julie, and is now applying a stereotype about an entire nationality to a specific individual to justify his matchmaking scheme.

structure.pattern_description: Lord Ponce takes a perceived trait of a large group ('French people') and applies it universally to every member (Julie) without sufficient evidence that the trait holds for all, or that Julie specifically possesses it. He assumes the generalization is absolute truth to support his conclusion.
structure.formal_form: Most/Some observed members of Group G have Property P. Individual X is a member of Group G. Therefore, Individual X definitely has Property P.
structure.why_wrong: Nationality does not guarantee a specific skill or behavior. Even if many French people are great kissers, it is logically invalid to assume every single French person shares this trait. The sample size of 'French people' as a monolith is insufficient to predict the attributes of a specific individual like Julie.
structure.counterpoint: Statistical trends can exist within populations, but they cannot dictate the characteristics of a specific individual. A valid argument would require evidence specific to Julie's abilities, not just her nationality.

assessment.identification_prompt: Lord Ponce claims Julie must be a great kisser solely because she is French. Is his reasoning logically sound?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Lord Ponce and attempts to set up the date based on his logic.
Player feels unsure but suspects the logic might be flawed without being able to explain why.
Player identifies that not all French people are the same but struggles to name the specific logical error.
Player correctly identifies the hasty generalization, noting that a group trait cannot be automatically applied to an individual.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, explaining that the premise relies on a stereotype rather than evidence specific to Julie, and suggests seeking direct evidence of her skills instead.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: You arrange the date, but Julie is unimpressed and leaves early. Lord Ponce insists you just didn't try hard enough, failing to see his assumption was wrong.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: You politely decline, pointing out that Julie's skills are her own, not defined by her passport. Lord Ponce pauses, realizing he was being presumptuous, and asks how else he might find a suitable match.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Overenthusiastic, stereotypical, impulsive, and socially oblivious.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But everyone knows it! It's in their blood! Are you saying you know better than centuries of romance?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Ponce to interview Julie about her interests first, shifting the focus from national stereotypes to individual compatibility.

scenario.context: In the dimly lit holding cell of the Iron Ward, a stern City Watchman blocks the path to the evidence locker, refusing to release a confiscated herb pouch.
scenario.text: Smoking pot is against the law because it is wrong; I know it is wrong because it is against the law.
scenario.speaker_context: Officer Grum, a by-the-book enforcer who believes legality and morality are identical and cannot conceive of a law being unjust or an act being illegal yet moral.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker claims the act is illegal because it is wrong, and then claims it is wrong solely because it is illegal. The premise (it is wrong) and the conclusion (it is against the law) rely on each other without any external evidence.
structure.formal_form: P1: Act X is against the law because it is wrong. P2: Act X is wrong because it is against the law. C: Therefore, Act X is against the law (and wrong).
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes the truth of the conclusion within the premise. To prove the law is justified (moral), one needs independent ethical reasoning. To prove the act is immoral, one needs ethical standards outside of mere legality. Using the law to prove morality and morality to prove the law creates a closed loop with no foundational support.
structure.counterpoint: Not all references to law and morality are circular. It is valid to say 'It is wrong because it causes harm, and therefore we made it law.' The fallacy occurs only when the only reason given for the morality is the law itself, and the only reason for the law is the morality.

assessment.identification_prompt: Officer Grum seems very certain of his stance. What is the actual reason he gives for why smoking pot is wrong?

rubric.description: Agrees with the officer or argues about drugs without noticing the logical flaw.
Feels the argument is unsatisfying or repetitive but cannot explain why.
Identifies that the officer is using the law to prove it's wrong and 'wrong' to prove it's law, calling it 'going in circles'.
Names the fallacy as begging the question or circular reasoning and explains that the premise assumes the conclusion.
Names the fallacy, explains the circular dependency between legality and morality, and notes that no independent evidence was provided for either claim.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at the two parts of his sentence. Does the second part give a new reason, or does it just repeat the first part in different words?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! He hasn't given us a real reason. He's just restating his conclusion as if it were evidence. Without an independent standard of 'wrongness,' his argument proves nothing.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Rigid, authoritative, and intellectually stagnant. Grum believes rules are self-justifying and gets frustrated when players ask 'why'.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't ask me why the rule exists! The rule exists because it's the rule! Breaking it is bad, and it's bad because it's broken!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out the circular logic to confuse Grum or lower his guard, allowing access to the evidence locker or forcing him to consult a superior for a 'real' reason.

scenario.context: In the Town Square, the accused stands trial for theft. The crowd is restless, and a prominent town elder, Magistrate Vane, steps forward to sway the jury before evidence is fully heard.
scenario.text: I don't see how you can believe he is not guilty of that crime. He's a terrible person and I can prove it. In fact, several years ago he was convicted of that same kind of crime.
scenario.speaker_context: Vane ignores the specific evidence regarding the current charge. Instead, he argues the defendant must be guilty now because accepting his innocence would mean acknowledging a 'terrible person' walks free, and he cites past bad behavior as proof of current guilt based on the undesirable outcome of acquittal.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a factual claim (guilt or innocence) should be accepted or rejected based on the perceived negative consequences of the alternative, rather than on direct evidence.
structure.formal_form: Accepting Claim P (that he is innocent) would lead to undesirable consequence C (a terrible person goes free). Therefore, Claim P is false (he is guilty).
structure.why_wrong: The truth of whether someone committed a specific crime depends solely on the evidence of that event. The moral character of the accused or the unpleasantness of them going free does not change the facts of the current case.
structure.counterpoint: It is understandable to fear a dangerous person remaining in society, but that fear is a policy concern for sentencing or surveillance, not proof of guilt for a specific new charge.

assessment.identification_prompt: Magistrate Vane seems very worried about the defendant's character and past. But does he provide any evidence about the crime happening today?

rubric.description: Agrees with Vane; believes the defendant's bad character proves current guilt.
Senses something is off but thinks the past conviction is strong enough proof.
Notices Vane is talking about the defendant's nature rather than the specific act.
Identifies that Vane is rejecting innocence because the consequences seem bad, not because of evidence.
Clearly articulates that the undesirability of the outcome (a guilty man going free) does not constitute evidence of the act itself.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If the defendant were a saint instead of a 'terrible person,' would Vane's argument about the past conviction still hold the same weight for this specific crime?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Why might a jury feel pressured to ignore evidence if they are afraid of the consequences of a 'not guilty' verdict?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Authoritative, fear-mongering, relies on reputation over facts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: We cannot risk letting a wolf back into the fold just because the shepherd is hesitant!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must present the lack of direct evidence for the current charge, separating the defendant's history from the current facts.

scenario.context: In the Grand Hall of Arguments, two scholars are debating the origins of humanity before a panel of judges. Scholar Elara presents evidence for evolutionary theory. Her opponent, Magister Thorne, seeks to discredit her by mocking her position rather than addressing her evidence.
scenario.text: Magister Thorne declares to the crowd: 'My opponent is trying to convince you that we evolved from monkeys who were swinging from trees; a truly ludicrous claim.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara argued for common ancestry based on genetic and fossil evidence. Thorne distorted this into the absurd claim that humans directly descended from modern tree-swinging monkeys to make the argument easier to ridicule.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne takes Elara's nuanced scientific position (common ancestry/evolution) and replaces it with a crude, exaggerated caricature (humans evolved directly from modern monkeys swinging in trees). He then attacks this caricature as 'ludicrous' instead of engaging with the actual evidence.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (evolution/common ancestry). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (descended from modern tree-swinging monkeys). Person B attacks P* as absurd. Person B concludes P is false.
structure.why_wrong: The criticism targets a fabricated version of the argument. Evolutionary theory does not claim humans descended from modern monkeys, but that both share a common ancestor. Attacking the distorted version proves nothing about the actual theory.
structure.counterpoint: Elara could reply: 'I did not say we evolved from modern monkeys swinging in trees. I said humans and monkeys share a common ancestor from millions of years ago. Please address the actual evidence I presented, not a caricature of it.'

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Magister Thorne misrepresent Scholar Elara's argument, and why is his attack ineffective against her actual point?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne or believes he has successfully disproven evolution.
Player feels Thorne is being mean or mocking, but cannot identify the logical error.
Player notices Thorne changed the argument but cannot clearly distinguish between 'common ancestry' and 'descended from monkeys'.
Player identifies that Thorne created a straw man by exaggerating Elara's claim into something absurd (modern monkeys) and attacked that instead of her real point.

Player fully explains the distortion: clarifies that evolution posits a shared ancestor, not direct descent from modern species, and notes that refuting the distortion does not refute the original theory.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at the specific words Thorne used: 'monkeys who were swinging from trees.' Did Elara actually say that, or is that an exaggeration designed to make her look foolish?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thorne built a weak 'straw man' argument that was easy to knock down, but it wasn't the argument Elara actually made. This is a classic diversion tactic.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Magister Thorne is an arrogant, traditionalist debater who relies on rhetoric and mockery rather than evidence. He speaks with a booming voice and uses dismissive gestures.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Ha! Can you believe she wants us to think we're just glorified apes swinging from vines? Preposterous!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select the dialogue option that corrects the definition of evolution, forcing Thorne to either engage with the real science or retreat in embarrassment, earning the 'Logic Shield' badge.

scenario.context: During the final debate in the town square of Oakhaven, the player stands before the podium as a neutral observer. The incumbent mayor is discussing economic policy when the challenger, Lara, takes the microphone to respond to a question about employment rates.
scenario.text: Lara leans into the microphone, her voice trembling with manufactured urgency: 'My opponent talks about statistics and gradual growth, but let me tell you what his plan really means. A vote for him is a direct vote for you losing your job. It means empty cupboards for your children and foreclosure on your homes. Do you want to be the one who destroyed this community? Vote for me, or say goodbye to your livelihood.'
scenario.speaker_context: Lara bypasses any discussion of actual economic data or policy details. Instead, she attempts to induce fear and guilt in the audience to force a decision without logical justification.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting a strong emotional response (fear, guilt, pity) in place of addressing the factual evidence or logical merits of an argument. Lara does not explain how the opponent's policy causes job loss; she simply asserts a terrifying outcome to provoke panic.
structure.formal_form: Claim P is supported by evidence E. Agent evokes emotion F (fear/guilt) unrelated to E. Agent implies P must be accepted/rejected because of F.
structure.why_wrong: The fear of losing a job does not constitute evidence that the opponent's policy will cause job losses. The emotional manipulation is designed to bypass critical evaluation of the actual economic plans.
structure.counterpoint: While job security is an emotional topic, a valid argument would link specific policies to projected employment data. Lara offers no such link, relying solely on the threat.

assessment.identification_prompt: Lara paints a scary picture of the future. But does she provide any reason to believe her opponent's plan actually leads to those outcomes?

rubric.description: Feels immediate fear and agrees with Lara based on the scary outcome described.
Senses something is manipulative but cannot articulate why the argument is logically flawed.
Notices Lara didn't provide evidence for her claim about job losses, only fear.
Identifies that Lara is using fear to replace evidence, recognizing the appeal to emotion.
Clearly names the fallacy, explains the disconnect between the emotional threat and the lack of causal evidence, and distinguishes between legitimate concern and manipulative fear-mongering.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at the connection between 'voting for the opponent' and 'losing your job.' Did Lara explain the mechanism, or did she just tell you to be afraid?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. She substituted a frightening scenario for actual proof. Now, how would you rephrase her argument to make it logical if she actually had data to support her claim?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Populist agitator, dramatic, prone to hyperbole, manipulative.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: They want to take your bread! They want to see you in the streets! Will you stand for it?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player selects dialogue option to 'Demand Evidence' or 'Point out the Fear Tactic,' causing Lara to stutter or shift topics, gaining influence with the rational voter bloc.

scenario.context: The player enters the Grand Archives and finds Head Librarian Veritas arguing with a novice scribe. The Librarian is trying to justify ignoring specific historical warnings by using a clever but flawed generalization.
scenario.text: Veritas declares loudly: 'Historians agree that studying the past is the best way to avoid repeating mistakes. Therefore, if we simply study the past, we are guaranteed to avoid repeating mistakes.'
scenario.speaker_context: Head Librarian Veritas is a brilliant but arrogant scholar who often uses semantic shifts to win debates. Here, he shifts the meaning of 'best way' (an optimal method among many, not a guarantee) to imply 'sufficient condition' (a method that ensures the result).

structure.pattern_description: The argument relies on shifting the meaning of the phrase 'best way.' In the premise, 'best way' means the most effective method available, but it does not imply certainty or sufficiency. In the conclusion, the term is treated as if it means a 'guaranteed solution' or 'sufficient condition.'
structure.formal_form: Premise: Method M is the 'best way' (most effective) to achieve Result R. Conclusion: Using Method M ensures Result R. Error: Equating 'most effective' with 'sufficient/guaranteed'.
structure.why_wrong: The argument fails because being the 'best' method does not mean the method is foolproof. One can use the best available strategy and still fail due to unforeseen variables. The term 'best way' changes from a comparative ranking to an absolute guarantee.
structure.counterpoint: A similar equivocation occurs with the word 'safe.' 'This is the safest car' (relative safety) does not mean 'This car cannot be damaged in a crash' (absolute safety).

assessment.identification_prompt: Head Librarian Veritas claims that studying the past guarantees we won't repeat mistakes. Is his reasoning sound? Identify the word or phrase that changes meaning.

rubric.description: Player accepts the argument as true because the premise sounds reasonable.
Player suspects the conclusion is too strong but cannot identify the specific linguistic flaw.
Player identifies that 'best way' is the problematic phrase but cannot explain the shift in meaning.
Player explains that 'best way' means 'most effective' in the premise but is treated as 'guaranteed' in the conclusion.
Player fully articulates the equivocation, noting that an optimal method is not a sufficient condition, and provides a counter-example where the best method still fails.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If 'running' is the best way to catch a bus, does running guarantee you will catch it? What if the bus leaves early?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Veritas is conflating optimization with certainty. Just because a method is superior doesn't mean it is infallible.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Arrogant, pedantic, relies on semantic tricks to maintain authority.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Ah, you see through my little linguistic sleight of hand? Perhaps you are ready for the Advanced Logic Wing.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player corrects the Librarian's logic, causing him to concede the point and grant access to a restricted section of the library as a reward for critical thinking.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Veridia, a charismatic merchant named Silas is trying to sell a new type of 'luck-enhancing' amulet to a crowd of skeptical adventurers.
scenario.text: Silas holds up a shimmering amulet and declares, 'This type of ad taps into a person's desire to be part of a group. Look around! Every successful guild in the city has bought these. If you aren't wearing one, you're clearly not serious about your next quest. Join the majority and secure your fate!'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas offers no proof of the amulet's magical properties, relying entirely on the claim that 'everyone else' is buying them to pressure the listener into conformity.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition is true or good solely because many people believe it or are doing it. It treats popularity as a substitute for evidence.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The number of people who believe something has no logical bearing on its truth value. Popularity can be driven by social pressure, marketing, tradition, or mass error, none of which constitute factual evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Widespread adoption can sometimes indicate utility if independent agents converge on a solution after separate investigation, but mere conformity or marketing hype is not evidence of truth.

assessment.identification_prompt: What actual evidence does Silas provide that the amulet enhances luck? Is the fact that 'every successful guild' bought one a valid reason to believe it works?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; believes the amulet must work because so many guilds bought it.
Feels hesitant about the claim but cannot articulate why popularity is insufficient evidence.
Notes that Silas provided no technical proof but fails to identify the specific 'bandwagon' logical error.
Identifies that Silas uses the number of buyers as the sole evidence and explains that popularity does not establish truth.
Names the bandwagon fallacy, explains why popularity is not evidence, identifies the appeal to social pressure, and distinguishes between consensus and proof.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every person in the kingdom believed the sky was green, would that actually make the sky green?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'many people believe X' might actually be a reasonable (though not definitive) clue that X is worth investigating?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Silas is a fast-talking, high-energy merchant who thrives on FOMO (fear of missing out) and crowd dynamics. He speaks quickly and uses inclusive language like 'us' and 'the smart ones'.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't be the odd one out! The wise choose what the many choose!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully points out that guilds might just be following a trend rather than verifying magic, causing Silas to drop the act and offer a discount based on actual (albeit minor) features.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling market square of Veridia, where a charismatic street vendor named Silas is loudly promoting his wares to a crowd of skeptical townsfolk.
scenario.text: Silas holds up a tube of sparkling paste. 'Listen well, friends! Four out of five dentists recommend Happy Glossy Smiley toothpaste brand. Therefore, it must be great.'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas is using a statistic about a small sample of experts (five dentists) to make a universal claim about the absolute quality of the product for everyone, ignoring that 'four out of five' still implies one dissenting expert and that 'great' is a subjective conclusion not fully supported by a simple recommendation count.

structure.pattern_description: Silas takes a specific statistic (4/5 dentists recommend) and leaps to a broad, unqualified conclusion ('it must be great'). This ignores the sample size (only 5 dentists surveyed?), the possibility of bias in who was asked, and the fact that a 20% dissent rate suggests the product is not universally 'great'.
structure.formal_form: n members of sample S (where S is small or potentially biased) have property P. Therefore, all members of population U have property P (or U is entirely defined by P).
structure.why_wrong: The sample size of five dentists is too small to definitively prove the product is 'great' for the entire population. Furthermore, the conclusion ignores the 20% of dentists in the sample who did NOT recommend it, making the universal claim of greatness logically unsound.
structure.counterpoint: Statistics can be useful, but a small sample size (n=5) cannot support a definitive, universal qualitative judgment without more context about how those dentists were selected and what criteria they used.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas claims the toothpaste 'must be great' because four out of five dentists recommend it. Is this conclusion logically guaranteed by his evidence?

rubric.description: Player accepts Silas's claim immediately, believing the majority vote proves the product is great.
Player feels unsure but cannot identify the specific logical gap between the statistic and the conclusion.
Player notes that one dentist didn't recommend it, suggesting the product might not be perfect, but misses the sample size issue.
Player identifies that five dentists is a very small sample size and that '4 out of 5' does not equal 'universally great'.

Player explicitly identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a sample of five is insufficient for a universal claim and highlighting the ignored dissenting opinion as proof the conclusion is overstated.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Silas grins. 'See? The majority speaks! Why doubt the experts?' He tries to hand you a tube before you can ask how many dentists were actually surveyed.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: You point out that five people isn't enough to judge the whole world, and that one dentist said 'no.' Silas falters, his smile dropping. 'Well... statistics are tricky, aren't they? Perhaps I exaggerated slightly.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, fast-talking, slightly deceptive merchant who relies on soundbites rather than deep analysis.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't let the numbers fool you, friend; let the shine convince you!
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player challenges the logic, Silas offers a discount but admits his pitch was 'marketing flair.' If the player buys, they receive a mediocre item that wears off quickly.

scenario.context: The player is in the Academy of Reason, speaking with a nervous first-year student named Pip who is visibly holding himself and pacing near the lecture hall door.
scenario.text: Pip whispers frantically, 'If I go to the bathroom now, I will miss the notes. If I miss the notes, I'll do poorly on the test. If I do poorly on the test, I won't get into college. If I don't get into college, my life is over. So, I absolutely cannot go to the bathroom.'
scenario.speaker_context: Pip is experiencing extreme anxiety and has constructed a causal chain where a single minor action (using the restroom) inevitably leads to a catastrophic life outcome without any possibility of interruption or alternative outcomes.

structure.pattern_description: While often categorized as a Slippery Slope, in this specific taxonomy context, Pip is making a hasty generalization about the必然 nature of future events based on a single hypothetical instance. He assumes that missing one set of notes guarantees test failure, which guarantees college rejection, ignoring all other variables (studying later, asking friends, retaking tests, other colleges). He generalizes a worst-case sequence from a single potential event.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurs. Therefore, Sequence A -> B -> C -> D (catastrophe) will inevitably occur. Therefore, A must never happen.
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes a deterministic chain of negative events without evidence. Missing notes does not guarantee failing a test; failing a test does not guarantee college rejection. The sample size of 'one missed lecture' is insufficient to generalize about the entirety of one's academic future.
structure.counterpoint: Planning for consequences is rational, but assuming a single minor mistake leads inevitably to total ruin is a logical error. One can miss notes and still succeed through other means.

assessment.identification_prompt: Pip believes that going to the bathroom will inevitably ruin his entire life. Is his conclusion that he 'absolutely cannot go' justified by the evidence?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Pip and tells him to stay put to avoid ruining his life.
Player feels Pip is overreacting but cannot explain the logical flaw in the chain of events.
Player identifies that one step (missing notes) does not guarantee the next (failing), but misses the broader generalization issue.
Player identifies the flaw in the causal chain, noting that missing notes doesn't inevitably lead to life failure.

Player explicitly identifies the hasty generalization: Pip is generalizing a catastrophic life outcome from a single, manageable event, ignoring all mitigating factors and alternative paths to success.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if you miss one page of notes, is it truly impossible to ever get into college? Are there no other ways to learn the material?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Pip is taking one small possibility and generalizing it into an inevitable disaster. He's ignoring all the ways he could recover from missing a few minutes of class.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, high-strung, prone to catastrophizing, diligent but easily overwhelmed.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But what if the professor calls on me and I don't know the answer because I was in the stall? It's the start of the end!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Pip to take a bathroom break by listing three realistic ways he can catch up on missed notes, breaking the false causal chain.

scenario.context: The player enters the Alchemist's Guild hall where Elder Thorne is arguing with a group of apprentices about the dangers of new recreational substances.
scenario.text: Elder Thorne points a shaking finger at a poster of a cigarette. 'Mark my words! One cigarette will lead any youth straight to addiction. It is the first step on an inevitable path to ruin. If a young person tries even a single one, they are lost forever.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elder Thorne is a cautious traditionalist who fears change. He is taking the specific risk of one instance (trying one cigarette) and asserting a universal, inevitable outcome (addiction) for every single youth without evidence of probability or individual variance.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne claims that a single instance of behavior (smoking one cigarette) universally and inevitably leads to a specific extreme outcome (addiction) for all members of a group (youth). He ignores statistical reality, individual differences in physiology and willpower, and the distinction between possibility and certainty.
structure.formal_form: Instance X occurred for subject S. Therefore, for all subjects in population P, instance X will inevitably lead to outcome Y.
structure.why_wrong: The leap from 'one cigarette' to 'certain addiction' is unsupported. While addiction is a risk, stating it as an inevitable result of a single trial for every youth is a massive overgeneralization. It confuses a potential slippery slope with a guaranteed causal chain.
structure.counterpoint: While it is true that many addictions start with a first use, not every first use results in addiction. A valid argument would discuss increased risk or probability, not absolute inevitability based on a single data point.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elder Thorne claims that trying just one cigarette guarantees addiction for any youth. Is this conclusion logically sound based on the evidence provided?

rubric.description: Player accepts Thorne's warning as absolute fact and agrees that one cigarette guarantees ruin.
Player feels the statement is too strong but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Player identifies that not everyone who tries a cigarette becomes addicted, challenging the 'all' claim.
Player explicitly identifies the hasty generalization, noting that Thorne treats a possible outcome as an inevitable universal law based on insufficient evidence.
Player identifies the fallacy, explains the difference between risk and certainty, and suggests a more accurate probabilistic statement Thorne could have made.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne seems very certain. But think about people you know or stories you've heard: does everyone who tries something once immediately lose all control? What is the difference between 'can happen' and 'will happen'?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Thorne is letting fear drive his logic. He takes a real risk and exaggerates it into an absolute rule. How could he rephrase this to be truthful without lying about the certainty?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, dogmatic, well-meaning but prone to catastrophizing.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You don't understand the danger! It only takes one slip!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Thorne to update the guild's warning pamphlets to reflect 'high risk' rather than 'certain doom,' improving the guild's credibility with the youth.

scenario.context: The player enters the Guild Hall of Healing Arts to speak with Master Thorne, a senior alchemist known for his rigid adherence to tradition. He is arguing vehemently against a new bill that would allow licensed psychologists to prescribe medication.
scenario.text: If the government allows psychologists to prescribe medications, there will be no basis to block them from obtaining competence and legal authority to conduct other traditionally medical procedures such as diagnosing minor skin irritations, treating a sprained ankle, setting a broken bone, and even performing neurosurgery. Once we allow this first step, the floodgates will open to total medical chaos.
scenario.speaker_context: Master Thorne is using a slippery slope argument that relies on a hasty generalization. He assumes that granting one specific, limited authority (prescribing meds) automatically implies the ability and right to perform all possible medical procedures, ignoring the existence of regulatory boundaries, specialized training requirements, and legal distinctions between different medical acts.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne generalizes from a single permitted action (prescribing medication) to an extreme and unsupported conclusion (performing neurosurgery).
