He treats the entire spectrum of medical practice as a single, undifferentiated block, ignoring the vast differences in skill, training, and regulation required for each procedure. He assumes that because a boundary is moved once, no boundaries can exist.
structure.formal_form: Entity E is granted permission for action A1. Action A1 is part of the set of Medical Actions M. Therefore, Entity E must be granted permission for all actions in M, including the most extreme An.
structure.why_wrong: The argument fails because it ignores the specific criteria and limitations that distinguish different medical procedures. Granting permission for A1 does not logically necessitate granting permission for A2 through An. Regulatory bodies are perfectly capable of drawing lines between prescribing pills and performing brain surgery; the sample of 'one allowed action' is insufficient to prove that 'all actions will be allowed.'
structure.counterpoint: While it is valid to ask where the line will be drawn, assuming the line cannot be drawn at all based on a single change is a logical leap. Boundaries are successfully maintained in many professions where roles expand incrementally.

assessment.identification_prompt: Master Thorne claims that allowing psychologists to prescribe meds means they will soon be performing neurosurgery. Does the evidence support this extreme conclusion?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne, believing that any expansion of rights inevitably leads to total loss of control.
Player feels the conclusion is too extreme but cannot explain the logical gap between prescribing meds and surgery.
Player identifies that prescribing meds and performing surgery are different skills, but does not explicitly name the generalization error.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that Thorne assumes one small change proves all changes will happen without evidence of regulatory failure.

Player fully deconstructs the argument, noting that the set of 'medical procedures' is not a monolith, and that distinct licensing requirements prevent the slide from prescribing to neurosurgery, effectively refuting the generalization.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne seems very certain. But think about driving: if we allow someone to drive a car, does that mean they are automatically allowed to fly a jet? Why or why not?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Just because one door opens doesn't mean every door in the hallway falls off its hinges. Regulations can be specific.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Rigid, traditionalist, alarmist, protective of professional hierarchy.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It is the thin end of the wedge, I tell you! First pills, then bones, then brains! Where does it end?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can present a counter-example of a profession that expanded its scope (e.g., nurses gaining prescription rights) without descending into chaos, convincing Thorne to lower his hostility.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling mess hall of the Ironvale Academy. Helga, a health-conscious alchemist apprentice, is trying to warn her friend Hugh about his lunch choices. Hugh, a hearty blacksmith apprentice known for his large appetite, holds a greasy burger.
scenario.text: Helga: "You should not be eating that... it has been scientifically proven that eating fat burgers is no good for your health." Hugh: "You eat fat burgers all the time so that can't be true."
scenario.speaker_context: Hugh, a blacksmith apprentice who values practical experience over theory. He is defensive about his diet and often deflects criticism by pointing out the hypocrisy of others rather than addressing the argument itself.

structure.pattern_description: Hugh dismisses Helga's scientific claim about the health risks of fatty burgers not by refuting the evidence or the logic, but by pointing out that Helga herself engages in the same behavior. He treats her hypocrisy as proof that her claim is false.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X is bad/untrue. Person P does X (or has done X). Therefore, X is not bad/untrue (or P's claim is false).
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a claim (e.g., 'fatty burgers are unhealthy') is independent of the person making the claim. Even if Helga is a hypocrite for eating them, the scientific evidence regarding health risks remains valid. Hugh's response attacks the messenger's consistency rather than the message's content.
structure.counterpoint: Pointing out hypocrisy is relevant when assessing a person's credibility, moral authority, or right to preach, but it does not logically disprove the factual accuracy of their statement. If Helga said, 'I am a perfect health guru,' then her eating burgers would refute that specific claim about herself, but not the general health facts.

assessment.identification_prompt: Hugh seems to think he has won the argument by catching Helga in a contradiction. But does Helga eating burgers actually change the scientific facts about cholesterol and heart disease? What is Hugh really attacking here?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Hugh, believing that Helga's hypocrisy makes her statement false.
Player feels Hugh's response is unfair or mean but cannot explain the logical error.
Player identifies that Hugh is attacking Helga's behavior instead of her argument.
Player explains that the truth of the health claim exists independently of whether Helga follows her own advice.
Player explicitly names the 'Tu Quoque' fallacy and articulates that hypocrisy does not equal factual incorrectness.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a smoker tells you 'Smoking causes cancer,' is he lying just because he smokes? Or is the medical fact still true regardless of his habits?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Hugh committed the 'Tu Quoque' fallacy. He tried to invalidate the science by pointing out Helga's hypocrisy, but a hypocrite can still tell the truth.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, pragmatic, relies on 'common sense' and personal observation over book learning. Easily embarrassed when caught in bad habits.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't lecture me on health when I saw you finishing a second slice of cake yesterday!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to point out the logical flaw to help Helga defend her point, or side with Hugh to boost his morale but miss the learning opportunity. Choosing the logical path grants 'Logic Points' and improves Helga's trust.

scenario.context: The player stands in the town square of Oakhaven during a sudden downpour. A frustrated farmer named Silas is shouting at the local weather oracle, who looks dejected.
scenario.text: Silas points an accusing finger at the oracle. 'You predicted clear skies for all of May, yet it rained today! Obviously, you are completely unreliable and your forecasts are worthless garbage.'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas is angry because a single day of rain contradicted a monthly forecast. He is judging the oracle's entire professional reliability based on one data point (one day) out of roughly thirty, ignoring the complexity of weather prediction and the possibility that the rest of the month was accurate.

structure.pattern_description: Silas takes a single instance of an incorrect prediction (rain on one specific day in May) and extrapolates it to a universal conclusion about the oracle's character and professional capability ('completely unreliable', 'worthless garbage'). The sample size of one error is insufficient to invalidate an entire month of forecasting or a career.
structure.formal_form: Instance X from Population P has property Q (error). Therefore, all members of P (or the source of P) have property Q (total unreliability).
structure.why_wrong: One mistake does not prove total incompetence. Weather forecasting involves probabilities, and a single deviation from a prediction does not negate the accuracy of the other 29 days of May or the oracle's general skill. Silas is ignoring the base rate of success.
structure.counterpoint: While repeated failures would justify a claim of unreliability, a single data point is statistically insignificant for such a broad condemnation. Critical thinking requires evaluating the ratio of successes to failures, not just isolating a failure.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas claims the oracle is 'completely unreliable' because it rained on one day despite a forecast for clear skies. Is this conclusion supported by the evidence?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Silas that one mistake proves the oracle is worthless.
Player feels Silas is being too harsh but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Player notes that one day is not enough to judge the whole month.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a sample size of one error cannot support a universal claim about total unreliability.

Player provides a comprehensive critique: identifies the fallacy, explains the insufficiency of the sample size relative to the population (30 days), and suggests that reliability should be measured by overall accuracy rates rather than isolated incidents.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If a student gets one math problem wrong on a 50-question test, does that mean they know nothing about math? How is Silas making a similar leap?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Silas is letting his anger over one rainy day cloud his judgment of the oracle's overall performance. One data point rarely defines a whole set.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Silas is a pragmatic but short-tempered farmer who values results above nuance. He speaks loudly and uses absolute terms when frustrated.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! Don't defend him! One lie is all it takes to break trust. If he can't get May right, how can we trust him for harvest season?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can calm Silas by presenting the oracle's successful predictions for the rest of the month, unlocking a quest where the oracle helps predict a storm to save Silas's crops, redeeming his reputation.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Oakhaven, the player confronts a merchant known for dumping sick animals. When challenged on the rising number of stray dogs and cats suffering in the alleys, the merchant refuses to discuss his specific actions or legal responsibilities.
scenario.text: The merchant spits on the ground and gestures wildly at the shivering strays nearby. 'Thousands of pets are left homeless and hungry because lousy people turn them out on the streets instead of taking care of them! Look at their suffering! How can you stand there judging me when the world is so cruel?'
scenario.speaker_context: The merchant deflects blame for his own negligence by invoking general pity for the animals and guilt in the accuser, avoiding any admission of his specific role in the problem.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting an emotional response (pity for the animals, guilt for the observer) in place of addressing the factual claim regarding the speaker's own responsibility. The speaker shifts focus from 'who caused this' to 'how sad this is'.
structure.formal_form: Claim P (Speaker is responsible for harm) is challenged. Agent evokes Emotion F (pity/guilt) regarding the victims. Agent implies Claim P should be disregarded or that they are not at fault because Emotion F is so strong.
structure.why_wrong: The fact that many pets are suffering is tragic, but it does not logically prove or disprove whether this specific merchant contributed to the problem. The emotional weight of the suffering is irrelevant to the factual question of the merchant's specific actions.
structure.counterpoint: Compassion for the animals is valid and important, but it cannot serve as evidence to exonerate the merchant from the specific accusation of dumping pets.

assessment.identification_prompt: The merchant describes a terrible situation that makes you feel sad. But did he actually answer the question about whether he threw those pets out himself?

rubric.description: Feels overwhelmed by sadness for the animals and accepts the merchant's implication that the accuser is being cruel.
Feels conflicted; recognizes the animals are suffering but is unsure if the merchant's defense is logical.
Notices the merchant didn't deny dumping the pets, but struggles to articulate why the sadness of the situation doesn't excuse him.
Identifies that the merchant is using the tragedy of stray animals to distract from his own specific actions.
Explicitly names the appeal to emotion, separates the general tragedy from the specific accusation, and explains that pity does not equal innocence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside the sad sight of the stray animals for a moment. Regardless of how many are hungry, did the merchant say 'I did not throw them out' or 'I am not responsible'? Or did he just talk about how sad it is?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. The suffering of the animals is real, but the merchant used that suffering as a shield to avoid answering for his own choices. Compassion doesn't change the facts of who did what.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, performative, and manipulative; uses public sentiment as a weapon to avoid accountability.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: How dare you accuse me when there is so much suffering? Are you heartless?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must calmly restate the specific evidence against the merchant, acknowledging the tragedy but insisting it does not absolve him of the specific act of dumping pets.

scenario.context: Inside the bustling Town Square of Veridia, a heated trial is underway. The crowd is restless, and a prominent town crier named Silas is trying to sway the jury before evidence is presented.
scenario.text: Silas shouts to the assembled crowd: 'Everyone already believes that the defendant killed her husband, and that many people can't be wrong! Look at the faces around you; the whole town knows the truth.'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas is attempting to bypass factual evidence by leveraging the sheer volume of public opinion as proof of guilt.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true simply because a large number of people believe it or act upon it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe X. Therefore, X is true.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief does not determine its truth value. Large groups can be misinformed, biased, or manipulated. Truth depends on evidence and logic, not headcounts.
structure.counterpoint: While consensus among experts after rigorous independent verification can be strong evidence, mere popular opinion among the general public without such verification is not evidence of truth.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does Silas provide any actual evidence of the crime, or does he only cite the number of believers?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument; assumes the crowd cannot be wrong about the defendant's guilt.
Feels uncertain but cannot articulate why the crowd's size is irrelevant to the facts.
Notes that Silas didn't show physical evidence but fails to identify the specific logical error regarding popularity.
Identifies that Silas uses the number of believers as the sole proof and explains that popularity does not equal truth.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains the distinction between popular opinion and factual evidence, and notes how this tactic pressures the jury socially rather than logically.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every person in this square believed the sky was green, would that actually change the color of the sky?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a scenario where 'everyone believing something' might actually be a useful clue, even if it isn't absolute proof?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Boisterous, manipulative, and reliant on mob mentality. Silas speaks loudly and uses sweeping gestures to emphasize the crowd.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look around you! The whole town knows the truth!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a counter-argument highlighting that truth is based on evidence, not votes, causing Silas to lose credibility with the judge.

scenario.context: In the Grand Council Chamber of the Academy, High Councilor Vane argues against a proposed ban on violent simulation games for minors.
scenario.text: High Councilor Vane declares: 'Violent video games are directly related to gun violence in schools and should be banned for teens. Furthermore, the school day should start an hour later.'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane attempts to link two unrelated policy proposals. He implies that because banning games might have negative social consequences (or perhaps he is conflating the fear of violence with the need for later start times), the specific claim about the game-violence link must be accepted or acted upon without evidence, while simultaneously pivoting to an unrelated scheduling change to distract from the lack of causal proof.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a factual claim should be accepted or rejected, or a specific policy enacted, based solely on the desirability or undesirability of the outcome, rather than on evidence connecting the cause and effect.
structure.formal_form: If we do not accept claim P (or do action A), undesirable consequence C will occur. Therefore, P is true (or we must do A).
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a causal claim (games cause violence) depends on empirical evidence, not on how scary the potential outcome is. Similarly, the merit of starting school later is a separate issue; linking them without logical connection exploits fear rather than reason.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to consider consequences when making policy decisions. However, one must first establish that the cause-and-effect relationship is real before acting on it. Vane skips the evidence step entirely.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane paints a frightening picture of school violence and suggests a ban, then immediately jumps to changing school start times. Does the fear of violence prove that games are the cause, or that later start times are the solution?

rubric.description: Agrees with Vane completely; the risk of violence is too high to question the logic.
Feels something is off about connecting games to start times but cannot explain why.
Notices that Vane uses fear to push the ban but fails to separate the two distinct topics.
Identifies that Vane assumes the game-violence link is true because the consequence is bad, and that the start time is a non-sequitur.
Explicitly names the Appeal to Consequences and explains that the truth of the causal link requires data, not just fear of the outcome, and identifies the red herring of the school start time.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine a world where violent games had zero effect on behavior. Would Vane's argument for the ban still hold up if the only reason was 'we are scared'?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: How could the Council investigate the actual link between games and violence before deciding on a ban, separate from their feelings about school safety?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Alarmist, authoritative, prone to slippery slope arguments.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: We cannot risk our children's lives on a technicality! The danger is real, so the solution must be immediate!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present statistical data separating correlation from causation and demand a committee review for the start-time proposal independently.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Oakhaven, a street vendor named Silas is trying to sell a peculiar blue potion to a crowd of skeptical adventurers.
scenario.text: Silas holds up a vial of glowing blue liquid and shouts, 'Don't just stand there staring! Look at the line behind me! Everyone is doing it; every true hero in the kingdom is drinking this Stamina Elixir right now. If all these brave souls are buying it, it must be the real deal. You don't want to be the only one left without it, do you?'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas offers no ingredients list, no testimonials of actual performance, and no magical certification. His entire argument rests on the fact that many people are currently purchasing the item.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or an action correct solely because a large number of people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good/correct.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or action does not constitute evidence of its truth or value. Crowds can be mistaken, manipulated, or acting on incomplete information. Truth is determined by evidence and logic, not headcounts.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate utility (e.g., many people use a specific tool because it works), this is only valid if the adoption is based on independent verification. In this case, the crowd is likely following each other blindly, creating a feedback loop rather than providing evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: What actual evidence does Silas provide that the potion improves stamina? Is the fact that 'everyone is doing it' a valid reason to believe it works?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; believes the potion must work because so many people are buying it.
Feels unsure about the potion but cannot articulate why the crowd's behavior is not proof of quality.
Recognizes that Silas hasn't provided facts about the potion but fails to identify the specific logical error of appealing to popularity.
Identifies that Silas uses the crowd's actions as the sole evidence and explains that popularity does not guarantee truth or effectiveness.
Explicitly names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains the disconnect between popularity and evidence, and notes how social pressure is being used to bypass critical thinking.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in the village suddenly started jumping off the bridge, would that make it a safe thing to do?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing it' might actually be useful information, even if it's not logical proof?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, fast-talking, and slightly manipulative. He feeds off the energy of the crowd and uses FOMO (fear of missing out) as his primary sales tactic.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Come on, don't be the odd one out! The whole party is drinking it!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully points out that a crowd can be wrong, causing Silas to stammer and admit he has no proof, which disperses the crowd and reveals the potion is just colored water.

scenario.context: The player enters the Grand Confectionery Hall in the city-state of Helvetia. Master Chocolatier Gustav is proudly presenting his latest thesis to the Guild of Sweetmakers, pointing to a large mural depicting national statistics.
scenario.text: Master Gustav gestures grandly to the mural. 'Behold the miracle of our craft! Global chocolate consumption is highest right here in Switzerland, yet our people remain among the trimmest in the entire industrialized world. The data is undeniable. Therefore, it is perfectly reasonable to conclude that eating chocolate helps keep your weight down. We should encourage the kingdom to eat even more!'
scenario.speaker_context: Gustav is a passionate but logically flawed artisan. He observes a correlation between high chocolate consumption and low obesity rates in Switzerland but incorrectly infers that the former causes the latter. He ignores confounding variables such as the Swiss lifestyle, high levels of physical activity (hiking, skiing), portion control habits, or the fact that high consumption might be spread across a very active population.

structure.pattern_description: Gustav observes that two variables are correlated (high chocolate consumption and low average weight) and infers that one causes the other (chocolate causes weight loss). However, correlation does not establish causation. There are four possibilities: (1) chocolate causes weight loss, (2) being thin causes people to eat more chocolate, (3) a common cause drives both (e.g., an active lifestyle allows for higher caloric intake including chocolate while maintaining low weight), or (4) the correlation is coincidental. The fallacy lies in jumping to conclusion (1) without ruling out the others.
structure.formal_form: A and B are correlated. Therefore A causes B. (But: A could cause B, B could cause A, C could cause both, or the correlation could be coincidental.)
structure.why_wrong: Correlation between two variables does not establish that one causes the other. Gustav has not ruled out reverse causation, a common cause (like an active lifestyle or metabolic factors), or coincidence. Promoting chocolate consumption based solely on this correlation could lead to weight gain if the underlying confounding variables (like high activity levels) are not present in those who increase consumption.
structure.counterpoint: Correlations can be evidence for causation when combined with a plausible biological mechanism, temporal ordering, and elimination of confounders. The fallacy is in jumping directly from correlation to causation without doing that additional work. A classic counter-example: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents are highly correlated, but eating ice cream does not cause drowning; rather, hot weather (a common cause) increases both swimming and ice cream consumption.

assessment.identification_prompt: Master Gustav claims that because Switzerland has high chocolate consumption and low obesity rates, chocolate must cause weight loss. What is the logical flaw in his reasoning?

rubric.description: The player accepts Gustav's conclusion as true or fails to identify any logical issue.
The player suspects the conclusion is wrong but cannot explain why, or attributes it to 'chocolate being bad' without addressing the logic.
The player identifies that correlation does not equal causation but cannot offer alternative explanations for the data.
The player correctly identifies the false cause fallacy and suggests one plausible alternative explanation (e.g., active lifestyle).

The player fully deconstructs the argument, identifying the false cause fallacy, explaining why correlation is insufficient, and listing multiple confounding variables (lifestyle, portion control, metabolism) that better explain the trend.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Gustav beams, 'Exactly! More chocolate for everyone means a slimmer kingdom!' (The kingdom's health metrics begin to decline as citizens overindulge without the accompanying activity levels).
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Gustav pauses, stroking his chin. 'Hmm... perhaps it is not the cocoa itself, but the mountain hikes we take to burn it off? Or maybe we simply eat smaller portions of higher quality? I shall revise my thesis before presenting to the King.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Enthusiastic, proud, slightly dogmatic about his craft, but open to evidence if presented gently.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The data is undeniable! Look at the mural!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Gustav to investigate confounding variables before changing national dietary policy, preventing a public health decline.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling town square of Veridia as the evening news broadcast plays on a large public screen. Senator Halloway has just been accused of corruption and taking bribes by the news anchor. A crowd has gathered, murmuring about the scandal. Before the player can form an opinion, Councilor Vane steps forward to address the concerned citizens.
scenario.text: Councilor Vane raises his voice over the crowd. 'Do not believe a word of what you just heard! The senator is right to tell us that we should all be very wary of the things we hear in the media, because we all know how very unreliable the media can be.'
scenario.speaker_context: Councilor Vane, a staunch ally of Senator Halloway known for his defensive rhetoric and tendency to deflect criticism by attacking the messenger rather than addressing the message.

structure.pattern_description: Instead of addressing the specific evidence of corruption and bribery presented against the senator, Vane dismisses the accusation solely by attacking the source (the media). He argues that because the media is allegedly unreliable, the specific claims of corruption must be false, ignoring the substance of the accusation entirely.
structure.formal_form: Source S claims X (Senator is corrupt). Source S has property Q (Media is unreliable). Therefore, X is false.
structure.why_wrong: The reliability of a source in general does not automatically negate a specific claim without evidence. Even if the media is sometimes unreliable, the accusation of bribery requires a direct rebuttal regarding the evidence, finances, or conduct of the senator. Dismissing the claim based only on the source's identity avoids engaging with the actual argument.
structure.counterpoint: Questioning a source's credibility is valid if there is specific evidence of bias or error regarding the current claim. However, a blanket statement that 'media is unreliable' is insufficient to disprove a specific, serious allegation like bribery without further investigation into the facts.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane is quick to defend the senator, but look closely at his reasoning. Does he provide any evidence that the senator is innocent, or does he only talk about the news station?

rubric.description: Player accepts Vane's argument completely, believing the media is too unreliable to ever be trusted about corruption.
Player feels Vane is being defensive but cannot explain why his logic is flawed.
Player identifies that Vane is attacking the media instead of talking about the bribery accusations.
Player explains that the general unreliability of the media does not prove the senator is innocent of this specific crime.
Player articulates that Vane committed an ad hominem fallacy by dismissing the evidence of corruption solely based on the source, failing to address the substance of the bribery claims.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a known liar tells you the sky is blue, are they wrong about the sky? Can a flawed source still report a true fact?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Vane sidestepped the actual issue. To prove the senator's innocence, he needs to address the bribery evidence, not just insult the news station.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, loyal to a fault, uses deflection as a primary debate tactic.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think I don't know how the press works? They twist everything! Don't let them fool you into doubting our leader based on their lies!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player successfully points out the lack of direct evidence in Vane's defense, causing the crowd to demand a factual response regarding the bribery allegations rather than accepting the deflection.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Veridia, a street performer named Jax is trying to sell a mysterious 'Luck Stone' to a crowd of onlookers.
scenario.text: Jax holds up a dull gray rock and shouts, 'Don't just stand there staring! Look at this line! Hundreds of people have bought one today. If it didn't work, would all these folks be carrying them? No! Since everyone is buying it, it must be true that this stone brings great fortune. You don't want to be the only one missing out, do you?'
scenario.speaker_context: Jax relies entirely on the size of the crowd and the number of sales to prove the stone's magical properties, offering no actual demonstration or evidence of its power.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or a product must be effective simply because a large number of people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or action does not constitute logical evidence for its truth or efficacy. Crowds can be mistaken, manipulated, or acting on tradition rather than fact.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate quality (e.g., many experts agreeing after independent study), mere crowd behavior in a market setting is often driven by social pressure or hype, not verification.

assessment.identification_prompt: What specific proof does Jax offer that the stone actually brings luck? Is the fact that 'hundreds of people' bought it sufficient evidence?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; believes the stone must work because so many people bought it.
Feels unsure about the claim but cannot articulate why the crowd's behavior isn't proof.
Recognizes that Jax hasn't shown the stone working but fails to identify the flaw in using popularity as evidence.
Identifies that Jax uses the number of buyers as the sole proof and explains that popularity does not guarantee truth.
Explicitly names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains the difference between social proof and factual evidence, and notes the potential for mass error or manipulation.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every person in this town suddenly believed the sky was green, would that actually change the color of the sky?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing it' might actually be a useful piece of information, even if it's not logical proof?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, fast-talking, and slightly manipulative street performer who feeds off crowd energy.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look at this line! Hundreds of people have bought one today... it must be true!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player points out that a crowd can be wrong, causing Jax to lose his sales pitch momentum and admit he has no real proof, allowing the player to walk away without spending gold.

scenario.context: The player finds a nervous student named Leo pacing outside the Academy Library, muttering to himself before a major exam.
scenario.text: Leo wrings his hands. 'I am torn between studying for the quiz or not. But, I know that if I don't study for the quiz, I will fail. If I fail the quiz, I get a D in the class. If I get a D, it will lower my GPA. If my GPA lowers, I can't play football. If I can't play football, I don't get a scholarship. No scholarship, no college. No college, no life!'
scenario.speaker_context: Leo is catastrophizing a single potential event (failing one quiz) into an inevitable chain reaction that destroys his entire future. He assumes a single data point (one bad grade) guarantees a universal outcome (no life), ignoring all intermediate variables and possibilities for recovery.

structure.pattern_description: Leo takes one possible negative outcome (failing a quiz) and generalizes it to an absolute, unavoidable conclusion about his entire life trajectory. He treats a single event as a sufficient sample to predict a complex, multi-year future with 100% certainty, ignoring the vast number of other factors that influence GPA, scholarships, and life success.
structure.formal_form: Event X occurred (or might occur). Event X leads to Y. Y leads to Z... therefore, the ultimate catastrophic outcome Z_final is inevitable. (Treating a single link in a long causal chain as a deterministic predictor of the final outcome without evidence for the strength of each link).
structure.why_wrong: The argument assumes a rigid, unbreakable chain of causality based on a single hypothetical failure. It ignores mitigating factors (e.g., retaking the class, improving grades later, non-athletic scholarships, alternative career paths). One bad grade does not statistically guarantee 'no life'; the sample size of one event is insufficient to support such a massive generalization about one's entire future.
structure.counterpoint: While consequences are real, assuming a single mistake dictates an entire life story is a logical error. Probabilities exist at every step; failing a quiz lowers the probability of a perfect GPA, but it does not reduce the probability of a successful life to zero.

assessment.identification_prompt: Leo claims that failing one quiz will inevitably lead to having 'no life.' Is this conclusion logically supported by the evidence of a single quiz?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Leo, believing that one failed quiz definitely ruins everything.
Player feels Leo is being too dramatic but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Player identifies that the chain of events is unlikely but misses the specific generalization error.
Player identifies that Leo is making a huge generalization from a single event, noting that one grade doesn't determine the whole future.

Player explicitly identifies the hasty generalization/slippery slope, explains that the sample size (one quiz) is insufficient to predict a life outcome, and lists specific broken links in the causal chain (e.g., grade recovery, other scholarships).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: have you ever made a mistake before that didn't ruin your entire life? Does one bad moment really erase all future possibilities?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Leo is taking one small data point and blowing it up to cover his whole existence. There are many paths to success, and one quiz is just a tiny sample of his academic career.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, catastrophic thinker, prone to spiraling into panic over minor setbacks.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's over! One wrong answer and it's all downhill from here!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must help Leo list three alternative outcomes for each step in his chain (e.g., 'If I get a D, I can retake the class') to break the hasty generalization.

scenario.context: In the Grand Hall of the University of Aethelgard, a heated debate erupts regarding the new 'Mandatory Ether-Study' curriculum. A senior student representative stands before the council to justify the change.
scenario.text: We must adopt this curriculum immediately. Certainly this is the case at most colleges in America nowadays; if all those institutions have chosen this path, it must be the correct one for us too.
scenario.speaker_context: The speaker offers no data on student outcomes or curriculum quality, relying entirely on the fact that other colleges are doing it as proof of its validity.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition is true or a course of action is right solely because many people or institutions believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Most X do/believe Y. Therefore, Y is true/correct for us.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or practice does not constitute evidence of its truth or efficacy. Large groups can be mistaken, influenced by trends, or acting without sufficient information.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate a proven standard (e.g., safety protocols), it only becomes evidence if the adopters independently verified the results. Mere imitation is not verification.

assessment.identification_prompt: What specific evidence does the student provide that the new curriculum improves education? Is the fact that other colleges use it enough?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; assumes that because many colleges do it, it must be the best choice.
Feels unsure about the argument but cannot articulate why popularity is insufficient evidence.
Recognizes that no specific benefits of the curriculum were listed, but misses the logical flaw in using popularity as proof.
Identifies that the speaker uses the actions of other colleges as the sole proof and explains that popularity does not guarantee correctness.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that institutions can follow trends without evidence, and distinguishes between 'common practice' and 'proven efficacy'.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every college in the land suddenly decided to teach that the earth is flat, would that make it true?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing what other colleges do would actually be useful evidence, rather than just a popularity contest?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest but conformist student leader who fears being left behind by peer institutions. Speaks with confident repetition.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Everyone else is doing it! We can't be the only ones left out. It's the standard now!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must challenge the NPC to provide independent data on student success rates rather than citing enrollment statistics from other schools.

scenario.context: In the bustling trade hub of Oakhaven, the Merchant Guild is debating whether to invest in a new 'Motivation Protocol' for all warehouse staff. A junior advisor presents a case study to the Guild Master.
scenario.text: In a study designed by a famous academic to test the effects of pleasant imagery on motivation, employees were shown images of baby animals and beautiful nature scenes for their first five minutes at work. Amazingly, results showed a 10 percent leap in profits in the first quarter and record earnings over the course of a year. So, showing employees pleasant images is a great way to increase their motivation and improve productivity.
scenario.speaker_context: The 'famous academic' cited is Dr. Aris Thorne, a renowned expert in Medieval Literature and Art History. While famous in his field, he has no background in organizational psychology, behavioral economics, or statistical analysis of workplace productivity.

structure.pattern_description: The advisor accepts the conclusion about workplace productivity solely because a famous academic (an expert in literature/art) conducted the study, ignoring the mismatch between the academic's field of expertise and the subject matter.
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is expert in domain D. P is in domain D*. Therefore P is true. (But D ≠ D*.)
structure.why_wrong: Fame or expertise in one domain (Medieval Literature) does not grant automatic authority in an unrelated domain (Workplace Psychology/Profit Analysis). The validity of the study depends on its methodology, not the reputation of the author in an irrelevant field.
structure.counterpoint: Citing an authority is valid when the authority is an expert in the specific domain relevant to the claim. If Dr. Thorne were a leading organizational psychologist, this appeal would be reasonable.

assessment.identification_prompt: The advisor claims the protocol works because a 'famous academic' proved it. What specific type of academic is Dr. Thorne, and does that make him an expert on profit margins?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely because the source is described as a 'famous academic'.
Feels unsure but cannot identify why the academic's fame might be insufficient proof.
Notices the academic studies literature/art, not business, but struggles to explain why this invalidates the profit claim.
Identifies that the academic's expertise in literature does not translate to expertise in workplace psychology or economics.

Clearly names the Appeal to Irrelevant Authority fallacy, explains the domain mismatch between Art History and Profit Analysis, and notes that methodology matters more than the author's fame in this context.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If a famous chef told you how to fix a broken engine, would you trust them just because they are famous? How is this different?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Suppose the study was actually peer-reviewed by actual psychologists, but Dr. Thorne just funded it. Does his name still carry the same weight for the conclusion?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Eager but naive junior advisor who equates 'fame' with 'truth' and wants to impress the Guild Master with big names.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But Guild Master, Dr. Thorne is celebrated across three kingdoms! If he says baby pictures make gold coins appear, who are we to doubt a mind so brilliant?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out the specific field of Dr. Thorne's expertise to the Guild Master, prompting a request for a review by a qualified economist before approving the budget.

scenario.context: In the bustling town square of Veridia, a crowd has gathered around a soapbox orator named Silas who is rallying support for a new city ordinance.
scenario.text: Silas shouts to the growing crowd: 'We must pass this ordinance immediately! Look around you; everyone here agrees it is the right path. The whole town is behind this idea. When this many people think something should be done, it must be the correct choice. You don't want to be the only one standing against the will of the people, do you?'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas offers no specific benefits or data regarding the ordinance. His entire argument rests on the fact that the current crowd agrees with him, using social pressure and popularity as proof of correctness.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition must be true or good simply because a large number of people believe it or are doing it. It treats popularity as evidence of truth.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The number of people who believe something has no logical bearing on whether it is actually true or beneficial. Popularity can be driven by social pressure, misinformation, tradition, or mob mentality, none of which constitute factual evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Widespread consensus among independent experts after rigorous investigation can be meaningful evidence. However, this is distinct from a spontaneous crowd agreement or a appeal to general public opinion without underlying data.

assessment.identification_prompt: What actual evidence does Silas provide that the ordinance is good? Is the fact that 'everyone agrees' a valid reason to accept it?

rubric.description: Finds Silas convincing solely because a large crowd supports the idea.
Feels hesitant about the argument but cannot explain why popularity is insufficient evidence.
Notes that Silas provides no specific facts but fails to explicitly identify the appeal to popularity as the flaw.
Identifies that Silas uses the number of supporters as his sole evidence and explains that popularity does not establish truth.

Names the bandwagon fallacy, explains why popularity is not evidence, identifies the social pressure component ('don't want to be the only one'), and distinguishes between mob opinion and evidential convergence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Suppose every person in this square believed the sky was green. Would that make the sky actually green?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'many people believe X' might give you a reason to investigate X further, even if it doesn't prove X is true?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic but manipulative agitator who thrives on group dynamics and fears of exclusion.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Join the movement! Don't be left behind while the rest of us move forward!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out that Silas has offered zero facts about the ordinance itself, only an appeal to the crowd's size, causing the crowd to pause and demand actual details.

scenario.context: The party is traveling through the arid wastes of the Scorch. Rick, the group's pragmatic scout, is trying to make a quick decision about their schedule. Tina, a mage prone to dramatic interpretations, responds to his binary question.
scenario.text: Rick: 'I need to know if we should stop for lunch or not. You are either hungry or not hungry, which is it?' Tina: 'If being hungry is being able to eat, I am always hungry.'
scenario.speaker_context: Rick asked a simple binary question about current appetite to decide on a lunch break. Tina ignored the context of 'needing food now' and redefined 'hungry' as the abstract 'capacity to eat,' attacking a distorted version of Rick's premise rather than answering his actual question.

structure.pattern_description: Tina takes Rick's specific question about immediate physical need ('Are you hungry right now?') and replaces it with an extreme, abstract definition ('Are you capable of eating?'). She then answers this fabricated definition ('I am always hungry') instead of addressing Rick's actual inquiry.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (Are you currently in need of food?). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (Is the state of hunger defined as the ability to eat?). Person B attacks or answers P*. Person B concludes the interaction based on P*, ignoring P.
structure.why_wrong: Tina's response is irrelevant to Rick's decision-making process. By redefining 'hungry' to mean 'always able to eat,' she creates a straw man that makes her answer technically true but practically useless for deciding whether to stop for lunch.
structure.counterpoint: Rick could reply: 'I'm not asking about your theoretical capacity to eat, Tina. I'm asking if your stomach is growling right now so we know whether to unpack the rations.'

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Tina's response misrepresent Rick's question about stopping for lunch?

rubric.description: Player accepts Tina's answer as valid and misses the logical disconnect.
Player feels Tina's answer is unhelpful but cannot explain why logically.
Player notices Tina changed the definition of 'hungry' but does not identify it as a misrepresentation of Rick's intent.
Player identifies that Tina constructed a straw man by redefining 'hungry' as 'able to eat' to avoid answering the specific question about current appetite.
Player fully articulates that Tina attacked a distorted version of the premise (abstract capacity vs. immediate need) and explains how this derails the decision-making process.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at the definition of 'hungry' Rick implies versus the one Tina uses. Are they talking about the same thing?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Tina substituted a trivial truth (we can always eat) for the relevant fact (are we starving now?), creating a straw man to sidestep the decision.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Tina is intellectually agile but often uses semantic trickery to avoid mundane tasks or decisions she finds boring.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: If hunger is merely the potential for consumption, then I am a vessel of endless void!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must press Tina to answer the practical question ('Yes' or 'No' to lunch) by exposing her semantic shift, restoring the party's momentum.

scenario.context: In the Grand Library of Aethelgard, a heated debate erupts among scholars regarding the validity of the Ancient Migration Theory. A young scribe attempts to settle the argument by citing a famous figure.
scenario.text: Ross Geller, an evolutionary biologist and perhaps the foremost expert in the field, says that evolution is true. Therefore, it's true.
scenario.speaker_context: The speaker is a novice scribe who assumes that because Ross Geller is an expert in biology, his word alone proves the historical migration theory without needing evidence specific to archaeology or history.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker asserts a claim is true solely because an expert in a related but distinct field (biology) says so, ignoring the need for evidence specific to the claim's actual domain (historical migration).
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is expert in domain D. P is in domain D*. Therefore P is true. (But D ≠ D* or evidence is missing).
structure.why_wrong: Expertise in one scientific domain (biology/evolution) does not automatically validate claims in a different domain (historical migration patterns) without specific evidence. The truth of a claim depends on evidence, not just the status of the person stating it.
structure.counterpoint: Citing an authority is valid when they are a genuine expert in the specific field relevant to the claim and when their consensus reflects the current evidence. The fallacy occurs when the authority is irrelevant or when their word replaces evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: The scribe claims the theory is true just because Ross Geller said so. Is Ross Geller an expert in the specific field required to prove this historical theory?

rubric.description: Accepts the claim immediately because Ross Geller is an expert.
Feels unsure but cannot identify why the expert's opinion might not be enough.
Notices Ross is a biologist but doesn't explain why that matters for a history theory.
Identifies that biology expertise does not automatically prove historical migration theories.
Clearly explains the domain mismatch between evolutionary biology and historical archaeology, noting that evidence is needed regardless of the speaker's fame.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If a famous chef said a specific medicine cures headaches, would you take it just because they are a famous chef?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Even experts must provide evidence relevant to the specific question. How could the scribe ask for that evidence instead of just accepting the name?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest but naive; tends to rely on fame and titles rather than digging into primary sources.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But everyone knows Ross Geller! He wrote the book on bones! If he says it happened, it happened!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Guide the scribe to consult the Archaeology Guild records or ask for fossil evidence linking the migration to the biological data.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Oakhaven, a heated debate erupts near the fountain regarding the proposed ban on single-use plastic bags. A local merchant has just presented a detailed report on environmental impact and cost-effective alternatives. Before the crowd can discuss the merits of the report, a rival trader steps forward to shut down the conversation.
scenario.text: Why should we listen to his proposal on banning plastic bags, rather than considering the content of what the person is saying? He's just a teenager who still lives with his parents and has never run a real business in his life!
scenario.speaker_context: Barnaby Thorne, a gruff, older shopkeeper who feels threatened by new ideas. He relies on tradition and often dismisses younger voices by attacking their age and experience rather than their arguments.

structure.pattern_description: Barnaby rejects the proposal to ban plastic bags solely by attacking the proposer's personal circumstances (age, living situation, lack of business ownership) instead of addressing the environmental data or economic alternatives presented in the report.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P has property Q (irrelevant to the truth of X). Therefore, X is false or should be ignored.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of an argument depends on its evidence and logic, not the characteristics of the person presenting it. A teenager can present accurate data about plastic pollution just as well as an experienced CEO. Barnaby provides no counter-evidence to the report itself.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if the argument explicitly relies on the speaker's authority or specific experience as a premise (e.g., 'You should trust my advice on farming because I have farmed for 40 years'). In this case, the argument was about environmental facts, not the speaker's personal authority.

assessment.identification_prompt: Barnaby is very focused on who is speaking. Look closely at his words: does he mention any facts from the report, or does he only talk about the speaker's background?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Barnaby, believing the speaker's age invalidates the proposal.
Player feels Barnaby is being mean or unfair but cannot identify the logical error.
Player identifies that Barnaby is attacking the person instead of the argument but cannot name the fallacy.
Player correctly identifies the ad hominem fallacy and explains that the speaker's age is irrelevant to the environmental data.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, explains why the personal attack fails logically, and demands evidence regarding the plastic ban itself.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if a child told you the stove was hot, would you ignore them just because they are a child? What matters is whether the stove is actually hot, not who says it.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Barnaby tried to distract everyone from the actual evidence by focusing on the speaker's age. That is a classic Ad Hominem attack.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Grumpy, traditionalist, defensive of the status quo, dismissive of youth.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Back in my day, we didn't need fancy reports from kids to know what's good for business!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must choose a dialogue option that redirects the crowd's attention back to the specific data points in the merchant's report, forcing Barnaby to address the facts or look foolish.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Veridia, the player encounters a heated debate near the town fountain. A wealthy merchant is arguing against a recent proposal to fund a dangerous ice-rescue mission for two trapped whales.
scenario.text: It is ridiculous to have spent thousands of dollars to rescue two whales trapped in the ice. Why, look at all the people trapped in jobs they don't like.
scenario.speaker_context: The merchant, Lord Vane, does not address the ecological value of the whales, the success probability of the rescue, or the budget specifics. Instead, he argues the rescue effort is 'ridiculous' (false/wrong) solely because pointing out this expenditure highlights the unpleasant reality of human labor dissatisfaction.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a factual claim or proposed action should be rejected because accepting it would lead to undesirable psychological or social outcomes, rather than addressing the merit of the claim itself.
structure.formal_form: Accepting Claim P (or doing Action A) highlights undesirable consequence C. Therefore, P is false (or A is ridiculous).
structure.why_wrong: The validity of a rescue mission or the truth of a statement does not depend on whether acknowledging it makes us feel uncomfortable about other unrelated problems (like bad jobs). The existence of one problem does not negate the importance of solving another.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to compare budget priorities (opportunity cost), but Vane is not arguing about the budget; he is dismissing the whale rescue as 'ridiculous' because thinking about it makes us sad about human jobs. The emotional consequence of the thought does not change the factual value of the whales or the rescue.

assessment.identification_prompt: Lord Vane claims the whale rescue is ridiculous. Is he giving a reason why the rescue itself is bad, or is he just pointing out a sad fact about human jobs?

rubric.description: Agrees with Vane; believes the sadness of human jobs makes the whale rescue worthless.
Feels the argument is unfair but cannot explain the logical disconnect.
Notices Vane is talking about human jobs instead of the whales or the cost.
Identifies that Vane is rejecting the rescue based on the uncomfortable feeling it causes regarding other issues.
Names the appeal to consequences and explains that the existence of human suffering does not logically invalidate the value of saving whales.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If nobody had bad jobs, would the whale rescue suddenly become a good idea? If not, then the jobs aren't the real reason the rescue is 'ridiculous'.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Vane is using the pain of one problem to distract from solving another. Can you think of a time when someone dismissed a small kindness because 'bigger problems exist'?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Cynical, pragmatic, dismissive of emotional causes, focuses on harsh realities.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't get sentimental. Look at the real tragedy right here in the streets.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player points out that two wrongs (bad jobs and ignoring whales) don't make a right, or that solving one problem doesn't require ignoring others.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling courtyard of the Academy of Reason. Two students, Elara and Kael, are debating the proposed curriculum changes. Elara has just presented a well-researched argument citing historical data and student performance metrics to support her view that coding should be mandatory. Kael, looking frustrated that he cannot refute her data, turns to address the crowd and the player directly.
scenario.text: Kael crosses his arms and sneers, 'You are clearly just too young to understand this issue! Your brain hasn't even finished developing, so your opinion on curriculum reform is worthless.'
scenario.speaker_context: Kael, a senior student known for his arrogance and reliance on status rather than evidence. He often feels threatened by younger students who outperform him academically.

structure.pattern_description: Kael dismisses Elara's argument solely based on her age ('too young', 'brain hasn't finished developing'). He attacks her personal characteristic (youth) instead of addressing the historical data or performance metrics she presented.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P has property Q (age/youth). Therefore, X is false or P's claim should be dismissed.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of an argument depends on the evidence and logic provided, not the age of the person presenting it. A young person can present valid data and sound reasoning. Kael provides no counter-evidence to Elara's points; he merely insults her demographic.
structure.counterpoint: Age might be relevant if the argument specifically relied on life experience that a young person objectively could not have (e.g., 'I remember when this law was passed'). However, Elara's argument was based on general data and logic, which are accessible regardless of age.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kael seems very confident in his dismissal. But look closely: did he mention any of the data Elara shared? What specific reason does he give for ignoring her argument?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael, believing age invalidates the argument.
Player feels Kael is being mean or unfair but cannot explain the logical error.
Player identifies that Kael is attacking Elara's age instead of her points.
Player explains that the truth of the claim is independent of the speaker's age.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, noting that Kael offered zero counter-evidence to the data presented.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if a child correctly states that 2+2=4, is the math wrong because they are a child? How does that apply here?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Kael tried to win by attacking the messenger rather than the message. Elara's data stands until someone disproves the data itself.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Arrogant, defensive, relies on social hierarchy and intimidation rather than intellect.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't lecture me, kid. You haven't lived enough life to know better.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player successfully points out the irrelevance of age to the data, causing Kael to stammer and retreat, while Elara gains respect from the crowd.

scenario.context: In the bustling tech district of Neo-Veridia, a street vendor named Jax is aggressively marketing the latest 'OmniPhone X' just before its official release.
scenario.text: Jax gestures to a massive crowd forming around his stall: 'Look at this line! Everyone is buying the new iPhone that's coming out this weekend. You have to buy it too. Don't be the only one left behind with an old model when the whole world is upgrading.'
scenario.speaker_context: Jax relies entirely on the visual of the crowd and the fear of missing out to drive sales, offering no technical specifications or reasons why the phone is actually better.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition is true or an action is correct solely because a large number of people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people are doing X. Therefore, you should do X / X is the right choice.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of an action or belief does not constitute evidence of its truth, quality, or suitability for an individual. Crowds can be mistaken, manipulated by marketing, or acting on social pressure rather than rational evaluation.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate reliability (e.g., a safety standard adopted by all experts after rigorous testing), mere consumer trends driven by hype do not provide logical justification for purchase.

assessment.identification_prompt: What specific reasons does Jax give for why the phone is good? Is the fact that 'everyone is buying it' a valid reason for you to buy it?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; believes the phone must be good because the crowd is buying it.
Feels pressured to agree but cannot articulate why the crowd's behavior isn't a logical reason.
Recognizes that Jax didn't list any features but fails to explicitly identify the 'everyone is doing it' flaw.
Identifies that Jax uses the crowd size as the only evidence and states that popularity does not prove quality.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that popularity is not evidence of merit, and notes the emotional manipulation (fear of missing out) used by the speaker.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in the city suddenly started jumping off a bridge, would that make it a safe or smart thing for you to do?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing something' actually is a good reason to do it yourself?

game_hooks.npc_personality: High-energy, fast-talking street hustler who feeds off crowd momentum and uses FOMO (fear of missing out) as a primary weapon.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't let the line move without you! Join the revolution!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully points out that a crowd doesn't equal quality, causing Jax to stutter and eventually admit he hasn't even used the phone himself, breaking the spell over the nearby NPCs.

scenario.context: In the bustling guild hall of Oakhaven, the project lead Barbara has proposed a risky new marketing strategy. The team is hesitant, and tensions are high as the deadline approaches.
scenario.text: Barbara crosses her arms and stares down the team. 'Look, we can either agree with my plan right now, or we can just let the entire project fail. There is no other option on the table.'
scenario.speaker_context: Barbara, a high-pressure project manager who equates disagreement with sabotage and often uses ultimatums to force compliance.

structure.pattern_description: A disjunction is presented as exhaustive when it is not. Barbara forces a choice between total agreement with her specific plan or total project failure, ignoring alternatives like modifying the plan, seeking external consultation, extending the deadline, or testing a hybrid approach.
structure.formal_form: A v B, ~A, therefore B. But the real situation is A v B v C v D..., so ~A does not entail B.
structure.why_wrong: Barbara presents only two options — agree or fail — but the disjunction does not exhaust the relevant space. Multiple unmentioned alternatives exist, such as negotiating changes to the plan or finding a compromise.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or is a false dichotomy. Sometimes the options genuinely are exhaustive (e.g., 'The light is either on or off'). The critical question is whether the disjunction covers the full space of relevant possibilities in this specific context.

assessment.identification_prompt: Barbara claims you must either accept her plan exactly as is or let the project fail. What is logically flawed about how she has framed this choice?

rubric.description: Accepts the framing as true or responds only with emotional agreement/disagreement.
Senses something is unfair or too extreme but cannot articulate the logical error.
Identifies that other options exist (like changing the plan) but does not name the fallacy or explain the structural error.
Names the false dichotomy and provides at least one concrete alternative to the two options presented.

Explains that the disjunction is not exhaustive, names the fallacy, offers multiple alternatives, and notes that disjunctive syllogism only works when the initial 'either/or' covers all possible cases.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Barbara gave you exactly two paths. Are those really the only two things the team could do? Try to think of a third possibility that isn't 'agree completely' or 'fail completely'.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Under what conditions would an either/or framing actually be legitimate in a project meeting? Can you think of a scenario where there truly are only two options?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Authoritarian, impatient, and prone to catastrophizing; she views nuance as weakness.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Stop wasting time with 'what ifs'. It's my way or the highway. Choose now.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully identifies a middle-ground solution (e.g., a pilot test of Barbara's plan), de-escalating the tension and proving that the 'failure' outcome was not inevitable.

scenario.context: The player enters the smoky back room of the Rusty Anchor tavern, where an old sailor named Captain Hargrove is holding court. He is coughing heavily but waving away concerns from a young apprentice.
scenario.text: Hargrove takes a long drag from his pipe and gestures with it emphatically. 'Don't listen to the healers, boy. I've smoked this blend every day for sixty years, and look at me! I haven't got a hint of lung cancer. Therefore, smoking doesn't cause lung cancer. It's all a myth invented by the tea merchants.'
scenario.speaker_context: Captain Hargrove is using his own single data point (his personal health despite heavy smoking) to make a universal claim about the safety of smoking for everyone, ignoring statistical evidence and the possibility that he is a statistical outlier.

structure.pattern_description: Hargrove draws a universal conclusion ('smoking doesn't cause lung cancer') based on a sample size of one (himself). He ignores the vast amount of contrary evidence and the fact that one survivor does not disprove a statistical trend.
structure.formal_form: Instance X has property P (survived without cancer) despite condition C (smoking). Therefore, condition C never leads to not-P (cancer) for any instance.
structure.why_wrong: A single anecdote cannot override large-scale statistical data. The fact that one person survived does not mean the risk does not exist; Hargrove may simply be lucky or have unique genetic factors. Generalizing from n=1 to 'all people' is logically invalid.
structure.counterpoint: Anecdotal evidence can be a starting point for investigation, but it is insufficient to establish a universal rule or disprove a well-supported statistical correlation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Captain Hargrove claims smoking is safe because he hasn't gotten sick. Is his personal experience enough to prove that smoking never causes cancer?

rubric.description: Player accepts Hargrove's argument as true because he is an experienced sailor.
Player doubts the claim but cannot explain the logical flaw, perhaps just citing authority figures instead.
Player notes that one person's experience might not apply to everyone but lacks specific terminology.
Player identifies the error as generalizing from a single case (n=1) and explains that outliers do not disprove trends.
Player explicitly names 'Hasty Generalization,' explains the difference between anecdotal and statistical evidence, and notes the possibility of survivorship bias.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Hargrove nods sagely. 'Exactly! You have sense, unlike those frightened rabbits in the medical tent.'
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Hargrove pauses, coughs, and frowns. 'Well... I suppose I am just one old salt. Maybe the odds are against the others, even if they weren't against me.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Stubborn, charismatic, relies on tradition and personal grit over science, dismissive of 'book learning'.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Bah! Statistics are for cowards who can't trust their own eyes!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Hargrove to visit the town healer for a check-up by acknowledging his luck while explaining the risk to others.

scenario.context: The player enters the Grand Hall of Carnivora, where High Steward Gorm is addressing a crowd of hesitant citizens regarding the rising popularity of plant-based diets.
scenario.text: There is a strong movement of people who choose not to consume meat, citing reasons ranging from health benefits to achieving an ideal physique. This is a ludicrous idea. Human beings have consumed meat for thousands of years without severe problems, provided it is eaten in appropriate amounts. Many claim that being vegan leads to a healthier, stronger body and mind. Actually, studies show our bodies are perfectly capable of digesting and utilizing nutrients found in animal foods. Thus, there is no health reason to completely avoid animal foods. Do not put unnecessary restraints on yourselves. You should enjoy life to the fullest and consume meat.
scenario.speaker_context: High Steward Gorm observes that humans have historically eaten meat and remained healthy. He incorrectly concludes that because meat consumption preceded current health in the population, meat is the sole cause of that health, and conversely, that avoiding meat (veganism) must therefore be unhealthy or unnecessary. He ignores other factors like modern medicine, varied diets, and the fact that correlation (history of meat eating) does not prove causation (meat is required for health).

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Post hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Gorm argues that because humans have eaten meat for thousands of years and survived/thrived, meat consumption is the cause of that thriving, and therefore avoiding it is wrong. This assumes that temporal precedence or historical correlation implies direct causation, ignoring that humans could thrive for other reasons or that meat might be incidental rather than causal to the specific health outcomes mentioned.
structure.formal_form: Event A (eating meat) has historically occurred alongside Event B (human survival/health). Therefore, A causes B, and not-A must cause not-B (unhealth).
structure.why_wrong: The argument commits the false cause fallacy by assuming that because two things happened together over time (meat consumption and human existence), one caused the other. It fails to consider that humans might be healthy due to other factors (clean water, shelter, varied diet including plants) and that the absence of meat does not logically necessitate poor health. It also ignores evidence that specific health benefits can be achieved through vegan diets.
structure.counterpoint: Just because humans have done something for a long time doesn't mean it is the sole cause of their success, nor that stopping it causes failure. For example, humans wore animal skins for thousands of years, but stopping that practice hasn't made us freeze to death because we developed other solutions. Similarly, health is multifactorial.

assessment.identification_prompt: High Steward Gorm claims that because humans have eaten meat for thousands of years without issue, avoiding meat must be unhealthy and unnecessary. What logical error is he making regarding the relationship between history and health?

rubric.description: The player accepts Gorm's argument as fact without questioning the link between history and health.
The player suspects the argument is weak but cannot identify the specific logical flaw.
The player identifies that Gorm is making an assumption about health based on history but mislabels the fallacy.
The player correctly identifies that Gorm assumes causation from correlation/history (False Cause) but misses the nuance of ignoring alternative causes.

The player fully explains that Gorm commits the False Cause fallacy by assuming historical meat consumption caused human health, ignoring that health is multifactorial and that avoiding meat does not logically lead to poor health.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Gorm insists, 'It is simple history! We ate meat, we survived. You stop eating meat, you break the chain of survival!' Consider: Did eating meat *cause* survival, or were there other factors? Could one survive without it?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because two things happen together over time doesn't mean one causes the other. Gorm ignores the possibility that humans thrived due to many factors, not just meat, and that a vegan diet can also support health.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Traditionalist, loud, confident, relies heavily on 'the way things have always been' rather than data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't let these new-fangled ideas starve you! The ancestors ate meat and lived to be giants!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Gorm that health is complex by presenting evidence of healthy vegan athletes or historical populations that thrived on plant-based diets, breaking his false causal link.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling hallway of Oakhaven High during a student council meeting. A group of students is debating a proposal to allow cell phones in the cafeteria for educational research. Jamie, a sophomore known for organizing successful charity drives, has just presented a slide deck showing how phones could access digital textbooks and nutrition facts instantly.
scenario.text: Brad, a senior who prides himself on 'old school' rules, crosses his arms and sneers. 'Students who want cell phones in school have no idea what they're talking about. They're just distracted kids who can't focus for five minutes without scrolling.'
scenario.speaker_context: Brad, a senior student council member who often dismisses underclassmen ideas. He values tradition and frequently attributes negative motives to younger students without engaging with their specific proposals.

structure.pattern_description: Brad attacks the character and mental state of the students ('distracted kids', 'can't focus') rather than addressing Jamie's specific argument about using phones for digital textbooks and nutrition research. He assumes their identity as students automatically invalidates their knowledge.
structure.formal_form: Person P (students) claims X (phones are useful for learning). Person P has property Q (being distracted kids). Therefore, P has no idea what they are talking about and X is false.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of the proposal depends on the evidence presented (access to textbooks, nutrition data), not on the general behavior of students. Even if some students are distracted, it does not logically follow that the specific educational use case proposed is invalid or that the proponents lack understanding.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if the argument relies entirely on the person's authority or testimony.
