game_hooks.resolution_path: Player can use logic to calm Silas down, potentially gaining a discount on future items as an apology, or choose to leave the shop angrily.

scenario.context: The player enters the Grand Hall of the Capital, where a traveling merchant named Silas is arguing with a group of poor petitioners near the throne room entrance.
scenario.text: Silas gestures broadly at the golden pillars. 'Look at this place! The United States is the wealthiest nation in the world. So every American is wealthy. Why should I spare a single copper for you beggars when your entire countrymen swim in gold?'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas is using the macroeconomic status of the United States (the wealthiest nation) to make an immediate, universal claim about the financial status of every individual citizen, ignoring income inequality and poverty within the nation.

structure.pattern_description: Silas takes a property of the whole (the nation's aggregate wealth) and incorrectly applies it to every single part (every individual American) without evidence. He assumes that because the average or total is high, there are no exceptions, which is a classic hasty generalization based on insufficient sampling of the population's diversity.
structure.formal_form: Population P has property Q (high aggregate wealth). Individual X is a member of P. Therefore, Individual X has property Q (is wealthy).
structure.why_wrong: Aggregate statistics do not guarantee individual outcomes. A nation can be the wealthiest in the world while still containing millions of citizens living in poverty. The sample size of 'the nation' does not justify a claim about 'every single person' without accounting for distribution.
structure.counterpoint: While it is statistically more likely for a random American to be wealthier than a random citizen of a poorer nation, it is logically invalid to claim that *every* American is wealthy. Generalizations about averages cannot be applied universally to individuals.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas claims that because the US is the wealthiest nation, every American must be wealthy. Is this conclusion logically sound based on his premise?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Silas, accepting that national wealth guarantees individual wealth.
Player feels something is wrong but cannot explain the difference between national averages and individual reality.
Player identifies that not everyone is rich but fails to name the logical error or explain the sample size issue.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a national average does not apply to every single individual.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, noting the difference between aggregate data and individual distribution, and provides a counter-example (e.g., homeless populations in wealthy nations).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if a classroom has the highest average test score in the school, does that mean every single student got an A?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because the 'pie' is big doesn't mean everyone gets a large slice. Silas is ignoring the distribution of wealth.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Arrogant, materialistic, and dismissive of the poor; believes money equates to moral worth.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't tell me about hardship! Your country prints money like water!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Silas that his generalization is flawed to unlock a donation from him, or expose his logic to the petitioners to boost their morale.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling cafeteria of the Academy of Reason. A student named Jack is leaning over a trash bin, looking visibly ill, while his friend Milo stands nearby holding an empty bag of spicy snacks.
scenario.text: Milo points accusingly at the empty bag of Hot Cheetos in Jack's hand and declares to the room, 'Everyone look! Jack threw up immediately after he ate those Hot Cheetos. It is a scientific fact: eating Hot Cheetos causes vomiting. We must ban them from the cafeteria before everyone gets sick!'
scenario.speaker_context: Milo observed two events happening in sequence (eating snacks, then vomiting) and immediately concluded the first caused the second. He ignores other possibilities, such as Jack having a stomach virus, eating something else earlier, or having a sensitive stomach unrelated to the specific brand of snack. The temporal proximity does not prove causation.

structure.pattern_description: Milo observes that Event B (vomiting) occurred after Event A (eating Hot Cheetos) and infers that A caused B. This is the 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' (after this, therefore because of this) error. He fails to consider alternative explanations like coincidence, a common cause (e.g., a bug going around), or reverse causality (though less likely here, the logic holds that sequence != cause).
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred. Event B occurred after A. Therefore, A caused B. (Flaw: Temporal sequence does not establish causal mechanism; confounding variables or coincidence are ignored.)
structure.why_wrong: Just because one event follows another does not mean the first caused the second. Milo has not ruled out that Jack was already sick, ate something else, or that the vomiting was coincidental. Banning the snacks based on a single data point without establishing a mechanism is irrational.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one needs more than just temporal order. We would need to see a consistent pattern across many subjects, a plausible biological mechanism, and the elimination of other variables (e.g., did others who ate the Cheetos get sick? Did Jack eat anything else?).

assessment.identification_prompt: Analyze Milo's argument. Does the fact that Jack got sick after eating the snacks prove the snacks made him sick? Identify the logical flaw in jumping from sequence to cause.

rubric.description: Fails to identify any logical error; agrees that the snacks definitely caused the vomiting solely because of the timing.
Suspects the logic is weak but cannot articulate why; vaguely suggests it might be a coincidence.
Identifies that sequence does not equal cause but offers limited alternative explanations.
Clearly identifies the 'post hoc' fallacy and lists at least two plausible alternative causes (e.g., virus, other food).

Masterfully deconstructs the argument, explaining why temporal proximity is insufficient for causation and outlining the specific evidence needed to prove Milo's claim (mechanism, sample size, controls).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If you sneeze after seeing a bright light, does the light cause the sneeze every time? Or could you just have a cold? What other reasons might Jack be sick?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Correlation in time is not causation. To prove the Cheetos are the culprit, we'd need to see if other students who ate them also got sick, or if Jack has eaten them before without issue.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Milo is an anxious, overzealous safety monitor who jumps to conclusions quickly to 'protect' others, often causing unnecessary panic.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's obvious! A ate, then B happened! We must act now before the whole school collapses!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player calms the cafeteria by pointing out alternative causes for Jack's illness, preventing an unjust ban on Hot Cheetos and teaching Milo to seek evidence before blaming.

scenario.context: The player stands in the muddy courtyard of the Ironhold Barracks. Sergeant Kael is reviewing the conduct of Private John, a soldier who has repeatedly been caught sleeping on watch and neglecting his equipment. The Captain asks for a recommendation on whether John can be rehabilitated through extra training.
scenario.text: Sergeant Kael spits on the ground and shakes his head. 'Did John ever give up his bad habits? No, because he is simply a lazy good-for-nothing. You cannot teach discipline to a slacker like him. He is a lost cause and a stain on this unit.'
scenario.speaker_context: Kael does not cite specific recent incidents, analyze the root causes of John's behavior, or evaluate the potential success of a training regimen. Instead, he applies global negative labels ('lazy,' 'good-for-nothing,' 'slacker,' 'lost cause') to John's character to dismiss the possibility of improvement without engaging with the actual question of habit change.

structure.pattern_description: Kael substitutes negative character labels for a substantive assessment of John's behavior or potential. Rather than addressing whether John's habits have changed or if training could work, he attaches dismissive terms to John to justify rejecting the proposal for rehabilitation. The labels serve as a shortcut to condemnation, bypassing evidence.
structure.formal_form: Question Q asks about the status or change of Subject S. Critic attaches negative label L to S. Critic concludes the answer to Q is negative based solely on L, without examining evidence of S's current state or actions.
structure.why_wrong: Labels are static judgments, not dynamic analyses. Calling someone a 'slacker' describes a perceived trait but does not prove that specific habits cannot be changed or that recent efforts have failed. It assumes the conclusion (that John cannot improve) by defining John as inherently flawed, ignoring the possibility of growth or context.
structure.counterpoint: Character assessments are valid when based on a consistent, long-term pattern of behavior directly relevant to the task. The fallacy occurs when a label is used as a conversation-stopper to avoid analyzing specific evidence of change or the feasibility of a proposed solution.

assessment.identification_prompt: Sergeant Kael seems certain that John cannot change. But look closely at his reasoning: does he provide any evidence about John's recent actions or the training plan, or does he just use insulting names?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael, believing that calling John a 'slacker' proves he cannot change.
Player senses Kael is being mean but cannot articulate why his logic is flawed regarding the habits.
Player identifies that Kael is using negative labels but thinks this might still be a valid reason to reject the training.
Player recognizes that Kael is using labels ('lazy', 'slacker') as a substitute for evidence about whether John's habits have actually changed.

Player clearly explains that Kael's name-calling is a logical fallacy because it assumes John's nature is fixed without examining the specific question of habit modification or providing data on John's recent conduct.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if I call a broken sword 'useless,' does that fix the metal? If I call John a 'slacker,' does that actually prove he can't learn new habits? What evidence is missing?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Kael is using labels as a shield. By calling John a 'lost cause,' he avoids having to look at the actual records of John's behavior or the details of the training plan. That is Name Calling.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Gruff, cynical, and set-in-his-ways. Kael values tradition and immediate results over potential and rehabilitation. He speaks in short, dismissive bursts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't waste my time with 'potential.' A rotten apple doesn't become fresh just because you polish it. John is what he is.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a log of John's last week of duty (showing improvement) to force Kael to drop the labels and address the actual data, unlocking the 'Rehabilitation Quest' branch.

scenario.context: The player finds Pip, a nervous first-year apprentice at the Arcane Academy, pacing outside the examination hall. He is clutching a movie ticket stub and looking unusually confident despite having failed the last three quizzes.
scenario.text: I passed my math test after going out to the movies the night before! It's obvious now. I should go to the movies the night before every single math test from now on. It's my lucky ritual!
scenario.speaker_context: Pip is experiencing a momentary success and has immediately attributed it to the most recent distinct event (going to the movies), ignoring other factors like the difficulty of the specific test, his actual study habits prior to the movie, or simple chance. He is committing a post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy.

structure.pattern_description: Pip observes that event B (passing the test) occurred after event A (going to the movies) and concludes that A caused B. This ignores the possibility that the correlation is coincidental, that a third factor caused both, or that the sequence is irrelevant to the outcome.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred. Event B occurred subsequently. Therefore, A caused B.
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession does not imply causation. Passing a test is likely the result of studying, understanding the material, or the specific questions asked, not the act of seeing a film. Pip has not established a causal mechanism linking cinema attendance to mathematical proficiency.
structure.counterpoint: While rituals can provide psychological comfort which might indirectly help performance via reduced anxiety, claiming the movie itself caused the intellectual mastery of the subject is a logical error. To prove causation, one would need to control for other variables (e.g., study time) across multiple trials.

assessment.identification_prompt: Pip believes going to the movies caused him to pass. What is the logical flaw in assuming that because the movie happened before the success, it caused the success?

rubric.description: Fails to identify any flaw; agrees that movies cause better test scores.
Identifies that the connection seems weak but cannot explain why logically.
States that correlation does not equal causation but lacks specific application to the scenario.
Correctly identifies the post hoc fallacy and suggests alternative causes (e.g., studying, easy test).
Comprehensively explains the temporal vs. causal distinction, debunks the ritual, and proposes a valid method to test the hypothesis (controlled experiment).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if you ate a blue berry before the test, would the berry be the cause? Just because one thing happens before another doesn't mean it made it happen.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Pip is confusing sequence with consequence. He needs to look at his study notes, not his ticket stub, to understand why he passed.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, superstitious, eager to find simple solutions to complex problems, prone to magical thinking.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Do you think I should see a comedy or an action movie before the history final? I need to replicate the conditions exactly!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Pip to analyze his study hours instead of his entertainment choices. If successful, he adopts a study schedule; if failed, he spends all his gold on movie tickets and fails the next exam.

scenario.context: In the bustling hallway of the Academy of Minds, Professor Aris attempts to explain the curriculum requirements to a hesitant student, Leo, who is worried about his schedule.
scenario.text: Professor Aris leans in urgently: 'It's important for you to take this psychology course. Sign up today. Don't wait. If you don't, you'll never understand human behavior, you'll fail your future leadership exams, and your entire career path could collapse before it even begins.'
scenario.speaker_context: Aris does not explain the course content, its relevance to the degree, or the evidence for its utility. Instead, he argues the student must enroll solely by highlighting the catastrophic personal consequences of not doing so.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim or course of action must be accepted (or rejected) based solely on the positive or negative outcomes of believing it, rather than on evidence supporting the claim itself.
structure.formal_form: If you do not accept X, bad consequence Y will happen. Therefore, you must accept X (or X is true/necessary).
structure.why_wrong: The potential negative consequences of not taking an action do not prove that the action is the correct one, nor do they validate the premises behind the recommendation. The merit of the course depends on its content and value, not just the fear of failure.
structure.counterpoint: While future consequences are important for decision-making, using fear of a worst-case scenario as the sole argument bypasses critical evaluation of whether the specific solution (the course) actually prevents that outcome.

assessment.identification_prompt: Professor Aris paints a scary picture of your future. But did he give you any actual reasons why this specific psychology course is valuable or necessary?

rubric.description: Agrees to sign up immediately because the consequences of not doing so sound too terrible to risk.
Feels pressured and anxious but cannot identify what is missing from the argument.
Notices the professor is talking only about bad outcomes, not about the class itself.
Identifies that the argument relies on fear of consequences rather than evidence for the course's value.
Names the appeal to consequences fallacy and articulates that negative outcomes do not validate the proposed solution without further evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine there was a different class that prevented those same bad outcomes even better. Would Aris's argument still hold up if he couldn't explain why this specific class works?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Fear is a motivator, not evidence. How could you ask Aris to rephrase his argument to focus on the actual merits of the course?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Intense, fast-talking, slightly manipulative academic who uses high-pressure tactics.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Think of the ruin! The shame! All because you hesitated to click 'Enroll'!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player successfully requests a syllabus or evidence of the course's efficacy, causing Aris to pause and switch to a factual explanation, unlocking the 'Critical Thinker' badge.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling town square of Veridia during the annual Budget Assembly. Two candidates are debating the proposed tax reduction plan. Candidate Elara has just finished presenting a spreadsheet showing how lower taxes could stimulate local business growth. Before the player can ask a question, her opponent, Councilor Bram, steps up to the microphone.
scenario.text: Bram sneers at the crowd. 'My opponent suggests that lowering taxes will be a good idea, but this is coming from a woman who eats a pint of Ben and Jerry's each night! How can we trust her fiscal judgment when she has no self-control with ice cream?'
scenario.speaker_context: Councilor Bram, a seasoned politician known for his sharp tongue and tendency to deflect difficult policy questions with personal insults. He is currently trailing in the polls and desperate for a win.

structure.pattern_description: Bram attacks Elara's personal habit (eating ice cream) and implies a lack of self-control, rather than addressing the economic data or logic behind her tax reduction proposal. He attempts to discredit the argument by discrediting the person.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X (lowering taxes is good). Person P has property Q (eats ice cream nightly/is undisciplined). Therefore, X is false or should be dismissed.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of an economic argument depends on evidence, data, and logical reasoning, not on the personal habits or character of the person presenting it. Elara's ice cream consumption has no logical connection to the potential effects of tax policy on the local economy. Bram provides zero counter-evidence to her spreadsheet.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if the argument explicitly relies on the person's authority or credibility as a premise (e.g., 'You should follow my diet plan because I am disciplined'). Since Elara's argument relied on economic data, her personal diet is irrelevant.

assessment.identification_prompt: Bram is trying to make the crowd laugh at Elara. But look closely at his reasoning: does mentioning ice cream actually prove that lowering taxes is a bad idea?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Bram or believes the ice cream habit proves Elara is unfit to discuss taxes.
Player feels Bram is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why his logic is flawed.
Player identifies that Bram is attacking Elara personally instead of her argument.
Player explains that personal habits (ice cream) are irrelevant to the specific topic (economic tax policy).
Player fully articulates that the truth of the tax proposal stands independently of Elara's character, and identifies the formal structure of the ad hominem fallacy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if a mathematician who loves junk food tells you 2+2=4, is the math wrong? Why does the speaker's snack choice matter for tax rates?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Bram is distracting the crowd with a personal insult because he likely doesn't have a good economic counter-argument. You've spotted the red herring.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Bram is a populist agitator who relies on emotional manipulation and mockery rather than policy details. He gets defensive when pressed on facts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Oh, so you think eating dessert makes someone bad at math? Maybe you should check your own fridge before judging the budget!
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player correctly identifies the fallacy, Bram stammers and is forced to address the actual tax numbers, lowering his approval rating but increasing the town's understanding of the issue. If the player fails, the crowd boos Elara, and the tax debate is derailed.

scenario.context: The player enters the Grand Archive of Chronos, where Historian Valerius is arguing against granting suffrage to women. He points to a timeline on the wall connecting historical milestones.
scenario.text: Valerius taps his staff on a stone timeline. 'Look at the evidence before you! For centuries, women had no vote, and the world remained free of nuclear annihilation. It was only after the movement for women's suffrage succeeded that humanity developed the atomic bomb. The correlation is undeniable. Granting women the vote directly caused the creation of nuclear weapons. To ensure our survival, we must revert to the old ways.'
scenario.speaker_context: Historian Valerius has identified a temporal sequence where women's suffrage preceded the invention of nuclear weapons. He incorrectly infers that the former caused the latter, ignoring the complex scientific, geopolitical, and military factors (such as WWII and the Manhattan Project) that actually drove nuclear development.

structure.pattern_description: Valerius observes that Event A (women getting the vote) happened before Event B (nuclear weapons were created) and infers that A caused B. This is a classic 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' error. The mere sequence of events or their co-occurrence over a broad timeline does not establish a causal link. The actual causes of nuclear weapons involve advancements in physics, wartime urgency, and government funding, which are independent of voting rights.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, A caused B. (Flaw: Temporal precedence is necessary but not sufficient for causation; confounding variables or coincidence are ignored.)
structure.why_wrong: Valerius fails to provide a mechanism linking voting rights to nuclear physics. He ignores the true common causes or independent drivers (e.g., global conflict, scientific discovery) that led to nuclear weapons. The timing is coincidental relative to the specific causal chain of nuclear development.
structure.counterpoint: While temporal order is a requirement for causation, it is not proof. Many things happen after breakfast (e.g., the sun rises higher), but breakfast does not cause the sun's position. Valid causation requires a plausible mechanism and the elimination of alternative explanations.

assessment.identification_prompt: Historian Valerius claims that women's suffrage caused the invention of nuclear weapons because one happened before the other. What logical fallacy is he committing, and why is his conclusion unsupported?

rubric.description: The player accepts Valerius's argument as true or fails to identify any logical error.
The player senses the argument is weak but cannot name the specific fallacy or explain the flaw clearly.
The player identifies that correlation or timing does not equal causation but does not explicitly name the 'False Cause' or 'Post Hoc' fallacy.
The player correctly identifies the False Cause (Post Hoc) fallacy and explains that the timing is coincidental, noting the lack of a direct link.

The player provides a comprehensive rebuttal: identifies the fallacy, explains the error in assuming temporal sequence implies causation, and suggests actual causes (e.g., wartime physics research) to dismantle the argument.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Valerius nods solemnly. 'If the timeline fits, the cause must be real. Are you suggesting science and politics are unrelated?'
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Valerius pauses, stroking his beard. 'Hmm. You argue that the bomb arose from the pressures of war and the breakthroughs of physicists, not the ballot box. Perhaps I have confused the calendar with the cause.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Pedantic, traditionalist, overly reliant on superficial patterns in history, resistant to social change.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The timeline never lies, adventurer! Sequence is the mother of consequence!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Valerius to update his historical model by separating correlation from causation, unlocking the 'Critical Historian' achievement and gaining access to the restricted military archives.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling market square of Logos City, where a frantic merchant named Correlus is shouting at a crowd gathered around his stall, which is covered in charts and graphs.
scenario.text: Correlus points aggressively to a chart showing two rising lines. 'Look at this undeniable proof! Over the last decade, the number of people wearing sunglasses has increased dramatically. In that exact same period, the number of ice cream cones sold has also skyrocketed. The connection is clear: wearing sunglasses causes people to crave ice cream! If we want to boost the economy, we must mandate that everyone wears sunglasses all year round. It is simple cause and effect!'
scenario.speaker_context: Correlus has identified a genuine positive correlation between sunglasses sales and ice cream sales but has incorrectly inferred that one causes the other. He ignores the common cause: hot weather (summer), which increases both the desire for eye protection and the desire for cold treats.

structure.pattern_name: False cause / Cum hoc ergo propter hoc
structure.pattern_description: Correlus observes that two variables (sunglasses usage and ice cream sales) rise together and infers that the first causes the second. However, correlation does not establish causation. There are four possibilities: (1) sunglasses cause ice cream cravings, (2) ice cream causes sunglasses usage, (3) a common cause drives both, or (4) the correlation is coincidental. The actual explanation is a common cause: seasonal heat.
structure.formal_form: A and B are correlated. Therefore A causes B. (But: A could cause B, B could cause A, C could cause both, or the correlation could be coincidental.)
structure.why_wrong: Correlation between two variables does not establish that one causes the other. Correlus has not ruled out reverse causation, a common cause, or coincidence. Mandating sunglasses would not increase ice cream sales in winter because the underlying driver (heat) would be missing.
structure.counterpoint: Correlations can be evidence for causation when combined with a plausible mechanism, temporal ordering, and elimination of confounders. The fallacy is in jumping directly from correlation to causation without doing that additional work. A classic parallel: ice cream sales correlate with drowning incidents, but eating ice cream does not cause drowning; hot weather causes both swimming and ice cream consumption.

assessment.identification_prompt: Correlus claims that wearing sunglasses causes people to buy ice cream based on his chart. What is the flaw in his reasoning?

rubric.description: The player accepts Correlus's conclusion that sunglasses cause ice cream sales without question.
The player suspects something is wrong but cannot articulate why, perhaps suggesting the data is fake.
The player identifies that the two events happen at the same time but does not identify the missing link.
The player correctly states that correlation does not imply causation and suggests a third factor might be involved.
The player explicitly identifies the 'common cause' fallacy, explaining that hot weather causes both increased sunglasses use and increased ice cream sales, rendering the direct causal link false.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about when people usually wear sunglasses and when they usually eat ice cream. Is there a specific time of year when both happen more often?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because two trends move together doesn't mean one pushes the other. Often, a third hidden variable is pulling the strings on both.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Overconfident, data-obsessed, but logically naive. Speaks quickly and uses grand gestures when pointing at charts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The numbers don't lie, adventurer! Sunglasses equal ice cream! It's the law of the market!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must explain the concept of a 'common cause' (summer heat) to Correlus. Upon understanding, he realizes his mandate would fail in winter and thanks the player, offering a discount on his wares.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling courtyard of the Academy of Reason, attempting to mediate a dispute between two students, Kael and Jory. Kael has just presented a well-researched argument about why the library hours should be extended, citing usage statistics and student sleep patterns. Jory, looking visibly agitated, turns away from Kael's data to address the player directly.
scenario.text: Jory crosses his arms and sneers, 'My best friend says you're a liar, so I'm not going to talk to you or listen to a word you say.'
scenario.speaker_context: Jory, a stubborn student who relies heavily on peer validation and often dismisses opposing views based on social reputation rather than evidence.

structure.pattern_description: Jory refuses to engage with the player's potential arguments or Kael's previous points solely because a third party (his best friend) labeled the player a 'liar'. He attacks the player's character via association instead of addressing the substance of the discussion.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person Q (associated with P or judging P) says P is untrustworthy. Therefore, X is false or should not be discussed.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a claim or the validity of an argument depends on evidence and logic, not on the character of the person presenting it or the opinions of their friends. Even if the player were a liar, their current argument could still be factually correct. Jory provides no counter-evidence to the library hours proposal.
structure.counterpoint: Character assessments are relevant only when the argument relies entirely on the speaker's testimony or authority (e.g., 'Believe me because I am honest'). If the player had said, 'You must trust my word alone without proof,' then questioning their honesty would be relevant. However, since the debate is about library policy and data, personal attacks are irrelevant.

assessment.identification_prompt: Jory seems unwilling to listen. But look closely: did he address Kael's statistics or your potential response? What specific reason did he give for shutting down the conversation?

rubric.description: Player accepts Jory's refusal and ends the conversation, believing the friend's accusation invalidates the player.
Player feels Jory is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why his reasoning is flawed.
Player identifies that Jory is attacking the person instead of the argument but misses the 'guilt by association' aspect.
Player clearly identifies that Jory is committing an ad hominem fallacy by relying on a third-party insult rather than evidence.
Player explains that the truth of the library hours argument is independent of the player's reputation and demands evidence regarding the proposal itself.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if a known liar says '2 + 2 = 4', is the math wrong? How does that apply to Jory's refusal to discuss the library hours?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Jory is attacking the messenger, not the message. To win this debate, you need to steer him back to the actual data about library usage.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defensive, clique-oriented, easily swayed by peer opinion, avoids intellectual effort.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I don't care what the charts say! If my bestie says you're fake, you're fake!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player successfully redirects the conversation to the objective data, forcing Jory to either engage with the facts or admit he has no real counter-argument.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling marketplace of Oakhaven. Two merchants are debating the safety of a new trade route through the Whispering Woods. Merchant Elara has just presented a map showing the cleared paths and guard schedules. Before the player can offer an opinion, Merchant Borin steps forward to shut down the discussion.
scenario.text: Borin crosses his arms and sneers. 'Why should we trust Elara's plan to use the Whispering Woods? Look at her! She drives a fancy enchanted carriage and wears silk robes. She must be wealthy and out of touch with the dangers common folk face. Her proposal is obviously reckless.'
scenario.speaker_context: Merchant Borin, a gruff trader who sells basic goods. He prides himself on being 'one of the people' but often dismisses valid arguments by attacking the speaker's status rather than their evidence.

structure.pattern_description: Borin rejects Elara's proposal about the trade route solely because of her perceived wealth and lifestyle (driving a fancy carriage, wearing silk). He assumes her personal circumstances make her incapable of understanding danger, ignoring the actual data she presented regarding cleared paths and guard schedules.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P has property Q (wealth/status, irrelevant to the truth of X). Therefore, X is false or reckless.
structure.why_wrong: The validity of a trade route proposal depends on objective factors like path safety, guard presence, and terrain, not on the financial status of the person proposing it. A wealthy person can present accurate data just as a poor person can. Borin provides no evidence against the map or the guard schedule; he only attacks Elara's character.
structure.counterpoint: Personal circumstances are only relevant if the argument explicitly relies on them. If Elara had argued, 'We should take this route because I am so wealthy I can hire extra guards,' then questioning her actual ability to pay would be relevant. However, she argued based on existing guard schedules, making her wealth irrelevant.

assessment.identification_prompt: Borin seems convinced that Elara's wealth makes her plan dangerous. But look closely at his reasons: does he mention any specific flaw in the map or the guard schedule, or is he only talking about Elara herself?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Borin, believing that wealthy people cannot understand danger or that Elara's plan is bad because she is rich.
Player feels Borin is being mean or unfair to Elara but cannot explain why his logic regarding the trade route is flawed.
Player identifies that Borin is attacking Elara's character instead of her argument but struggles to articulate why wealth is irrelevant to the map's accuracy.
Player clearly states that Borin commits an ad hominem fallacy by ignoring the evidence (maps/guards) and focusing on Elara's status, noting that wealth does not determine factual accuracy.

Player provides a comprehensive rebuttal identifying the fallacy, explaining the irrelevance of the personal attack to the specific premises of the argument, and suggesting how to redirect the debate to the actual evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a poor merchant presented the exact same map and guard schedule, would the route suddenly become safe? Or is the safety of the route independent of who is holding the map?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Borin is distracting everyone from the actual data. To evaluate the trade route, we need to look at the Whispering Woods' current conditions, not Elara's bank account.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Borin is populist and suspicious of elites, often using class resentment to win arguments rather than logic. He respects the player if they challenge him with hard facts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't let her fancy carriages fool you! She doesn't know what it's like to lose a cart to goblins!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to expose Borin's fallacy to gain respect from the town council (Logic path) or mediate by asking Elara to provide even more concrete proof to satisfy Borin's unfounded fears (Diplomacy path).

scenario.context: The player arrives in the town square of Oakhaven, where Mayor Thorne is addressing a frantic crowd of parents near the closed school gates. He holds a clipboard with attendance records and closure notices.
scenario.text: Mayor Thorne points emphatically at the shuttered school windows. 'Look at the evidence! All the schools in this area had to keep closed for most of the week. And now, look at the result: many parents have withdrawn their children from the local schools entirely. It is undeniable that keeping the schools closed for those few days caused the parents to lose faith and pull their children out. If we had just kept them open, none of these withdrawals would have happened.'
scenario.speaker_context: Mayor Thorne observes two events occurring in sequence: school closures followed by student withdrawals. He assumes the first event caused the second. However, he ignores a likely common cause, such as a severe local health crisis (e.g., a flu outbreak or contamination) that forced the schools to close for safety and simultaneously frightened parents into withdrawing their children regardless of the closure duration.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne observes that Event A (school closures) happened before Event B (parents withdrawing children) and infers that A caused B. This ignores other possibilities: B could have been caused by the same underlying factor that caused A (a common cause), or B might have happened anyway due to unrelated factors. The most likely scenario is a common cause, such as a disease outbreak, which necessitated closures and independently scared parents.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred. Event B occurred after A. Therefore, A caused B. (Flaw: Ignores common causes, reverse causation, or coincidence.)
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession does not prove causation. Thorne fails to consider that a third variable (like a health emergency) likely caused both the closures and the parental fear. Blaming the closure itself misidentifies the root problem and leads to ineffective solutions.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one must rule out confounding variables. For instance, if schools in a neighboring town remained open during the same health crisis and parents there also withdrew children, it would prove the closures were not the cause. Correlation in time is necessary but not sufficient for causation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Mayor Thorne claims the school closures caused the parents to withdraw their children. Is this a valid causal conclusion, or is he committing a logical fallacy? Identify the flaw in his reasoning.

rubric.description: The player accepts the Mayor's conclusion without question or cannot identify any logical issue.
The player suspects the reasoning is weak but cannot articulate why or identify the specific fallacy.
The player identifies that just because one thing happened after another doesn't mean it caused it (post hoc), but does not suggest an alternative explanation.
The player correctly identifies the False Cause fallacy and suggests that a third factor (common cause) might be responsible for both events.

The player fully deconstructs the argument, identifying the post hoc error, proposing a specific common cause (e.g., illness/outbreak), and explaining how testing this hypothesis would disprove the Mayor's claim.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: What if something dangerous was happening in the town that forced the schools to close AND made parents scared? Would the closure still be the main reason they left?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! The closures and the withdrawals are likely both symptoms of a larger problem, not cause and effect. Fixing the schedule won't solve the parents' fear if the underlying threat remains.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Mayor Thorne is pragmatic but hasty, prone to jumping to conclusions to appear decisive in a crisis. He values order over nuance.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: We must reopen the schools immediately! That is the only way to stop the exodus. The closure itself is the poison!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must investigate the town for a common cause (e.g., find reports of a water contamination or virus) and present this evidence to Thorne to shift his focus from reopening schools to addressing the actual threat.

scenario.context: In the Town Square of Veridia, the player confronts Councilor Vane about his proposal to defund the city library to build a new statue. When pressed for data on the statue's economic benefit, Vane abandons the numbers.
scenario.text: Councilor Vane leans forward, his voice trembling slightly: 'How can you sit there with your charts and cold calculations? Think of the children! Think of the pride that swells in our chests when we see a monument to our heritage. Do you want to be the one who tells a child they cannot have a beautiful symbol of our unity because we were too busy counting coins? Look at the faces of our ancestors; they did not count costs, they built glory!'
scenario.speaker_context: Vane is avoiding the specific question about the library's budget and the statue's ROI. Instead, he attempts to make the player feel guilty for prioritizing facts over sentimental imagery.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting an emotional response (pride, guilt, pity) in place of addressing the factual evidence or logical argument. Vane does not provide data on the statue's value; he tries to make the player feel ashamed for asking for data.
structure.formal_form: Claim P is supported by evidence E. Agent evokes emotion F unrelated to E. Agent implies E should be disregarded because of F.
structure.why_wrong: Whether the statue makes people feel proud or whether ancestors built glory does not change the mathematical reality of the library's budget deficit or the statue's cost. The emotional appeal is a distraction designed to bypass the factual inquiry.
structure.counterpoint: Emotions are relevant to community morale, but they cannot replace the need for fiscal solvency. One can honor ancestors without bankrupting the education system; the two are not mutually exclusive, and the emotional argument does not prove the statue is affordable.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Vane speaks passionately about children and ancestors. But did he actually answer the question about the library's funding numbers?

rubric.description: Is moved by Vane's speech about children and ancestors and agrees to drop the funding issue.
Feels conflicted; recognizes the numbers are missing but feels too guilty to press the point.
Notices Vane changed the subject to emotions but struggles to articulate why pride doesn't pay the bills.
Identifies that Vane is using emotional appeals (guilt/pride) to deflect from the lack of financial evidence.
Names the appeal to emotion, clearly distinguishes the factual question (budget) from the emotional one (pride), and explains that feelings do not validate the financial plan.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside the images of children and ancestors for a moment. The ledger shows a deficit if we cut the library. Has Vane explained how the statue generates enough revenue to cover that loss?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Pride and heritage are important, but they are not line items in a budget. Vane needs to show the math, not just the sentiment.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic but evasive; uses grand gestures and a trembling voice to manipulate sympathy.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You speak of coins, I speak of souls! Can your calculator measure the weight of history?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must select the dialogue option: 'Your passion is noted, Councilor, but it does not balance the ledger. Show me the projected revenue.'

scenario.context: At the Royal Academy's strategy briefing, the cadets are discussing how to allocate volunteer hours for the upcoming city-wide emergency services drill. Cadet Elara suggests a cautious approach regarding first-year participation.
scenario.text: Cadet Elara says: 'We should prohibit all cadets from assisting on emergency services missions. Some cadets are so immature they won't ever stop goofing around.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara takes a specific concern about immature cadets goofing around and exaggerates it into a universal claim that 'some cadets won't ever stop,' using this extreme characterization to justify a total ban on all cadets, rather than addressing the actual nuance of who might be ready.

structure.pattern_description: Elara distorts the reality of the cadet corps by claiming some are permanently incapable of seriousness ('won't ever stop goofing around') to support an extreme conclusion (banning all cadets). She attacks this exaggerated version of the cadets' behavior rather than evaluating individuals on their actual merit or proposing targeted supervision.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (some cadets need supervision). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (some cadets are incorrigibly immature and will never change). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that the original proposal for participation is invalid, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: The argument relies on an exaggerated characterization of cadet immaturity. Asserting that some cadets 'won't ever stop' goofing around is an unsupported extreme that ignores the possibility of growth, training, or the maturity of other cadets. The conclusion (total prohibition) does not logically follow from the actual, more moderate premise that some might be immature.
structure.counterpoint: Elara, you're assuming that because some cadets are immature now, they will never be responsible. That's an exaggeration. We could instead implement a mentorship program where mature cadets supervise the younger ones, rather than banning everyone.

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Cadet Elara misrepresent the situation regarding cadet maturity to support her argument for a total ban?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Elara or fails to see any issue with her reasoning.
Player feels the conclusion is too harsh but cannot identify the specific logical error.
Player notices Elara is being negative about cadets but does not identify the exaggeration of 'never stopping' as the core flaw.
Player identifies that Elara exaggerated the immaturity of cadets (claiming they will never change) to make her total ban seem reasonable.

Player clearly articulates that Elara constructed a 'straw man' by distorting the premise of cadet immaturity into an absolute, unchangeable trait to justify an extreme conclusion that doesn't fit the actual situation.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider the phrase 'won't ever stop.' Is it realistic to say a student will never mature? What is Elara ignoring by making such a strong claim?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. By painting all cadets with the brush of permanent immaturity, she avoids the harder work of distinguishing who is ready and who isn't. That is the essence of the Straw Man fallacy.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elara is a rigid traditionalist who prefers strict rules over nuanced judgment. She often speaks in absolutes to shut down debate.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's simple logic! If they can't be serious now, they never will be. Better safe than sorry.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must point out the exaggeration in Elara's claim about cadets never maturing, prompting her to concede that a mentorship system might be a viable alternative to a total ban.

scenario.context: In the Sunlit Classroom of the Academy, Master Thaddeus notices that Apprentice Elara has not submitted her written assignment on quadratic formulas. He asks for an explanation.
scenario.text: Master Thaddeus: 'Why don't you have your homework today?' Apprentice Elara: 'Well, I did my homework! I was actually really interested in all that info about the quadratic formula. Would you like to hear the song that I wrote to memorize it?'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara does not address the fact that she failed to submit the required written work. Instead, she argues that her assignment should be accepted (or her lack of submission forgiven) because the consequence of her alternative method (a song) is her own enthusiasm and a creative output, substituting this positive outcome for the actual requirement.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim or action should be accepted/rejected based on the desirability of its consequences rather than on evidence or adherence to rules.
structure.formal_form: Action/Claim P leads to desirable consequence C. Therefore, P satisfies requirement R (or P is correct).
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a factual claim or the fulfillment of a specific requirement (like submitting written homework) does not depend on whether the alternative action has pleasant or interesting consequences. Enthusiasm and songs do not negate the failure to submit the assigned task.
structure.counterpoint: While Elara's enthusiasm and song are positive outcomes, they are irrelevant to the binary fact of whether the specific written homework was submitted. Consequences are relevant to motivation, but not to the verification of task completion.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elara seems very proud of her song. But does her excitement prove that she completed the specific assignment Master Thaddeus asked for?

rubric.description: Accepts Elara's excuse; believes the song counts as homework because it shows interest.
Feels something is off but thinks the song might be a valid substitute due to effort.
Notices Elara talked about a song instead of the written paper, but isn't sure why that matters.
Identifies that Elara is using the positive result (a cool song) to distract from the missing requirement.
Names the appeal to consequences; explains that desirable outcomes do not change the fact that the specific criteria for the assignment were not met.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Elara had written a terrible song that made everyone cry, would that mean she definitely didn't do the homework? Or is the quality of the song irrelevant to the submission status?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where the consequences of an action would legitimately change whether a rule is applied? How is this classroom scenario different?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest, creative, slightly evasive, eager to please
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But the melody captures the essence of the parabola perfectly! Doesn't that count for extra credit?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must gently point out that while the song is impressive, the specific requirement was a written derivation, and enthusiasm cannot substitute for the missing document.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling town square of Veridia where Pastor Pete is addressing a small crowd, attempting to convince them of a spiritual revival.
scenario.text: Pastor Pete raises his hands triumphantly. 'Rejoice! People are turning to God everywhere! I have interviewed ten people today, and 9 out of 10 told me they have a personal relationship with Jesus Christ.' Fred, a skeptical local, steps forward and asks, 'That is impressive, but where exactly did you find these people you interviewed?' Pastor Pete beams, 'Right here in my own church, of course!'
scenario.speaker_context: Pastor Pete is enthusiastic but logically flawed. He surveyed only members of his own congregation (a biased, non-random sample) and is using their high rate of belief to claim that 'people everywhere' are converting. He ignores the fact that he did not survey anyone outside his church.

structure.pattern_description: Pastor Pete draws a broad conclusion about the general population ('people everywhere') based on a sample taken exclusively from a specific subgroup (his church attendees). The sample is not only small (n=10) but also heavily biased because church attendees are far more likely to have a relationship with Jesus than the general public.
structure.formal_form: Sample S is taken from population P. S has property Q. Therefore, all (or most) of P has property Q. (Flaw: S is not representative of P).
structure.why_wrong: The sample is unrepresentative. Surveying people inside a church guarantees a higher probability of finding believers than surveying the general population. Concluding that 'people everywhere' are converting based solely on church-goers is a classic hasty generalization fueled by selection bias.
structure.counterpoint: Generalizations are valid only when the sample is both large enough and randomly selected to represent the whole population. If Pete had surveyed 1,000 people randomly across the entire city, his conclusion might hold weight.

assessment.identification_prompt: Pastor Pete claims people everywhere are turning to God because 9 out of 10 people he asked in his church said so. Is his evidence sufficient to support his claim about 'people everywhere'?

rubric.description: Player accepts Pete's claim as true because the number (9 out of 10) sounds high.
Player feels something is off but cannot explain why the location of the interview matters.
Player notes that interviewing only church members might skew the results but doesn't fully articulate the sampling error.
Player identifies that the sample is biased because it was taken entirely within a church, making it unrepresentative of the general population.
Player clearly identifies the hasty generalization, explains the selection bias (sampling only believers to prove universal belief), and suggests a better method (random sampling outside the church).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about where Pete found these people. If you walk into a bakery and ask people if they like bread, will 9 out of 10 say yes? Does that mean everyone in the world loves bread?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! By only asking people already inside his church, Pete guaranteed a high success rate. He cannot use that specific group to make claims about the whole world.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Pastor Pete is well-meaning, overly optimistic, and lacks statistical literacy. He speaks with great enthusiasm and uses grand gestures.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The numbers don't lie, friend! Nine out of ten! The revival is upon us!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to gently correct Pete's logic, prompting him to conduct a proper survey in the town square, which unlocks a 'Critical Thinker' badge and improves the town's trust metric.

scenario.context: In the heated town hall of Patriot's Peak, a fiery orator named Silas Vane addresses a crowd gathered to discuss the new North American Free Trade Agreement.
scenario.text: Silas leans into the microphone, pointing a finger at the audience: 'If you are a true American, you will ask your congressman to vote against NAFTA. Look around this room! Every real patriot here knows the truth. To support this deal is to turn your back on everything we stand for.'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas equates being a 'true American' with holding a specific political view, implying that the majority opinion in the room (or the idealized majority of patriots) defines the correct stance, rather than presenting economic evidence.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition is true or a course of action is right because many people believe it or because it aligns with the identity of a popular group.
structure.formal_form: Group X believes Y. Therefore, Y is true/right. (Or: If you belong to Group X, you must believe Y.)
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or its alignment with a group identity does not constitute logical evidence for its truth. A large number of people can be mistaken, and defining membership in a group by a specific belief excludes valid dissenting opinions without refuting them.
structure.counterpoint: While consensus among experts in a specific field can be evidential, appealing to the general sentiment of a national or social group ('true Americans') is a rhetorical device, not a logical proof.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does Silas provide any economic data or logical reasons why NAFTA is bad, or does he rely on the label of being a 'true American'?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; assumes that being a true American necessitates this specific vote.
Feels pressured by the statement but cannot articulate why the logic is flawed.
Recognizes that Silas is using emotional pressure but fails to identify the specific appeal to popularity/identity.
Identifies that Silas uses the 'true American' label as a substitute for evidence and notes that popularity does not equal truth.
Explicitly names the Bandwagon fallacy (or Appeal to Identity), explains that group membership does not validate a claim, and demands actual evidence regarding the trade deal.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every person in this room believed the earth was flat, would that make it flat? Does being a 'true American' depend on agreeing with Silas, or on something else?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a scenario where knowing what 'true Americans' generally believe might be useful, even if it doesn't prove a specific policy is correct?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, aggressive, and deeply tribal. Silas thrives on us-vs-them dynamics and uses social cohesion as a weapon.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't tell me you're one of the ones who doesn't care about our heritage! The whole town is with me on this!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must calmly point out that patriotism is not a monolith and ask for specific facts about the trade deal, causing Silas to sputter and lose the crowd's blind support.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Logos City, a street performer named Hype is trying to sell a mysterious 'Luck Potion' to a crowd of skeptical adventurers.
scenario.text: Hype holds up a glowing vial and shouts, 'Don't just stand there questioning the ingredients! Look around you! Everyone is buying it, so you should be too! If all these smart adventurers are drinking it, it must work!'
scenario.speaker_context: Hype avoids answering questions about the potion's effects or ingredients, relying entirely on the fact that a crowd has gathered to buy it as proof of its efficacy.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or an action correct simply because a large number of people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or action does not constitute logical evidence for its truth or value. Crowds can be mistaken, manipulated, or acting on incomplete information.
structure.counterpoint: While consensus among experts after rigorous testing is valuable, mere popularity among a general crowd without independent verification is not evidence of truth.

assessment.identification_prompt: What actual evidence does Hype provide that the Luck Potion works? Is the fact that 'everyone is buying it' a valid reason to believe it works?

rubric.description: Accepts Hype's argument; believes the potion must work because so many people are buying it.
Feels unsure about the argument but cannot articulate why popularity is not proof.
Recognizes that Hype didn't explain how the potion works, but misses the specific flaw of using popularity as evidence.
Identifies that Hype uses the crowd's behavior as the only evidence and states that popularity does not prove effectiveness.
Correctly names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that crowds can be wrong, and distinguishes between social proof and factual evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in the city suddenly believed the sky was green, would that actually make the sky green?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing it' might be useful information, even if it doesn't prove something is true?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Energetic, fast-talking charlatan who feeds off crowd energy and uses social pressure to close sales.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Come on, don't be the only one left out! Join the movement!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player points out that the crowd might just be following each other blindly, causing Hype to sputter and the crowd to disperse, revealing the potion is just colored water.

scenario.context: The player enters the Grand Library's logic wing, where a nervous scribe named Elian is frantically organizing scrolls. He stops the player to warn them about a specific section of the archive.
scenario.text: Elian points a trembling finger at a massive shelf labeled 'Section B'. 'Do not touch any scroll in Section B!' he whispers urgently. 'I pulled one scroll from that section yesterday, and it was written in a cipher I could not break. Therefore, every single scroll in Section B is written in an unbreakable cipher. The whole section is useless to us!'
scenario.speaker_context: Elian has examined exactly one scroll out of hundreds in Section B. Because that single instance had a specific property (being unreadable to him), he has concluded that the entire population of scrolls in that section shares that property.

structure.pattern_description: Elian observes a single instance (one scroll) from a large population (Section B) possessing a specific trait (unbreakable cipher) and immediately concludes that all members of the population share that trait. This ignores the high probability of variation within such a large collection.
structure.formal_form: A is part of B. A has property X. Therefore, all of B has property X.
structure.why_wrong: A sample size of one is statistically insufficient to make a universal claim about a large group. The single scroll Elian found might be an outlier, a rare exception, or simply the only one of its kind in the section. Generalizing from n=1 to 'all' is a logical leap without evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Inductive reasoning relies on samples, but the strength of the conclusion depends entirely on the sample size and representativeness. If Elian had checked 90% of the scrolls and found them all coded, his conclusion would be strong; with one scroll, it is a fallacy.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elian claims every scroll in Section B is unreadable because the one he checked was unreadable. Is his conclusion logically sound?

rubric.description: Player accepts Elian's warning and avoids Section B entirely, believing the whole section is useless.
Player feels skeptical but cannot explain why one bad experience doesn't prove the whole section is bad.
Player notes that one scroll is not enough to judge the whole section but fails to name the logical error.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a sample size of one cannot support a universal claim about hundreds of scrolls.
Player fully deconstructs the argument: identifies the fallacy, explains the insufficiency of the sample size (n=1), and suggests that the single scroll may be an outlier rather than the rule.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Elian shakes his head. 'But if one is broken, surely the rest are too! Why risk it?'
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Elian pauses, looking at the single scroll in his hand. 'You... you're right. Just because this one is difficult doesn't mean the others are. I was letting fear do my thinking for me.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, risk-averse, and prone to catastrophizing based on limited data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: One bad apple spoils the bunch! Or in this case, one bad scroll spoils the shelf!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Elian to test a second or third random scroll from Section B, proving his generalization false and unlocking the 'Archivist's Courage' achievement.

scenario.context: In the bustling student union of Oakhaven Academy, Mabel, the stern Head of Discipline, proposes removing the physical student newspaper from the main hallway because it often creates litter and blocks foot traffic. She suggests moving it to a digital-only format or a designated reading nook. Reacting to this, Jaxon, a passionate but impulsive student activist, immediately jumps to a conclusion in front of a crowd.
scenario.text: Mabel wants to get rid of the student newspaper. Next she will probably want to ban free speech! She won't want us to speak at all! She will make it a law that you cannot speak in public.
scenario.speaker_context: Mabel proposed a specific logistical change regarding the physical placement of the newspaper. Jaxon recharacterized this limited administrative decision as a total ban on free speech and public speaking, an extreme position Mabel never suggested.

structure.pattern_description: Jaxon inflates Mabel's modest proposal (relocating the physical paper) into an extreme position (banning all free speech and public speaking) and then attacks that extreme version. His criticism targets the fabricated position, not Mabel's actual logistical concern.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (move the newspaper). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (ban all speech). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position is tyrannical, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: Jaxon's criticism targets a fabricated version of Mabel's proposal. Moving a newspaper stand does not equate to banning free speech or making public speaking illegal. His objections about total silence are irrelevant to the actual proposal about hallway clutter.
structure.counterpoint: Mabel could reply: 'I said move the paper stand, not ban speech. Students can still talk, protest, and publish online. Can we discuss the litter problem I actually raised instead of imagining a dictatorship?'

assessment.identification_prompt: What is wrong with Jaxon's response to Mabel's proposal about the newspaper?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Jaxon or believes Mabel truly intends to ban all speech.
Player senses Jaxon is overreacting but cannot explain why his logic is flawed.
Player notices Jaxon exaggerated Mabel's idea but fails to clearly distinguish between the newspaper issue and free speech.
Player identifies that Jaxon misrepresented Mabel's argument (moving the paper became banning speech) and attacked the misrepresentation instead of the real proposal.
Player explicitly names the 'Straw Man' fallacy, explains the distortion mechanism, and articulates how the original proposal remains unaddressed.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at what Mabel actually said she wanted to do. Did she mention laws or stopping people from talking? Or did she just talk about the newspaper's location?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Jaxon built a 'straw man'—a fake, scary version of Mabel's argument that is easy to knock down, while ignoring her actual point about hallway clutter.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jaxon is fiery, reactive, and prone to dramatic hyperbole. He cares deeply about rights but lacks patience for nuance, often escalating minor administrative issues into existential threats.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Wait, so you're saying if we let her move the paper, she'll silence us all? That's exactly what tyrants do! First the paper, then our voices!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must calmly de-escalate the crowd by restating Mabel's actual proposal and asking Jaxon to address the specific issue of litter rather than the imagined ban on speech.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling press gallery of the Capital Dome. A heated debate is underway regarding the new Infrastructure Bill. Representative Halloway has just finished presenting a complex argument involving budget allocations and projected job growth. Before the player can analyze the data, Senator Vane takes the podium to respond.
scenario.text: Senator Vane sneers into the microphone, pointing an accusatory finger at Representative Halloway. 'Why should we waste a single second debating Halloway's infrastructure plan? The man is a giant idiot who couldn't balance a checkbook if his life depended on it. His proposal is garbage because he is incompetent.'
scenario.speaker_context: Senator Vane, a seasoned politician known for his sharp tongue and aggressive debate style. He often relies on personal attacks to distract from weak policy positions.

structure.pattern_description: Senator Vane attacks Representative Halloway's intelligence and personal competence ('giant idiot', 'couldn't balance a checkbook') rather than addressing the specific details of the infrastructure plan, such as budget allocations or job projections. He asserts the plan is 'garbage' solely based on his negative assessment of Halloway's character.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P has property Q (negative personal trait). Therefore, X is false.
structure.why_wrong: The truth or validity of an argument (the infrastructure plan) is independent of the personal characteristics of the person presenting it. Even if Halloway were unintelligent, his plan could still be mathematically sound and beneficial. Vane provides no evidence against the plan itself, only an insult against the proposer.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are only relevant if the argument rests entirely on the person's authority or credibility as a witness. If Halloway had argued, 'You should trust this plan because I am a genius economist,' then questioning his intelligence would be relevant to that specific premise. However, since the argument relies on data, the personal attack is irrelevant.

assessment.identification_prompt: Senator Vane seems very confident in his dismissal of the plan. But look closely at his reasons: is he discussing the budget numbers and job projections, or is he talking about Representative Halloway himself?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Vane, believing the plan is bad because Halloway is an 'idiot'.
Player feels Vane is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why his logic is flawed.
Player identifies that Vane is insulting Halloway but fails to connect it to the lack of evidence against the plan.
Player recognizes that Vane is attacking the person instead of the argument, noting the absence of counter-evidence.
Player explicitly states that the validity of the infrastructure plan is independent of Halloway's intelligence and demands evidence regarding the policy itself.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: Can a person who makes mistakes still come up with a good idea? Does calling someone an idiot prove their math is wrong?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Vane tried to win by insulting the messenger rather than disproving the message. To defeat this argument, we must demand evidence about the infrastructure bill itself, not Halloway's resume.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Aggressive, dismissive, relies on charisma and intimidation over facts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't listen to the source, look at the trash they're selling! Anyone with eyes can see Halloway is unfit to lead this discussion.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select a dialogue option that redirects the conversation to the specific data points in the Infrastructure Bill, forcing Vane to either address the facts or retreat.

scenario.context: The player stands in the dusty archives of the Great Library, attempting to mediate a dispute between two scholars regarding the location of the lost Sunken City. Scholar Elara has just presented a map derived from ancient star charts and geological surveys. Before the player can examine the evidence, Master Thorne, a senior archivist, interrupts.
scenario.text: Master Thorne scoffs, waving a hand dismissively at Elara's map. 'You are not a credible resource person on this matter. You haven't even finished college, let alone earned your master's sigil. Why should we trust the theories of a dropout?'
scenario.speaker_context: Master Thorne, a rigid and traditionalist senior archivist who values hierarchy and credentials above all else. He is often impatient with younger scholars who challenge established norms.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne rejects Elara's argument (the location of the Sunken City) solely based on her lack of formal credentials (not finishing college). He attacks her status rather than addressing the star charts, geological data, or logic she presented.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P lacks credential/status Q. Therefore, claim X is false or unworthy of consideration.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a claim depends on the evidence and reasoning supporting it, not the educational status of the person making it. A dropout can present valid data, just as a master can present false theories. Thorne provides no counter-evidence to the map itself.
structure.counterpoint: Credentials are relevant when assessing the likelihood of expertise in complex fields where verification is impossible for the listener. However, in this case, the evidence (maps and charts) is present and can be evaluated on its own merits, making the attack on her degree irrelevant to the truth of the specific claim.

assessment.identification_prompt: Master Thorne seems very confident in his dismissal. But look closely: did he point out any errors in Elara's map or star charts, or did he only talk about her schooling?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne, believing that lacking a degree automatically makes Elara's map wrong.
Player feels Thorne is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why his logic is flawed.
Player identifies that Thorne is attacking Elara's background instead of her argument.
Player explains that the validity of the map depends on the data, not Elara's degree, and notes that Thorne offered no counter-evidence.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, distinguishing between the source's credibility and the argument's merit, and suggests evaluating the star charts directly.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if a child correctly said '2 + 2 = 4', would it be wrong just because they are a child? Does the person change the math?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Thorne tried to win by attacking the messenger, not the message. The star charts are either accurate or they aren't, regardless of Elara's diploma.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elitist, dismissive, authoritative, relies on tradition.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Credentials define competence. Without the sigil, you have no voice here.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to examine the map independently (bypassing Thorne), challenge Thorne to find a specific error in the data, or use a 'Logic' skill check to expose his fallacy to the room, lowering his reputation.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Veridia, a flashy holographic advertisement projects above a clothing stall, catching the player's attention.
scenario.text: A commercial shows a group of friends all hanging out wearing clothes from a popular clothing company. The narrator asks, 'Isn't it obvious? Everyone is wearing these brands. This is an example of why you should buy them too.'
scenario.speaker_context: The advertisement relies entirely on the visual of a popular group to persuade viewers, implying that the clothing's value is derived solely from its widespread adoption rather than its quality or price.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or an action correct simply because a large number of people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good/correct.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or action does not constitute logical evidence for its truth or value. Crowds can be mistaken, influenced by marketing, or acting on social pressure rather than facts.
structure.counterpoint: While popularity can sometimes indicate social utility or safety in numbers (e.g., choosing a busy restaurant over an empty one), it never proves an objective fact or inherent quality without additional evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the commercial provide any evidence about the quality of the clothes, or does it only mention how many people are wearing them?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument: assumes the clothes must be good because everyone is wearing them.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why popularity isn't proof of quality.
Recognizes that no specific evidence about the clothes was given, but doesn't name the logical error.
Identifies that the argument uses popularity as the sole evidence and explains that this does not prove quality.
Explicitly names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains the disconnect between popularity and truth, and notes the role of social pressure in the ad.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in the city suddenly started jumping off a bridge, would that make it a safe or smart thing to do?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing it' might actually be useful information, even if it's not logical proof?

game_hooks.npc_personality: A slick, fast-talking holographic merchant avatar who speaks in trends and hype, constantly referencing what 'everyone' is doing.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look at the crowd! Do you really want to be the only one out of style? Join the movement!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player points out that popularity does not equal quality, causing the hologram to glitch and switch to listing actual product features.
