scenario.context: Inside the bustling Grand Bazaar of Oakhaven, a street vendor named Silas stands atop a crate, surrounded by a crowd of eager customers holding copies of the latest hit album, 'Echoes of the Void'.
scenario.text: Silas holds up a vinyl record high above his head, shouting over the din: 'Don't just stand there staring! Look at this line! Look at these sold-out signs! Lots of people bought this album, so it must be good. Do you really think thousands of music lovers could be wrong? Grab yours before the next shipment arrives!'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas is using the sheer volume of sales and the presence of a crowd as the sole proof of the album's artistic quality, avoiding any discussion of the music itself.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or a product must be good simply because a large number of people believe it or have purchased it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/buy X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: Popularity is not a measure of truth or quality. Crowds can be mistaken, influenced by marketing, or acting on herd mentality. The merit of an album lies in its composition and performance, not its sales figures.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate quality (e.g., if experts independently converge on a solution), in consumer markets, popularity is often driven by trends and social pressure rather than objective merit.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas claims the album is good because 'lots of people bought it.' Does the number of buyers actually prove the music is high quality?

rubric.description: Agrees with Silas; assumes that high sales automatically mean the album is excellent.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why popularity might not equal quality.
Recognizes that Silas didn't describe the music, but doesn't explicitly identify the logical error regarding popularity.
Identifies that Silas is using the number of buyers as evidence and explains that popularity does not guarantee quality.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that sales can be driven by hype rather than merit, and distinguishes between popularity and objective artistic value.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in town suddenly started eating gravel, would that make gravel delicious?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing many people like something is actually useful information, even if it's not proof of quality?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Energetic, fast-talking huckster who feeds off crowd energy and uses FOMO (fear of missing out) to drive sales.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Everyone's got one! Don't be the odd one out!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player points out that a bad movie can also have a big opening weekend, causing Silas to stutter and admit he hasn't actually listened to the album himself.

scenario.context: The player enters the quiet, dimly lit study of Elder Thorne in the village of Oakhaven. The Elder is pacing nervously, clutching a medical scroll, having just returned from the capital where his grandchild received standard immunizations.
scenario.text: Elder Thorne slams the scroll onto the desk, his voice trembling with conviction. 'It is undeniable! My grandchild was perfectly healthy until the day they received those vaccinations. Immediately after the needles, the diagnosis of autism came down. The timing is proof enough. The vaccines are the sole cause of this affliction, and we must ban them from our village to protect our children.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elder Thorne is a loving but fearful grandfather who has observed a temporal sequence (vaccination followed by diagnosis) and incorrectly interpreted it as a causal relationship. He is ignoring the fact that the age at which vaccines are administered coincides with the age at which autism symptoms typically become noticeable, regardless of vaccination status.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne observes that Event A (vaccination) occurred before Event B (autism diagnosis) and concludes that A caused B. This is the 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' (after this, therefore because of this) error. He fails to consider that the two events may be coincidental or that a third factor (developmental timing) explains why they appear together. The scientific consensus is that autism is a neurodevelopmental condition present before birth, with symptoms emerging around the same age routine vaccinations are scheduled.
structure.formal_form: Event A occurred before Event B. Therefore, A caused B. (Flaw: Temporal succession does not prove causation; coincidence or common causes are possible.)
structure.why_wrong: The argument relies solely on the timing of events to establish causation. It ignores extensive epidemiological evidence showing no link between vaccines and autism. It also overlooks the confounding variable of age: children are vaccinated at 12-18 months, which is also when autism symptoms often first become apparent to parents and doctors. Correlation in time does not equal causation.
structure.counterpoint: To establish causation, one needs more than just temporal order; one requires a plausible biological mechanism, consistency across large populations, and the elimination of confounding variables. In this case, large-scale studies involving millions of children have found no difference in autism rates between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups, disproving the causal link despite the temporal coincidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: Analyze Elder Thorne's argument. Does the fact that the diagnosis happened after the vaccination prove the vaccination caused the diagnosis? Identify the logical flaw.

rubric.description: The player accepts Thorne's conclusion as fact or fails to identify any logical error.
The player suspects the argument is weak but cannot articulate why, or simply states 'vaccines are safe' without addressing the logic.
The player identifies that timing alone is not proof but struggles to explain the alternative explanation (coincidence of age).
The player correctly identifies the 'post hoc' fallacy and explains that two events happening in sequence does not mean one caused the other.

The player fully deconstructs the fallacy, identifying the temporal error, explaining the confounding variable (age of symptom onset vs. vaccination schedule), and referencing the lack of mechanistic evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne insists, 'But the timing is too perfect to be a mistake! If you prick the skin and then the trouble starts, the prick must be the cause.' Consider: If you eat breakfast and then it rains, did your breakfast cause the rain?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Precisely. Just because the diagnosis followed the shot doesn't mean the shot caused the condition. It's like saying roosters cause the sun to rise because they crow before dawn. The symptoms of autism naturally emerge around the same age children get vaccinated, creating an illusion of cause and effect.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, protective, deeply traditional, and susceptible to fear-based reasoning. He acts out of love, not malice.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I saw it with my own eyes! One day he was babbling, the next day after the needle, he withdrew. How can you say it's not the cause?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present the 'Coincidence of Age' evidence card or successfully pass a Logic Check to reveal the statistical data showing autism rates are identical in unvaccinated children, calming Thorne's fears and preventing the village from banning medicine.

scenario.context: The player is resting at a campfire with a young squire named Elian who is debating politics with a group of travelers.
scenario.text: Elian crosses his arms defiantly. 'My parents are Democrats, and they are good people. Therefore, all Democrats must be good people.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elian is reasoning from a sample size of two (his parents) to a population of millions. He assumes that because his specific examples possess a positive trait, the entire group shares that trait.

structure.pattern_description: Elian draws a universal conclusion about all members of a political party based solely on the character of his two parents. The sample size is infinitesimally small relative to the total population of the group, making the inference logically invalid.
structure.formal_form: Observed n instances of X from population P (where n=2 and P is very large). All observed instances had property Q. Therefore, all members of P have property Q.
structure.why_wrong: Two individuals cannot represent the diversity of a massive political group. There is no logical guarantee that the traits of the parents extend to every other member. This ignores the high probability of variation within the group.
structure.counterpoint: While personal experience is valuable data, it only becomes statistically significant for generalization when the sample is large enough and randomly selected to be representative of the whole.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elian claims that because his parents are good people, all Democrats must be good. Is his evidence sufficient to support this conclusion?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Elian, accepting that family experience proves the rule for the whole group.
Player feels unsure but suspects the statement might be too broad without knowing why.
Player identifies that two people are not enough to judge a whole group but cannot name the error.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, explaining that a sample of two is too small to represent millions.
Player fully deconstructs the argument, noting the sample size issue, the lack of random selection, and explaining how one could properly test the hypothesis (e.g., larger diverse sample).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: if you met two rude people from a distant city, would that mean everyone in that city is rude? How many people would you need to meet to be sure?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Judging a massive group by just two examples is a classic hasty generalization. Your parents are great, but they are just two data points in a sea of millions.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest, loyal to family, slightly naive, eager to defend his upbringing.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But they are the only Democrats I know! If they are good, surely the rest are too?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player guides Elian to understand that while his parents are good, he needs more evidence before making claims about the entire party, perhaps suggesting he talk to other Democrats with different views.

scenario.context: The player stands in the misty ruins of the Sunken Library, debating the existence of mythical sea-folk with Captain Thorne, a skeptical privateer who prides himself on only believing what he can touch or see.
scenario.text: Captain Thorne crosses his arms and scoffs at your suggestion that mermaids might be real. 'You can't prove that mermaids actually don't exist,' he declares loudly to the crew, 'and therefore it is perfectly reasonable to say that they do. Anyone who denies it is just a closed-minded landlubber afraid of the deep.'
scenario.speaker_context: Thorne shifts the burden of proof entirely onto the skeptic. Instead of providing evidence for mermaids, he argues that the inability to disprove them is sufficient proof of their existence, while simultaneously labeling dissenters as 'closed-minded' to discourage counter-argument.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne claims a proposition is true simply because it has not been proven false. He ignores the logical principle that the burden of proof lies with the person making the positive claim. Additionally, he uses labeling ('closed-minded landlubber') to attack the character of anyone who disagrees, rather than addressing the lack of evidence.
structure.formal_form: Proposition P has not been proven false. Therefore, P is true. (Optional: Anyone who doubts P is labeled L).
structure.why_wrong: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Many things cannot be disproven (e.g., invisible dragons), but that does not make them real. The truth of a claim depends on positive evidence supporting it, not on the failure of others to refute it.
structure.counterpoint: In legal systems, a defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty, which is a specific procedural rule, not a general logical law. In general reasoning, if no evidence exists for a claim after rigorous testing, it is rational to withhold belief, not to affirm the claim.

assessment.identification_prompt: Captain Thorne says we should believe in mermaids because we can't prove they don't exist. Is the lack of disproof enough to make something true?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Thorne, believing that if you can't disprove it, it must be true.
Player feels unsure but suspects Thorne might be manipulating the argument.
Player identifies that Thorne is shifting the burden of proof but misses the labeling aspect.
Player correctly identifies that absence of disproof is not proof, and notes the use of insults.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, explaining why the burden of proof lies with the claimant and how the label serves to silence valid skepticism.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: Can you prove that there isn't a tiny, invisible teapot orbiting Mars? Just because you can't disprove it, does that mean it's definitely there?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! The burden of proof is on the person making the claim. Thorne is hiding his lack of evidence behind a logical trick and name-calling.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Arrogant, superstitious, and defensive about his lack of formal education. He uses bluster and insults to cover gaps in his knowledge.

game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must present a 'Logic Lens' item or choose a dialogue option that forces Thorne to provide positive evidence for mermaids, causing him to grumble and change the subject.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling hallway of the Capitol Building, overhearing a heated debate between two lobbyists regarding the new Infrastructure Tax Bill. Senator Halloway has just finished presenting a complex economic model showing how the tax increase will fund critical bridge repairs without impacting small businesses. Before the player can review the charts, a wealthy donor named Marcus Sterling steps forward to dismiss the proposal.
scenario.text: Sterling waves a hand dismissively at the charts. 'The Senator voted for the tax increase? It's not hard to understand why when you consider that he is a millionaire and has never had to worry about money. Obviously, he doesn't care about the struggle of regular folks, so his plan must be flawed.'
scenario.speaker_context: Marcus Sterling, a self-made millionaire and major campaign donor known for his populist rhetoric but often conflating a politician's wealth with their policy merits.

structure.pattern_description: Sterling attacks the Senator's personal financial status (being a millionaire) and implies a lack of empathy due to his wealth, rather than addressing the specific economic data, bridge repair needs, or small business protections outlined in the tax proposal.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X (Tax increase is good). Person P has property Q (is wealthy/doesn't worry about money). Therefore, claim X is false or motivated by bad intent.
structure.why_wrong: The Senator's personal wealth is irrelevant to the logical validity of the tax proposal. The argument stands or falls on the economic data presented: will the bridges get fixed? Will small businesses suffer? Attacking the Senator's bank account provides no evidence that the math in the proposal is incorrect.
structure.counterpoint: Personal financial interest is relevant only if the argument relies on the person's impartiality as a primary premise (e.g., 'I recommend this stock because I have no stake in it'). Here, the Senator is arguing for a policy's outcome, not his own neutrality.

assessment.identification_prompt: Sterling seems convinced that the Senator's wallet dictates his logic. But look closely at the charts the Senator presented: do any of them mention the Senator's bank account? What exactly is Sterling attacking—the data or the man?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Sterling, believing the Senator's wealth automatically invalidates the tax plan.
Player feels Sterling is being mean or unfair but cannot explain why the argument is logically flawed.
Player identifies that Sterling is attacking the Senator's character/wealth instead of the tax proposal.
Player explains that the Senator's wealth is irrelevant to the factual accuracy of the economic projections and bridge repair needs.
Player fully deconstructs the fallacy, noting that a valid rebuttal would require addressing the specific line items in the budget, not the proposer's net worth.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a poor person proposed a bad math equation, would it suddenly become correct? The truth of the proposal depends on the numbers, not who wrote them.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Sterling tried to distract everyone from the actual data by focusing on the Senator's lifestyle. That's a classic deflection.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Populist Agitator: Loud, gestures frequently, appeals to emotion over fact, suspicious of elites.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Follow the money! That's what I always say. You can't trust a guy who drives a limo to fix potholes!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player presents the 'Small Business Exemption Clause' from the Senator's chart, forcing Sterling to address the actual policy detail rather than the Senator's wealth.

scenario.context: In the bustling marketplace of Techhaven, a group of friends gathers around Susie, who has just unboxed a retro flip-phone. The crowd is skeptical until one friend points out the trend.
scenario.text: Susie bought a flip-phone, so all of her friends bought flip-phones.
scenario.speaker_context: A peer observer noting the sudden shift in behavior among the friend group solely based on Susie's initial action, implying the action is correct because the group followed it.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a proposition is true or an action is correct simply because many people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Person A did X. Therefore, everyone else should do X (or X is the right choice).
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of an action or belief does not constitute evidence of its truth or value. The friends may have bought the phones due to social pressure or mimicry, not because the flip-phone is objectively superior or the right choice for them.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate utility (e.g., a widely used software tool), it is only evidential if the adoption is based on independent verification of quality, not mere imitation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the fact that Susie's friends bought flip-phones prove that buying a flip-phone was a good idea? What evidence is missing?

rubric.description: Accepts the statement as logical; assumes the group action validates the choice.
Senses something is off but cannot articulate why popularity isn't proof.
Identifies that the friends might just be copying Susie without good reason.
Explicitly states that the number of buyers is not evidence of the phone's quality or the correctness of the purchase.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains the lack of independent evaluation by the friends, and distinguishes between social conformity and rational decision-making.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in the city suddenly started eating paint, would that make paint a healthy food?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing it' actually is a good reason to do something yourself?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Trend-conscious teenager who speaks quickly and relies heavily on social proof.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Wait, if Susie did it and now EVERYONE has one, it must be the meta! We can't be the only ones without flip-phones!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must convince the NPC to evaluate the phone's features (battery life, durability) rather than just following the crowd to unlock the 'Critical Thinker' badge.

scenario.context: Inside the bustling Grand Stadium of the capital, moments after the championship game concludes. The crowd is a sea of new jerseys appearing out of nowhere.
scenario.text: A spectator turns to their friend, gesturing at the sudden surge of supporters in the stands: 'Look at this! Now that the Chiefs are going to the Super Bowl, everybody is suddenly a fan. They must be the greatest team in history if everyone loves them this much.'
scenario.speaker_context: The speaker observes the rapid shift in public allegiance and incorrectly interprets this sudden popularity as objective proof of the team's superior quality or historical greatness.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or a thing must be good solely because a large number of people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: Popularity is a measure of social trend, not factual accuracy or intrinsic quality. People often join trends due to social pressure, fear of missing out, or recent success, none of which validate the underlying claim about greatness or truth.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread consensus among experts after independent verification can be evidence, the spontaneous reaction of a crowd to a sports victory is purely emotional and social, not evidential.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the fact that 'everybody is suddenly a fan' prove the team is the 'greatest in history'? What other reasons might people be becoming fans right now?

rubric.description: Agrees with the speaker; assumes that if everyone is a fan, the team must objectively be the greatest.
Feels unsure but cannot articulate why popularity might not equal greatness.
Recognizes that people are just jumping on the bandwagon but fails to explicitly link this to the logical error in the argument.
Identifies that the speaker uses the sudden increase in fans as proof of greatness and explains that popularity does not equal quality.
Names the Bandwagon fallacy, explains that the surge is likely due to recent victory (recency bias) rather than historical greatness, and distinguishes social trends from objective merit.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If every person in the stadium suddenly started wearing their shirts inside out, would that make it the correct way to wear a shirt?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a scenario where a large number of people believing something actually does provide good evidence that it is true?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Enthusiastic but easily swayed sports fan who gets caught up in the energy of the crowd.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Everybody's doing it, so it must be right! Don't you want to be part of the winning side?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player points out that fair-weather fans appear after victories, but this doesn't change the team's actual historical stats or prove they are the 'greatest' compared to past legends.

scenario.context: In the Grand Hall of the Merchant's Guild, a junior accountant questions the fairness of the wage structure. The Guildmaster, a charismatic but evasive leader, stands to address the room.
scenario.text: The Guildmaster smiles broadly and spreads his arms. 'Sure, we haven't given raises to our employees in more than ten years. However, we do pride ourselves on providing customer service in over seven different languages.'
scenario.speaker_context: The Guildmaster avoids addressing the core issue of stagnant wages. Instead, he points to a positive attribute (multilingual service) to distract from the negative reality, implying that the good consequence (service quality) negates the need for raises.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim or situation should be accepted or rejected based on the desirability of its consequences, rather than on evidence or logical relevance. In this specific variant, a positive outcome is used to distract from a negative fact.
structure.formal_form: Fact A has negative implication X. But Fact A also leads to positive consequence Y. Therefore, X is not a valid concern (or A is acceptable).
structure.why_wrong: The existence of a positive side effect (multilingual service) does not logically refute the validity of the complaint regarding stagnant wages. Two things can be true simultaneously: the service is excellent, AND the wages are unfairly low. The consequence does not change the fact.
structure.counterpoint: While providing multilingual service is a commendable achievement, it is irrelevant to the economic calculation of whether employees deserve a raise. The two issues are logically independent.

assessment.identification_prompt: The Guildmaster highlights a great achievement. But does speaking seven languages actually fix the problem of no raises in ten years?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument; believes the great service justifies the lack of raises.
Feels something is off but thinks the service might be a fair trade-off.
Notices the Guildmaster changed the subject from wages to language skills.
Identifies that the positive consequence (service) does not logically address the negative fact (no raises).
Explicitly names the fallacy (Appeal to Consequences/Red Herring) and explains that the truth of the wage stagnation is independent of the service quality.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If the Guild offered service in twenty languages but still paid nothing, would that make the lack of pay acceptable?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a scenario where the positive consequence would actually be relevant to the decision of giving a raise?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charismatic, deflective, proud of surface-level achievements, avoids direct financial accountability.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Think of the prestige! Think of the customers from across the seas! Is that not worth a little patience regarding coin?
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must press the NPC to address the wage ledger directly, ignoring the distraction of the language banners until the NPC admits the two issues are separate.

scenario.context: The player is studying in the Royal Academy library with two fellow students, Nicholas and Alexis. They are preparing for the upcoming AP Language exam. Nicholas makes a bold claim about biological classification to test his knowledge.
scenario.text: Nicholas states confidently, "An apple is a vegetable." Alexis immediately rolls her eyes and retorts, "Don't listen to Nicholas; he is failing AP Language."
scenario.speaker_context: Alexis, a high-achieving student who prides herself on her academic record. She is often quick to dismiss peers who struggle academically, equating current grades with total intellectual validity.

structure.pattern_description: Alexis rejects Nicholas's claim solely based on his current academic performance (failing the class) rather than addressing the factual accuracy of his statement about apples. She uses his status as a struggling student as proof that his specific claim is false.
structure.formal_form: Person P claims X. Person P has property Q (irrelevant to the truth of X). Therefore, X is false.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of the statement 'An apple is a vegetable' depends on botanical definitions, not on Nicholas's grade in a language class. Even a student failing a course can make a true statement, and a top student can make a false one. Alexis provides no evidence regarding botany.
structure.counterpoint: Personal characteristics are relevant if the argument relies on the person's expertise or credibility as a primary premise. If Nicholas had argued, 'You should trust my definition because I am the top student in Biology,' then pointing out his failing grade in a related field would be a valid challenge to his authority. However, he simply made a claim, so his grades are irrelevant to its truth.

assessment.identification_prompt: Alexis seems very sure of herself. But look closely: did she explain why an apple is or isn't a vegetable? Or did she just talk about Nicholas's grades?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Alexis, believing Nicholas must be wrong because he is failing the class.
Player feels Alexis was mean or unfair but cannot identify the logical error.
Player identifies that Alexis attacked Nicholas instead of the argument but struggles to name the specific fallacy.
Player correctly identifies the ad hominem fallacy and explains that grades do not determine botanical facts.
Player fully deconstructs the argument, noting that the truth value of the claim is independent of the speaker's academic status, and provides the correct botanical classification.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: If a student who fails math says '2 + 2 = 4', are they wrong because of their grade? How does that apply here?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Alexis committed an ad hominem fallacy. She attacked the arguer (Nicholas) rather than the argument (the classification of an apple). By the way, botanically, an apple is actually a fruit, specifically a pome, so Nicholas was factually wrong, but Alexis's reasoning for dismissing him was still flawed.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Alexis is competitive, status-conscious, and tends to use academic hierarchy as a weapon in debates. She respects authority and grades above all else.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look, I don't have time to debate basic facts with someone who can't even pass the midterm. Check the textbook if you don't believe me.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to correct Alexis's logic (gaining Logic XP) or fact-check Nicholas's claim (gaining Biology XP). Choosing both unlocks a 'Scholar' badge.

scenario.context: The player enters the Student Council Chamber where Laura, the Class President, is pacing nervously in front of a whiteboard covered in fundraiser ideas.
scenario.text: Laura points to 'Dance' on the board, then aggressively crosses it out. 'I was ready to sponsor the dance. It's a great idea. But then I found out that those girls from the North Hall clique support it too. Since they like it, it must be a terrible plan for the rest of us. We are doing a race instead.'
scenario.speaker_context: Laura is letting her personal dislike for a specific group of students dictate her policy decision. She assumes that because a small, specific group she dislikes supports an idea, the idea itself must be bad for everyone, ignoring the merit of the proposal.

structure.pattern_description: Laura rejects a proposal solely because a small, specific group (the girls she dislikes) supports it. She generalizes that 'what they like must be bad for us' based on her bias against them, rather than evaluating the proposal on its own merits. This is a form of hasty generalization where the sample (the disliked group) is used to make a universal claim about the quality of the event for the whole class.
structure.formal_form: Group G supports proposal P. Group G has negative trait T (in the speaker's view). Therefore, proposal P has negative quality Q for the entire population.
structure.why_wrong: The preferences of a specific subgroup do not determine the objective value of a proposal for the entire class. Laura is ignoring the possibility that the dance could be popular with many other students who are not in that clique. Her conclusion relies on an insufficient and biased sample to judge the whole.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to consider the source of an idea, but rejecting an idea entirely based only on who supports it, without examining the idea itself, is a logical error. A good idea remains good even if disliked people agree with it.

assessment.identification_prompt: Laura decides against the dance solely because a group she dislikes supports it. Is her reasoning logically sound?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Laura, believing that if 'those girls' like it, it must be bad.
Player feels Laura is being unfair but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Player identifies that Laura is letting personal bias affect her decision but misses the generalization aspect.
Player recognizes that Laura is making a broad conclusion about the event's quality based on the preferences of a single, small group.
Player explicitly identifies the hasty generalization: Laura assumes the dance is bad for everyone just because a specific subgroup she dislikes likes it, ignoring independent merit.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it: If your enemy suggested breathing air, would you stop breathing? Does who supports an idea change whether the idea itself is good?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Just because a specific group supports an idea doesn't make the idea bad for everyone else. Laura needs to evaluate the dance on its own merits, not based on who else likes it.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Laura is stressed, overly competitive, and prone to letting personal grudges cloud her judgment as a leader.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I can't let them win by having their idea chosen! We need a race, something they clearly didn't think of!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player convinces Laura to separate the idea from the people, leading to a vote where the dance wins by a landslide, proving her generalization wrong.

scenario.context: The player enters the Alchemist's Guild hall, finding Master Thorne staring intensely at a half-eaten box of enchanted chocolates on his workbench. He seems to be arguing with himself about his recent binge.
scenario.text: Master Thorne gestures wildly at the empty wrappers. 'I can't stop eating these chocolates. It must be that I really love chocolate, or that I seriously lack willpower. I know for a fact that I really love chocolate; therefore, I cannot lack willpower.'
scenario.speaker_context: Master Thorne is a brilliant but logically flawed alchemist who often confuses sufficient conditions with necessary ones. He believes that because one cause (love of chocolate) is present, the alternative cause (lack of willpower) must be absent, ignoring that both could be true simultaneously.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne reasons from 'If I lack willpower OR I love chocolate, then I eat them' (implicitly treating them as exclusive or confusing the logic) to 'I love chocolate, therefore I do not lack willpower.' More accurately, he treats the presence of one sufficient cause as proof that the other potential cause is false, or he misapplies a disjunctive syllogism by failing to establish mutual exclusivity.
structure.formal_form: P or Q. P. Therefore not Q.
structure.why_wrong: This is a formal fallacy when 'or' is inclusive. The fact that Thorne loves chocolate does not logically exclude the possibility that he also lacks willpower. Both conditions can be true at the same time. Denying one based on the affirmation of the other is invalid unless the options are explicitly mutually exclusive.
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would only be valid if Thorne had established: 'Either I love chocolate OR I lack willpower, but not both.' Without that exclusive constraint, loving chocolate explains the behavior but does not exonerate his willpower.

assessment.identification_prompt: Master Thorne seems relieved that his love for chocolate proves he has strong willpower. Does liking chocolate actually prove he isn't weak-willed?

rubric.description: Agrees with Thorne that loving chocolate means he has willpower.
Suspects Thorne is making an excuse but cannot identify the logical flaw.
Recognizes that someone can both love chocolate AND lack willpower simultaneously.
Identifies that Thorne incorrectly treats two compatible causes as mutually exclusive.
Names the fallacy (affirming a disjunct / denying the antecedent variant), explains inclusive vs exclusive 'or', and notes that both premises can be true.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about a time you ate something you loved even though you promised not to. Did you love it? Yes. Did you lack willpower in that moment? Could both be true?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. If the statement was 'Either I love chocolate OR I lack willpower, but not both,' his logic would hold. But since he didn't say 'not both,' he's falling for a logical trap.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Eccentric, defensive about his habits, prone to over-intellectualizing simple weaknesses to avoid guilt.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But surely, a true connoisseur's passion overrides mere impulse! It's not weakness, it's appreciation!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to point out the flaw gently, earning Thorne's respect and a recipe, or challenge him harshly, causing him to storm off and lock his lab.

scenario.context: The player stands in the bustling courtyard of Oakhaven Academy just before the class treasurer elections. A senior student named Marcus is loudly discouraging a group of first-years from voting for a candidate named Donald.
scenario.text: Marcus crosses his arms and sneers at the first-years. 'Did you really vote for Donald as class treasurer? Didn't you hear that his uncle was imprisoned for embezzling $1.5 million? If the apple doesn't fall far from the tree, Donald is definitely a thief too. You'd be crazy to let someone with that bloodline manage our funds.'
scenario.speaker_context: Marcus is relying on a single data point (Donald's uncle) to make a definitive claim about Donald's character and future actions. He ignores Donald's own history, qualifications, or the fact that one relative's crime does not determine another's behavior.

structure.pattern_description: Marcus draws a universal conclusion about Donald's character ('Donald is definitely a thief') based on a single instance involving a different person (his uncle). The sample size (one relative) is insufficient to support a generalization about Donald's entire moral compass or competence.
structure.formal_form: Individual X (uncle) has property Q (thief). Individual Y (Donald) is related to X. Therefore, Individual Y has property Q.
structure.why_wrong: One person's actions do not dictate another's, even within a family. Generalizing the behavior of an entire individual based solely on a relative's crime ignores individual agency, personal history, and the vast majority of people who do not follow their relatives' negative paths. The sample size of 'one uncle' is statistically meaningless for predicting Donald's behavior.
structure.counterpoint: While family environment can influence behavior, it is not a deterministic rule. Assuming guilt or specific traits by association without direct evidence of those traits in the individual is a logical leap.

assessment.identification_prompt: Marcus claims Donald must be a thief because his uncle was one. Is this evidence sufficient to prove Donald is untrustworthy?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Marcus and decides not to vote for Donald based solely on his uncle's history.
Player feels unsure but cannot explain why the uncle's actions don't automatically apply to Donald.
Player suspects Marcus is being unfair but identifies the issue only as 'family isn't everything' without addressing the logical structure.
Player identifies that Marcus is making a hasty generalization, noting that one relative's crime is insufficient evidence to judge Donald's character.

Player explicitly identifies the hasty generalization, explains that the sample size (one uncle) is too small to predict Donald's behavior, and notes that individuals are responsible for their own actions, not their relatives'.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Marcus nods confidently. 'Exactly! Blood tells. Best to be safe than sorry.' (The player misses the chance to challenge the flawed logic).
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Marcus pauses, looking slightly embarrassed. 'Well... I suppose you're right. I shouldn't judge him without knowing him first. Maybe he's different.'

game_hooks.npc_personality: Cynical, protective of the group's resources, prone to gossip and stereotypes.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You can't trust a [Family Name]; they all have sticky fingers.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince the first-years to evaluate Donald based on his own platform and past deeds rather than his lineage, potentially unlocking a 'Fair Judge' achievement.

scenario.context: In the bustling courtyard of the Academy of Reason, a young noble named Elara is preparing for her birthday gala. She stands by the guest list, visibly distressed as she speaks to the player, who acts as her logic tutor.
scenario.text: Elara crosses her arms and pouts. 'Look at this list. All of my true friends are coming to my birthday party. If Micah doesn't show up, she might as well just tell me to my face that she doesn't like me at all. There is no middle ground here.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara, an emotional noble student who tends to interpret social slights as absolute rejections.

structure.pattern_description: Elara presents a situation where only two outcomes exist: Micah attends the party (proof of liking) or Micah absents herself (proof of disliking). This ignores numerous other reasons for absence, such as prior commitments, illness, family emergencies, or simply missing the invitation.
structure.formal_form: A v B, ~A, therefore B. (Where A = Micah likes me/comes, B = Micah dislikes me/doesn't come). The error is assuming A and B are the only exhaustive possibilities regarding attendance and affection.
structure.why_wrong: The speaker falsely assumes that attendance is the sole indicator of affection and that absence is the sole indicator of dislike. The disjunction is not exhaustive; many neutral or positive reasons for absence exist.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or scenario is false. If the statement were 'Either Micah is alive or she is dead,' the dichotomy holds. The fallacy occurs only when relevant middle grounds or alternative options are artificially excluded.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elara claims Micah's absence proves she doesn't like her. What is flawed about limiting the possibilities to just these two options?

rubric.description: Agrees with Elara or offers purely emotional comfort without addressing the logic.
Suggests Micah might have another reason but fails to identify the logical structure of the error.
Identifies that there are other reasons for not coming but does not explicitly name the false dichotomy.
Names the false dichotomy and explains that attendance does not equal affection, offering specific alternative reasons for absence.

Fully deconstructs the argument: identifies the false dichotomy, explains that the disjunction (like vs. dislike based on attendance) is not exhaustive, and provides multiple concrete counter-examples to break the binary.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Elara sees only two paths: come to the party or hate me. Can you think of a third path where someone cares about you but still cannot attend?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent. You've shown the choice isn't binary. Now, how could you phrase a response to Elara that acknowledges her feelings while correcting this logical leap?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dramatic, sensitive, prone to catastrophizing social interactions, but eager to learn logical frameworks to manage her anxiety.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: But if she liked me, she would move heaven and earth to be there! Unless... wait, did she mention a family trip last week?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player helps Elara draft a non-accusatory message to Micah asking about her schedule, leading to a quest update where Micah sends a gift and an apology note, validating the player's logical intervention.

scenario.context: The player enters the Grand Bestiary, a magical zoo where creatures are categorized by strict logical rules. A sign at the entrance to the Aquatic Wing reads: 'If it is a fish, it lives in water.' The player stands before a pen containing a donkey.
scenario.text: The Curator points to the donkey and declares: 'No donkeys are fish. Some asses are donkeys. Therefore, some asses are fish.' He gestures proudly, believing he has proven the donkey belongs in the water.
scenario.speaker_context: The Curator is an eccentric scholar who believes that negating a category membership (not being a fish) somehow forces membership in a related category (being a fish) through a chain of unrelated premises. He confuses the exclusion from a group with inclusion in that same group via a middle term.

structure.pattern_description: The Curator implicitly reasons: 'If it is a fish, it lives in water (or has aquatic traits). This creature is not a fish. Therefore, it has aquatic traits (is a fish).' More accurately, he treats the premise 'No donkeys are fish' as if it implies 'Some non-fishes are fish' through the middle term 'asses/donkeys', violating the rule that a negative premise cannot yield an affirmative conclusion about the same class, effectively denying the antecedent condition of being a fish to conclude one is a fish.
structure.formal_form: If P (is a fish) then Q (has aquatic nature). Not P (is a donkey/not a fish). Therefore Q (is a fish).
structure.why_wrong: The fact that something is not a fish does not make it a fish. The premises establish that donkeys are NOT fish. Concluding that some asses ARE fish directly contradicts the first premise and illogically assumes that denying the category 'fish' results in belonging to 'fish'.
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would only hold if the rule was 'Everything that is not a fish IS a fish,' which is a contradiction. Valid logic dictates: If no donkeys are fish, and some asses are donkeys, then some asses are NOT fish.

assessment.identification_prompt: The Curator claims the donkey is a fish based on these statements. Look closely at the first sentence: 'No donkeys are fish.' Does his conclusion match that fact?

rubric.description: Accepts the Curator's conclusion that the donkey is a fish.
Senses the conclusion is wrong because donkeys aren't fish, but cannot explain the logical break.
Notices the contradiction between 'No donkeys are fish' and 'Some asses are fish' but misses the structural error.
Identifies that the argument denies the condition of being a fish only to affirm it, violating the initial premise.

Explicitly identifies the formal fallacy (denying the antecedent or contradictory conclusion), explains that 'No A are B' combined with 'Some C are A' must yield 'Some C are not B', and corrects the Curator.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If no donkeys are fish, and the animal is a donkey, how can it possibly be a fish? What rule did the Curator break?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent. Now, if the sign said 'All water-dwellers are fish,' and the donkey lives on land, could we prove it's not a fish? How does that structure differ?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Pedantic, confidently incorrect, obsessed with classification despite lacking basic logical consistency.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Observe the elegance of my deduction! The premises are clear, the conclusion is inevitable!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player corrects the Curator, causing him to blush and move the donkey to the Terrestrial Wing, rewarding the player with a 'Logic Lens' item.

scenario.context: The player visits the village apothecary where Old Man Hemlock is boasting about his robust health to a group of skeptical villagers during flu season.
scenario.text: I've never had the flu because I take my vitamins every day.
scenario.speaker_context: Hemlock takes a daily multivitamin and has indeed avoided the flu this year. However, he ignores other factors such as his isolationist lifestyle, frequent hand washing, or simple luck, attributing his health solely to the supplements without evidence of a causal link.

structure.pattern_description: Hemlock observes that event B (taking vitamins) precedes or accompanies event A (not getting the flu) and concludes that B causes A. He fails to consider that the correlation might be coincidental, that a third factor (like hygiene) causes both, or that the vitamins have no effect on influenza prevention.
structure.formal_form: Event B occurs before/with Event A. Therefore, B causes A. (Flaw: Ignores alternative explanations like coincidence, reverse causation, or common causes.)
structure.why_wrong: Temporal succession or correlation does not prove causation. Avoiding the flu could be due to many factors (immune system strength, lack of exposure, hygiene) unrelated to vitamin intake. Assuming the vitamins are the sole cause without controlling for other variables is a logical error.
structure.counterpoint: While vitamins support general immune function, claiming they are the definitive cause of avoiding a specific viral infection like the flu requires clinical evidence, not just anecdotal observation. One could take vitamins and still get the flu, or skip them and stay healthy due to other precautions.

assessment.identification_prompt: Identify the logical flaw in Hemlock's reasoning regarding his health and vitamin usage.

rubric.description: Fails to identify any logical error; accepts the statement as factual truth.
Suspects the statement might be wrong but cannot articulate why or confuses it with lying.
Identifies that vitamins might not be the only reason but does not name the specific fallacy or explain the correlation/causation distinction.
Correctly identifies that correlation does not imply causation and lists at least one alternative explanation (e.g., hygiene, luck).
Precisely identifies the 'False Cause' fallacy, explains the difference between correlation and causation, and provides a robust counter-example or alternative causal mechanism.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider: If your neighbor also takes vitamins but gets the flu, does that change your view on what causes immunity?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent. You recognized that just because two things happen together doesn't mean one caused the other. What other factors could explain Hemlock's good health?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Superstitious, confident, slightly dogmatic about traditional remedies, dismissive of modern science.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't question the pills, lad! They're the shield that keeps the red death away!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player must present evidence of someone who takes vitamins but got sick, or someone who doesn't take them and stayed healthy, to break Hemlock's false certainty and unlock the 'Critical Thinker' badge.

scenario.context: In the smog-choked alchemy district of Veridia, a frantic merchant named Silas blocks your path. He holds a canister of experimental hairspray that has accidentally created a minor, localized fog. He is panicking as city guards approach.
scenario.text: Silas grabs your arm, eyes wide with terror. 'Listen! The guards think this fog is dangerous. We either ban hairspray forever right now, or the world will end! There is no middle ground!'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas, a nervous alchemy merchant prone to catastrophic thinking and exaggeration when under pressure.

structure.pattern_description: The speaker presents two extreme options as the only possibilities, ignoring a spectrum of moderate alternatives. Silas claims the only choices are a total ban on hairspray or global apocalypse, ignoring options like regulating usage, improving ventilation, or simply waiting for the fog to dissipate.
structure.formal_form: A v B, ~A, therefore B. But the real situation is A v B v C v D..., so ~A does not entail B.
structure.why_wrong: Silas constructs a disjunction that is not exhaustive. He ignores all intermediate solutions between 'total ban' and 'world ending,' such as partial restrictions, safety tests, or containment procedures.
structure.counterpoint: Not every either/or statement is a fallacy. If the options truly are exhaustive (e.g., 'The light is either on or off'), the reasoning holds. The error here is assuming exhaustion where none exists.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas claims we must either ban hairspray or face the end of the world. What is logically flawed about this choice?

rubric.description: Accepts Silas's panic and agrees that the world will end without a ban.
Senses Silas is overreacting but cannot explain the logical error.
Identifies that other options exist (like regulation) but does not name the fallacy.
Names the false dichotomy and explains that Silas is ignoring moderate alternatives between the two extremes.
Fully articulates that the disjunction is not exhaustive, names the fallacy, lists specific ignored alternatives, and explains why the conclusion does not follow from the premises.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Silas says those are the only two options. Can you think of a third thing the city could do instead of banning everything or dying?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. When does an 'either/or' statement become a legitimate logical constraint rather than a fallacy?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, dramatic, prone to worst-case scenarios, speaks rapidly.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't you see? It's all or nothing! If we don't act now, it's over!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player calms Silas by listing three reasonable regulatory steps, proving the 'world end' scenario is not the only alternative to a ban.

scenario.context: In the Grand Hall of Debates, a novice scholar named Elara argues for stricter regulations on dangerous magical experiments to prevent accidental summonings. The arrogant High Mage Valerius, who profits from unregulated research, steps forward to refute her.
scenario.text: Elara states: 'We must require safety wards on all summoning circles to prevent accidental demon incursions.' High Mage Valerius scoffs: 'So Elara wants to ban all magic entirely! She wishes to return us to the dark ages, lighting our homes with candles and healing our sick with mud packs. We cannot let one fearful scholar destroy the progress of centuries!'
scenario.speaker_context: Elara proposed specific safety measures for summoning circles. Valerius recharacterized this as a total ban on all magic and a return to primitive living, an extreme position Elara never suggested.

structure.pattern_description: Valerius inflates Elara's specific proposal (safety wards for summoning) into an extreme position (banning all magic and reverting to primitive life) and then attacks that extreme version. His criticism targets the fabricated position, not Elara's actual argument.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P. Person B restates P as the distorted P*. Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position has been refuted, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: Valerius's criticism targets a fabricated version of Elara's proposal. Requiring safety wards does not equate to banning all magic or abandoning modern healing. His objections about candles and mud packs are irrelevant to the actual proposal of safety regulations.
structure.counterpoint: Elara could reply: 'I said safety wards for summoning, not a ban on all magic. Safety measures do not stop progress; they ensure it continues without disaster. Can we discuss the specific wards I proposed?'

assessment.identification_prompt: What is wrong with High Mage Valerius's response to Elara's proposal?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Valerius or sees no problem with his response.
Player senses something is off or feels Valerius is being unfair but cannot articulate why.
Player notices that Valerius exaggerated Elara's proposal but does not clearly distinguish the original safety measure from the total ban.
Player identifies that Valerius misrepresented Elara's argument (safety wards became a total ban) and attacked the misrepresentation instead of the real proposal.
Player explicitly names the 'Straw Man' fallacy, explains how the distortion works, and provides the correct counter-argument to restore the original context.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at what Elara actually asked for versus what Valerius claims she wants. Did she mention banning healing magic or using candles?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent! You spotted that Valerius built a 'straw man' to knock down. He attacked an argument nobody made to avoid addressing the real issue of safety.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Arrogant, dismissive, uses hyperbole to intimidate opponents, protective of the status quo.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think you can out-debate me? Everyone knows [Player Name] wants to strip us of our power!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must select the dialogue option that clarifies Elara's actual position, causing Valerius to lose face in front of the council and forcing a vote on the safety wards.

scenario.context: In the bustling cafeteria of Oakhaven Academy, a group of students gathers around a new juice bar station during lunch rush.
scenario.text: Everyone I know is making fruit smoothies for quick, portable meals, so smoothies must be really good for you.
scenario.speaker_context: A popular student influencer trying to convince their hesitant friend to join the trend, relying entirely on the number of participants rather than nutritional facts.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a claim must be true or an action must be beneficial solely because many people believe it or are doing it.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore, X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The popularity of a belief or action does not constitute evidence of its truth or value. Crowds can be misinformed, influenced by trends, or acting without critical evaluation.
structure.counterpoint: While widespread adoption can sometimes indicate practical utility or social consensus, it is not a logical proof of inherent quality or truth without independent verification.

assessment.identification_prompt: Does the speaker provide any nutritional evidence for why smoothies are healthy, or do they only mention how many people are making them?

rubric.description: Accepts the argument completely; assumes that because everyone is doing it, it must be healthy.
Feels unsure about the claim but cannot articulate why popularity is insufficient evidence.
Recognizes that no specific health benefits were listed but fails to identify the reliance on popularity as the core flaw.
Identifies that the argument relies solely on the number of people participating and states that popularity does not prove health benefits.
Explicitly names the bandwagon fallacy, explains that trends do not equal facts, and notes that the speaker provided zero nutritional data.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If everyone in the school started eating chalk because it was trendy, would that make chalk a healthy snack?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Can you think of a situation where knowing 'everyone is doing it' might actually be useful information, even if it doesn't prove something is true?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Energetic, trend-focused student who equates popularity with quality and fears missing out.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Come on, don't be the only one left out! Look at the line!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player successfully points out that trends aren't evidence, prompting the NPC to check the actual ingredients list for the first time.

scenario.context: The player stands before the Town Council in the village of Oakhaven. Elder Thorne, a respected but anxious community leader, is arguing vehemently against a proposed construction project near the local lake.
scenario.text: If we allow a single housing development to be built on Sunny Lake, a massive resort will come next, and soon we won't have any wilderness left in the entire region!
scenario.speaker_context: Elder Thorne is extrapolating a catastrophic, total loss of wilderness based solely on the approval of one small housing development. He assumes a deterministic chain of events without evidence that the first step inevitably leads to the extreme final outcome.

structure.pattern_description: Elder Thorne takes a single instance (one housing development) and generalizes it into an inevitable, extreme sequence of events leading to total wilderness loss. This is a hasty generalization because it assumes that one small change guarantees a specific, massive outcome without considering regulatory limits, community pushback, or the possibility that the development remains isolated.
structure.formal_form: Event X occurred (or is proposed). Therefore, extreme Event Y and Event Z will inevitably follow, resulting in total outcome Q.
structure.why_wrong: The argument fails because it treats a single data point (one development) as sufficient proof of an unstoppable trend. It ignores the many variables that could stop the progression (zoning laws, economic factors, environmental protections) and assumes the worst-case scenario is the only possible outcome.
structure.counterpoint: While it is prudent to consider long-term consequences, a valid argument requires evidence that the specific steps (development -> resort -> no wilderness) are causally linked and probable, not just theoretically possible. One example does not prove a universal rule of escalation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elder Thorne claims that allowing one housing development means we will soon have no wilderness left. Is this conclusion supported by the evidence provided?

rubric.description: Player agrees completely with Thorne, believing the development will definitely destroy all wilderness.
Player feels the claim is too strong but cannot explain the logical gap between one house and no wilderness.
Player identifies that the jump from 'one development' to 'no wilderness' is large but labels it simply as 'exaggeration' without identifying the generalization error.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, noting that one instance does not prove an inevitable chain of events leading to total loss.

Player fully deconstructs the argument, explaining that Thorne is generalizing from a sample size of one to a universal outcome, ignoring intervening variables like zoning laws or community intervention that could break the chain.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Thorne seems very certain. But does one small building really guarantee that the whole forest disappears? What might stop a resort from being built after the houses?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Thorne is assuming a slippery slope without evidence. Just because one step is taken doesn't mean the entire staircase must be climbed.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, protective of tradition, prone to catastrophizing, deeply cares about the land but lacks nuance in risk assessment.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You don't understand! It always starts small. First a few cabins, then a hotel, then a highway! If we say yes to this, we say yes to the end of Oakhaven as we know it!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can present precedents where developments were built without leading to resorts, or propose a binding zoning agreement that legally prevents future expansion, satisfying Thorne's fear without halting progress.

scenario.context: In the bustling market square of Veridia, two merchants are debating the upcoming Winter Solstice festival. Merchant A is suggesting a minor adjustment to the greeting scripts for seasonal employees to be more inclusive of various traditions.
scenario.text: Merchant A says: 'Many stores are telling their employees to say Happy Holidays instead of Merry Christmas.' Merchant B reacts angrily: 'This is crazy! Why are they trying to get rid of Christmas?!'
scenario.speaker_context: Merchant A noted a shift in phrasing ('Happy Holidays' vs 'Merry Christmas'). Merchant B interpreted this specific phrasing change as an active attempt to eliminate the Christmas holiday entirely, attacking an extreme position that was never stated.

structure.pattern_description: Merchant B takes Merchant A's observation about a change in greeting phrases and distorts it into an accusation that someone is trying to abolish the Christmas holiday itself. B attacks this fabricated extreme goal rather than addressing the actual topic of employee greeting scripts.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (stores are using different greetings). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (someone is trying to eliminate Christmas). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position is wrong or crazy, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: The criticism targets a fabricated version of the situation. Changing a greeting phrase is not equivalent to trying to 'get rid of' a holiday. The emotional reaction is based on a misrepresentation of the original statement.
structure.counterpoint: Merchant A could reply: 'I didn't say anyone wants to get rid of Christmas. I only mentioned that some stores are asking staff to use a broader greeting like Happy Holidays. That doesn't mean Christmas is being cancelled.'

assessment.identification_prompt: What is logically flawed about Merchant B's response to Merchant A's statement?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Merchant B or sees no problem with the angry reaction.
Player senses Merchant B is overreacting but cannot explain why logically.
Player notices Merchant B changed the topic from greetings to eliminating the holiday but does not identify the specific distortion technique.
Player identifies that Merchant B misrepresented Merchant A's point (greeting phrasing vs. abolishing Christmas) and attacked the misrepresentation.
Player explicitly names the 'Straw Man' fallacy, explains how the original statement was exaggerated, and provides the correct interpretation of Merchant A's intent.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at what Merchant A actually said. Did they mention 'getting rid' of anything, or just changing a phrase? How did Merchant B change the meaning?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct! Merchant B constructed a 'Straw Man' by exaggerating a simple change in wording into a conspiracy to destroy a tradition, making it easier to attack.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Merchant B is traditional, quick-tempered, and prone to seeing cultural shifts as personal attacks.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's an attack on our heritage! First they change the words, next they ban the trees!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must calmly clarify the distinction between 'greeting preferences' and 'holiday abolition' to de-escalate Merchant B's anger and restore logical discourse in the market.

scenario.context: The player stands in the war room of the Capital, where President Aris Thorne is addressing his cabinet and the player character regarding the recent aircraft disaster over the border.
scenario.text: President Thorne slams his hand on the map table. "The government is convinced that it was a bomb that brought down the aircraft. Our countrymen believe it was a bomb. A survey done just a few days after the crash indicates that almost seventy percent of the people believe it was a terrorist's bomb. Therefore, we must act immediately on the certainty that this was an act of terrorism."
scenario.speaker_context: President Thorne is under immense pressure to respond to a national tragedy. He is conflating public opinion (a survey taken during a state of shock and grief) and political conviction with factual evidence regarding the mechanical cause of the crash.

structure.pattern_description: The President concludes that the crash was definitely caused by a bomb based primarily on a public opinion survey conducted shortly after the event. He generalizes the beliefs of 70% of respondents (who are likely reacting emotionally rather than forensically) to establish an objective fact about the crash's cause, ignoring the need for physical evidence or expert investigation.
structure.formal_form: Population P believes proposition X is true (based on a survey taken at time T). Therefore, proposition X is objectively true.
structure.why_wrong: Public belief, especially immediately following a traumatic event, is not evidence of factual reality. The sample (public opinion) is biased by emotion, lack of technical knowledge, and media speculation. A majority belief does not constitute proof of a mechanical or criminal cause; only forensic data can do that.
structure.counterpoint: While public sentiment is crucial for political decision-making and morale, it cannot replace empirical evidence in determining the physical cause of an accident. Consensus does not equal correctness in matters of forensic science.

assessment.identification_prompt: President Thorne claims the crash was definitely a bomb because 70% of people believe it was. Does public opinion prove the cause of the crash?

rubric.description: Player agrees with the President, accepting the survey as proof of the bomb.
Player expresses doubt but cannot explain why a survey is insufficient evidence for a physical cause.
Player notes that people might be guessing or emotional, but doesn't fully identify the logical gap between belief and fact.
Player identifies that the President is making a hasty generalization, confusing popular belief with forensic evidence.
Player explicitly explains that the sample (public opinion) is biased by emotion and lack of expertise, and that a survey cannot determine mechanical failure vs. terrorism without physical data.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If 70% of people believed the earth was flat, would that make it flat? What kind of evidence do we actually need to find a bomb?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Fear and speculation spread faster than facts. We need the black box data, not a popularity contest, to know the truth.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Authoritative, stressed, prone to decisive action based on intuition and public pressure rather than slow deliberation.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The people know the truth in their hearts! We cannot wait for bureaucrats to count screws while our enemies laugh!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must persuade the President to halt the immediate military retaliation and authorize a proper forensic investigation team before declaring war.

scenario.context: The player encounters a weary traveler named Kael resting by the roadside near the starting line of the Grand Marathon. Kael looks exhausted and is bandaging a blistered foot.
scenario.text: Kael shakes his head bitterly. 'Trying to finish a marathon is impossible. I know because I tried it once and failed miserably. No human can actually complete that distance.'
scenario.speaker_context: Kael attempted the marathon exactly one time and did not finish. He is using this single personal failure to make a universal claim about human capability regarding marathons.

structure.pattern_description: Kael draws a universal conclusion ('no human can complete a marathon') based on a sample size of one (his own failed attempt). The sample is insufficient to support a claim about the capabilities of the entire human population, especially given that thousands successfully complete marathons regularly.
structure.formal_form: Observed 1 instance of X (my attempt) having property Q (failure). Therefore, all instances of X (all human attempts) have property Q.
structure.why_wrong: A single data point, particularly one influenced by individual variables like training, health, or conditions on that specific day, cannot justify a universal negative claim about a large population. It ignores the existence of successful runners.
structure.counterpoint: Personal experience is valuable data, but it becomes a fallacy when treated as representative of the whole without sufficient statistical backing. If Kael said 'Marathons are very hard,' that would be reasonable; saying they are 'impossible' is the error.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kael claims finishing a marathon is impossible for anyone because he failed once. Is his evidence sufficient to support this conclusion?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael that marathons are impossible based on his story.
Player feels Kael might be wrong but cannot explain the logical flaw.
Player notes that one person's failure doesn't mean everyone fails, but lacks specific terminology.
Player identifies the hasty generalization, noting the sample size of one is too small for a universal claim.

Player fully deconstructs the argument: identifies the fallacy, explains the insufficiency of n=1 against a global population, and distinguishes between subjective difficulty and objective impossibility.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider: If you tripped once, would you say walking is impossible for everyone? How many successful runners would it take to prove Kael wrong?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Kael is letting one bad experience cloud his judgment of reality. Thousands finish marathons every year; his sample size is just too small to support such a broad claim.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Defeated, cynical, and projecting his own limitations onto the world. He speaks with absolute certainty despite having limited data.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Don't bother trying, kid. I did it once and nearly died. It can't be done.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Convince Kael to watch the race finish line with you. Seeing others succeed forces him to update his mental model and retract his universal claim.

scenario.context: In the Academy of Reason, a student named Kael approaches Professor Thorne's desk after receiving a graded assignment. Kael failed to submit the required homework and has just been given a zero for the assignment.
scenario.text: Professor Thorne says: 'You are receiving a zero because you didn't do your homework.' Kael reacts angrily: 'Are you serious? You gave me a zero because you hate me????'
scenario.speaker_context: Thorne stated a specific consequence for a specific action (no homework equals zero). Kael ignored this specific claim and instead attacked a fabricated, extreme motive (that the professor hates him), which was never suggested.

structure.pattern_description: Kael distorts Thorne's specific administrative decision (grading based on missing work) into an emotional, personal attack (hatred). He then argues against this fabricated motive rather than addressing the actual reason for the grade.
structure.formal_form: Person A advances position P (Grade is zero due to missing homework). Person B restates P as the distorted P* (Grade is zero due to hatred). Person B attacks P*. Person B concludes that A's position is invalid, but P* is not P.
structure.why_wrong: The professor's statement was about academic policy and cause-and-effect regarding the missing assignment. The student's response invents a malicious intent ('hate') that was never present in the original statement, making the rebuttal irrelevant to the actual argument.
structure.counterpoint: Kael could reply: 'I understand I get a zero for missing the work, but I don't agree that this means you hate me. Can we discuss how I can make up the assignment?'

assessment.identification_prompt: How does Kael's response misrepresent Professor Thorne's actual statement?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael that the professor must hate him or sees no logical error.
Player feels Kael is overreacting but cannot explain the logical disconnect.
Player notices Kael brought up 'hate' which the professor didn't mention, but doesn't identify it as a distortion of the argument.
Player identifies that Kael replaced the professor's specific reason (missing homework) with an extreme, fabricated motive (hatred) to attack.
Player clearly articulates that Kael constructed a 'straw man' by exaggerating a grading decision into personal animosity, rendering his counter-argument irrelevant to the actual policy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Look closely at what the professor actually said. Did he mention feelings or hatred? Or did he state a rule about homework?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct! Kael ignored the real issue (the missing homework) and fought against an imaginary enemy (the professor's hatred) instead.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Kael is impulsive, emotionally reactive, and tends to personalize criticism, often feeling persecuted by authority figures.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: It's always personal with you guys! You're all out to get me!
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must guide Kael to separate the academic consequence from personal intent, allowing him to apologize for the outburst and ask about extra credit.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling market square of Oakhaven. A local merchant named Silas is arguing heatedly with a traveler wearing German-style clothing, drawing a small crowd.
scenario.text: Silas points an accusing finger at the traveler. 'That German, Fred, just stole my wallet right from my belt! I knew it. All Germans are thieves, every single one of them. You shouldn't let any of their kind into this town!'
scenario.speaker_context: Silas has had his wallet stolen by one individual named Fred, who happens to be German. He immediately extrapolates this single negative event to characterize the entire nationality of Germans as thieves.

structure.pattern_description: Silas observes one instance of theft committed by a German individual and concludes that all members of the German nationality are thieves. The sample size (n=1) is statistically insignificant relative to the population (all Germans), making the universal claim unsupported and logically invalid.
structure.formal_form: Observed 1 instance of X (Fred) from population P (Germans). Instance X had property Q (thief). Therefore, all members of P have property Q.
structure.why_wrong: A single data point cannot support a universal generalization about a massive population. The behavior of one individual does not represent the behavior of the whole group. This ignores the vast majority of Germans who are not thieves and assumes a causal link between nationality and criminal behavior without evidence.
structure.counterpoint: While past experience can inform caution, forming a definitive rule about an entire group based on a single encounter is irrational. Valid inductive reasoning requires a representative and sufficiently large sample size.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silas claims that because Fred (a German) stole his wallet, all Germans are thieves. Is this conclusion logically sound based on the evidence provided?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Silas, accepting that all Germans are thieves based on Fred's action.
Player feels the statement is unfair but cannot explain the logical error regarding sample size.
Player identifies that one person does not represent a whole group but fails to name the specific fallacy.
Player correctly identifies the hasty generalization, noting that a sample size of one is insufficient to judge an entire nationality.

Player provides a comprehensive rebuttal identifying the hasty generalization, explaining the statistical inadequacy of n=1, and distinguishing between individual responsibility and group characteristics.
